case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Company’s Reply Submissions dated 17/10/2025 Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: On the issue of whether the Claimant’s dismissal was with just cause or excuse, would be no longer an issue which had already been conclusively decided by the High Court in the Judicial Review Application upon which this Industrial Court bound to follow as ordered, not to relitigate the issue of whether the Claimant’s dismissal was with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Company’s Reply Submissions dated 17/10/2025 Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: In the instance case, it shall be the duty of the workman to mitigate against loss but the burden of proving that the workman has not done so lies with the employer. Such mitigation shall be made against back wages only. No deduction be made in respect of the compensation in lieu of reinstatement. In view of the fact that it is not in dispute that the Claimant has been dismissed without just cause or excuse, the sole is issue to be determined by this Court is the quantum of compensation and backwages to which the Claimant is entitled.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Company’s Reply Submissions dated 17/10/2025 Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: Section 4(1) Minimum Retirement Age Act 2012 stipulates that the minimum retirement age is 60 years. As the Claimant is 64 years old this year (2025) and has passed the statutory retirement age, reinstatement may not be the most appropriate remedy. The Claimant has long surpassed the statutory threshold. There is no contractual clause displacing the statutory age. The Claimant had worked for the Company for more than four (4) years from 14/04/2014 until her dismissal on 06/08/2018. Therefore, the calculation of completed years of service would be four (4) completed years.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Company’s Reply Submissions dated 17/10/2025 Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content:
Notwithstanding that, pursuant to the Practice Note No. 3 of 2019, paragraph 2.3 has stipulated that the Court shall not order that the workman be paid compensation in lieu of reinstatement if the workman is incapable of being reinstated (e.g., statutory age of retirement). In Abdul Latif Abdul Malik v. Malaysia Airport Sdn. Bhd. [2022] 3 ILR 598, the learned Chairman had opined that:
"[70] In this present case, the claimant who has attains of 61 years and 4 months old has passed his statutory age of retirement. The claimant who has passed his retirement age is not entitled for compensation in lieu of reinstatement and is only limited to backwages (See Unilever (M) Holdings Sdn. Bhd. v. So Lai & Anor [2015] 2 ILR 265). In accordance to para. 2.3 of Industrial Court of Malaysia Practice Note No. 3 of 2019; "The court shall not order that the workman be paid compensation in lieu of reinstatement if the workman is incapable of being reinstated (e.g., statutory age of retirement)."

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Company’s Reply Submissions dated 17/10/2025 Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: Undoubtedly, the Claimant’s age, where she was already 63 years old when she filed this reference claim herein to the DGIR. The Claimant is not entitled to compensation in lieu of reinstatement as the reinstatement is neither possible nor appropriate on the grounds that the Claimant has exceeded the statutory retirement age, making any claim for compensation in lieu of reinstatement untenable under the law.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Company’s Reply Submissions dated 17/10/2025 Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: Remedy of reinstatement as a relief sought by the Claimant is not harmonious in line with Industrial Relations due to the fact that the Claimant has been separated from the Company for more than six (6) years. Thus, reinstatement would be impractical and disruptive to the current operational structure. In the same sense, no deduction of post dismissal earning shall be ordered as she already passed mandatory retirement age.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: Pursuant to the Letter of Appointment dated 14/04/2014 (pages 15-16 of CLB) the Claimant was appointed as the Company’s Human Resources Manager with a basic salary of RM7,500.00 per month. Clause 3 of the same letter, provided that the Claimant was required to undergo a probationary period of six (6) months. The Company confirmed her employment and her role as a Human Resource Manager vide Letter of Confirmation dated 01/10/2014 (page 19 of CLB) effective 01/10/2014. In the same Letter of Confirmation, the Claimant’s salary will be revised from RM7,500.00 to RM8,500.00 per month with effect the same date of her confirmation i.e., 01/10/2014.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: The Claimant’s Letter of Confirmation dated 01/10/2014 was duly signed by the Company’s Farm Operation Manager, Eric Vigne which later no longer be working with the Company effective 10/07/2015 as he wished to work in the different field pursuant to the letter of Organization Changed dated 18/06/2015 to all employees from the CEO of the Company, Ang Ting Cheong (COW-1) known as T.C. Ang. In the same letter of Organization Changed dated 18/06/2015, the CEO decided that Eric Vigne’s position will be assumed by the Claimant as Operations and Human Resource Manager effective on the same date (10/07/2015) as this is the Company’s direction to not recruit from outside and provide opportunities to local talent within the Company. The Company will announce the new organization structure of Farm in coming days focusing on local team and inform all the employees to extend their support and co-operation to the Claimant as the new Company’s Farm Operations Manager.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: The CEO of the Company (COW-1) T.C. Ang also issued letter of Expanded Role dated 01/08/2015 (page 21 of CLB) to the Claimant in recognition of her expanded roles as Human Resources Manager and covering farm operations duties, the management of the Company had decided to update her designation to Operations Manager effective 01/08/2015. Her basic salary will be increased from RM7,500.00 to RM8,000.00 per month effective 01/08/2015 with allowance of RM2,500.00 per month in view of the expended responsibilities which will be paid to the Claimant along with her August 1, 2015 salary. Despite that the Claimant do not have the required aquaculture background to take up the expended responsibilities the Company recognize and appreciate her dedication, performance, support and contribution, and will support her in this working together as their work towards their goal of “Employer of Choice” in the journey towards better and more comprehensive benefits plus a more balanced work life.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: Nonetheless, the RM2,500.00 allowance was indeed a temporary allowance paid solely in relation to the Claimant’s expanded role, and not a fixed or contractual allowance forming part of her permanent wages. The allowance of RM2,500.00 was expressly tied to the Claimant’s temporary assumption of expended duties in respect of the farm operations. Once those responsibilities were removed and reallocated, the allowance ceased accordingly. It demonstrates beyond doubt that the RM2,500.00 allowance was never a fixed or contractual payment. The payroll records confirm that once her expanded responsibilities ceased, her salary reverted to RM8,000.00 with no continuing payment of the RM2,500.00 allowance. The Claimant raised no contemporaneous complaint or grievance at that material time, an omission that strongly implies her acceptance that the allowance had ended in accordance with its temporary nature. Thus, the Claimant’s last drawn basic salary as evidenced by payroll records was RM8,000.00 without the extra allowance of RM2,500.00.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: Thereafter, the Company was undergoing serious financial losses exceeding RM86.5 million from 2012-2017 as referred to the Company’s Statutory Financial Statements for years 2013 to 2017 (page 22-240 of COB). In the efforts to turnaround the Company, it has closed the headquarters at Ipoh of which the Claimant was aware of. The Company has also streamlined Finance team from 7 staff to 5 staff, do without the General Manager position, and sold off the Company’s assets and the Hatchery unit due to the financial losses faced by the Company.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: As part of a genuine restructuring exercise, the Company did not employ new staff to fill in the vacancies of Maintenance Manager and Farm Operation Manager instead asking the Claimant to fill the positions while remained the position as Human Resource Manager. That being the reason that the Company issued an organization update dated 18/06/2015 (page 290 of COB) formally announcing the Claimant’s new position despite knowing the Claimant may not have the required aquaculture background to take up the expanded responsibilities.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: Nevertheless, the Claimant never raised any objection over the said new position, but she had full control and updated the organization structure to create the Facilities and Maintenance Operations team (emails at pages 287-288, 294-301 of COB). The Claimant was also aware that no new personnel were to be recruited for the Company due to the ongoing restructuring process. As a result of the genuine restructuring and consolidation of functions, the Company determined that the Claimant’s role as Human Resource Manager was no longer required and accordingly her position was rendered redundant.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: In the Acknowledgement page (page 24 of CLB) of the letter of termination dated 26/07/2018, the Claimant duly acknowledged and signed on 06/08/2018 that she received a total of termination nett payment of RM20,667.91, whereof inter alia, it clearly stated that the last basic salary of the Claimant for 06/09/2018 – 05/10/2018 was for RM8,000.00 per month before her termination and/or before she left the Company.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: The Company exhibited payment advice from Maybank2e (page 280-281 of COB) for sum payment of RM20.667.91 to the Claimant pursuant to payment for date of end employment 06/08/2018 (page 281 of COB) for the same nett amount RM20,66791 which was received by the Claimant on 03/08/2018 of which was duly acknowledged receipt by the Claimant on 06/08/2018. The Claimant then signed the acknowledgement to acknowledge receipt of the letter of termination and the payment received on 03/06/2018 and to confirm that she understood and accepted the contents (pages 276-277 of COB).

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: Nonetheless, by reference to the Claimant’s salary slip for 2nd. Half Payroll – August 2015 dated 31/08/2015 (page 22 of CLB) the Claimant received basic rate salary of RM8,000.00. Similarly, in reference to the pay slip for 2nd. Half Payroll – June 2018 dated 30/06/2018 (page 25 of CLB) and pay slip for 2nd. Half Payroll – July 2018 dated 31/07/2018 (page 26 of CLB) it is abundantly clear and profound finding that the basic salary of the Claimant was RM8,000.00 per month. These contemporaneous documents and pay slips consistently show a basic salary of RM8,000.00 per month at the time of her termination, and not RM8,500.00 as alleged by the Claimant.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: Notably, the Claimant asserted that Mr. Eric Vigne had authority to approve salary adjustments, while on the other hand conceding that such approval required higher management and/or the CEO confirmation whereof the Company disputed consistently from the outset is the validity and authorization of any salary adjustment to RM8,500.00. On contrary, the only truly reliable evidence of what the Claimant was paid are the Company’s payroll records and payslips produce in evidence. All contemporaneous documents, testimony and payroll evidence confirm that the purported RM8,500.00 figure was never approved by the Company’s authorized decision makers.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: Conversely, the Claimant never raised any contemporaneous complaint or escalation to the CEO of Board when she continued to receive RM7,500.00 per month though she believed that she is entitled to RM8,500.00 per month. One would expect her as in her capacity as HR Manager, to have immediately sought redress or clarification from higher management. Her failure to do so, and her continued acceptance of RM7,500.00 per month without protest, speaks volumes against her credibility.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: Moreover, the Claimant conceded during cross-examination that Mr. Eric Vigne himself reported to higher management, including the CEO, except she approached COW-1 for a separate salary adjustment from RM7,500.00 to RM10,500.00. This speaks volume and it shows that she herself knew her salary would be RM7,500.00 and not RM8,500.00 even after the issuance of the Letter of Confirmation by Mr. Eric Vigne, and that only the CEO could approve salary changes. If so, there is no plausible reason why she would have abandoned her claim to the higher salary without even raising the matter with COW-1, unless she knew all along that the Letter of Confirmation was not validly authorized. Her silence and acquiescence amount to clear evidence that she herself recognized the Letter of Confirmation’s lack of validity. It relies on the Letter of Confirmation and the surrounding evidence showing that there was no authorized salary adjustment to RM8,500.00 per month.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: It is abundantly clear findings that the payroll records and payslips stand as the most reliable, contemporaneous evidence of the Claimant’s true wages, and the contemporaneous payroll records corroborate that her basic salary was increased from RM7,500.00 to RM8,000.00, not RM8,500.00, consistent with the Company’s case and directly contrary to her claim. If indeed RM8,500.00 had been approved or paid, this would have been reflected in the payroll but yet no such record exists.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: On final analysis, the Claimant’s contradictory narration in her evidence, selective reliance on unauthorized letters and acquiescence to payroll evidence showing her last drawn salary of RM8,000.00 collectively demonstrate that her claim to RM8,500.00 per month is unmeritorious and unsubstantiated by fact or law. This Court of considered view and finding, has satisfied on balance of probability that backwages to be awarded must be strictly computed on the basis of the verified last drawn salary of RM8,000.00 in compliance with the Second Schedule of the Industrial Relations Act 1967, and not on the speculative sum of RM11,100.00 advanced by the Claimant, which is without legal or evidential foundation.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content:
The calculation of remedy shall be in accordance with the following computation as below: -
(i) Basic last drawn salary before termination: RM8,000.00 x 24 = RM192,000.00
(ii) Deduction of termination net payment (severance sum) of RM20,667.91 which was credited into the Claimant’s bank account on 03/08/2018 (pages 272-275 & 280-281 of COB)
(iii) RM192,000.00 – RM20,667.91 = RM171,332.09

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: The amount of backwages as awarded above amounting of RM171,332.09 (Ringgit Malaysia: One Hundred Seventy One Thousand Three Hundred Thirty Two And Nine Cent Only) subject to any statutory deductions (if any) shall be paid by the Company to the Claimant through her representative Messrs. S. Ravichandaran & Anuar within thirty (30) days from the date of service of this Award to parties as set forth herein, so ordered.

case_name: Siti Azmah binti Mat Taib v Trapia Malaysia Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: In arriving the above decision, the Court has taken into account on totality of evidence as a whole submitted by the Company and the Claimant, the pleadings that have been filed by both parties and with regard to s. 30(5) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 which requires the Court to act in accordance with equity and good conscience and substantial merits of the case without regards on technicality and legal form.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: In the case of WONG CHEE HONG v. CATHAY ORGANIZATION (M) SDN BHD [1988] 1 CLJ 45; [1988] 1 CLJ (Rep) 298, the Court had stated the followings: “When the Industrial Court is dealing with a reference under s. 20, the first thing that the court will have to do is to ask itself a question (of) whether there was a dismissal, and if so, whether it was with or without just cause or excuse”.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content:
See the cases of MILAN AUTO SDN BHD v. WONG SEH YEN [1995] 2 MLRA, and HONG LEONG ASSURANCE SDN BHD v. WONG YUEN HOCK [1995] 1 MLRA 412. In the case of STAMFORD EXECUTIVE CENTRE v. PUAN DHARSINI GANESAN (1986) 1 ILR 101, it was held that:
‘..in a dismissal case, the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence. Burden of proof lies on the employer. He must prove that the workmen are guilty and it is not the workman who must prove that he is not guilty.’

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: The burden of proving that the dismissal was done with just cause and excuse, squarely rest upon the Employer/Company. (See PELANGI ENTERPRISE SDN BHD v. OH SWEE CHOO & ANOR (2004) 6 CLJ 157).

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content:
In the case of IREKA CONSTRUCTION BERHAD v. CHANTIRAVATHAN SUBRAMANIAM JAMES [1995] 1 MELR 373 it was decided that:
“It is a basic principle of industrial jurisprudence that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer to prove that he has just cause or excuse for taking the decision to impose the disciplinary measure of dismissal upon the employee. The just cause must be, either a misconduct, negligence or poor performance based on the facts of the case “.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: In the case of TELEKOM MALAYSIA KAWASAN UTARA v. KRISHNAN KUTTY SANGUNI NAIR & ANOR (2002) 3 CLJ 314 the Court of Appeal held that the standard of proof that is required in the Industrial Court is that of balance of probabilities. Even if there is misconduct like theft or any dishonest conduct, the standard of proof is still on balance of probabilities and not of beyond reasonable doubt. What this means is that the Company bears the burden of producing convincing evidence that the Company has good grounds for the dismissal and that the exercise of this decision is made with just cause or excuse. (WELTEX KNITWEAR INDUSTRIES SDN BHD v. LAW KAR TOY & ANOR [1998] 4 MLRH 774; [1998] 1 LNS 258). Where the dismissal is disputed, the burden of proof rests on the Claimant to show on balance of probabilities that he had been dismissed by his employer. In the present case, there is no dispute as to the dismissal, the only question now is whether the dismissal is done with just cause or excuse. See the Federal Court decision of GOON KWEE PHOY v. J & P COATS (M) BHD [1981] 1 MLRA 415.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: The Claimant was terminated vide letter of termination dared 27.9.2022. The Company admitted that the Claimant was terminated due to the seriousness of the misconduct. The Court must decide whether the termination was done with just cause or excuse. At this stage, the Court will evaluate the evidence and testimonies of the witnesses to decide if the termination was done with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: Misconduct was defined by O.P MALHOTRA in his book THE LAW OF INDUSTRIAL DISPUTE as “any conduct on part of an employee inconsistent with the faithful discharge of his duties towards his employer would be misconduct. Any breach of the express or implied duties of an employee towards his employer, therefore unless it be of trifling nature, would constitute an act of misconduct. In Industrial Law, the word ‘misconduct’ has acquired a specified connotation. It cannot mean inefficiency or slackness. It is something far more positive and certainly deliberate. The charge of ‘misconduct’, therefore, is the charge of some positive act or conduct which would be quite incompatible with express and implied terms of relationship of the employee to the employer.”

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: DR. V.G MHETRAS in his book called MISCONDUCTS ENQUIRY AND DISMISSALS defined misconduct as “In Industrial Law, ‘misconduct’ is a mode of behavior and conduct of an employee which is inconsistent with his relationship with the employer. It is an act or omission thereof which is contrary to the expected performance of his duties or in a variance with the faithful discharge of his obligations undertaken by him either expressly or impliedly in accepting the services. Misconduct in industry or legal-being contrary to the rule of right or natural justice, or violation of ‘justice according to law’.”

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content:
When an action is done willfully and deliberately, it is considered a misconduct and entails a punishment.” In the case of HONG LEONG EQUIPMENTS SDN BHD v. LIEW FOOK CHUAN & OTHER APPEALS [1996] 1 MELR 142, the Court of Appeal held that;
"The fact that an employer has conducted a Domestic Inquiry against his workman is, in my judgment, an entirely irrelevant consideration to the issue whether the latter had been dismissed without just cause or excuse. The findings of a Domestic Inquiry are not binding upon the Industrial Court which rehears the matter afresh. However, it may take into account the fact that a Domestic Inquiry had been held when determining whether the particular workman was justly dismissed.” See also SEELAN MANIAM v. MOX GASES SDN BHD (2012) 2 MELR 329.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: The Claimant avers that Domestic Inquiry (“DI”) was held by the Company with regards to the allegations. The case of DREAMLAND CORPORATION (M) SDN BHD v. CHOONG CHIN SOOI & ANOR (1987) 1 MLRA 357, was approved by the Federal Court in the case of WONG YUEN HOCK v. SYARIKAT HONG LEONG ASSURANCE SDN BHD (1995) 3 AMR 214, whereby the Courts held that the failure of an employer to hold a pre-domestic inquiry can be cured by the Industrial Court when it hears the reference of the employee for unfair dismissal. Further in the case of OSA HOLDINGS SDN BHD v. MAHESWARAN SABARATNAM (1995) 2 ILR 377, the Court held that a failure to convene a Domestic Inquiry would not render the dismissal as being without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: The core of the allegation here is a false claim made by the Claimant misrepresenting the claim as that of a guest’s vehicle. The Claimant was dismissed due to serious misconduct which made the Hotel lose the trust and confidence in him.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: The Company averred that the Claimant had misrepresented the Company into believing that the vehicle belongs to one of the guests of the Hotel. The Company averred that the Claimant failed to submit the claim firm, incident report and the quotation to COW2 being the Cluster Director of Finance instead the Claimant submitted the claim to the Company’s insurance provider Etiqa Takaful on 9.8.2022 when the alleged incident took place on 27.1.2022. The Claim should have been submitted to COW2 first

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: The Company refers to page 16 of COB1, email sent to COW2. The Company submitted that the Claimant had represented that the vehicle belonged to a guest of the Hotel. There is nothing on page 16 of COB1 where the Claimant indicated or misrepresented the Company that the vehicle belonged to the guest. However, reference made to page 15 of COB1, the Company submitted that the Claimant failed to inform or reveal to COW2 that the vehicle belongs to him. The Claimant had clearly written in the email to refer to the incident form (refer to page 21 to 25 of COB1). The incident report on page 21, clearly did not mention any with reference to the guest. The details given by the Claimant were his contact number and his car details. If COW2 had gone through the incident report, she would have known that the vehicle belonged to the Claimant. The email page 15 & 16 of COB1, clearly indicates that COW2 did not refer to the documents before communicating to the Claimant, COW1 also testified that there was no written Standard Operation Procedure (‘SOP”) with regards to the claim. COW1 stated that the Custer Director had an impression that the claim was for the guest and a follow up email was sent to the Claimant (refer to page 15 & 16 of the COB1). The Claimant’s counsel asked COW1 if he had verified with the Claimant who the guest was and COW1 answered that he did not. COW1 further testified that the document at page 9 of CLB1 was for the employee of the Hotel, which is consistent with the Claimant’s statement.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: The Company further submitted that the Claimant’s contention that others were aware the claim was for his own vehicle does not hold water as the Claimant employee of the Hotel are not allowed to make claims. On the other hand, the Claimant contended that there were 2 forms for the claim, the Team Member Incident report was for the employees where else the Internal Incident Report was for the Guests. When asked in the cross examination whether an employee can claim for accidents, COW1 stated that it depends on the nature of the accident and if its due to the employee’s own negligent, claim is not allowed.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: The Claimant stated that he had informed Mr. Ainuddin (‘Assistant Security Manager’) that the vehicle belonged to him. The Assistant Security Manager still employed in the Hotel, however the Company failed to bring the Assistant Security Manager as the witness to shed some light into this conflicting evidence. The only evidence with regards to the accident was forwarded by the Claimant himself vide WhatsApp, there is no other available evidence as the accident was alleged to have taken place on 27.12022 however the claim surfaced on 9.8.2022.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: COW2 on the other hand stated that he found out about the incident in August 2022 when the claim was submitted to COW2. Furthermore, COW2 testified that the form was presented for his signature by the Claimant while he was going out of the office and he was presented with the form in a rush and did not check the details in the form. COW2 also admitted that he did not check with the Finance whether the form was submitted in January or not. COW2 also admitted that the Claimant did not write false information in the claim form. When the Court asked COW2 whether he has never seen page 9 of CLB1 before, he answered no. Being the investigation officer for this allegation, he is expected to be aware of this very important document which is the Team member’s Incident Form. The Court is puzzled how could an investigation officer investigate the matter without going through the document. COW2 has stated that he had gone through all the documents including the cctv footage, the Claimant’s explanation to the show cause letter however in Court, COW2 testified that he has never seen the incident report before, according to COW2 the document was never provided to him during the investigation. There is no investigation report available in the Bundle to substantiate COW2’s evidence. COW2 also testified that he did not view the cctv footage during the investigation. COW2 admitted that he overlooked the claim form twice first when he signed the form and secondly during the investigation. COW2 signed the claim form on page 11 of COB1.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: COW1 and COW2 testified in Court that the Claimant verbally mentioned to them that the claim was for the guest of the Hotel however the Hotel did not provide any evidence to prove that the Claimant had stated that the claim was for the guest.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: The Company argued that according to the Employee Handbook (page 60 of COB1) which was handed to the Claimant, clearly states that the Hotel will not accept liability for the loss or damage to the Team member’s property. However, there was a claim form for the Team Member, and the Company did not at any material time during the claim or even during the investigation deny the Claimant’s right to claim. COW2 need not have signed the Claimant form in the first place. Alternatively, the Hotel could have just denied the claim at any time, which was not the case. On the other hand, COW2 and COW1 also testified that the Team Member’s Incident form was for employees to make the claim.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: The termination letter dated 27.09.2022 contained 2 allegations, 1st allegation was stated in the show cause letter however the 2nd allegation was never communicated to the Claimant vide the show cause letter. As the Court illustrated above, there was no cogent evidence adduced by the Hotel to prove the allegation of misrepresentation for a false claim. The Claimant did not at any material time misrepresent the Hotel into believing that the vehicle belonged to the Hotel guest. The Hotel claimed that the Hotel was under the impression that the claim was for the guest. The Hotel was under the impression that the vehicle belonged to the guests due to their own failure to verify the documents before the Claimant was charged. Both COW1 and COW2 testified that they did not verify the documents with the Claimant. The cctv footage was not clear whether the vehicle was damaged prior to the accident or on the incident. The Hotel failed to prove the case on balance of probabilities all the charges of misconduct against the Claimant. The Hotel has acted on a suspicion however there was no grounds and evidence to believe there was a reasonable suspicion. At most, the Hotel had merely casted doubt based on the surrounding circumstances. The Hotel has the burden to prove the case on balance of probabilities and not just casting doubts.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: This Court finds that, the Claimant was unfairly dismissed based on the reasons illustrated above. The Company was unable to adduce sufficient evidence to prove the charges on balance of probabilities. The Claimant’s termination purportedly was lacking in good faith, improper and unfair for reasons which I have enumerated herein above. Accordingly, the Court finds that the Claimant was dismissed without just cause or excuse. Therefore, the Claimant’s claim hereby allowed.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: Considering the facts of this case, the Court finds that reinstatement may not be an appropriate remedy. Therefore, the monetary award of compensation in lieu of reinstatement would be more suitable (KOPERASI SERBAGUNA SANYA BHS (SABAH) v. DR. JAMES ALFRED (SABAH) & ANOR [2000] 3 CLJ 758. This Court will thereby order compensation in lieu of reinstatement of one month salary for each year of completed service to the Claimant.

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content:
The Claimant’s last drawn salary was RM8,740.99 and for the purpose of calculation, this Court disregard variable figures such as reimbursement, allowances and commissions. The Court is also mindful of the provisions of Section 30(5), Section 30(6A) and The Second Schedule of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 in considering the appropriate relief to be awarded to the Claimant. Having considered all the above items and items 1 and 3 of the Second Schedule of the Act, the Claimant is ordered for back wages (maximum of 24 months) from his last drawn salary. The Claimant gave evidence that he was working after the dismissal therefore, the Court will make deductions from the back wages for the post dismissal earning.
Back wages of 24 month: RM8,740.99 x 12 months
= RM104,891.88 Deduction of 12 months for post dismissal earning Compensation in lieu of reinstatement of one month pay for each year of service:
RM8,740.99 X 4 month
= RM34,963.96
============ TOTAL
= RM 139,855.84
============

case_name: Samugam a/l Krishnan v Knights Bridge Avenue Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Vanithamany Sivalingam
content: It is hereby ordered that the total sum of Ringgit Malaysia One Hundred Thirty Nine Thousand Eight Hundred Fifty Five and Eighty Four Only (RM139,855.84) after statutory deductions if any, is to be paid by the Company to the Claimant’s solicitor Messrs Lavaniyan Nathan & Associates within 30 days from the date of this Award.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: III. The Function Of The Industrial Court
content: The role of the Industrial Court pertaining to a reference under section 20(3) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 is to ask itself a question whether there was a dismissal; and, if so, whether it was with or without just cause or excuse (Wong Chee Hong v. Cathay Organisation (M) Sdn. Bhd. [1988] 1 MLJ 92).

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The issues that arise in this case are:- (i) whether the Claimant’s prolonged illness and uncertainty as to when he will return to work frustrated his employment contract with the Company; (ii) if so, whether the dismissal of the Claimant by the Company was done with or without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content: The Claimant’s employment contract was terminated on the ground of frustration of contract due to the prolonged illness of the Claimant, wherein the Claimant had been on medical/hospitalization leave for 373 days.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content:
The letter entitled ‘Termination of your Contract of Employment due to frustration by reason of prolonged illness’ dated 17 May 2024 (“the Termination Letter”) (at pp. 25-26 of COB-1) issued by the Company to the Claimant states, inter alia, as follows:- “It is with regret that you have been on prolonged hospitalisation leave from 8.5.2023 till 11.5.2024. As per the Company’s record, the Medical Certificates (MC) for your hospitalisation leave that were given by you are as follows:-
Particular
Date Period No. of days 1. MC for Hospitalisation leave 18.5.23 8.5.23-24.5.23 17 2. MC for Hospitalisation leave 24.5.23 25.5.23-24.6.23 31 3. MC for Hospitalisation leave 23.6.23 25.6.23-29.7.23 35 4. MC for Hospitalisation leave 28.7.23 30.7.23-29.8.23 31 5. MC for Hospitalisation leave 29.8.23 30.8.23-29.9.23 31 6. MC for Hospitalisation leave 27.9.23 30.9.23-3.11.23 35 7. MC for Hospitalisation leave 3.11.23 4.11.23-8.12.23 35 8. MC for Hospitalisation leave 6.12.23 9.12.23-13.1.24 35 9. MC for Hospitalisation leave 12.1.24 14.1.24-17.2.24 35 10. MC for Hospitalisation leave 16.2.24 18.2.24-6.4.24 49 11. MC for Hospitalisation leave 19.3.24 7.4.24-11.5.24 35 On 13.5.2024, the Company received a further MC from you stating that your hospitalisation leave would be extended again from 12.5.2024 to 25.5.2024. You have been on hospitalisation leave due to your illness and/or medical condition for too long i.e. 373 days as at the date of this letter. The Management finds that your incapacity or illness is serious as it has prolonged for too long for more than a year. You are holding a key role and an important position in your department as Head of Security to oversee and ensure that the operations run smoothly. Your position has been vacant for too long and the Company had stretched its other personnel to cover and perform your duties and responsibilities in your absence. The Company is in a very difficult position for such a long time and could no longer afford to run its operation in such manner. In view of your prolonged illness and the uncertainty as to when you are fit to return to perform your duties as the Head of Security, the Management has no other alternative but to take this difficult decision to terminate your contract of employment with immediate effect due to frustration as a result of your prolonged illness”.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content: The Claimant suffered his first injury on 8 May 2023 whilst at work when he was carrying a 15kg box, when he felt numbness on his back. He was thereafter warded at the KPJ Selangor Specialist Hospital for 10 days and underwent a Posterior Lumbar Interbody Fusion (PLIF) surgery. He was on medical leave from 8 May 2023 until 29 July 2023, i.e. a total of 83 days (the medical certificates for the period between 8 May 2023 until 29 July 2023 are collectively exhibited at pp. 8 – 10 of COB-1). This was not disputed by the Claimant.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content: The Claimant’s medical leave was further extended for the period from 30 July 2023 until 6 April 2024, i.e. a total of 251 days (the medical certificates for the period between 30 July 2023 until 6 April 2024 are collectively exhibited at pp. 11 – 17 of COB-1). Again, this is not disputed by the Claimant.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content: Whilst being on medical leave during the period between 18 February 2024 until 6 April 2024, the Claimant suffered yet another injury to his back on 29 February 2024 and had to undergo a percutaneous disc compression surgery as well as a surgery to his right hand.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content: At this point in time, the Company understandably became agitated due to the numerous extensions to the Claimant’s medical leave which was stretching to almost one year at that point in time, and thus had written to the Claimant’s surgeon at KPJ Selangor Specialist Hospital, i.e. Dr. Askandar on 29 March 2024 (at pp. 21-22 of COB-1) inquiring about the Claimant’s projected return to work. Dr. Askandar replied via letter dated 3 April 2024 (at pp. 23-24 of COB-1) stating that it would take about 2 months before a patient, such as the Claimant, who had undergone percutaneous disc decompression surgery to be fit to work again.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content: Lo and behold, the Claimant went on yet another extended medical leave from 12 May 2024 to 25 May 2024 (at p. 19 of COB-1). After having been patient for almost 373 days whilst the Claimant was on continuous medical leave since 8 May 2023, this final tranche of medical leave was the straw that broke the camel’s back. The Company issued the Termination Letter on 17 May 2024 after having waited patiently for 373 days for the Claimant to return to work.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content: The Claimant meanwhile contends, amongst other things, that the Company had been unfair to his predicament when they failed to wait for one more month before he was fit to return to work on 26 June 2024. However, the Company was still in the dark as at 17 May 2024 whether the Claimant would ever be able to return to work.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content: It must be borne in mind that the Company waited more than one year for the Claimant to recover and be fit again to resume his duties in the Company. They had given the Claimant sufficient time and opportunity for him to recover fully and return back to work. During the Claimant’s absence, the Company had to re-deploy some of their other staff to cover the Claimant’s duties and responsibilities. The Company is an on-going concern incorporated with the sole purpose of making profits in their business, and thus could ill afford to accommodate an employee who was prone to prolonged absences, either medically or otherwise. Rather than being an asset to the Company, the Claimant had instead became a liability.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content: The Claimant also contends that there can be no frustration of contract as the Company had allowed him to carry out light duties. It is pertinent to note however that out of the 373 days that the Claimant had been on medical leave, he had only performed the light duties between 15 January 2024 to 26 February 2024 ( as can be seen from the Daily Time Records for the months of January 2024 (at p. 27 of COB-1) and February 2024 (at p. 28 of COB-1)), i.e. a little over one month. Furthermore, it was the Claimant who had offered to do some light work. The Company never approached him to do any work during his medical leave, as medical leave are given for an employee to recuperate at home. The Claimant was technically on medical leave and the Company was unable to give any instructions of their own to the Claimant to carry out his duties and responsibilities as the Head of Security. In any event, the light work that the Claimant carried out was for approximately one month only out of the 373 days he had been on medical leave.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content: COW-2 testified as follows with regard to the issue of the Claimant performing light duties (COWS-2; Q & A Nos. 8 to 11):- “Q8. Based on the daily time record – detailed of the Claimant for the months of January and February 2024, did the Claimant report for duty? A8. Yes, he did. In January 2024, he did report for work between 15.1.2024 and 31.1.2024. In February 2024, he did report for work between the period of 1.2.2024 and 26.2.2024. Q9. Why did he still report for duty despite on hospitalization leave? A9. Sometime in January 2024, the Claimant met the Director of the Company to check if there were any light duties for him to perform. The Claimant was informed that there were light duties for him to do. On 15.1.2025, the Claimant agreed to return to work to perform some light duties with a schedule from 7 a.m. to 3.30 p.m. During the period from 15.1.2024 to 26.2.2024, the Company has assigned the Claimant with some administrative works i.e. communicating with the security agency regarding new agreement and work schedule of the Company’s security guard. Q10. What happened after 17.2.2024? A10. The Company subsequently received a hospitalization leave from the Claimant stating that he would be unfit to work for 49 days from 18.2.2024 to 6.4.2024. (See page 17 of COB-1) Q11. Did the Claimant report for duty in performing the light duties after 26.2.2024? A11. He did not”.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
section_title: V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons
content: In the case of Pauline Peck v. Saratim Insurance Agency Services Sdn Bhd [2010] 3 ILR 630 the learned Industrial Court Chairman, P Iruthayaraj D Pappusamy, considered the principles and/or factors in determining frustration of an employment contract due to an employee’s illness:- “1. One of the ways by which a contract of employment may come to an end apart from the dismissal of an employee is by the application of the doctrine of frustration. By 'frustration' it is meant that there has been such a change of circumstances that events make it physically impossible for a contract to be performed as for example, where the illness of the employee lasts or is likely to last for a prolonged period. It cannot be disputed that illness or incapacity which is permanent will frustrate the contract, and so will illness which is of so prolonged a nature as to prevent the employer from getting substantially what he has bargained for as it is also accepted that an employee must provide satisfactory performance of the work which he has contracted to do. (Kumpulan Guthrie Sdn. Bhd. v. K.P. Sukumari Amana Narayana Meon, Award No. 33 of 1973 "Kumpulan Guthrie"); 2. Whether a particular illness is of such a character as to put an end to the employment, is always a question of fact for the court to decide. (Kumpulan Guthrie); 3. The incapacity or illness should not be temporary, but serious and prolonged, so that the employee cannot be expected to perform his duties in the foreseeable future. In such circumstances, the employer has the right to terminate the employee's services. (A.T. Fernandez v. See Sun Estate, Award No. 64 of 1974); 4. Where without the fault of either party, some supervening event occurs which was not reasonably foreseeable at the time when the contract was made and which renders further performance of the contract totally impossible or something radically different from what the parties bargained for, the contract is forthwith discharged by operation of law. Absence of ill health may take the form of either of persistent brief absences over a long period of time, or a single long absence from work. In the latter situation it may exceptionally be the case that the contract is frustrated. Where this is the case there is in law no dismissal and therefore the employee's claim for unfair dismissal is bound to fail. (MHS Aviation Sdn. Bhd. v. Zainol Akmar Hj. Mohd Noor [2001] 2 ILR 336 (Award No. 419 of 2001); 5. Where there is a dismissal, the starting point for analyzing the duty of the tribunal in deciding whether or not the dismissal is fair, the court emphasized the importance of scrutinizing all the relevant factors. Every case depends on its own circumstances. The basic question which has to be determined in every case is whether, in all the circumstances, the employer can be expected to wait any longer and if so, how much longer? The relevant circumstances include "the nature of the illness, the likely length of the continuing absence, the need of the employers to have done the work, which the employee was engaged to do" (Spencer v. Paragon Wallpapers Ltd [1976] IRLR 373) 6. While the employers cannot be expected to be, nor is it desirable that they should set themselves up as medical experts, the decision to dismiss is not a medical question, but a question to be answered by the employers in the light of the available medical advice. (East Lindsey District Council v. Daubney [1977] IRLR 181) 7. In cases of intermittent absences from work due to ill-health there was no obligation on an employer to call medical evidence. An employer had to have regard to the whole history of the employment and to take into account a range of factors including - the nature of the illness; the likelihood of it recurring or some other illness arising; the length of the various absences and the spaces of good health between them; the need of the employer for the work done by the particular employee; the impact of the absences on others who work with the employee; the adoption and the carrying out of the policy; the important emphasis on a personal assessment in the ultimate decision and of course, the extent to which the difficulty of the situation and the position of the employer had been made clear to the employee so that the employee realises that the point of no return, the moment when the decision was ultimately being made may be approaching. (Lynock v. Packaging Ltd. [1988] IRLR 510) 8. The employers cannot be expected to go to unreasonable length in seeking to accommodate someone who is not able to carry out his job to the full extent. (Garricks (Caterers) Ltd v. V Nolan [1980] 1 IRLR 259)”

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
In fact, the Claimant himself in his testimony admitted the seriousness of the injuries that he had suffered, in particular the second injury sustained on 29 February 2024 (CLWS-1; Q & A No. 16):- “S.16 Didalam Ikatan Dokumen Syarikat muka surat 22 hingga 23, petikan dari surat doctor mengesahkan bahawa anda memerlukan cuti lebih kurang 2 bulan; “He was admitted from 29/02/2024 to 07/03/2024 for the above surgeries. Post operative, he has been advised to continue medical leave. In normal circumstances, it would take about 2 months before a patient who had undergone percutaneous disc decompression is fit to start work.
Muhammad Rifa’i’s condition will be reviewed on 11/05/2024”. Boleh beritahu kepada Mahkamah, tahap keseriusan pembedahan yang anda alami? J.16 Ya Yang Arif, saya telah mengalami 2 kali kemalangan/kecederaan yang melibatkan pembedahan tulang belakang, dan ianya berpunca dari kecederaan dan pembedahan pertama pada 10hb Mei 2023. Saya tekun dalam melakukan fisioterapi walau betapa sakit pun, tetapi demi mencari punca pendapatan, saya tekun dan rajin supaya saya dapat pulih dan kembali bekerja seperti sebelum ini. Menurut doctor, saya boleh melakukan kerja-kerja ringan dan saya juga telah lapor untuk bekerja. Saya tidak mengambil cuti sakit yang panjang seperti yang dikatakan oleh Syarikat “prolonged illness”. Apabila kali kedua pembedahan berlaku, kecederaan ini makin serius. Adalah wajar untuk diberikan rehat yang secukupnya kerana pembedahan yang melibatkan tulang belakang adalah satu pembedahan besar dan saya mempunyai risiko untuk cacat sepanjang hidup jika tidak dijaga dengan baik. Selepas pembedahan, saya dikira separa cacat hampir selama 1 bulan terlantar di katil dan berharap untuk pulih seperti biasa. Saya juga giat melakukan fisioterapi supaya dapat pulih seperti sediakala dan berharap dapat bekerja semula”.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: Due to the seriousness of the injuries suffered by the Claimant and the uncertainty as to when he would be able to return to work, the Company, after having waited 373 days, finally decided enough was enough and brought the Claimant’s employment contract to an end. The overwhelming evidence before the Court, despite the Claimant’s contention that he was working hard to regain fitness, is that there was no certainty as to when he would be fit again to work. The Claimant was eventually declared fit to work by his surgeon at KPJ Selangor Specialist Hospital, i.e. Dr. Askandar, on 26 June 2024 (at p. 11 of CLB-2) (which is almost one after his employment was terminated by the Company on 17 May 2024), which was a little too late taking into account the circumstances of the case. The Company was not expected to know at the time they terminated the Claimant’s employment contract on 17 May 2024 that he would be able to return to work on 26 June 2024, as he was still on prolonged medial leave at that point in time.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: In the case of Sathiya Kala Nagapan v. Malayan Banking Bhd [2016] 3 ILR 26 it was held by the learned Industrial Court Chairman, Mary Shakila G Azariah:- “It is the bank's pleaded case that the claimant was dismissed for 2 reasons - firstly that she had taken excessive medical leave from June 2009 to November 2011 that is 273 days and secondly, for being absent without approval for 35 days. The bank submits that her persistent absenteeism is an indication to not perform her contractual obligations arising under the contract of employment. In the case of General Tyre Retreaders Sdn Bhd v. Vadiveloo Munusamy [1996] 2 ILR 1419 (Award No. 532 of 1996) it was held that extensive absence causes inconvenience and has a disruption effect on the productivity of the business. There is a wealth of cases where it has been held that taking excessive medical leave can be a serious misconduct and attracts the punishment of dismissal. It has been held that when an employee takes excessive medical leave it indicates that he is unwilling to perform his duties as required under the contract of employment with the Bank. In Mastura Mohd Mokhtar v. Affin Bank Berhad [2014] 3 ILR 113 (Award No. 540 of 2014) it was held that where the employee is unable to perform her duties in accordance with the terms and conditions of service the employer can treat the contract of employment as frustrated. Based upon equity and good conscience and the substantial merits of the case in the said case it was held that the contract of employment was frustrated and the termination of the claimant's contract of employment was with just cause or excuse. The issue before the court as I glean it to be is whether the termination of the claimant's employment contract was the product of a unjust dismissal or frustration of contract. If the dismissal was unjust the claimant would been entitled to relief whereas frustration of contract would discharge the employer from any liability. At the time of her dismissal the claimant had been absent for 68 days from 1 December 2011 to 1 March 2012 and further 6 days on 5, 6, 19, 20, 25 and 27 January 2012 which she claimed to be on medical leave but failed to produce any documentation or supporting evidence to justify her absence. The court having analysed the facts and evidence in that from June 2009 to the date of her dismissal the claimant had absented herself for more than several hundreds of days having been on medical leave and unapproved leave and considering the fact that the claimant had taken no further steps to satisfy her employer that she was now certified medical fit for work it was reasonable for the bank to have considered her contract of employment as having being frustrated. As such there is no obligation or liability that the court can pin on the bank. Given the facts and evidence the bank was right to think that the contract was frustrated as a result of the claimant's persistent absenteeism. A contract is deemed frustrated where it is impossible for that contract to continue. In employment that means that the employment ends. It will occur only where the circumstances that lead to the consideration to terminate the contract were unforeseen and it is impossible to continue the employment relationship. Once frustrated each party is discharged from future obligations under the contract and neither party may sue for breach. There is no dismissal in law. Illness causing long term absenteeism from work renders an employee incapable of carrying out the functions of his job and the employer under these circumstances is entitled to treat the contract as at an end as the purpose of the contract is unachievable the contracts will take into account when determining if a contract has been frustrated in ill health absence will be nature of the job role itself, the employer's length of service, the length and effect of the illness, whether the employee needed replacing and whether it was reasonable for the employer to wait any longer for the employee to return to work. Applying these principles to the facts of the case where the evidence clearly shows that the claimant had taken excessive medical leave no doubt for a definite medical condition and certified by the Bank's panel doctors, bank was right in treating the contract of employment as having being frustrated. As held in Spencer v. Paragon Wallpapers Ltd (1977) ICR 301 where it was held that the basic question which has to be determined in such cases is whether in all the circumstances the employer can be expected to wait any longer and if so, how much longer? Every case will be different depending upon the circumstances. The court opines that it is not whether the bank knew that the claimant was on medical leave or that the medical certificates were from their panel doctors for a definite medical ailment that the claimant had suffered in the given instance. The point is the bank had been patient carrying the claimant through from June 2009 to November 2011 and through 2012”.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: Similarly here, the Company had waited patiently for more than a year, in fact 373 days to be exact, for the Claimant to be fit to resume work again. But alas, there was nothing forthcoming that indicated that the Claimant was on a road to recovery. Instead, whilst being on medical leave, the Claimant suffered yet another injury which placed him on yet another long run of medical leave.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: After having analysed the facts and evidence produced by both parties, the Court finds that the Company was fully justified in losing their patience when they issued the Termination Letter on 17 May 2024 when they had no other choice but to bring the Claimant’s employment contract on the ground of frustration of contract due to the Claimant’s prolonged and persistent absenteeism due to illness.

case_name: Muhammad Rifa'i bin Sulaiman v Pusat Perniagaan Matahari Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant’s case is hereby dismissed.

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content: Based on both the parties' case as stated above, it is apparent that the two (2) questions which the court has to ask are: (i) was there a dismissal; and (ii) if the answer to (i) is in the affirmative, was the dismissal with or without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content:
As stated in the case of Wong Chee Hong v Cathay Organisation (M) Sdn. Bhd. [1988] 1 CLJ 45; [1988] 1 CLJ (Rep) 298 by the then Supreme Court as follows:
“When the Industrial Court is dealing with a reference under S 20, the first thing that the court will have to do is to ask itself a question whether there was a dismissal, and if so, whether it was with or without just cause or excuse.”

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content: In this case, the fact of dismissal is not disputed. Therefore, the only issue which is left to be deliberated before the court is whether the dismissal of the Claimant by the Company was with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content:
Having established that there is a dismissal, the court refers to the principles established in the Federal Court case of Wong Yuen Hock v Syarikat Hong Leong Assurance Sdn. Bhd. & Anor [1995] CLJ 344 where it was held that: -
“On the authorities, we were of the view that the main and only function of the Industrial Court is dealing with a reference under section 20 of the Act (unless otherwise lawfully provided by the terms of the reference), is to determine whether the misconduct or irregularities complained of by the Management as the grounds of dismissal were in fact committed by the workman, and if so, whether such grounds constitute just cause or excuse for the dismissal.”

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content:
Based on the foregoing paragraphs 37 to 40 hereinabove, the court has a duty to consider the followings: -
i. Whether the Claimant is guilty of the allegations of
misconduct levelled against him by the Company; and
ii. If the allegations of misconduct had been proven by the Company against the Claimant, whether that misconduct is serious enough to warrant a dismissal of the Claimant by the Company.

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content:
In the case of Shell Malaysia Trading Co. Sdn Bhd v. National Union of Petroleum & Chemical Industry Workers [1986] 1 ILR 677, the Industrial Court stated that:
"The company cited various authorities from Soonavala's The Supreme Court on Industrial Law (1979 Edition) .... But one authority relied on by the company goes on to add:
It is for the management to determine whether the act of the workman constitutes misconduct and whether it merits an order of dismissal. However, in determining whether there has been such misconduct, it must have facts upon which to base its conclusions and it must act in good faith without caprice or discrimination and without motive of victimization or intimidation or resorting to unfair labour practice and there must be no infraction of the accepted rules of natural justice. When management does have facts from, which it can conclude misconduct, its judgement cannot be questioned provided the above mentioned principles are not violated."

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content:
In the case of Ireka Construction Berhad v Chantiravathan Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 11 (Award No. 245 of 1995) the following was stated:
“It is a basic principle of industrial jurisprudence that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer to prove that he has just cause and excuse for taking the decision to impose the disciplinary measure of dismissal upon the employee. The just cause must be, either a misconduct, negligence or poor performance based on the facts of the case.”

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content: Having the burden of proving, the standard in which the employer must prove that the act of terminating the employee was carried out with just cause or excuse is on a balance of probabilities (as established in the case of Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara v Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor [2002] 3 CLJ 314)

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content: Section 30(5) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 (Act 1977) requires the court to decide a case in accordance with equity and good conscience, as such, Gopal Sri Ram JCA in his decision in the case of Harris Solid States (M) Sdn Bhd & Ors v Bruno Gentil Pereira & Ors (1996) 4 CLJ 747 CA had stated that it is incumbent upon the court to have regard to substantial merits of the case rather than to technicalities.

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content: It is trite that the Claimant is not the one who must prove that he was not guilty of misconduct [see the case of Stamford Executive Centre v Dharsini Ganesan [1986] 1 ILR 101 (Award No. 263 of 1985)]. That burden is cast squarely upon the Company.

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content: The Company had dismissed the Claimant as he was found guilty of Charge no. 1, Charge no. 2 and Charge no. 3 as stated in the Company’s letter of dismissal dated 18.05.2018.

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content:
However, what needs to be proven on a balance of probabilities (as determined in the case of Sinnaiyah & Sons Sdn. Bhd v Damai Setia Sdn Bhd [2015] 7 CLJ 584) is the allegation of misconduct levelled against the Claimant. In the case of Konnas Maritime Services Sdn Bhd v Adi Negara Kamaruddin [2004] 8 CLJ 369, Faiza Thamby Chik J had stated the following:
“…that the reason for the dismissal of an employee is grounded on a set of facts known to the employer or a set of beliefs held by him at the time of dismissal. Such a test is measured against a standard of proof on a balance of probabilities. Here the court is faced with civil proceedings, the standard applicable is on a balance of probabilities…”

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content:
The foregoing proposition in law was enunciated in the case of Ferodo Ltd v Barnes (EAT) [1976] ICR 439 where His Lordship Kilner Brown J held at p. 440:
“The question which falls to be decided in circumstances such as these is not whether or not the alleged offence is proved but whether or not the employers after careful investigation, and after adopting the appropriate procedures enshrined in the Code of Practice, came to a reasonable decision that dismissal must follow.”
His Lordship went on further to state at p. 441: “... the law is quite plain and that what the industrial tribunal ought to do is, not ask itself the question which this tribunal did - "Are we satisfied that the offence was committed?" - but to ask itself the question, "Are we satisfied that the employers had, at the time of the dismissal, reasonable grounds for believing that the offence put against the employee was in fact committed?”

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content: Based on the foregoing, Charge 1, Charge 2 and Charge 3 has been made out and the Claimant is guilty of misconduct.

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content: Since misconduct has been proven via all the Charges, the question that arises now is whether this misconduct warrants a dismissal of the Claimant. It is the court's view that the Claimant by his action had failed to safeguard the trust and confidence entrusted upon him by the Company.

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content:
B.R. Ghaiye in Misconduct in Employment Chapter XIX at page 650 states:
"The relation between an employer and an employee is of a fiduciary character. The word "fiduciary" means belonging to trust or trusteeship. It means that whenever an employer engages a worker, he puts trust that the worker will faithfully discharge the service and protect and further the interest of the employer."

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content:
In Pearce v Foster [1886] (vol XV11) QBD 536 the Queen's Bench Division it was held as follows:
"The rule of law is that where a person has entered into the position of servant, if he does anything incompatible with the due or faithful discharge of his duty to his master, the latter has a right to dismiss him. The relation of master and servant implies necessarily that the servant shall be in a position to perform his duty duly and faithfully, and if by his own act he prevents himself from doing so, the master may dismiss him. And Lopes LJ in the same case at page 542 stated as follows:
"If a servant conducts himself in a way inconsistent with the faithful discharge of his duty in the service, it is misconduct which justifies immediate dismissal."

case_name: Sulaiman bin Ghazali v Ranhill SAJ Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Tengku Amir Zaki bin Tengku Abdul Rahman
content: Therefore, by a careful assessment of the evidence taken as a whole, grounded upon equity, good conscience and the substantial merits of this case pursuant to Section 30(5) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967, it is the finding of the court that the Company has established, on a balance of probabilities, the appropriateness of the Company’s action against the Claimant. In the circumstances of this case, it is the considered view of the court that it is unreasonable to expect the Company to have continued the Claimant’s employment. The Claimant's claim is hereby dismissed.

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content:
It was not disputed that the termination of the Claimant is based on poor performance. The law concerning dismissal on the grounds of poor performance is well settled. Poor performance, unlike misconduct, does not in itself constitute a disciplinary offence. However, it is widely recognised that constant inefficiency or inability to perform the duties of one’s employment can justify termination with just cause and excuse, provided procedural fairness is observed. In Khor Eng Khye v. Guinness Anchor Marketing Sdn Bhd [2006] 2 LNS 1784, the Court held that:
“Although the Industrial Court has held that poor performance is not misconduct per se, it is trite law that poor performance affords an acceptable basis for an employer to establish that the dismissal is with just cause or excuse under section 20 of the Industrial Relations Act 1967. The reason for this is that inefficiency or incompetence resulting in failure to perform the duties of the service destroys the whole reality of the contract from the point of view of the employer. The vast majority of employees make their employers the judges of their competence. Hence, so long as the employer acts bona fide, i.e., if he is genuinely discontented with an employee, he is quite entitled to dismiss the employee.” (see also Samsudin Amin v. Austral Enterprises Bhd, Award 47 of 1974).”
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content:
The case of Ireka Construction Berhad v. Chantiravathan a/l Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 11 establishes a clear framework for assessing claims of dismissal for poor performance. It was held that, to justify such a dismissal, the employer must establish on a balance of probabilities that:
(a) the employee was warned about the deficiencies in performance; (b) the employee was given sufficient opportunity to improve; and (c) despite such warnings and opportunities, the employee failed to demonstrate sufficient improvement.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content:
In Rooftech Sdn. Bhd. v. Holiday Inn, Penang, Award No. 166/86, the Industrial Court emphasised that inefficiency or poor performance must be supported by proper procedural safeguards, including written communications evidencing the employee’s shortcomings. Similarly, in Sitt Tatt Bhd v. Ong Chee Meng [2004] 2 ILR 388, it was held that the employer is the proper party to determine the standards and criteria for assessing employee performance, provided such assessment is conducted in good faith, objectively, and without mala fide intent. The court held as follows
“ … In my view, the company was fully entitled to terminate the claimant’s service if, upon evaluation, the claimant was found to have been unable to perform his job functions satisfactorily. How he is to be assessed and the yardstick to gauge his performance is best left to the company’s prerogative and judgment, so long as it is not tainted by mala fide intentions. It could well be based on performance per se or upon a combination of other variables and values such as suitability, aptitude, conduct, behaviour, mannerism and so forth.”
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content:
Based on the above authorities, the Court will determine the following issues:
(a) whether the Claimant’s alleged poor performance is established, assessed in light of:
(i) the Claimant’s prescribed scope of work, responsibilities, and her awareness of her duties; (ii) whether she was adequately warned of the specific performance deficiencies; (iii) whether she was afforded a fair and reasonable opportunity to improve, and if so, whether her performance nevertheless remained unsatisfactory; and
(b) whether the Company acted bona fide and in accordance with fair and reasonable procedures, including in its use and implementation of the Performance Improvement Plan (PIP).
(a) Whether the Claimant’s alleged poor performance is established,
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content:
The first issue for determination is whether the Company has, on the balance of probabilities, established that the Claimant was a poor performer. In considering this issue, the Court takes into account the Claimant’s job scope, her awareness of responsibilities, the alleged deficiencies in her work performance and the warnings issued by the Company, the opportunities afforded for the Claimant to improve, and her actual performance outcomes during the relevant period
(i) the Claimant’s prescribed scope of work, responsibilities, and her awareness of her duties;
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content: The Claimant held the position of Executive, CEO – Corporate Document Control, a role that carried clear, defined responsibilities, including the timely updating of manuals, strict adherence to submission deadlines, maintaining accuracy in the Company’s document control systems, and ensuring the quality of circulated documents. These responsibilities are neither ambiguous nor peripheral since they reflect the core of the operational integrity of the CEO’s office
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content: Under cross-examination, the Claimant conceded that she had applied for the post, attended an interview, and was fully apprised of the job description before accepting the position. This admission is highly material. It establishes that the Claimant was fully aware of the standards expected of her and that those standards formed the objective benchmark against which her performance must be measured. Any assertion of misunderstanding or misalignment of job expectations is therefore untenable.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content: The evidence presented establishes a clear and consistent chronology of escalating concerns communicated to the Claimant throughout 2018. Beginning in May 2018, the Company, through COW-1, issued a series of written communications expressly identifying deficiencies in the Claimant’s performance. Emails dated 4 May, 16, 19 and 21 September 2018, among others, documented repeated instances of frequent and unexplained absences, incomplete or substandard work, delays in critical manual updates, missed deadlines, and instances of unprofessional conduct. These warnings were neither isolated nor vague as they were specific, contemporaneous, and directed at core aspects of the Claimant’s responsibilities.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content:
