In particular, the 4 May 2018 email meticulously detailed out the Claimant’s deficiencies for discussion on 7 May 2018, including:
(a) regular emergency leave and medical leave taken without proper notification to her immediate supervisor; (b) repeated requests for time off; (c) failure to complete assignments such as posters and manual updates within the stipulated timelines; (d) substandard minutes of meetings coupled with late circulation; and (e) additional concerns categorised as “Any Other Business.”
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content:
The Claimant’s response on 7 May 2018 is highly material. In that email, she unambiguously acknowledged the legitimacy of the concerns raised and expressly apologised for her “unacceptable behaviour” and “poor performance,” giving her “word to improve.” The relevant contemporaneous admissions are reproduced as follows:
(a) “Please accept my apology of unacceptable behaviour for the past few months” [COB-1, pages 18 – 21 @ 18]
Leave (b) “I deeply apologise as this is unacceptable reason” [COB-1, pages 18 – 21 @ 19]
Leave (c) “after I took my medication I fell asleep the whole day and I admit that I failed to inform En. Zamry immediately” [COB-1, pages 18 – 21 @ 20]
Manual update (d) “As I spoke to Enck Zamry, I realized that I still need to update some info in order to prepare for upcoming audit Substandard minutes of meeting (e) “I’m admitting that I’m having difficulty to update a Minutes of Meeting…After our early discussion with En Zamry and Kak Hashimah, I’m giving you my words to improve my poor performance.” [COB-1, pages 18 – 21 @ 21]
These admissions were voluntarily made, contemporaneous with the events complained of, and directly in response to the specific deficiencies identified by the Company.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content: The Claimant in this case did not deny having received any of the emails issued to her throughout the relevant period. In fact, no challenge was presented as to their authenticity, receipt, or contents. This omission is significant. Where contemporaneous documentary evidence stands unchallenged, it allows the Court to give it full evidential weight. The Claimant’s failure to rebut, explain, or even dispute the numerous written communications detailing her performance shortcomings further strengthens the Court’s finding that repeated warnings were indeed issued and brought to her attention at the relevant time.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content: The legal requirement, as articulated in Ireka Construction (supra), is that an employee must be made aware of performance shortcomings before dismissal can be justified. Applying the principle and having considered the totality of the evidence, including the unchallenged documentary record and the Claimant’s own admissions, the Court finds that the Company has established, on a balance of probabilities, clear and adequate warnings regarding the Claimant’s poor performance were communicated. The requirement set out under Ireka Construction is therefore satisfied.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: The requirement to provide a reasonable opportunity to improve is not a mere technicality but a substantive pillar of fair employment practice and this opportunity need not be indefinite or perfect, but it must be genuine, sufficient, and commensurate with the circumstances.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: From the evidence, the Company’s intervention in addressing the Claimant’s performance deficiencies starts at an early stage and continues doing so over an extended period. The first intervention occurred 4 May 2018, when COW-1 issued an email requiring the Claimant to attend a Performance Issue Discussion on 7 May 2018 and expressly warning that immediate improvement was required. At this stage, no PIP had yet been triggered, as the Company was still attempting to deal with her shortcomings informally and afforded her an opportunity to correct her conduct. This communication marks the beginning of a sustained period during which the Company repeatedly put the Claimant on notice regarding her shortcomings and pressed for improvement.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: The opportunity afforded was not confined to a single meeting. The evidence shows that discussions continued throughout the following months. On 14 September 2018, COW-1 raised ongoing concerns about the Claimant’s discipline and performance. This was not a new matter, it reflects the continuation of the same issues flagged in May, indicating that the Company had, over several months, maintained active engagement with the Claimant regarding her deficiencies and had consistently provided verbal reminders and guidance.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: On 16 September 2018, COW-1 conveyed a complaint from the Corporate Occupational Safety and Health (COSH) Unit that the Claimant had taken home the CSO store keys while on leave, causing operational disruption. This incident demonstrated that performance concerns had expanded beyond the quality and timeliness of work to include conduct, accountability, and discipline. COW-1 raised the matter promptly, illustrating the Company’s continued commitment to guiding and correcting the Claimant’s behaviour.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: Similarly, on 21 September 2018, COW-1 forwarded to the Claimant a complaint from Puan Hashimah Hashim regarding the Claimant’s rude and inappropriate response to a work-related inquiry. This further illustrates that concerns about her conduct and that the Company promptly raised each issue with her as it arose, providing her with repeated opportunities to take corrective steps.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content:
After several months of growing concerns, the Company formalised its approach by instituting a formal PIP. On 2 October 2018, a meeting took place between the Claimant, COW-1, and the Human Capital Business Partner, Pn. Adlina during which the Claimant was informed that she would undergo a three-month Performance Improvement Plan (PIP). The PIP was comprehensive and targeted deficiencies in three key areas:
(a) work performance; (b) behaviour and discipline; and (c) computer application skills.
The Claimant acknowledged the PIP requirements in her email of 3 October 2018, demonstrating full awareness and acceptance of the expectations placed upon her.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content:
The PIP was structured, time-bound, and supported by scheduled Progress Check Point meetings. The purpose was not punitive but corrective providing the Claimant with a structured opportunity to improve with guidance and supervision.
The Claimant’s performance.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content:
The Claimant’s contention that there is no evidence of poor performance during the PIP is untenable. The contemporaneous record, coupled with her own admissions, demonstrates repeated failures to comply with the PIP framework and instructions issued by COW-1. Upon evaluating the evidence in its entirety, the Court identifies the following material non-compliances:
(a) Failure to submit the performance progress and achievement report
While the PIP itself did not expressly mandate progress updates, the Claimant was specifically instructed by COW-1 who is her immediate superior to submit her performance progress and achievement report prior to his leave. Despite this explicit instruction, the Claimant failed to submit the report by the stipulated date. Her failure to comply undermined the structured process of the PIP and deprived the Company of the ability to properly evaluate her performance. The absence of this report reflects a persistent lack of engagement with the corrective measures provided and constitutes a material failure to adhere to reasonable instructions within the performance management process.
(b) Failure to Communicate with his immediate superior (COW-1)
Despite explicit instructions issued on 17 October 2018 to notify COW-1 by email of any medical leave or related matters, the Claimant failed to comply. Instead, she chose to communicate via WhatsApp, in direct contravention of the instruction. This conduct reflects a conscious disregard for established procedures and a clear lapse in professional responsibility.
An employee genuinely committed to demonstrating improvement under a PIP would be expected to adhere strictly to reporting requirements and maintain proper communication with her supervisor. The Claimant did the opposite. Her decision to ignore the designated channel, despite being expressly directed otherwise, underscores a persistent failure to engage with the supervisory process central to the PIP.
This pattern of non-communication came to an immediate superior at the most critical stage of the PIP. As mentioned before, the Claimant was expressly required to submit her progress report before COW-1 commenced leave. She failed to do so and maintained complete silence until 3 January 2019. Her attempt to justify this lapse by asserting she had been unwell from 21 December 2018 and had sought treatment on 24 December 2018 does not assist her. The medical consultation on 24 December 2018 resulted in no medical certificate being issued and therefore did not relieve her of the obligation to communicate her status to her superior. Furthermore, the Claimant’s hospital admission was only supported from 26 December 2018 onwards. This leaves the period between 19 and 24 December 2018 entirely unaccounted for. During this crucial phase of the PIP, when she was expected to complete her outstanding tasks and submit her progress report, there was no communication, no explanation, and no attempt to fulfil or clarify her obligations.
At no point prior to that date did she offer any explanation or seek clarification, despite her knowledge of the reporting obligations.
The Court finds that this silence cannot be attributed to illness, as the Claimant was neither certified unfit for work nor hospitalised during the bulk of this period. Her failure to communicate, despite knowing the requirement to notify COW-1 by email, therefore reflects not incapacity but a continued pattern of disengagement. It undermines her assertion that she was compliant with or committed to the PIP process and instead supports the Company’s position that she was unwilling to participate meaningfully in the improvement measures offered to her.
(c) Bypassing the Immediate Supervisor
The Claimant’s decision to bypass COW-1 and communicate directly with higher management regarding critical deliverables contravened the reporting protocol outlined in the PIP. By circumventing her immediate supervisor, the Claimant deprived COW-1 of the opportunity to monitor, guide, and support her progress. Such behaviour undermines the fundamental purpose of a PIP, which depends on consistent engagement between the employee and the designated superior to facilitate improvement.
The Claimant's email of 3 January 2019 served as a de facto admission of her failures. The Claimant’s email of 3 January 2019 to COW-1 constitutes a de facto admission of these failures, confirming that she did not adhere to the prescribed communication and reporting obligations.
(d) Failure to Respond to Performance-Related Emails During the PIP Period
The Claimant's pattern of disengagement is evidenced by her failure to respond to her work performance during the PIP itself. The Company adduced an email from 13 October 2018, in which COW-1 explicitly highlighted several deficiencies requiring immediate justification, including:
(i) findings from the IOSA Dry Run concerning the Master Manual List;
(ii) the failure to maintain the CSO Info TV; and
(iii) non-conformances in the SMS training tracking sheet.
Despite these clear instructions, based on the document, the Claimant did not respond. A follow-up reminder was sent on 22 October 2018, yet she still failed to reply. This complete lack of response shows a serious disregard for the standards of diligence, accountability, and engagement expected in her role. It also undermines the very purpose of the PIP, which relies on active participation and communication between the employee and supervisor to address performance gaps.
This was not a minor lapse but a significant breach of her responsibilities. Any employee genuinely committed to improving under a PIP would, at a minimum, acknowledge and respond to direct queries from their supervisor. The Claimant’s failure to do so demonstrates that she did not take the process seriously. The Court finds that this behaviour forms part of a clear pattern of non-engagement, which justified the Company’s conclusion that the PIP had failed (e) Failure to complete Corporate Safety Management Manual (CSMM), Corporate Document Manual (CDM) and Document Control Policy Manual (DCPM)
The evidence clearly establishes that the Claimant failed to comply with the timelines set by COW-1 for completing the CSMM, CDM and DCPM manuals. She was expressly instructed in early September to finalise the CSMM by 14 September 2019, and the CDM and DCPM by 18 September 2019. The Claimant did not meet any of these deadlines.
As of 30 September 2019, COW-1 was still seeking an update on the status of these documents and informed her that he intended to review the manuals by 4 October 2019. Although the Claimant was on medical leave on 4 and 5 October 2019, there is no contemporaneous documentation showing that the manuals were completed or submitted for COW-1’s review within the stipulated period. Her subsequent email dated 3 January 2019, stating that she had updated “part” of the CSMM together with amendments to the CDM and DCPM on 21 December, further confirms that the work was neither completed within the assigned timeline nor delivered in full.
On the totality of the evidence, the Court finds that the Claimant failed to adhere to clear and reasonable deadlines set by her supervisor, and her delayed and partial submissions demonstrate non-compliance with the work requirements communicated to her.

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: Having considered the evidence, The Court finds that the Company afforded the Claimant a more than reasonable opportunity to improve, beginning with informal warnings in May 2018 and culminating in a formal, three-month PIP. This graduated process was genuine, sufficient, and commensurate with the circumstances.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content:
Despite this extensive opportunity, the Claimant’s performance remained unsatisfactory. Her persistent failures to comply with instructions, adhere to communication protocols, and engage meaningfully with the structured support of the PIP demonstrate a lack of commitment to the improvement process. Therefore, the Company has successfully established both that a fair opportunity was given and that the Claimant’s performance failed to meet the required standards thereafter.
(b) Whether the Company acted bona fide and in accordance with fair and reasonable procedures, including in its use and implementation of the Performance Improvement Plan (PIP).

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: The Court now turns to determine whether the employer demonstrates that it acted in bona fide and adhered to fair and reasonable procedures throughout the performance management process. This requirement ensures that employees are given a genuine opportunity to meet expected standards while allowing the employer to maintain operational efficiency and discipline.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: In this case, the Court’s attention is directed to how the Company implemented and managed the PIP, which was the culmination of its ongoing efforts to address the Claimant’s repeated performance issues. The key questions are whether the Company acted in good faith, whether the procedures it followed were fair and reasonable, and whether the entire process was conducted without any hint of malice, discrimination, or intimidation. The Court must determine whether the PIP was genuinely intended to help the Claimant improve, rather than to penalize or unfairly target her.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: Upon careful evaluation of the evidence, the Court is satisfied that the introduction and execution of the PIP clearly demonstrate the Company’s bona fide intention to support the Claimant’s improvement. In Sharifah Nurzehan Syed Hazani v. Petrofac (Malaysia-PM304) Ltd [2019] CLJU 1631, the Court affirmed that the use of a structured PIP with measurable indicators reflects a genuine effort by an employer to give the employee every reasonable opportunity to succeed. Here, the Company implemented a three-month PIP with clearly defined objectives, measurable targets, and scheduled review sessions. The structure was corrective, not punitive, and closely aligned with the principles articulated in Sharifah Nurzehan Syed Hazani (supra).
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: A further element of procedural fairness is the employee’s understanding of management’s dissatisfaction and the consequences of continued underperformance. The evidence before the Court is undisputed. The Claimant was repeatedly informed of the deficiencies in her work and the need for improvement. At all material times, she knew or ought reasonably to have known that her continued poor performance placed her employment at risk. This is not a case where an employee was uninformed or taken by surprise.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: The principle established in KC Mathews v. Kumpulan Guthrie Sdn Bhd [1981] CLJ Rep 62 is directly applicable to the present circumstances. The Federal Court held that no formal inquiry was necessary where the employee "knew at all times how dissatisfied his employer was with him and he must have known... that he was running the risk of dismissal. All he had to do was to produce the work required of him. He never did."
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: Similarly, in the present case, the Claimant’s acceptance of the PIP terms was an acknowledgment that she needed to demonstrate meaningful improvement. Yet, the evidence shows that she repeatedly failed to comply with key requirements, including submission of progress reports, adherence to communication protocols, and engagement with supervisory guidance. The Court finds that her inaction reflects a deliberate failure to engage with the remedial process offered.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: The Court has also examined the Claimant’s allegations that she was subjected to discrimination and intimidation by COW-1. These allegations were premised on her PIP placement, her medical leave pattern, and a prior complaint she lodged against COW-1 concerning the events of 19 September 2018. Having scrutinised the evidence, the Court finds that these assertions are unsupported and, on the balance of probabilities, appear to reflect the Claimant’s subjective reaction to legitimate supervisory oversight rather than any improper conduct.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: The chronology of events is instructive. The Claimant lodged her complaint against COW-1 immediately after the performance meeting on 19 September 2018 [COB-1, pp. 24–25; 57–58], during which concerns regarding her performance were discussed and she was informed of her impending placement under the PIP. The temporal proximity strongly suggests that the complaint was not prompted by misconduct on the part of COW-1 but was, on balance of probabilities, a reaction to being confronted with her own performance shortcomings.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: The Company, for its part, followed established procedures by referring the matter to the Business Integrity Department for investigation. The investigation, conducted independently, concluded that the complaint lacked merit and that the issues raised stemmed from the Claimant’s own performance deficiencies rather than any misconduct by COW-1. The Company’s adherence to a formal grievance process reinforces the Court’s finding that the Claimant was not subjected to a prejudicial or retaliatory environment.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: The Claimant's attempt to link her medical leave with alleged intimidation is similarly unpersuasive. The management of her leave was an administrative matter separate from performance oversight. There is no evidence to suggest that COW-1 acted in a retaliatory manner due to her absences. The record demonstrates that the Company’s concerns consistently focused on the quality, timeliness, and outcomes of her work during periods of attendance. Indeed, COW-1’s contemporaneous communications reflect a constructive approach, advising that the Claimant seek medical consultation or specialist care if required, further emphasizing that his concern was her wellbeing and performance rather than intimidation.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: In view of the evidence, the Court finds that the Company’s actions were consistently procedural, objective, and aligned with a genuine intention to support the Claimant’s improvement. Both the PIP and the handling of her complaint were conducted in accordance with established procedures and demonstrate good faith managerial practice. The allegation of intimidation is therefore rejected.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: This finding is consistent with the Industrial Court’s reasoning in Thurka Thevi Mohan v. Ace Greencemt Venture (M) Sdn Bhd [2025] 2 ILR 23 where the court affirms that an employer is entitled to manage an employee’s performance without this being construed as intimidation, provided the process is bona fide and procedural. In Thurka Thevi Mohan the court held that: “ It is trite law that how an employee is assessed and the yardstick to be used to gauge his/her performance is best left to the company’s prerogative and judgment so long as it is not tainted by mala fide intentions…"
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
section_title: (iii) Opportunity to Improve and whether her performance remains unsatisfactory
content: For the reasons comprehensively outlined above, the Court finds that the Company's conduct throughout the performance management process, culminating in the dismissal, constituted a genuine and bona fide exercise of its managerial prerogative. The procedures adopted were fair, reasonable, and proportionate in the circumstances. The Company acted within its rights in seeking to address the Claimant’s persistent underperformance, and the Court is satisfied that the dismissal was neither arbitrary nor motivated by malice, intimidation, or discrimination.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content:
Having carefully considered all the evidence, submissions of the parties, and the applicable legal principles, the Court makes the following findings:
(a) the Company has successfully established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Claimant’s poor performance was genuine, persistent, and incompatible with the standards reasonably expected of her role. The evidence demonstrates that the Claimant was well aware of her prescribed duties, scope of work, and reporting obligations. The record further demonstrates that she was repeatedly cautioned, both informally and formally, regarding specific deficiencies in her output, timeliness, organisation, and adherence to instructions. Not only was she expressly informed of these shortcomings, but she was also afforded a fair, structured, and reasonable opportunity to improve. The Company provided clear guidance and performance expectations and subsequently placed her under a structured PIP designed to address identified deficiencies. Despite these opportunities, the Claimant’s performance remained unsatisfactory. She failed to meet key deliverables, failed to adhere to reporting requirements, and showed no sustained improvement. Her explanations were inconsistent and did not displace the clear documentary evidence of ongoing deficiencies. On this basis, the Court finds that the substantive element of poor performance has been fully proven; and
(b) the Company acted throughout in good faith and in full accordance with fair and reasonable procedures. The performance management process adopted was neither rushed nor arbitrary. The evidence shows that the Company undertook progressive steps before implementing a structured PIP. The PIP itself was clear, measurable, time-bound, and designed to assist the Claimant in meeting expected standards. The Claimant was informed of the areas requiring improvement, the consequences of failing to improve, and the support mechanisms available to her. Allegations of discrimination, intimidation, or mala fide conduct were not substantiated by any credible evidence. On the contrary, the documentary record shows a consistent, objective, and transparent approach by the Company, including the independent investigation of the Claimant’s complaint, which was found to be unrelated to any improper conduct by her supervisor.
source_file: Award_1817-2025_Anis Nadhirah Binti Muhd Nazak  Mohd Nas.pdf

case_name: Anis Nadhirah binti Muhd Nazak @ Mohd Nasir v Malaysia Airlines Berhad
chairman: Noramilia binti Mohd Saad
content: For all these reasons, the Court concludes that both the substantive and procedural requirements for a dismissal based on poor performance have been fully satisfied. The Company’s decision was a bona fide exercise of managerial prerogative following months of documented concerns, reasonable opportunities for improvement, and the Claimant’s continued failure to meet essential performance expectations. The dismissal is therefore upheld as having been carried out with just cause or excuse. The Claimant’s claim is hereby dismissed.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
content: As was opined by His Lordship Raja Azlan (CJ Malaya) (as HRH then was) in the Federal Court decision of Goon Kwee Phoy v. J & P Coats (M) Bhd [1981] 1 LNS 30, it is trite that where representations are made and are referred to the Industrial Court for enquiry, it is the duty of that Court to determine whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse. If the employer chooses to give a reason for the action taken by him the duty of the Industrial Court will be to enquire whether that excuse or reason has or has not been made out. If it finds as a fact that it has not been proved, then the inevitable conclusion must be that the termination or dismissal was without just cause or excuse. The proper enquiry of the Court is the reason advanced by it and that Court or the High Court cannot go into another reason not relied on by the employer or find one for it.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
content: It has been settled that in cases where the dismissal was caused by the employer, it is the employer that must discharge the burden of proof that the dismissal is with just cause and excuse. This long settled principle was demonstrated in the case of Ireka Construction Berhad v. Chantiravathan Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 11 wherein the Learned Chairman opined that:- It is a basic principle of industrial jurisprudence that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer to prove that he has just cause and excuse for taking the decision to impose the disciplinary measure of dismissal upon the employee. The just cause must be, either a misconduct, negligence or poor performance based on the facts of the case.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
content:
On the standard of proof applicable, the Court of Appeal in the case of Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara v. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor [2002] 3 CLJ 314 had laid down the principle that the standard of proof that is required to prove a case at the Industrial Court is on the balance of probabilities wherein His Lordship Justice Abdul Hamid Mohamad, JCA opined:-
Thus, we can see that the preponderant view is that the Industrial Court, when hearing a claim of unjust dismissal, even where the ground is one of dishonest act, including "theft", is not required to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the employee has "committed the offence", as in a criminal prosecution. On the other hand, we see that the Courts and learned authors have used such terms as "solid and sensible grounds", "sufficient to measure up to a preponderance of the evidence," "whether a case... has been made out", "on the balance of probabilities" and "evidence of probative value". In our view the passage quoted from Administrative Law by H.W.R. Wade & C.F. Forsyth offers the clearest statement on the standard of proof required, that is the civil standard based on the balance of probabilities, which is flexible, so that the degree of probability required is proportionate to the nature of gravity of the issue. But, again, if we may add, these are not "passwords" that the failure to use them or if some other words are used, the decision is automatically rendered bad in law.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: LAW ON THE MISCONDUCT OF HARRASSMENT/SEXUAL HARRASSMENT
content: This Court had consistently taken the view that the right to livelihood is as fundamental as the right to life itself (see Kesatuan Pekerja Pekerja Perkilangan Perusahaan Makanan v Nestle Manufacturing (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd. [2023] 1 ILR 63). As such, it is imperative that any employee in search of this right to livelihood should be allowed to do so in a safe and secure working environment free of any aggression or harassment from any of the other employees or superiors. To this extent this Court views any acts of any employee or superior that causes a fellow employee to be put in an environment that causes fear or distress due to harassment or aggression as misconducts that warrants appropriate punishment depending on the circumstances of the case and the gravity of the alleged misconduct. When the harassment is added with acts which are sexual in nature giving rise to sexual harassment at work place then such misconduct cannot be tolerated at all under any circumstances. The punishment that will ensue may invariably be an outright dismissal depending on the seriousness of the act itself particularly if it is an objectionable conduct of the aggressor (see Kuldeep Singh Udham Singh v Tobacco Importers and Manufacturer Sdn Bhd [2022] 4 ILR 514).

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: It is the Company's stated case that the Claimant being a Technical Assistant had committed serious misconducts in that the Claimant had sexually harassed four (4) women employees, namely COW-1, COW-3, COW-5 and COW-6. Upon complaints being lodged and after commencing investigation, the Company issued four (4) separate Show Cause Letters to the Claimant with each letter corresponding to each allegation (pages 20 to 34 of COB-1) and the Claimant submitted his replies to the said Show Cause Letters. Upon receiving the Claimant’s responses, the Company issued a notice of DI informing him of the charges, the scheduled inquiry date and his rights. The DI was conducted on 16.12.2021 and the Claimant was represented by a Union Official.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content:
The Company preferred the following four (4) charges of misconduct against the Claimant namely:- (i) "Anda telah melakukan gangguan seksual terhadap seorang pekerja syarikat ini bernama Nur Irdina binti Bahari pada lebih kurang pukul 12:00 tengah hari, 22.11.2021 di Bilik Inspection, bahagian IMP. Anda telah dilaporkan masuk ke dalam bilik tersebut dan bercakap dengan pekerja bernama Hariz, Shahrul dan Anim. Ketika Irdina sedang melakukan kerja, anda bergurau dengan mereka dan telah melibatkan beliau dalam gurauan tersebut tetapi gurauan tersebut melampau, menjijikkan, lucah dan bermaksud kotor bagi beliau sebagai seorang perempuan. Anda telah mengeluarkan ayat iaitu “ko pernah buat ke dengan dia kalau ko cakap dia lemah” dan cuba ko tengok dia ni dari jauh dah nampak hebat diranjang."
(ii) “Anda telah melakukan gangguan seksual terhadap seorang pekerja syarikat ini bernama Sofhia Khaleeda binti Nazeri (206924) pekerja daripada Jabatan Engineering/QA. Kejadian telah berlaku pada lebih kurang pukul 10:45 pagi, bertarikh 23.11.2021 di Bilik Inspection, bahagian IMP. Anda telah dilaporkan masuk ke dalam bilik tersebut dan mengeluarkan kata-kata lucah yang melibatkan diri beliau dengan mengaitkan seorang pekerja bernama Shahrul yang ketika itu berada di bilik tersebut. Perkataan yang disebut adalah "eh kau lahni dengan Shahrul, sedap apa.” Pengadu juga melaporkan anda pernah mengeluarkan kata-kata kepada beliau seperti “malam jumaat ni, berapa round kau” dan "badan abang sakit-sakit la, tolong urutkan kejap”
(iii) “Anda telah melakukan gangguan seksual terhadap seorang pekerja syarikat ini bernama Lailatul Fatihah binti Hushaini (176776) pekerja daripada Jabatan Engineering/IQC. Kejadian telah berlaku pada bulan Oktober 2021 di Bilik Inspection, bahagian IMP. Anda telah dilaporkan sering mengajak pengadu pergi keluar makan dan tengok wayang bersama. Anda juga ada menyebut "kau kerja ke Sabtu ni, nanti balik abang ambik kau dekat depan kilang ea kita pergi makan, tengok wayang nak bermanja-manja dengan kau.” Selain itu anda juga pernah berkata "malam ni tolong urut abang ya, badan abang sakit-sakit lah”, tolong suapkan abang gula-gula tangan abang sakit lah”, kau takde pakwe ke? Tu Masrizal ada, pergilah dengan dia best apa nanti peluk-peluk dia.”
(iv) "Anda telah melakukan gangguan seksual terhadap seorang pekerja syarikat ini bernama Amelia binti Mohd Zailani (156612) pekerja daripada Jabatan Engineering/IQC. Kejadian telah berlaku pada bulan November 2021 di Bilik Inspection, bahagian IMP. Anda telah dilaporkan berkata "kau pernah tidur dengan pakwe kau kan" Selain itu anda juga pernah berkata "tolong urut abang jap”, “jom teman abang tengok wayang atau pergi makan ke.”

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content:
Code of Practice on the Prevention and Eradication of Sexual Harassment in the Workplace (1999) defines sexual harassment as:-
Any unwanted conduct of a sexual nature having the effect of verbal, non-verbal, visual, psychological, or physical harassment that might, on reasonable grounds, be perceived by the recipient as an offence, humiliation, or threat to their well-being.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content:
Section 2 of the Employment Act 1955 defines sexual harassment as:-
Sexual harassment means any unwanted conduct of a sexual nature, whether verbal, nonverbal, visual, gestural or physical, directed at a person which is offensive or humiliating or is a threat to his well-being, arising out of and in the course of his employment.”

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: The Claimant was charged with committing an act of sexual harassment against COW-1 on 22.11.2021, at approximately 12:00pm, in the Inspection Room. It was alleged that while COW-1 was performing her duties, the Claimant made lewd, offensive, and inappropriate remarks of a sexual nature, including, “Ko pernah buat ke dengan dia kalau ko cakap dia lemah" and "Cuba ko tengok dia ni, dari jauh dah nampak hebat di ranjang.”

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: It was COW-1's testimony that the incident occurred in the presence of five (5) individuals in the Inspection Room namely, herself, COW-2, CLW-2, CLW-3 and the Claimant. Of the five (5), COW-1 was the only female, while the remaining four (4) were male. COW-1, a Technical Assistant, was in the room assisting COW-2. During the interaction, the Claimant attempted to "match make" COW-1 with COW-2. When COW-1 responded by saying “tak nak" and "lemah", the Claimant made the inappropriate remarks – “ko pernah buat ke dengan dia kalau ko cakap dia lemah” and "cuba ko tengok dia ni dari jauh dah nampak hebat di ranjang”. These statements shocked and embarrassed COW-1, causing her to leave the room immediately and report the incident to COW-4, an Engineer in the IMP Department. COW-4 then advised her to lodge a formal complaint, which she did.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: COW-1 also testified that the Claimant had, on previous occasions, used sexually inappropriate language in her presence. However, she chose to ignore such remarks at the time out of respect for the Claimant, who was her senior and had long-standing service with the Company [Q&A No. 10 of COWS-1].

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content:
It is apparent to this Court that the Claimant's response to this charge varied at different stages, in his replies to Show Cause Letter, during DI, in his pleading and during cross-examination:-
(a) As per this reply dated 26.11.2021 to the show cause letter, he denied making any of the remarks (page 22 of COB-1];
(b) He later claimed the incident was a misunderstanding, suggesting that the word "lemah" had been misinterpreted (paragraph 24 of Statement of Case); and
(c) During cross-examination, he conceded to making one of the remarks "ko pernah buat ke dengan dia kalau ko cakap dia lemah”.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: This Court finds that such contradictions seriously undermine his credibility and strongly supports the conclusion that he did, in fact, make the sexually inappropriate remarks as charged.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: Furthermore, the evidence of COW-2 affirms that the Claimant was trying to pair him and COW-1 and that the Claimant indeed made the remark/statement “ko pernah buat ke dengan dia kalau ko cakap dia lemah”. CLW-2 affirms that the Claimant was trying to pair COW-1 and COW-2. CLW-3 affirms that the Claimant used words that is "lucah dan kotor" and that he made the remark/statement "ko pernah buat ke dengan dia kalau ko cakap dia lemah” (grievance report at page 10 of COB-1).

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: From the evidence of all the individuals present, including the Claimant's own admission, it is clear that at least the statement "ko pernah buat ke dengan dia kalau ko cakap dia lemah" was made by the Claimant. The remark implicitly questions whether COW-1 had engaged in sexual activity with COW-2 to be able to comment on him being "lemah" (weak) and in this context to be understood and interpreted by the Claimant as weakness in male sexual performance or stamina ("batin"). This remark was clearly intended and perceived as sexual in nature. This is further supported by the reaction of the witnesses, all of whom understood the remarks to reference sexual performance or bodily abilities, thus constituting unwanted and inappropriate conduct of a sexual nature.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: The Company also alleged that the Claimant proceeded to snap his fingers in front of his own private area, allegedly directed at COW-2. While the precise angle or positioning of the gesture may differ according to the witnesses' accounts, the intent behind it was clear and not in dispute. All three (3) witnesses, COW-2, CLW-2 and CLW-3 consistently testified that the gesture was made in a manner implying sexual inadequacy, specifically referring to male performance or "lemah tenaga batin." CLW-2 observed the gesture and interpreted it as referring to COW-2's private parts, while CLW-3 confirmed hearing the Claimant say, "ko lemah ke, tak naik ke”. It is apparent to this Court that these actions and remarks, taken together, clearly reinforces the sexually inappropriate and offensive nature of the Claimant's conduct during the incident.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: Based on the definitions of sexual harassment under the Code of Practice on the Prevention and Eradication of Sexual Harassment [supra] and Section 2 of the Employment Act 1955 [supra] this Court finds that the Claimant’s conduct and remarks, whether framed as a joke or not, clearly falls within the definition of sexual harassment.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content:
In the case of Abdul Halim Mohd Salleh v. Cagamas Berhad [2021] 4 ILR 284 the Industrial Court found, among others, that inappropriate comments, including a joke made by a superior, constituted sexual harassment and further held as follows:-
[18] In relation to charge 71 which had pertained to the claimant’s inappropriate intimate or personal enquiries against COW13, the claimant had stated that he had uttered the words in jest and that it had been meant as a joke. In cases of sexual harassment, the motive of the perpetrator is irrelevant. What is important is the effect that the conduct of the perpetrator has on the victim. His inappropriate enquiries, when looked at in totality, had given the impression that COW13 had been having an intimate or scandalous relationship with the CEO, which had humiliated and disgusted COW13, especially since it had been uttered in the presence of her other colleagues. The utterance of the enquiries, which had been personal and sexual in nature, had also been witnessed by COW6 and COW11. His conduct had been unbecoming of someone in his position and he had breached the Code of Ethics and the Guidelines. He had, by his actions, committed serious misconduct and been guilty of this charge.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content:
In the case of Vasuthevan Athaly v. Freescale Semiconductor (M) Sdn Bhd [2013] 1 ILR 73 (Award No : 1401 of 2012) the Industrial Court made an observation on what constituted sexual harassment:-
Ashgar Ali in his book "Dismissal from Employment and the Remedies", Lexis Nexis, 2007, describes "sexual harassment" as follows: "Sexual harassment refers to sexual conduct which is imposed on, and is unsolicited or unreciprocated by the recipient, for example, repeated unwelcome sexual comments, looks or physical contact, among others.” The key element in cases of sexual harassment is the feature that the acts of the alleged "perpetrator" are unsolicited or unreciprocated by the recipient. In other words, they are unwelcome.
The Code of Practice on the Prevention and Eradication Sexual Harassment at the Workplace (issued by the Ministry of Human Resources in 1999, and which acts as a guide), refers to sexual harassment as any "unwanted conduct of a sexual nature…" Ashgar Ali, taking the clue from the said code of practice enumerates the types of sexual harassment; and elaborates as follows:-
1. Verbal harassment : Making sexually suggestive comments such as jokes, jesting, kidding, sounds and questioning, for example, subjecting a female worker to sexually suggestive comments, the learned author goes on to observe:- ……
The Learned Author goes on to observe:
It has also to be borne in mind that many cases of sexual harassment may go unreported with the victim suffering in silence. In view of the social stigma and fears that the complainant may not be believed or taken seriously, and also the fear of reprisal, ie repercussions. Sometimes there is also a delay in reporting, as in cases where the complainant only plucks up the courage to come forward and report after seeing another colleague filing such complaint.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: In the case of Ahmad Zailani Junoh v. Alam Flora Sdn Bhd [2008] 2 LNS 0104 the Claimant was found guilty of sexual harassment for making inappropriate remarks to a subordinate, including a comment with sexual innuendo - "kalau mahu malam ini dengan suami awak, malam ini juga suami awak bagi ke?". The Industrial Court determined that the remarks caused emotional distress to the victim and constituted sexual harassment as defined by the Code of Practice on the Prevention and Eradication of Sexual Harassment in the workplace. The dismissal of the Claimant was upheld as justified due to the severity of the misconduct.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content:
Based on the consistent and corroborated testimonies of the witnesses present, including the Claimant's own admissions, this Court finds that Charge (i) has been established on a balance of probabilities. The Claimant's conduct, which included sexually suggestive remarks, offensive gestures, and inappropriate insinuations, was clearly unwelcome, demeaning, and offensive to COW-1. The remarks were made openly in a shared workspace, in the presence of other male colleagues, and had the immediate effect of causing embarrassment and discomfort to the complainant.
Charge (ii)

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: Charge (ii) is about the Claimant having committed an act of sexual harassment against COW-3 on 23.11.2021, at approximately 10:45am in the Inspection Room of the IMP Department. During the incident, the Claimant made a lewd remark involving COW-3, CLW-3 and the Claimant. The remark uttered by the Claimant was, "eh kau lahni dengan Shahrul, sedap apa” . The Claimant was also charged with having made prior inappropriate remarks of a sexual nature to COW-3 on other occasions, "malam jumaat ni, berapa round kau” and “badan abang sakit-sakit la, tolong urutkan kejap".

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: According to the testimony of COW-3, while she was performing her duty with CLW-3 in the Inspection Room, the Claimant entered the Inspection Room and attempted to "match make" her with CLW-3 with the remark: "eh kau lahni dengan Shahrul, sedap apa". The remark shocked and embarrassed COW-1, causing her to immediately leave the room and report the incident to COW-4. COW-4 then advised her to lodge a formal complaint, which she did (page 2 of COB-1).

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: This Court finds that the evidence of CLW-3 both during cross-examination and in his grievance report, clearly supports the account provided by COW-3. He affirmed that the Claimant was attempting to "match make" him with COW-3 during the incident, thereby reinforcing the sexually suggestive context of the remark and lending credibility to COW-3's version of events.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: While CLW-3 had stated that he did not hear the specific phrase "sedap apa”, he candidly admitted that he was not paying full attention at the material time. However, he unequivocally confirmed that he observed COW-3 leaving the Inspection Room immediately after the Claimant made the remark, which he believed was an attempt by COW-3 to distance herself from the Claimant. It is apparent to this Court that this reaction is consistent with someone who had just been subjected to an inappropriate and embarrassing comment and it further corroborates COW-3's account of the incident.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: It was established that COW-4 and COW-8 confirmed that COW-4 had informed COW-8 who is the Claimant's Superior about the complaint made by COW-3 as well as the earlier complaint by COW-1. Following this, COW-8 testified that he instructed En. Kamal from the same department to notify the Claimant of the complaints. Subsequently, the Claimant approached COW-8 and stated that he had already explained the situation to COW-4 claiming that the incidents were merely jokes and had been misunderstood. This corroboration supports the conclusion that the Claimant did, in fact, acknowledge having made the remarks and sought to characterize them as jokes rather than denying them outright.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: With regard to the issue of COW-3’s inability to dissect or translate every element of the Claimant’s statement word-for-word, this Court finds that does not negate its offensive and sexual nature. The remark was delivered in Malay colloquial slang with an unmistakable sexual undertone. It is apparent the phrase”sedap apa", when used in this context implies sexual pleasure, and when paired with the reference to her being "with Shahrul" (“kau lah ni dengan Shahrul”), it suggests a physical relationship. Both COW-3 and CLW-3 clearly understood the remark to be sexual in nature, as evidenced by their immediate emotional and physical responses, COW-3 leaving the room in embarrassment, and CLW-3 acknowledging that COW-3 may be avoiding the Claimant by immediately leaving the Inspection Room.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: It is also the finding of this Court that the lack of full understanding of every exact word does not negate a sexual harassment claim if the overall conduct creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive environment and causes actual emotional or psychological harm to the victim. It is not necessary for a victim to pinpoint every precise remark; rather, the focus is on whether the conduct was sufficiently oppressive and persistent to cause alarm and distress to the victim - Mohd Ridzwan bin Abdul Razak v. Asmah bt Hj Mohd Nor [2013] 9 CLJ 243.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content:
Hence, Charge (ii) has been proven on a balance of probabilities. The Claimant's conduct towards COW-3 was not only offensive and demeaning but also consistent with a pattern of inappropriate behaviour previously directed at other female employees.
Charge (iii)

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: With regard to this charge, the Claimant was charged for sexually harassing COW-5 from the Engineering/IQC Department. The incident allegedly took place in October 2021 in the Inspection Room, IMP section, whereby the remarks made to COW-5 were, "Kau kerja ke Sabtu ni, nanti balik abang ambik kau dekat depan kilang ea kita pergi makan, tengok wayang nak bermanja-manja dengan kau”, Malam ni tolong urut abang ya, badan abang sakit-sakit lah”, Tolong suapkan abang gula-gula tangan abang sakit lah" and “Kau takde pakwe ke? Tu Masrizal ada, pergilah dengan dia best apa nanti peluk-peluk dia.”

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: This Court finds that each statement made by the Claimant contains inappropriate innuendos, suggestive invitations, and flirtatious overtones that were uninvited and directed toward a junior colleague in the workplace. The use of terms such as "tolong suapkan abang gula-gula”, “bermanja-manja dengan kau”, “tolong urut abang", Kau takde pakwe ke" and "peluk-peluk dia” are all suggestive of intimacy, physical affection, which are entirely inappropriate and without doubt sexual in nature.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: In Rosni Turnin v. SWM Environment Sdn Bhd [2019] 2 LNS 2948, the Industrial Court upheld the dismissal of a supervisor for sexually harassing several female colleagues. Notably, the court acknowledged that some of the complainants could not furnish precise details or lodge contemporaneous reports due to fear or other constraints. Nevertheless, the court emphasized that the absence of strict corroboration did not invalidate their complaints. When viewed holistically and in light of the employer's duty to provide a safe working environment, the complainants' testimonies were deemed sufficiently reliable to justify dismissal.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: As submitted by the Company’s Counsel, this Court had considered the pattern of conduct exhibited by the Claimant in relation to COW-1, COW-3 and COW-6. In all three (3) instances, the alleged misconduct occurred in the same location, namely the Inspection Room of the IMP Department and involved the Claimant making sexually charged or suggestive remarks under the pretext of "joking" or "banter". The Inspection Room has, based on the evidence, become a recurring setting in which the Claimant directed inappropriate comments toward female employees. The similarity in context, language, tone and manner strongly indicates a consistent behavioural pattern rather than isolated misunderstandings or coincidental interpretation.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: This Court can consider the surrounding circumstances and cumulative effect of the conduct in assessing the reliability of a sexual harassment complaint. Where a pattern emerges, especially involving similar victims, settings, and behaviours, it strengthens the conclusion that the conduct did in fact occur as alleged - Rosni Turnin v. SWM Environment Sdn Bhd [supra].

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: Furthermore, this Court also finds that there is no evidence whatsoever to suggest that any of the complainants, namely COW-1, COW-3, COW-5 or COW-6 were motivated by ill intent or personal vendetta against the Claimant. No evidence was led to demonstrate that these individuals had any prior conflicts, animosity, or reasons to conspire against the Claimant. In the absence of proof of mala fide intent, the Court is entitled to treat their complaints as bona fide expressions of grievance.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content:
Hence, this Court finds that Charge (iii) has been proven on a balance of probabilities by the Company.
Charge (iv)

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: With regard to this charge, the Claimant was charged for sexually harassing COW-6, from the Engineering/IQC Department. The incident took place in November 2021 in the Inspection Room, IMP section, whereby the remarks made to COW-6 was “Kau pernah tidur dengan pakwe kau kan, “Tolong urut abang jap” and “Jom teman abang tengok wayang atau pergi makan ke”. In addition, COW-6 also gave evidence that the Claimant touched her arm when they were alone in the Inspection Room.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: It is apparent to this Court that this charge is similar to Charge (iii) and as such the legal and factual findings made by this Court with regard to Charge (iii) are applicable to this charge.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: EVALUATION AND FINDINGS OF THIS COURT
content: Hence, Charge (iv) has been proven on the balance of probabilities by the Company.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: In relation to the grievance report, it was suggested during cross-examination that the grievance reports relied upon by the Company were inappropriate as the witnesses who made the report were not aggrieved persons and that the contents were not recorded verbatim but written by COW-7, the Human Resource personnel responsible for documenting the investigation. All individuals referenced as makers of the grievance reports, including the Claimant's own witnesses signed their own report and affirmed the accuracy and truth of the contents of their respective reports during the proceeding in Court. It is the finding of this Court that the said suggestion is a mere technicality and therefore without merit.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: With regard to the issue of procedural fairness, the Claimant alleges that the Company conducted a procedurally unfair disciplinary process. However, the evidence demonstrates that the Company fully complied with established industrial relations procedures and the principles of natural justice. Upon receiving complaints of sexual harassment, the Company promptly initiated a formal investigation, interviewing the complainants and relevant witnesses. The Claimant was issued detailed Show Cause Letters, each outlining the factual basis of the charges, and he was given sufficient opportunity to provide written responses. He also admitted in cross-examination that he understood the charges. DI was then convened in accordance with proper procedures. The Claimant was served with a notice specifying the charges, date, time, and venue, and informing him of his rights, including representation, calling witnesses, and cross-examining the Company’s witnesses. These rights were fully observed. The Claimant was represented by a Union Official and both were given full opportunity to cross-examine witnesses and present a defence. After the DI was concluded, the notes of proceedings were provided to the Claimant and his representative, who signed them. The DI’s findings and the Company’s decision to dismiss were subsequently communicated to him, together with a right of appeal. Notably, during cross-examination the Claimant admitted that the Company had complied with all procedural steps including issuance of Show Cause Letters, the right to representation, the opportunity to challenge witnesses and the right to appeal.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: Based on the facts, it is finding of this Court that there is no procedural unfairness as alleged by the Claimant. In fact, the Claimant’s own admission during cross-examination that the procedures were followed further undermines his allegation.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: The Claimant also alleges that he was targeted and falsely accused of sexual harassment because of his role as a Union EXCO Member, claiming that the Company particularly Encik Nor Azmin viewed him as a threat due to tensions during collective bargaining. He suggests that the charges were fabricated to remove him. However, this Court finds that this allegation is entirely unsupported by evidence. The disciplinary proceedings were initiated only after formal complaints of sexual harassment were lodged by multiple employees, which the Company was legally obliged to investigate. The Claimant himself admitted during cross-examination that the Company took action only after receiving these complaints.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: The Claimant also attempted to suggest that the complainants’ letters were orchestrated by the Company. This Court finds that this was refuted by the testimonies of COW-1, COW-3, COW-5, and COW-6, each of whom explained clearly how and why they prepared their complaints. None of the complainants demonstrated any ill motive, their evidence was consistent, credible and corroborated – [see Magendran Gunasekharan v. Mattel (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd [2024] 1 ILR 188]. Even suggestions of collusion, such as questions to COW-5 regarding a WhatsApp exchange with the Claimant’s sister, were firmly denied. Importantly, the Claimant conceded that without these employee complaints, the Company would not have commenced disciplinary proceedings, confirming that the Company was responding to grievances and not acting out of political hostility.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: This Court finds that there is no evidence that the Claimant was targeted, victimized, or subjected to disciplinary action because of his role as a Union EXCO Member. The evidence overwhelmingly shows that the Company acted only after receiving multiple independent sexual harassment complaints and was fulfilling its duty as an employer. The complainants’ testimonies were credible, consistent, and untainted by any political motive. The allegation of being targeted due to his EXCO position is not proven and unsupported by any facts.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: Further, the Claimant alleges that he was selectively prosecuted because of his position as a Union EXCO Member. This Court is of the view that this selective prosecution requires evidence that others in similar circumstances committed comparable misconduct but were not subjected to disciplinary action. Here, the Claimant himself admitted that all four (4) sexual harassment complaints were directed solely at him and that no other employee and/or EXCO Member was implicated.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: In fact, during cross-examination the Claimant confirmed that another EXCO Member within the Company was not subjected to any disciplinary action and this alone undermines the claim of anti-Union targeting. This Court agrees with the Company that if it intended to suppress Union Leadership, it would logically have acted against more than one EXCO Member. The fact that only the Claimant faced disciplinary proceedings and only after multiple independent complaints, shows that the Company’s actions were based on misconduct not Union politics. Furthermore, the upon being questioned, the Claimant conceded that he had no evidence to support his theory that disciplinary proceedings were initiated because of his EXCO status.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: It is finding of this Court based on the facts of this case that the Company responded appropriately and responsibly to credible complaints, fulfilling its obligation to ensure a safe and respectful workplace. The disciplinary action taken was a proportionate and necessary response to the serious allegations, not a retaliatory measure.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: Hence, with regard to the allegation of selective prosecution raised by the Claimant, this Court finds that there is no basis whatsoever for his allegation. The Claimant was the only employee against whom complaints were made and he provided no evidence that others in similar circumstances were treated differently. The existence of another EXCO Member who faced no disciplinary action further disproves any claim of anti-Union targeting.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: It is also apparent to this Court that throughout the disciplinary process, the Claimant repeatedly highlighted his role as an EXCO Member of the Union, referencing it in each of his show cause replies and in his correspondence with the Company. These repeated references were not incidental, rather, they reflected an attempt to use his Union position as a shield against disciplinary action.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: In the case of Kandu Sugang & Anor v. Trienekens (Sarawak) Sdn Bhd [2012] 1 CLJ 996 and Pamol Plantations Sdn Bhd, Johore v. Vengkatajalam s/o Govindasamy [1994] 2 ILR 974, the Industrial Court makes it clear that Union Officials are not above workplace rules. Holding a Union Office does not grant immunity from disciplinary action nor does it excuse misconduct. An employee remains an employee first, bound by contractual obligations and subject to lawful discipline.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: This Court finds that the Claimant’s attempt to rely on his EXCO position as a form of immunity is misconceived. Union status does not shield an employee from disciplinary action nor elevate them above the standards expected of other employees.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: With regard go the issue of failure to lodge a police report, this Court finds that lodging a police report is not a mandatory requirement in cases of workplace sexual harassment as affirmed in Sitt Tatt Bhd v. Flora Gnanapragasam & Anor [2006] 1 MLJ 497 and relied upon in Magendran Gunasekharan [supra]. The law does not impose an obligation on the victim to initiate criminal proceedings. Instead, what matters is whether the employer, upon receiving a complaint, acted responsibly and in accordance with its duty to provide a safe work environment

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: The Claimant also asserted that the Company had failed to give due consideration to his twenty-seven (27) years of service and his alleged clean disciplinary record before deciding to terminate his employment.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: While the Claimant initially stated that he had no disciplinary record, he later acknowledged during cross-examination the existence of disciplinary entries in the Company's records. In particular, he confirmed the records of his disciplinary entries recorded in the DI Notes at page 119 of COB-1, which reflects prior instances of misconduct. Hence, the Claimant is not free of disciplinary issues.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: This Court finds that even if he had a clean disciplinary record, it is well-established that long service and past good conduct do not grant immunity nor operate as a defence to serious misconduct, particularly where the misconduct concerns sexual harassment. In the case of Hong Leong Bank Berhad v. Adrian Joseph D’Cruz [2005] 2 LNS 1904, the Court considered the Claimant's long tenure and good performance but found these irrelevant in the face of egregious misconduct. The Claimant had made inappropriate sexual comments in the workplace. The Court upheld the dismissal, stating that such behaviour particularly in a professional setting was inexcusable and warranted termination.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: This Court would also state that it is settled principle in industrial jurisprudence that an employer is not required to prove every charge levelled against an employee in order to justify dismissal. Rather, a single established charge of sufficient gravity may, on its own, constitute just cause and excuse for termination, provided it is proven on a balance of probabilities. This position is clearly affirmed in the case of Ahmad Rasly Haji Osman v. Padiberas Nasional Berhad [2015] 1 LNS 1427 wherein multiple charges were preferred against the employee, but the Court ultimately upheld the dismissal based solely on one proven charge. The Court held that even where other charges fail, a serious act of dishonesty or misconduct that is established on the evidence is sufficient to support the employer's decision.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
section_title: Other Issues raised by the Claimant
content: This Court finds that the said principle applies equally in cases involving allegations of sexual harassment, where the nature of the misconduct is inherently serious and implicates the safety and dignity of others in the workplace.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
content: Based on the totality of the evidence presented, the Company had proven all the four (4) charges on a balance of probabilities. The Claimant's actions and/or remarks toward COW-1, COW-3, COW-5 and COW-6 were clearly unwanted, inappropriate, and offensive in nature and tantamount to sexual harassment. Accordingly, the Claimant's dismissal was with just cause and excuse.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
content: It is seeming to this Court that that the Company has taken the charges preferred against the Claimant seriously in order to ensure that the employees were not being intimidated and/or humiliated and/or offended at any given time by the Claimant. It is the duty of the Company to ensure that such acts are not committed by any person what more the Claimant having served the Company for twenty-seven (27) years.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
content: As a Technical Assistant of twenty-seven (27) years of service with the Company, the Claimant should lead by example and to demonstrate sufficient seniority qualities. The Claimant is also expected to possess a greater degree of integrity to ensure save environment for his colleagues but instead he was the person intoxicating the working environment with an intolerable and unacceptable behaviour.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
