content: Aligning myself to the judicial pronouncements in the aforesaid cases and based on the facts and circumstances of the present case in its entirety and the totality of the evidence and upon reading respective written submissions, this Court is of the considered view that the Company had successfully proved on the balance of probabilities the appropriateness of the Company’s action against the Claimant. In the circumstances of this case, it is the considered view of this Court that it is unreasonable to expect the Company to have continued the Claimant’s employment.

case_name: Mohamad Hizam bin Suwardi @ Surip v Chemi-Con (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Eswary Maree
content: In conclusion, having considered all pleadings, evidences and submissions available before this Court and bearing in mind Section 30(5) of the 1967 Act to act according to equity, good conscience and the substantial merits of the case without regard to technicalities and legal form, this Court finds that the dismissal was with just cause and excuse. Accordingly, the Claimant's claim is hereby dismissed.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: It behoves this Court to make a ruling on this issue before proceeding to hear the merits of the striking out Application filed herein.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content:
Section 29(fa) and (g) of the Act reads: “29. The Court may, in any proceedings before it:
(fa) Order a case to be struck off or reinstated (g) Generally direct and do all such things as are necessary or expedient for the expeditious determination of the matter before it”.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: Clearly, Section 29 of the Act does not limit or afford restricted control over the Court’s powers to struck off or reinstate or take all measures necessary or expedient for the expeditious determination of the matter. The provision, in substance, empowers the Court to strike out a case or reinstate a case that has been struck off while (g) allows the Court to consider whatever necessary or expedient to avoid unnecessary delay or inconvenience.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: The Act is silent on the proper stage for filing an application under Section 29 (fa) and (g) of the Act. Had delay be a determining factor of whether such an application ought to be entertained, the legislature would have expressly provided so by mandating that the Court consider delay as a material consideration. In the absence of such clear proviso, delay cannot be construed as a bar to the Court’s jurisdiction to hear and determine a striking out application, more so, when an objection is raised on a threshold jurisdiction of the Industrial Court.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: Accordingly, the Court may exercise this striking out power at any stage of the proceedings, provided that it is satisfied that the objection concerns a jurisdiction issue and it serves to avoid unnecessary time, effort and resources of all parties. Section 29(fa) of the Act is plain in its meaning and contains no words that imposes any temporal restrictions on its usage or confines its application to any particular stage of the proceedings when a striking out is based on a specific provision of the Act. If an application seeking the Industrial Court to exercise Section 29(fa) on grounds of s 52 of the Act, it ought to be heard at the earliest possible opportunity as the circumstances in which it is worded, it is left to the discretion of the Industrial Court to exercise its powers pursuant to such application.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: In the present case, the fact that Pernas has not yet commenced its case and that the application was not heard earlier or filed before the commencement of the trial, does not bar Pernas from raising the fundamental issue of jurisdictional objection. If it is demonstrated that the Court lacks the jurisdiction, it therefore cannot confer jurisdiction upon itself through parties’ acquiescence or act. And neither should the Industrial Court assume the requisite jurisdiction merely because the hearing has started. The Court must therefore, ascertain that in compliance with the Act it does not lacks the threshold jurisdiction to determine the reference.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: In the judgment of the Court of Appeal in the case of Institut Integrity Malaysia v Roziah Harun & Anor [2024] 6 MLRA 809, it was stated that where clear evidence is presented for the determination of a jurisdictional issue of the Industrial Court, for the Industrial Court to dealt with such issue summarily, it is open for a party to take the route via s 29(fa) of the Act to have the case struck out.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: Clearly, in this case, the Minister’s reference is not quashed for purposes of challenging the Industrial Court’s threshold jurisdiction and no prohibition order was obtained by Pernas to prevent the Industrial Court from adjudicating this matter. Parties therefore are fully entitled to have their issues canvassed and ventilated before the Court. Once a Minister’s reference has been obtained, except for limited grounds, no matters can be dealt with by mere affidavit evidence and neither can a matter be struck out. The principle in Kathiravelu Ganesan & Anor v Kojasa Holdings Bhd [1997] 1 MELR 10; [1997] 1 MLRA 372; [1997] 2 MLJ 685; [1997] 3 CLJ 777; [1997] 3 AMR 2484 has made this trajectory of the role and function of the Industrial Court clear enough.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: For an objection on grounds of jurisdictional threshold to be taken up at a full hearing would make Section 29(fa) to be quite redundant thereby defeating the purpose of its introduction and amendment of Section 29 of the Act. The Court of Appeal in Institut Integrity (supra) held that s 29(fa) of the Act may be invoked in a fit and proper case - where evidence points conclusively that s 52 of the Act applies to oust the jurisdiction of the Industrial Court. Section 52 therefore acts as an exception to the situations described in Kathiravelu Ganesan’s (supra) case.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: This Court shall therefore determine on the application by Pernas based on its affidavit evidence to see if the reasons advanced as required under s 52 of the Act support a case that is fit and proper to be concluded under Section 29(fa) of the Act.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: The Court must be satisfied that Pernas falls within the ambit of Section 52 which provides that “Parts II, III, IV, V and VI shall not apply to any Government service or to any service of any statutory authority or to any workman employed by Government or by any statutory authority.”

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: In support of its case, Pernas position is that it is an agency owned by the MOF (incorporated) with clear government responsibilities or mandates. As it is also under the supervision of MECD, Pernas financial accounts and documents are subject to audit by the National Audit Department. Its Board of Directors consists of two members from the Malaysian Government Ministries i.e. MOF and MECD. Pernas is listed as one of the agencies under the Ministry based on the official MECD portal. Pernas main goal is to support bumiputera economic delevepment policies under the Malaysia Plan.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: A conclusive proof of its agency stature is the letter from Jabatan Audit Negara (JAN) dated 16.04.2021 exhibited in the supporting Affidavit. The letter reads: “Pengauditan Terhadap Pengurusan Perbadanan Nasional Berhad” 2. Sukacita dimaklumkan Jabatan Audit Negara (JAN) akan menjalankan pengauditan terhadap pengurusan syarikat Perbadanan Nasional Berhad (PNS). Pengauditan ini Adalah selaras dengan Seksyen 5(1)(d) Akta Audit 1957 yang memberi kuasa kepada Ketua Audit Negara untuk mengaudit sesebuah syarikat yang berdaftar di bawah Akta Syarikat 2016 yang menerima geran/pinjaman daripada Kerajaan Persekutuan atau negeri dan sesebuah syarikat di mana lebih daripada separuh modal saham berbayar dipegang oleh Kerajaan Persekutuan/Kerajaan Negeri/Agenci Kerajaan. PNS telah diwartakan dalam Perintah Audit (Akaun Syarikat) 2017 [P.U. (A) 294] sebagai salah satu syarikat yang perlu diaudit oleh JAN.”

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: The relevance of the foregoing content in the JAN letter is seen in the case of Ramana Dayaram Shetty v International Airport Authority of India And Others (1979) 2 SCC 489 referred to in Institut Integriti (supra) judgment, where it was stated that: “14. A corporation may be created in one of two ways. It may be either established by statute or incorporated under a law such as the Companies Act 1956 or the Societies Registration Act 1860. Where a corporation is wholly controlled by Government not only in its policymaking but also in carrying out the functions entrusted to it by law establishing it or by the character of its incorporation, there can be no doubt that it would be an instrumentality or agency of Government.” 15. But if extensive and unusual financial assistance is given and the purpose of the Government in giving such assistance coincides with the purpose for which the corporation is expected to use the assistance and such purpose is of public character, it may be a relevant circumstances supporting an inference that the corporation is an instrumentality or agency of Government.” The following paragraphs then states as follows: “…… But “a finding of State financial support plus an unusual degree of control over the management and policies might lead one to characterise an operation as State action”.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: The letter from JAN is evident that Pernas is funded by the Government and by virtue of Section 5 (1)(d) Audit Act 1957, it empowers JAN to conduct an Audit to ensure the purpose and objective of the Government policy is carried out. Basically, it acts as a safeguard of any profits, funds received or assets used to be align in accordance with the policy. This characteristics which controls its finance does not make it to be a GLC or a mere private corporation.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: The obvious difference between a GLC and a government agency is that a GLC is a company with a commercial objective in which the government has a controlling stake while a government agency is primarily engaged in matters of high public interest.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: The Claimant argues that the contracts entered into by Pernas are commercial in nature which bind Pernas itself and not the Government.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: The Court is of the view that the mere fact that Pernas enters into contracts of commercial nature, does not, by itself, divest it of its position as a Government agency. Its legal paradigm remains unaffected merely because it undertakes commercial transactions. The agency, whilst having its objective intact, often enters into commercial transactions so long as it continuous to function as an instrument of the Government and carries out the mandate entrusted to it in furtherance of Government policy. There is no legal requirement that for Pernas to retain its character as an instrument of the government, the Government must be privy to every contract which it enters. The fact that the Government has continuously funded Pernas, is an important indicator which supports the characteristics of its standing as a Government agency.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: The Claimant sought to argue that the Objects Clause in the MOA sets out business objects such as investment, trading and related commercial activities and other profit driven activities consistent with a commercial company structure, not within the functions of a statutory authority or government department.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: It is vital to look at the function and role Pernas plays and the purpose of its establishment. To achieve its vision of supporting economic development policies under the Malaysia Plan and to develop bumiputra entrepreneurs specifically through investments, it is of no surprise that the activities that Pernas carries out could overlap with transactions which are commercial in nature. Thus by involving in investment trading and related commercial activities, Pernas should not be seen as vitiating from its true purpose but rather diversify to achieve the policy.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: It was further submitted by the Claimant that the “Guidelines for Directors Appointment by the MOF and reference to the Red Book are merely governance tools to regulate the behaviour of directors nominated by the Government which do not confer any statutory powers to Pernas.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: It is my considered view that the “Guidelines” are indicative of significant and substantive involvement of the Government at the management stage which fits the role of Pernas as an Government instrumentality or agency.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: For completeness, the other reasons raised by Pernas to prove that it comes within s 52 is the involvement of non-profitable activities carried out solely on humanitarian grounds for example the Palestine Humanitarian fund collection. The National Sports Day and MECD Family Day 2024 Programme were carried out with the aims to strengthened relationship between MECD residents and agencies and Pernas was the recipient of the “Best International Government Agency Franchise Development” Award in Abu Dhabi in March 2024.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: By receiving the Best International Government Agency Franchise Development Award, it is evident that the Government has never rebuked Pernas or regarded it as anything other than one of its instrumentalities, as such information is available to the public at large.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: The foregoing reasons would all lead to the conclusion that Pernas is a instrumentalities of the Government. This result in the Industrial Court lacks the requisite threshold jurisdiction to proceed to hear and determine the Claimant’s representation emanating from the Minister’s reference under s 20(1) of the Act.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: This Court allows prayer 1 of the encl 34 of Pernas’ Application to struck out the Claimant’s Case under Section 29(fa) and/or Section 29(g) of the Act.

case_name: Nor Fardzliah binti Jaafar v Perbadanan Nasional Berhad
chairman: Amrik Singh
content: The Claimant’s case is hereby struck off.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The fact that the Company dismissed the Claimant is an undisputed fact and/or agreed by both parties. The issue, which remains disputed by the parties, is whether the Claimant was dismissed with just cause and excuse, in which the Claimant reiterates that the Claimant's employment with the Company was terminated without just cause and excuse.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In this regard, refer to the case of Yap Kit Seong V. Inti Iabs Sdn Bhd [2023] 4 ILR 610, wherein it was held as follows: ‘’[11] In the case of Wong Chee Hong V. Cathay Organization (M) Sdn Bhd [1988] 1 CLJ 45; [1988] 1 CLJ (Rep) 298, the court had stated the followings: When the Industrial Court is dealing with a reference under s. 20, the first thing that the court will have to do is to ask itself a question (of) whether there was a dismissal, and if so, whether it was with or without just cause or excuse. [12] In a case involving retrenchment, the issues before the court essentially are whether there existed circumstances, which justified the retrenchment exercise undertaken by the Company and whether the Company had acted bona fide in retrenching the claimant. Arkitek Akiprima Sdn Bhd V. Lianq Siew Fatt & Anor [2002] 1 ILR 150 (Award No. 11 of 2002). It is an established principle that the burden is on the employer to prove their case against the claimant and to justify the retrenchment exercise on a balance of probabilities. Liew Soon Cheonq V. Aljazeera International (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd [2016] 4 ILR 360 (Award No. 1065 of 2016). Reference also made to the case of Ireka Construction Berhad V. Chantiravathan Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 11 (Award No. 245 of 1995). [13] It is incumbent for the Company to prove on the standard of balance of probabilities that it has grounds to justify its exercise of retrenchment. (Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara V. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor [2002] 3 CLJ 314).’’

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In cases of unfair dismissal, the burden of proof lies with the Company to prove that the dismissal process adhered to proper procedures and that the Claimant was dismissed for just cause or excuse.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Referring to the case of Niall Atholl Murray V. Baker Hughes (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd. & Anor [2018] MELRU 1194, the court reaffirmed the principle that the burden of proof in an unfair dismissal case lies with the employer: “In an unfair dismissal case, the burden of proof is on the employer to discharge as stated in the case of Stamford Executive Centre V. Dharsini Ganesan [1986] 1 ILR 101: “It may further be emphasised here that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer. He must prove the workman guilty and it is not the workman who must prove himself not guilty. This is so basic a principle of industrial jurisprudence that no employer is expected to come to this Court in ignorance of it.”. [14] Further, in order to successfully defend an unfair dismissal claim, the burden of proof is on the employer to show that the reason for dismissing the employee falls into one of the two categories set out in subsection 20(3) of Act…. [177] the termination of the employee will be deemed to have been unjust unless an employer can prove that the employee was dismissed for a just cause or excuse. Even if an employer succeeds in proving that there was a reason for the dismissal of the employee, it is for the Industrial Court to decide whether the dismissal was warranted or not in accordance with, inter alia, the principles of equity, good conscience and the substantial merits of the case (subsection 30(5) of Act 177).”

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The dismissal will be deemed unjust unless the employer can prove that the dismissal was for just cause or excuse. Even if the employer provides a reason for the dismissal, it is for the Industrial Court to determine whether the dismissal was justified, considering principles of equity, good conscience, and the substantial merits of the case.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In light of the principles established in the cited cases, it is clear that the burden of proof in an unfair dismissal case lies with the Company. The Company must provide convincing evidence that the dismissal was conducted following proper procedures and that the Claimant was dismissed for just cause or excuse.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Company must demonstrate the validity of the dismissal with clear evidence of misconduct or other grounds for dismissal. Moreover, if the Company's reasons are unsubstantiated or fail to meet the required standard, the dismissal will be deemed unjust. The Industrial Court will assess whether the dismissal aligns with the principles of equity, good conscience, and the substantial merits of the case.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
Primarily, it is the duty of the Industrial Court to determine whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse. In Goon Kwee Phoy V. J & P Coats (M) Bhd [1981] 2 MLJ 129, Raja Azlan Shah CJ:
“If the employer chooses to give a reason for the action taken by him, the duty of the Industrial Court will be to enquire whether the excuse or reason has or has not been made out”. His Lordship went on to hold that if the Industrial Court finds that this has not been proved, “then the inevitable conclusion must be the termination or dismissal was without just cause or excuse”.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Federal Court in Milan Auto Sdn. Bhd V. Wong She Yen [1995] 4 CLJ 449 held that the function of the Industrial Court in dismissal cases on a reference under section 20 is two-fold. Firstly, to determine whether the misconduct complained of by the employer has been established, and secondly whether the proven misconduct constitutes just cause or excuse for the dismissal.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: Whenever a Company had caused the dismissal of the workman, it is incumbent on the part of the Company to discharge the burden of proof that the dismissal was with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: It is trite law that the Company bears the burden to prove that the Claimant had committed the alleged misconduct and the conduct warrants the Claimant’s dismissal. The Company must prove the Claimant guilty and it is not the Claimant who must prove himself not guilty.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: This principle was laid down by His Lordship Mr. Justice Raja Azlan Shah C. J. (Malaya) (now His Royal Highness the Sultan of Perak) in the case of Goon Kwee Phoy V. J & P Coats (M) BHC) [1981] 2 ML J 129. The relevant passages are found at p. 1 36 of the report : “Where representations are made and are referred to the Industrial Court for enquiry, it is the duty of that court to determine whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse. If the employer chooses to give a reason for the action taken by him, the duty of the Industrial Court will be to enquire whether that excuse or reasons has or has not been made out. If it finds as a fact that it has not been proved, then the inevitable conclusion must be that the termination or dismissal was without just cause or excuse. The proper enquiry of the court is the reason advanced by it and that court or the High Court cannot go into another reason not relied on by the employer or find one for it”. [ Emphasis added]

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: In Wong Yuen Hock V. Syarikat Hong Leong Assurance Sdn Bhd & Another Appeal [1995] 3 CLJ 344, in delivering the grounds of judgment of the Federal Court, His Lordship Mr. Justice Mohd Azmi FCJ stated as follows at p.352 of the report: - “On the authorities, we were of the view that the main and only function of the Industrial Court dealing with a reference under s. 20 of the Act (unless otherwise lawfully provided by the terms of the reference), is to determine whether the misconduct or irregularities complained by the management as the grounds of dismissal were in fact committed by the workman, and if so, whether such grounds constitute just cause or excuse.’’

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: The burden of proof in an unfair dismissal claim lies on the employer to prove on a balance of probabilities that the employee is guilty of the allegation or the reason for the dismissal. This principle was expounded in Stamford Executive Centre V. Dharsini Ganesan [1986] 1 ILR 101, [Award No.263 of 1985] [1985] 2 MELR 245. “In a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer. The employer must prove the workman guilty and it is not the workman who must prove himself not guilty. This is so basic a principle of industrial jurisprudence that no employer is expected to come to this Court in ignorance of it.”

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: In Wong Chee Hong V. Cathay Organisation Malaysia Sdn Bhd [1987] 1 MELR 32; 1 MLRA 346, the Supreme Court held that: “Where the Industrial Court is dealing with reference under s20, the first thing that the Court will have to do is to ask itself a question whether there was a dismissal, and if so, whether it was with or without just cause or excuse.”

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: In the case of Ireka Construction Bhd. V. Chantiravathan Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 11 it was held that: “It is a basic principle of industrial jurisprudence that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer to prove that he has just cause and excuse for taking the decision to impose the disciplinary measure of dismissal upon the employee. The just cause must be either a misconduct, negligence or poor performance based on the facts of case.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: In Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara V. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor [2002] 3 CLJ 314 at the Court Appeal held that the standard of proof for cases heard before the Industrial Court is “on the balance of probabilities”: ‘’In our view the passage quoted from Administrative Law by H.W.R. Wade & C.F. Forsyth offers the clearest statement on the standard of proof required, that is the civil standard based on the balance of probabilities, which is flexible so that the degree of probability required is proportionate to the nature of gravity of the issue.”

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: In Tyco Engineering and Construction (M) Sdn Bhd V. James Francis Trimble [2000] 2 MELR 678, the Industrial Court outlined the law on the burden of proof as follows: “The burden of proof that the dismissal was with just cause or excuse is on the employer which is on the balance of probabilities to adduce cogent and convincing evidence being the real reason by dismissing the employee. This is the principle of industrial jurisprudence”.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: Based on the case of Colgate Palmolive (M) Sdn Bhd V. Yap Kok Foong & Another Appeal [2001] 3 CLJ 9, it now remains to be considered whether the termination was with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: ISSUES WHICH WERE RAISED THROUGHOUT THE PROCEEDINGS

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Findings of Fact a) Position of Signatories
content: The evidence establishes that by late 2019 the Claimant was effectively the sole authorised bank signatory at MIMA. The three directors named in his contract (Dr. Rizal himself, Puan Zaharizan Md. Zin, and Tan Sri Dato’ Sri Ahmad Ramli were supposed signatories. On 24.10.2019, Puan Zaharizan gave notice of resignation as a Board member and signatory. Tan Sri Dato’ Sri Ahmad Ramli (Chairman) was ill and never completed bank formalities. In cross-examination, the Company’s own witnesses confirmed that by November 2019 only Dr. Rizal could sign MIMA cheques. COW-1 (Puan Aspamurni) agreed, “for November 2019”, the company had only one signatory, Dr. Rizal,” so payments could not be processed with only him. COW-2 (Puan Suhaila) likewise agreed that as of November 2019 the only available signatory was the Claimant. Thus, factually, the Claimant was the only active authorised signatory during the material period, apart from his own role.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: b) Appointment and Duties of Encik Azman
content: In October 2019, the Claimant offered Encik Mohamed Azman bin Mohd Aris (Encik Azman) a position titled “Senior Researcher / Head of Administration & Finance”. Encik Azman began his duty on 01.11.2019. He reported to the Claimant. Under the Company’s rules, a Director of Administration & Finance (DOAF) is a (Grade A-II) post requiring Board approval, whereas Head of Admin/Finance (Grade A-III) did not. The evidence shows that Encik Azman duties and benefits were essentially those of a DOAF. His contract (COB3, p.20) contained the DOAF job description. He was provided with a reserved parking bay paid for by MIMA (normally reserved for DG and DOAF). The Claimant admitted that although Encik Azman’s title was “Head of Admin/Finance,” for all intents and purposes he was acting as DOAF. In particular, COW-1 conceded that even though the official posts were vacant, it was company practice to keep paying parking spaces for DG and DOAF. She agreed that it was practical to allow Encik Azman to use the paid-for DOAF parking (incurring no extra cost) rather than leave it unused. The Director of Transport’s circular (Pekeliling No. 2/2002) indeed restricts parking only to the DG and DOAF, but the evidence (including the Board resolution) shows MIMA did extend the privilege to Encik Azman as a practical measure.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Encik Azman did not submit a Statutory Declaration of non-bankruptcy as required by the Handbook. In December 2019, Maybank notified MIMA that Encik Azman could not be registered as signatory due to insolvency matters. The Claimant met the Maybank manager (Puan Fazlien) on 26.11.2019. He was told Encik Azman had an old debt now in the Insolvency Department, and that until cleared he could not sign. A lawyer was recommended to “clear” Encik Azman’s record. The Claimant admitted he was told Maybank was no longer pursuing the debt itself but was unclear if Encik Azman was bankrupt. The Company ran an Insolvency Department search (as at COB7 p.18) and found Encik Azman was an undischarged bankrupt (the creditor was Dana Harta Urus Sdn. Bhd.)

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: On the facts that the Claimant never obtained Encik Azman’s SD nor independently verified his status. He assumed his staff had secured it. After learning of Maybank’s refusal, the Claimant did not seek an alternative signatory or appoint the recommended lawyer during the nine-month period. He testified he “did not think to appoint someone else” because he believed Encik Azman’s issue would be resolved. The Company’s submissions characterize this as deliberate concealment, but the Claimant maintains he genuinely thought Maybank would allow Encik Azman to sign if given time (he later secured an attorney for that purpose).

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: With only one signatory (the Claimant), available, urgent payments became problematic. To meet payroll and bills between November 2019 and July 2020, the Claimant devised a temporary procedure. He and senior finance staff agreed to transfer funds from MIMA’s account into the personal accounts of COW-1 (Puan Aspamurni) and COW-2 (Puan Suhaila), from which they would promptly pay MIMA’s vendors. This method was documented by a series of “Payment Memos” (COB-4–COB-5) showing the purpose and amounts for each transaction. The payments made were legitimate company expenses (salaries, HRDF levies, project costs, etc.) all supported by invoices and approved cheques. The finance witnesses confirmed that these payments were indeed on behalf of MIMA and for its benefit. COW-1 and COW-2 agreed that no company funds were misused; each transaction was reversed within a day once payment cleared the personal account.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Although MIMA’s financial rules ordinarily require payments by crossed cheques and advance Board approval (as at COB-I pp. 163, 173), the Claimant explained that the arrangement was a stopgap due to lack of signatories and aborted Board meetings. The record shows the Claimant did not inform the Board in writing about this arrangement, but he did seek to convene Board meetings, unsuccessfully. All scheduled Board meetings in December 2019 were aborted and the Board ignored the Claimant’s urgent emails on 15.11.2019 requesting an emergency meeting after the Mr. Captain Sebastian incident. In cross-examination, the Claimant admitted it was a “serious situation” and agreed with questioning that he did not nominate another signatory during the nine months. He claimed he briefed the new Chairman (Dato’ Seri Saripuddin) orally in January 2020, but no formal Board approval was recorded.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: e) Incident with Captain Martin Sebastian
content: The undisputed facts are that on 14.11.2019 Captain Martin Sebastian (Captain Sebastian), (a Company Senior Fellow) attacked and injured the Claimant in the MIMA parking lot. The Claimant immediately lodged a police report on 14.11.2019, (as at COB-6 p.173) and sent an email on 15.11.2019, (as at CLB-2 p.218) to all Board members recommending Captain Sebastian be placed on immediate garden leave. He repeatedly urged the Board to act. A Board meeting was scheduled for 03.12.2019 (to consider Captain Sebastian’s insubordination and this incident), but it was aborted. It was rescheduled for 18.12. 2019, but was also cancelled.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: e) Incident with Captain Martin Sebastian
content: In the face of continued Board inaction, the Claimant (as Acting DG) unilaterally appointed Messrs. Zul Rafique & Partners in November 2019 to advice on the disciplinary measures to take against Captain Sebastian. He did so immediately after the incident and before any Board directive, stating it was to assist the Board’s decision. After legal services were rendered, the Claimant authorized payment of RM6, 417.13 (as at invoice dated16.12.2019) and RM4, 313.35 (as at invoice dated 26.2.2020) to Messrs. Zul Rafique & Partners. Captain Sebastian was later convicted under Section 323 of the Penal Code. Voluntarily causing hurt on 20.01.2020. This confirms the gravity of Captain Sebastian’s attack. The Claimant did not personally profit and used legal counsel to further MIMA’s interests.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: It is also settled that an employee’s single act of misconduct can justify summary dismissal if it strikes at the root of the contract. However, even when misconduct is proven, the sanction must be fair and proportionate. The Federal Court in Norizan Bakar V. Panzana Enterprise [2013] 6 MLRA 613; 9CLJ 409; 6MLJ 605 reiterated that the Industrial Court has jurisdiction to consider whether dismissal was an excessive punishment for the proven misconduct. The “doctrine of proportionality” empowers the Court to substitute what it deems an appropriate penalty if dismissal would be too harsh. Similarly, appellate authority recognizes that repeated or serious breaches (e.g. involving public safety or trust) may justify dismissal but lesser misdeeds by long-serving employees may call for lesser sanctions.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Analysis First Charge (DOAF Appointment without Board Approval)
content: The Company alleges the Claimant tried to make Encik Azman a DOAF (Grade A-II) despite knowing he was a bankrupt, and then circumvented the requirement for Board approval by titling him “Head of Admin/Finance” instead. It points out that Encik Azman’s letter carried the DOAF job description and he received DOAF parking and a DOAF-range salary (RM8, 000 compared with his demanded RM10, 000). The Claimant admitted Encik Azman never swore the required SD for non-bankruptcy and that Encik Azman had asked for a higher salary; he argues Encik Azman was paid only as a Senior Researcher.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Findings of the Honourable Court of the first charge
content: The evidence shows the Claimant offered Encik Azman a Grade A.III role rather than Grade A-II. Encik Azman’s letter (as at page 15 (COB-3) did use the DOAF job description, but Encik Azman’s title and salary were that of a Grade A-III position. COW-1 admitted during cross that, Encik Azman’s tasks were those of DOAF only “in name,” and that the only difference was the name of the post. In context, the Board’s actions suggest they did not consider this subterfuge a serious issue, on 12.11.2019 (shortly after Encik Azman’s hire) the Board actually passed resolutions to add Encik Azman as an authorised signatory for all of MIMA’s banks. The Board thereby tacitly accepted Encik Azman as DOAF or Head of Admin/Finance. The Claimant also promptly sought to regularize Encik Azman’s authority.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Findings of the Honourable Court of the first charge
content: On balance of probabilities, this Honourable Court find this charge only partially proved. It is not disputed that Encik Azman was not asked for the SD, a lapse under the Handbook. However, the Claimant’s credible explanation is that he genuinely believed Encik Azman’s employment was properly authorized, he testified that the board had approved Encik Azman’s remuneration and parking. That Encik Azman was treated as Head of Admin/Finance by mutual agreement. No Board member contradicted this, and the Board’s own resolution confirms Encik Azman’s status. There is no evidence the Claimant knowingly defrauded the Board. Rather, he appears to have been overly optimistic that Encik Azman would clear his insolvency issues and thus did not seek formal reclassification.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Even if this conduct breached internal rules (appointing without an SD or formal Board approval), it involved no dishonesty or loss to the Company. The Claimant argues that he acted in good faith and that the position Encik Azman filled was indeed needed. In these circumstances, this Honourable Industrial Court find the misconduct was at most a procedural violation. Applying the case of Menon V. Brooklands (Selangor) Rubber Co Ltd [1968] MRLA 844 [1968] 2MLJ 186, only wilful disobedience of a lawful order or repudiation of contract terms would justify dismissal. Here, the Claimant did not wilfully deceive the Company or derive personal gain. He remained cooperative with the Board and ultimately engaged a lawyer to resolve Encik Azman’s status. The punishment of dismissal is manifestly disproportionate to this lapse. This Honourable Court accordingly conclude that First Charge, even if technically made out, does not amount to just cause for summary dismissal.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Second Charge (Failure to Verify Encik Azman’s Bankruptcy and Installing Him as Signatory)
content: The Company’s charge is that on learning, Encik Azman might be bankrupt; the Claimant kept Encik Azman on and pushed to make him an authorised signatory. It points out that Maybank expressly told the Claimant, that Encik Azman could not be registered until cleared by the Insolvency Department and advised hiring a lawyer.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Second Charge (Failure to Verify Encik Azman’s Bankruptcy and Installing Him as Signatory)
content: The Claimant admitted he was told an old debt existed but claimed Maybank was no longer pursuing it. The Company argues the Claimant “suspiciously” failed to verify Encik Azman’s status: he did not request the SD, did not hire the recommended lawyer, and did not run the Insolvency search, even though he urgently needed a second signatory. Indeed, when the Company later checked, Encik Azman’s insolvency was confirmed by an outside creditor, contradicting the Claimant’s account. The Company submits this charge is proved, the Claimant knowingly concealed Encik Azman’s ineligibility and thus breached his duties.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Findings of this Honourable Court to the Second Issue
content: The Claimant acknowledges that Encik Azman never presented the required SD. He says he trusted his finance unit to obtain it and assumed Maybank would eventually allow Encik Azman to sign after the debt was no longer pursued. He insists he did not “know” Encik Azman was bankrupt. While the Claimant’s testimony was inconsistent on whether he knew Encik Azman had to swear an SD, it was clear he had notice of a “debt in Insolvency Department” and was urged to have it cleared by a lawyer. He did later instruct a firm (Jagjit Singh & Co) to follow up on that debt after leaving MIMA.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Findings of this Honourable Court to the Second Issue
content: However, find the Company’s allegations largely unproven. There is no direct evidence that the Claimant actively concealed anything, at most he was negligent in not following up. The finance witnesses agreed that Encik Azman was only prevented from signing at Maybank, not at other banks, and the Board had already approved him for three of four banks. The Claimant attempted to appoint Encik Azman, but when Maybank balked, he simply waited. This Honourable Court have no proof that Encik Azman remained “installed” as signatory (COB documents show he was never registered at Maybank). The Claimant’s failure to run an Insolvency check or hire a lawyer, while imprudent, appears to be due to oversight rather than fraud.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Findings of this Honourable Court to the Second Issue
content: Credibility wise, the Claimant was forthcoming that he misunderstood the situation. The Company’s attack on his truthfulness (calling him “very untruthful”) is based on inferences not on any admission by the Claimant. On balance, the evidence falls short of showing “clear proof” (as required) that the Claimant knowingly allowed a bankrupt person to become signatory.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Even if a prima facie breach occurred (failing to verify Encik Azman’s status), this was not a deliberate breach of an essential term. There was no financial loss to MIMA, Encik Azman had ceased to be signatory at the bank that mattered. The Industrial Court has frequently held that mere negligence or error (absent dishonesty) does not of itself justify dismiss. Here, the Claimant’s motive was to ensure continuity of payments, not personal gain. Considering his length of service and the fact that the Board ultimately recognized Encik Azman’s role, this Honourable Court conclude that even if this charge were partially proved, it would not amount to “just cause or excuse” for summary dismissal.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Company alleges that from Nov 2019 to July 2020 the Claimant “devised a scheme” directing MIMA funds into subordinates’ personal bank accounts without BOD oversight. It criticizes the Claimant for not appointing any alternative signatory or informing the Board of the arrangement. The particulars (in COB -) show 11 transactions passed through Puan Aspamurni and Puan Suhaila accounts. The Company concedes that no theft occurred (“no monies were stolen”) but insists the arrangement itself was serious misconduct breaching MIMA’s financial procedures. The Claimant defends that the “Payment Method” was an interim necessity, all banks had no available signatory (Encik Azman disqualified, since Tan Sri Ramli) and urgent payments had to be made. He argues he did not hide it in bad faith; on the contrary, he documented each payment and noted the urgency. He also notes COW-1’s admission that the payments were company expenses and for the company’s benefit.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Findings of this Honourable Court to this issue
content: The documents and testimony firmly establish the facts: the Claimant instructed Puan Aspamurni and Puan Suhaila to process payments via their personal accounts, with memos explaining each transaction. There is no dispute these payments were genuine. The witnesses agreed they were on behalf of MIMA (e.g. salaries, levies, conference costs) and the Claimant paid no overdrafts or fees. The Claimant’s evidence (and the memos) shows all transactions were reversed within a day once cleared (COW-1 said the funds “came out” by next morning). Thus, substantively, no misappropriation of funds occurred and no one personally profited.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Findings of this Honourable Court to this issue
content: Procedurally, the arrangement did violate MIMA’s Treasury rules (which require crossed cheques and Board approval for payments). The Claimant admitted he never informed the full Board in writing about this arrangement, though he did raise the issue with the Acting Chairman (who was briefed orally). The explanations for not selecting another signatory (waiting for Encik Azman) and for not convening the Board (meetings were aborted) are plausible. On credibility, the Claimant and witnesses gave consistent accounts of the scheme; the Company offered no contradictory evidence (the officers who could have approved a third signatory or called the Board were not called as witnesses).

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Even assuming the arrangement breached internal procedures, it was done for no ill motive. The Industrial Court must ask, was it reasonable for the Company to dismiss him for this?

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Under the doctrine of proportionality, the fact the Claimant was in a pinch and acted to avoid default on payments is highly mitigation. Comparable cases have distinguished between misconduct (fraud or gross negligence) and a mere error of judgment in management.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Here, the Claimant involved his most senior deputies and created written trails, this was not a secret scheme but an improvised solution to an extraordinary problem (no authorized signatories). He faced a genuine dilemma and chose what he believed was best for the Company. In the circumstances, although this conduct was irregular, this Honourable Court find it does not justify dismissal. It is not a wilful disobedience of a lawful order, but a questionable exercise of managerial discretion in crisis. The sanction of summary dismissal would be excessive and unfair.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Fourth Charge (Conflict of Interest in Captain Sebastian Case)
content: The Company charged that after the physical altercation with Captain Sebastian, the Claimant improperly appointed solicitors and paid them, despite his personal interest. The charge notes the Claimant had already declared a conflict during a May 2019 Board meeting (when Captain Sebastian’s earlier insubordination was tabled).

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Fourth Charge (Conflict of Interest in Captain Sebastian Case)
content: It argues that by November 2019, the Claimant’s interest had only increased (he was the complainant in the police report) and thus he should have abstained from any decision on Captain Sebastian’s case. Instead, he pursued legal action for MIMA without Board approval and personally consulted outside counsel after leaving MIMA (as at Jagjit Singh’s email at CLB-4 p.3).

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Fourth Charge (Conflict of Interest in Captain Sebastian Case)
content: The Claimant’s evidence is that he was the victim of a grave assault, which constituted a reportable act of insubordination. On 14.11.2019, he lodged a police report and at 3:24 a.m. on 15.11.2019, he emailed all Directors describing the incident and recommending Captain Sebastian be placed on garden leave. His email urged the Board to convene urgently, the Board members did call him back, and he reiterated the need for a meeting.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Fourth Charge (Conflict of Interest in Captain Sebastian Case)
content: The Board scheduled a meeting for 03.12. 2019 to address Captain Sebastian’s misconduct and this incident, but it did not take place. By mid-December, the Board’s attempts to meet were abortive. Therefore, as Acting DG he took the initiative to retain Messrs. Zul Rafique & Partners in late November 2019 to advise on disciplinary proceedings.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Fourth Charge (Conflict of Interest in Captain Sebastian Case)
content: He testified that the purpose was to help the Board decide what to do. It was not to prosecute Captain Sebastian personally but to seek legal guidance. He then authorized payment of the firm’s invoices once received. The Claimant did not hide these steps, he had already sent his email to the Board and the retention of counsel was for legal advice for the Company.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Findings of the Honourable Court to this issue
content: The facts of the Captain Sebastian incident are undisputed and well documented. The Claimant’s proactive steps (reporting to police, emailing directors, hiring counsel) were transparent. There is no evidence Captain Sebastian’s employment or the payments to Messrs Zul Rafique & Partners went forward without the Board’s knowledge. Indeed, by January 2020 Captain Sebastian was in court and later convicted. The Claimant’s earlier declaration of conflict (May 2019) related to a different matter, he maintained he did not treat Captain Sebastian’s criminal case as a “personal benefit” issue but as a serious disciplinary matter requiring legal input. No Company policy or law is shown that he could not engage a lawyer in this emergency.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Honourable Court find that while the Claimant may have had a conflict of interest (being the complainant), his actions on Captain Sebastian’s case were effectively part of his duty as Acting DG. The Board’s own neglect (failure to meet for two months) forced the Claimant to act on an urgent situation.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: There is no suggestion he benefited personally (indeed, he later pursued Captain Sebastian’s appeal privately). On balance of probabilities, this charge is not proved as misconduct warranting dismissal. At most, it shows a breakdown in communication, it does not betray disloyalty or malice by the Claimant. Terminating an employee for addressing a violent assault upon himself (and attempting to protect the Company) would be inequitable. No just cause is shown.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant also argued he had a legitimate expectation to become DG. This Honourable Court note that any such expectation was expressly limited by his contract clauses, which subjected the promotion to “MIMA’s rules and regulations”. The law is that a “legitimate expectation” arises only if an employer’s promise or consistent policy gives rise to a contractual right or precondition. Here, the Company consistently advertised the DG post and chose other candidates (2018, 2020) while the Claimant did not object at the time.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: He even offered to interview for the position. In any event, a mere expectation without contractual or statutory basis cannot convert a dismissal for purported misconduct into unfair dismissal. Thus, this argument does not assist the Claimant, and in our view, no legitimate expectation to be appointed DG was established.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Having considered the testimony and documents, this Honourable Court find the Claimant’s evidence generally credible. He gave detailed contemporaneous evidence of his actions, and Board emails (as at CLB--2, COB6) and the payment memos corroborate much of his account. The finance officers’ statements (which was COW-1, COW-2) during cross-examination supported his version of the financial arrangements.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In contrast, the Company’s case relied heavily on inferences from the Claimant’s omissions (as not running insolvency checks), rather than contradictory factual testimony. There are no evidences from the witness, COW-1, COW-2; COW-3 testified that the Claimant was deceitful. In particular, the Company did not call as witnesses any of the senior Board members (such as Tan Sri Dato’ Sri Ramli or Dato’ Mohamed Suffian, who led the relevant committees). On this record, there is insufficient evidence of mala fides or ill intent by the Claimant. His errors, if any, appear to have been made in good faith to address urgent issues.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In weighing the punishment, this Honourable Court must apply the equitable “substantial merits” test. Even if the Claimant’s actions technically violated Company rules, they were done under duress of circumstances and with the aim of preserving Company operations. The Claimant had six (6) years three (3) months and one (1) day years of service, a clean record, and no previous warnings. He had been “groomed” for leadership, which suggests the Board valued his contribution. Termination of such a long-serving executive for procedural lapses (none involving dishonesty or loss) would be unduly harsh. Under Norizan Bakar V. Panzana Enterprise [2013] 6 MLRA 613; 9CLJ 409; 6MLJ 605 and related jurisprudence, the Court must substitute a just penalty when appropriate.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Honourable Court conclude that even if some misconduct is found, the sanction of summary dismissal is manifestly disproportionate. A reasonable employer would not have dismissed an employee of the Claimant’s standing for the irregularities in question.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: For the above reasons, the industrial court finds that the Company has failed to prove that the Claimant’s dismissal was with just cause or excuse. The misconduct charges were either not established or not of such gravity as to justify summary dismissal in fairness. The dismissal is therefore without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
It is settled law that where the misconducts were proven, the Industrial Court is duty bound to move on to consider whether the proven misconducts constitute just cause or excuse for the dismissal as stated in the Federal Court cases of Wong Yuen Hock (Supra) And Milan Auto (Supra).
Punishment Disproportionate to the Misconduct.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In support, we rely on the Federal Court authority of Norizan Bin Bakar V. Panzana Enterprise Sdn Bhd [2013] 6 MLJ 605 ("PANZANA case") which held as follows in the head notes at p.606 of the report. (3) In deciding whether a proven misconduct constituted just cause or excuse for dismissal the Industrial Court had power to decide, using the doctrine of proportionality of punishment which was inbuilt into the IRA and acting in accordance with equity, good conscience and the substantial merits of the case as mandated by s 30(5) of the IRA, whether the punishment of dismissal was appropriate or too harsh in the circumstances (see paras 35-36 & 39) of the case. (4) The Industrial Court could therefore substitute its own view, in place of the employers, as to what was the appropriate penalty for an employee's misconduct and go on to decide the relief to be granted by taking into account the claimants’ contributory misconduct (see para 39).’’

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Industrial Court in Kesatuan Kebangsaan Pekerja-Pekerja Bank Semenanjung Malaysia V. Malayan Banking Bhd [2012] 1 MELR 469 at p.480 of the report had discussed on the reasonableness of the employer's action in dismissing an employee. Referring to the judgment in Southern Bank Bhd V. Kamarudin Othman and Anor [2005] 6 CLJ 379 which followed the Federal Court decision in Ng Hock Cheng V. Pengarah Am Penjara & Ors [1998] 1 CLJ 405, the Industrial Court went on to state that the principle of proportionality of punishment must be reconciled with the test of reasonableness.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In Foley V. Post Office HSBC Bank Plc. (Formerly Midland Bank Plc.) V. Madden [2000] I.C.R 1283, the Court of Appeal stated as follows on the test for a reasonable employer at pp. 1292 - 1293. “It was also made clear in Iceland Frozen Food Ltd, at pp.24G-25B that the members of the tribunal must not simply consider whether they personally think that the dismissal is fair and they must not substitute their decision as to what was the right course to adopt for that of the employer. Their proper function is to determine whether the decision to dismiss the employee fell within the band of reasonable responses "which a reasonable employer might have adopted." ‘’In one sense it is true that, if the application of that approach leads the members of the tribunal to conclude that the dismissal was unfair, they are in effect substituting their judgment for that of the employer. Bui that process must always be conducted by reference to the objective standards of the reasonable employer which are imported by the statutory reference to their own subjective views of what they would in fact have done as an employer in the same circumstances.”

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In the case of Foley V. Post Office (Supra), the Court of Appeal had stated that the test of reasonableness or unreasonableness action of an employer must always be conducted by reference to the objective standard of the hypothetical reasonable employer and not by reference to their own subjective views of what they in fact would have done as an employer in the same circumstances.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In an earlier Court of Appeal decision in Union of Construction, Allied Trades and Technicians V. Brain [1981] ILR 542, his Lordship Donaldson L. J. had this to say whether the employer had acted reasonably or otherwise at p.550 of the report as follows: "Has the employer satisfied us that in the circumstances (having regard to equity and the substantial merits of the case) he acted reasonably in treating this conduct as a sufficient reason for dismissing the employee" see subsection (3). Whether someone acted reasonably is always a pure question of fact, so long as the tribunal deciding the issue correctly directs itself on the matters, which should and should not be taken into account. However, where Parliament has directed a tribunal to have regard to equity - and that, of course, means common fairness and not a particular branch of the law - and to the substantial merits of the case, the tribunal's duty is very plain. It has to look at the question in the round and without regard to a lawyer's [as at page 36 of 54] technicalities. It has to look at it in an employment and industrial relations context and not in the context of the Temple and Chancery Lane. It should therefore be very rare for any decision of an industrial tribunal under this section to give rise to any question of law. In addition, this is quite plainly, what Parliament intended. Of course, a tribunal can approach this simple question in a way, which is other than that which Parliament intended. However, where Parliament has given to the tribunal so wide a discretion, in my judgment, appellate courts should be very slow indeed to find that the tribunal has erred in law. When I refer to appellate courts, I do not mean only the Court of Appeal, because, although the Employment Appeal Tribunal calls itself a tribunal, it, like its predecessor, is declared by statute to be a superior court of record. It is now, after all, nearly 10 years since it was pointed out in Earl v Slater & Wheeler (Airline) Ltd. [1972] I.C.R. 508 that the reasonableness or otherwise of an employer's conduct must depend upon what he knew or ought to have known when he dismissed the employee.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In considering the reasonableness or unreasonableness response of the employer, another Division of the Industrial Court in Ricwil (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd V. Tham Chai Wan [2004] 3 ILR 293, after perusing Union Construction, Allied Trades & Technician (Supra) And Foley V. Post Office (Supra) decided that, taking into consideration the circumstances under which the Claimant committed the offence, punishment of dismissal was too harsh. The relevant passage is found at pp.302 303 of the report. "I am only able to consider the question of fairness of the company's response in the context of the reason found for the 37 of 54 dismissal, which in the instant case is the claimant's retort to COW-1 to "sack her". A punishment of dismissal for an act of insubordination as in the instant case arising under the circumstances described will be totally out of proportion to the graver men of the offence. Moreover, in this connection, I am aided by OP Malhotra the Law of Industrial Dispute, Vol 2, 6th End, at pp. 1294 and 1295 where the learned author writes: In order to avoid the charge of vindictiveness, justice, equity and fair play demand that the punishment must always be commensurate with the gravity of the offence charge. [as at Rama Kant Misra V. State of Uttar Pradesh 1982 Lab IC 1790, 1792 (SC)] Based on the discussion thus far the reasonable and inescapable conclusion cannot be other that the company had no just cause or excuse for the dismissal of the claimant. That being so, I find the claimant's dismissal by the company to be wrong.”

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The High Court in Sunmugam Subramaniam V. Jg Containers (M) Sdn Bhd & Anor [2000] 6 CLJ 521, overturned the Industrial Court's decision that upheld the employer's decision to dismiss the Claimant for misconduct on account of severity of the punishment.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: His Lordship Faiza Thamby Chik J in Sunmugam's case (Supra) quoted with approval at p. 535 of the report the dicta of M.P. Thakkar in the case of RM Parmer V. Gujarat Electricity Board [1983] 1 CLJ 261 as follows. “When different categories of the penalties can be imposed in respect of the alleged fault one of which is dismissal from service, the disciplinary authority perforce is required to consult himself for selecting the most appropriate penalty from out of the range of penalties available that can be imposed, having regard to the nature, content and gravity of the default. Unless the disciplinary authority reached the conclusion that having regard to the nature, content and magnitude of the fault committed by the employee concerned it Should be absolutely unsafe to retain him in service the maximum penalty of dismissal cannot be imposed. If a lesser penalty can be imposed without, seriously jeopardising the interest of the employer the disciplinary authority cannot impose the maximum penalty of dismissal from service. He is bound to ask his inner voice and rational faculty why a lesser penalty cannot be imposed”.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In the case of Abu Samah Othman V. Oriental Assemblers Sdn Bhd [2007] 3 ILR 1, the Johor Baharu High Court held that the punishment of dismissal was disproportionate to the offence that it merits the Court's intervention herein. His Lordship Syed Ahmad Helmy J stated as follows at p.6 of the report: “[16] Again on the principles of judicial review as laid down by the Court of Appeal decision in Menara Pan GlobaI Sdn Bhd V. Arokianathan a/I Sivapiragasam [2006] 2 CLJ 501 same is distinguishable in that it did not take into account the Federal Court decision on Ramachandran (supra) and also it did not touch on the issue or proportionality of sentence” [17] In any event to my mind the punishment meted out is disproportionate to alleged offence and bearing in mind that the applicant had been working for the respondent for nine years and there was no complaint about his work performance the punishment of dismissal is rather harsh as intercase of Sunmugam Subramaniam V. JG Container (M) Sdn Bhd & Anor [2000] 6 CLJ 521; Ricwil (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd V. Tham Chai Wan [2004] 3 293.”

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: There is a band of reasonableness, which a reasonable employer should consider before reaching a decision to impose the extreme penalty of dismissal. In deciding whether the Company had acted reasonably, refer in the dictum in Foley V. Post Office (Supra) which stated that reasonableness or unreasonableness action of the employer must be conducted by reference to the objective standard of the hypothetical reasonable employer and not by reference to their own subjective views of what they in fact would have done as an employer in the same circumstances.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Rely on the dictum of M.P. Thakkar J in the case of RM Parmer V. Gujarat Electricity Board [1983] 1 LLJ 261 cited in Sunmugam's case (Supra) which stated as follows at p.535 of the report. "If a lesser penalty can be imposed without seriously jeopardising the interest of the employer, the disciplinary authority cannot impose the maximum penalty of dismissal from service. He is bound to ask his inner voice and rational fault why a lesser penalty cannot be imposed.’’

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Industrial Court in Ang Tin Huat V. The Store (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd [2014] 1 ILR 85 ("The Store case") found the claimant guilty as charged for the 'unauthorised" Use of company money and stated that he could not be absolved himself of accountability for the use of financial assets or physical property of the company. Therefore, the claimant had been wrong from a perspective of the fiduciary relationship existing between the employer and employee.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The learned Chairman in Ang Tin Huat (supra) also went on to discuss the fiduciary nature of relationship by referring to decided cases and works of well-known authors as follows at pp. 100-102 of the report. In Azahari Shahrom & Anor V. Associated Pan Malaysia Cement Sdn Bhd [2010] 1 ILR 423 (Award No. 101 of 2010 p. 436) this court was of the view that: “It is trite that the association between employer and employee out of necessity is fiduciary in nature. There has to be mutual trust and confidence that one would deal with the other in all fairness and rectitude over the rights and obligations flowing between the parties under the employment agreement. If one does an act or commits an omission, which is inconsistent with that fiduciary relationship, then that act or omission will be mala fide. This principle has equal application as against the employer and the employee in their respective position viz. the employment relationship between them.’’

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Further, at paras 47, 48 and 49 at p. 105 of the report, the learned Chairman held that in equity and good conscience and the substantial merits of the case, the dismissal was excessively harsh, unjust and disproportionate. The relevant passage is reproduced below: [47] ‘’Applying the test as prescribed in Taylor V. Parsons Peebele Nei Bruce Peebles Ltd (supra), and if viewed in equity, good conscience and the substantial merits of this case; the termination in this instance appears excessively harsh, and disproportionate, taking into consideration the overall fidelity owed by the claimant to the company in the general scheme of things; [48] That there were other sanctions available in the "armoury of punishment" open to the company is trite. That they chose the ultimate one and applied it against the claimant in this instance was somewhat draconic, to say the least. Surely after 28 years of loyal service the claimant deserved a modicum of mercy; and [49] Hardly a reasonable reaction from a reasonable employer in the whole circumstances of the case.”

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In regard to the doctrine of proportionality, his Lordship Lee Swee Seng J, in THE STORE case referred to the Federal Court decision in PANZANA case and stated as follows at p. 17 of the report: “[42] Recently the Federal Court has clearly approved the application of the doctrine of proportionality in determining whether the dismissal of a workman can be upheld in a reference under s. 20(3) IRA. In other words, in determining whether the dismissal was for a just cause and excuse, the Industrial Court is entitled to ask itself if the dismissal, being the maximum punishment that could be meted out by an employer for the misconduct of its employee, is proportionate to the severity of the misconduct that the employee is guilty of. In the event that it is not, the Industrial Court would be perfectly justified in holding that the dismissal was without just cause and excuse in that it was disproportionate to the gravity of the misconduct and in assessing compensation, the Industrial Court may take into consideration the contributory conduct of the dismissed employee.’’

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Federal Court has placed the doctrine of proportionality in such cases beyond a pale of doubt in the relevant dicta of His Lordship Raus Sharif PCA in Norizan Bakar V. Panzana Enterprise Sdn Bhd [2013] 9 CLJ 409. ‘’The whole scheme and structure of managing industrial relations and disputes for the private sector under the IRA is that the doctrine of proportionality is applicable in any consideration as to whether dismissal is for just cause and excuse. Thus an employer under a reference under s. 20(3) IRA has both the burden of Droving the misconduct and also justifying that the dismissal is proportionate in the circumstances of the case.”

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Industrial Court in Warren Zawawi Hussein V. Wagner Global Services (M) Sdn Bhd [2012] 3 ILR 34, found that the employee had lied to the Company's chairman when he denied sending carbon copies of his email to other officers in the company. ‘’The company stated that despite of giving the claimant 3 opportunities to speak the truth, the claimant was adamant and maintained his position.’’ ‘’The claimant explained that it was his worst human error and was due to his mental and physical exhaustion.’’

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Industrial Court found for a fact that the claimant had indeed committed the misconduct. Then it went on to consider whether the dismissal was with just cause or excuse. The relevant passage at page 51 is reproduced below: "[39] In England, there is a need of the employer to have acted reasonably in dismissing an employee. In the case of Sandhu V. DES [7978] 1 RLR 208 it was held that the tribunal must still go on to consider whether the dismissal was reasonable. In the words of Sir John Donaldson, MR the Court has to consider whether the dismissal was fair on the facts before it.’’

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In Sundararaj M Ramasamy & Ors V. Nittsu Transport Services (M) Sdn Bhd (2014) 2 MELR 268, the Learned Chairman held that the Company has established the misconduct of illegal picket and that the said illegal picket was a serious misconduct. However, on the quantum of punishment, the Court held that it was too harsh and excessive and held the dismissal to be without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Using the doctrine of proportionality of punishment, the court next consider the issue as to whether the punishment of dismissal was too harsh in the circumstances.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Following these principles, the claims of the following claimants are allowed applying the test under the second limb of Milan Auto. Claimant's six (6) years and three (3) months of Unblemished Service Is a Relevant Factor

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
