chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In reaching its decision that the dismissal was excessive and harsh though the Claimant had past record of misconduct, the learned chairman in Wan Encik Azman Wan Hussein V. Perusahaan Sadijr Timah Malaysia (Perstima) Berhad [2013] 3 ILR 97 held that it was without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
In the case of Ahmad Kamaruzaman Azizan V. Continental Tyre (M) Sdn Bhd) [2015] 4 ILR 489 the Court found that the Claimant's misconduct of leaving the work place earlier without any approval form his superior was proven. However, the Learned Chairman held that the punishment of dismissal was harsh and without just cause or excuse. The relevant passage at pp 506-507 of the report is reproduced below: ‘’[54] The next issue is whether this established misconduct entitles the company to dismiss the claimant on the basis of just cause or excuse; i.e., was the ultimate sanction in industrial jurisprudence appropriate in this case. [55] It must be borne in mind that in deciding on the appropriate punishment for misconduct the company ought to be bound by the rules of fairness. To do this the company must demonstrate that it had fully or at least substantially appraised the actual breaches or misconduct perpetrated by the claimant as against his antecedents with the company. Did he have a record of past employment infringements? What was the nature, the magnitude or seriousness of those infringements? Was he adequately warned, advised or counselled over his previous infringements The failure of the company to adduce evidence on the prevailing state of affairs and particulars that were taken into account and/or evaluated, peculiar to the claimant, leading to the decision to terminate renders the company's action subject to the intervention of this court Equity and good conscience in the whole circumstances of this case demand it; and even more so given the long years of service rendered by the claimant to the company and duly acknowledged by them on the very day of the dismissal! In the premises, it is the ruling of this court that the punishment of dismissal in the instant case was harsh and for that reason it is hereby set aside as being without just cause or excuse”. [Emphasis added]
No Financial Loss and Reputation of Company Not Tarnished

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: There was no evidence at all to show that the Company had suffered any financial loss or its reputation tarnished as a result of the Claimant's alleged misconduct.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In this present action, the Claimant did not have any history of misconduct, which were proven by the Company; therefore, the Company’s decision to terminate the Claimant’s employment was procedurally unfair and done is an unjust manner.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
This Court is of the view that the following facts should also be taken into consideration in making an appropriate order:
a) The Claimant has served the Company for over six (6) years and three (3) months and one (1) day clean disciplinary record. During the Claimant’s tenure of service, the Claimant had no disciplinary issues with the Company.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In the present case, as mentioned earlier, this Court is satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Company had failed to made out the case of misconduct against the Claimant. As such, the termination of the Claimant is now rendered as null and void.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In addition, when carrying out any disciplinary actions, the employer must ensure that the existing law, rules and procedures are adhered to. In this regard, it has been the practice of the Industrial Court to look at the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony 1975 (“the Code”) in determining the issue of fairness. Though the Code has no legal force and its acceptance is voluntary, it is still relevant for the purpose of considering the overall reasonableness of the employer’s action.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Clause 41 and 42 of the Code is a provision on Procedure for Disciplinary Action as follows : “41. An employer should ensure that a fair, effective and expeditious procedure exists for dealing with disciplinary matters. Such procedure may be established in consultation with the employees’ representatives or trade as appropriate. The employer should define and make known to each employee the rules of work and the disciplinary action, which may follow if they are broken. Penalties should be graduated according to the seriousness of the offence. An employee should not, be dismissed except in cases of gross misconduct, be dismissed for a first offence. 42. The disciplinary procedure should be in writing and be made known to each employee. The proceedings should be conducted in accordance with the rules of natural justice”

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The High Court in Credit Corporation (M) Bhd V. Choo Kam Sing & Anor [1998] 2 MELR 256 noted that although the Code has no legal force, it is nevertheless relevant factor to be looked at for the purpose of considering the overall reasonableness of the employer’s action in dismissal cases. In fact, section 30(5A) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 empowers the Industrial Court in making an award to take into consideration the requirements of the Code.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In view of all the above and after taking into consideration the evidence adduced during the Trial , this Court is satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Company had failed to prove that the termination of the Claimant was with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
Furthermore, in the case of Jessica Barthy Das Sivadas V. American Express (M) Sdn Bhd [2023] 4 ILR 374, it was held as follows: - ‘’ [14] The burden of proof in an unfair dismissal claim lies on the employer to prove on a balance of probabilities that the employee is guilty of the allegation or the reason for the dismissal. This court will now refer to the case of Ireka Construction Berhad V. Chantiravathan Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 11 (Award No. 245 of 1995), in which case it was stated that: ‘’It is a basic principle of industrial jurisprudence that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer to prove that he has just cause and excuse for taking the decision to impose the disciplinary measure of dismissal upon the employee. The just cause must be either a misconduct, negligence or poor performance based on the facts of the case. It went further to state that: “The only issue for this court to determine now is whether the Companies, on a balance of probabilities has established the poor performance of the claimant. As far as unsatisfactory performance is concerned the Industrial Court has laid down that in order to justify the dismissal of the claimant on this ground, the Company has to establish:
(ii) that the claimant was warned about his poor performance; (iii) that the claimant was accorded sufficient opportunity to improve; and (iv) that notwithstanding the above, the claimant failed to sufficiently improve his performance.’’
However, the Company had failed to establish the above mentioned requirements, as it is undisputed that the Company had failed to adduce any positive evidence to show that the Claimant was warned pertaining to any of the alleged acts. Subsequently, the Claimant was suspended immediately after the allegations were raised by the Company.’’

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Whether The Claimant’s Dismissal by the Company Was Proportionate
content: This Honourable Court found that the Claimant’s dismissal from the Company was not proportionate as it was done in a haste and sudden manner.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Whether The Claimant’s Dismissal by the Company Was Proportionate
content:
Refer to the above mentioned case of Gartner Research & Advisory (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd wherein in holding that the Company needs to strike a balance between severity of an employee's conduct and the sanction imposed, the court held as follows:- [32] Further, in the Court of Appeal case of Ngiam Geok Mooi V. Pacific World Destination East Sdn Bhd [2001] 3 ILR 229, the Court explained the need to strike a balance between severity of an employee's conduct and the sanction imposed. [33] In Ngiam's case the appellant was dismissed from her employment for insubordination of her superior's orders which are as follows: "(i) refused to follow her superior's instructions to make payment for a Companies-related expense and to make adjustments to the Budget 2009/2010; and (ii) wrote an e-mail saying that she won't report to the said superior." [34] In the said case, the Court of Appeal found that the employer's decision to dismiss the employee was harsh and grossly disproportionate to the misconduct committed having taken into consideration the following factors:
(i) the appellant had worked for the respondent for 20 years; (ii) the appellant had an unblemished employment record; (iii) the appellant was instrumental in setting up the respondent's headquarters in Penang and the branch office in Kuala Lumpur; (iv) the appellant's tireless and faithful service to the respondent is evidenced by the profits earned by the respondent; (v) the appellant had committed a single act of insubordination; and (vi) the said insubordination was the appellant's first misconduct in her long years of service. There was no history of past misconduct, even no warning was given to her at any point of time.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Whether The Claimant’s Dismissal by the Company Was Proportionate
content:
The Claimant refers to the case of Benjamin Lim Siaw Ming V. Syarikat Sesco Berhad [2023] 2 ILR 591, in holding that the employee’s dismissal was not proportionate when other means were less severe sanctions were available, the court held as follows:- ‘’Proportionality of Punishment [87] The claimant raised the issue of proportionality of punishment and submits that the punishment of dismissal was too harsh and disproportionate to the seriousness of the charges of misconduct. [88] The Companies, on the other hand submits that the dismissal of the claimant was with just cause and excuse. [89] The Federal Court in Norizan Bakar V. Panzana Enterprise Sdn Bhd [2013] 9 CLJ 409; [2013] 6 MLJ 605 held that the Industrial Court is duty bound to consider proportionality of punishment when exercising its powers under s. 30(5) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 to act according to equity, good conscience and substantial merits of the case. [90] The proportionality principle requires the court to strike a balance between the severity of an employee's conduct and the sanction imposed. In the present case, whether such alleged misconducts constitute just cause or excuse for the dismissal of the claimant from the Companies? [91] In the present case, this court is of the view that the following facts should also be taken into consideration in making an appropriate order:
(i) the claimant has served the Company for 13 years with clean disciplinary record. During the claimant's tenure of service, the claimant had no disciplinary issues with the Companies; (ii) the claimant was also the victim of the scam whereby he did a Master's Program in Human Resource for three years which cost him a sum of RM25,000; (iii) despite the involvement of the other employees, only the claimant and one Lucilla Mary Joseph were terminated from the Companies; (iv) COW3 who was also involved in the conduct of the career development programs was never issued with any warning letter or subjected to any disciplinary action by the Companies; (v) despite the Companies’ finding of negligence against COW4 who was the Companies’ engineer, COW4 was only issued with a warning letter; (vi) COW5 and COW8 who were responsible in executing the contract agreements to appoint PSSB as the course provider were only issued with a warning letter, and were promoted in their respective positions in the Companies; and (vii) although the Company found that COW7 was negligent, COW7 who was the Companies’ Manager of Legal Affairs was only issued with a warning letter and was promoted by the Companies. [92] In passing a just and appropriate order, the Industrial Court is obliged to do a balancing exercise. It was held by the Court of Appeal in Tan Poh Thiam V. Industrial Court of Malaysia & Anor [2015] 1 LNS 1534 (Civil Appeal J-01-414-12-2013) that: [4] Industrial law jurisprudence does not permit any form of oppressive conduct on the part of an employer having the objective of dismissing the employee on "just cause or excuse" based on trivial allegations; based on matters that could have been dealt with appropriately with proper operating system or management system instead of taking drastic steps to dismiss the employee. ‘’The Industrial Court in the Malaysian context is obliged to do a balancing exercise taking into account such factors as the nature of complaint the conduct of the employer, the operating and management system that is in place, the reason advanced by the employee as well as his conduct, and the gravity of the allegation; in order to ascertain whether the employee's act or omission qualifies as a misconduct to attract s. 20 on Industrial Relations Act 1967 (IRA 1967). The proposition is fortified by s. 30 of IRA 1967.’’ [93] In the present case, the dismissal of the claimant was without just cause or excuse on the ground that the charges were defective ab initio and therefore there is no further need to look into the merits of the Company’s case. This court holds that the dismissal of the claimant constitutes unlawful termination and was in breach of the principles of natural justice. [94] In any event, this court is convinced that the claimant could have been dealt with appropriately with proper management system. The Company could have opted for other lesser forms of punishment instead of taking drastic steps by terminating his service. Hence, it is now safe to conclude that the dismissal of the claimant was disproportionate to the alleged misconducts. [95] In Goodyear Malaysia Bhd and National Company of Employees in Company Manufacturing Rubber Products (Award No. 88 of 1986) it was held that; ‘’It must be noted that not all misconduct deserves dismissal, which has been described as the capital punishment in industrial relations. Important circumstances, which mitigate the offence of the workman, should be taken into account by the employer before he can be said to have made a fair and reasonable decision to dismiss. For example, a workman's past record of good service, or the management's own actions or omission which contributed to the misconduct, are mitigating factors which any reasonable employer would take into account before dismissing length and quality of service, good untainted record, and past service awards and recognition must also be taken as extenuating circumstances when an employer decides the appropriate punishment for the misconduct.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Whether The Claimant’s Dismissal by the Company Was Proportionate
content: In this present instance, the Company had dismissed the Claimant from his employment in a haste and arbitrary manner, in which the allegations were raised in a sudden manner and were done in bad faith by the Company. The Company could had dealt with the allegations (if proven) in a less severe fashion such as providing a proper management and/or understanding the issues surrounding its employees, particularly the Claimant in this instance.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Whether The Claimant’s Dismissal by the Company Was Proportionate
content: It is trite the onus remains on the Company to prove that the Claimant was dismissed with just cause and excuse, wherein the Claimant submits that the Company had failed to prove its allegations.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Whether The Claimant’s Dismissal by the Company Was Proportionate
content: Pursuant to section 30(5) of the IRA1967 and after having considered the totality of the evidence adduced, this Court is of the view that the Company had failed to establish on the balance of probabilities that the dismissal of the Claimant from his employment with the company was with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Whether The Claimant’s Dismissal by the Company Was Proportionate
content: This Court having ruled that the Claimant was dismissed without just cause or excuse, will now consider the appropriate remedy for the Claimant.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: For the above reasons, this court finds that the Company has failed to prove that the Claimant’s dismissal was with just cause or excuse. The misconduct charges were either not established or not of such gravity as to justify summary dismissal in fairness. The dismissal is therefore without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: By Section 30(5) IRA 1967, this Court may order reinstatement or compensation. The usual relief is reinstatement with back wages, or compensation in lieu of reinstatement and back wages (capped at 24 months’ salary) for the period of unemployment. Given the Claimant’s senior position and long tenure, the primary relief is reinstatement to his former position (or equivalent), with continuity of service. The Company shall pay the Claimant’s back wages from 2 May 2021 (date of termination) to the date of this Award, subject to the statutory cap of 24 months. In addition, in lieu of reinstatement (should reinstatement not be practicable), the Company shall pay compensation amounting to one month’s salary on the service of the Claimant to satisfaction of the unjust dismissal claim.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Honourable Court trust the parties will co-operate to effect reinstatement if desired, but if not, the compensation sum is declared due forthwith. Interest on any unpaid award shall run at the statutory rate from the date of this Award until payment.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Section 30(5) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 empowers this Honourable Court to make an order for reinstatement or, in lieu thereof, award compensation and back wages. The guiding principle, as consistently affirmed by the superior courts, is that reinstatement remains the primary remedy in cases where the dismissal is found to be without just cause or excuse, unless reinstatement has become impracticable due to exceptional circumstances.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In Assunta Hospital V. Dr A. Dutt [1981] 1 MLJ 115, the Federal Court held that reinstatement is the normal and primary relief, as the Industrial Court’s function is to restore the employee to the position, he would have held but for the unjust dismissal. Similarly, in Hotel Jaya Puri Bhd V. National Union of Hotel, Bar & Restaurant Workers [1980] 1 MLJ 109, the Court emphasized that reinstatement should not be denied merely on the ground of strained relations unless such strain renders continued employment impossible.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This position was reaffirmed in Sime UEP Properties Bhd V. Chu Ah Poi [2008] 9 CLJ 73 (CA), where the Court of Appeal observed that compensation is a secondary remedy and should only be awarded when reinstatement is clearly impracticable. The Court reiterated that the Industrial Court must examine the surrounding facts to determine whether reinstatement can realistically be implemented.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In the present case, the Claimant had served the Respondent with an unblemished record prior to the dismissal. The dismissal was found to be without just cause or excuse, and no evidence was adduced to show that the employment relationship had deteriorated to such an extent that reinstatement would be untenable. The Claimant’s position remains available within the organizational structure, and no evidence was led to suggest redundancy or closure of the role.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Accordingly, this Honourable Court finds that reinstatement is both legally justified and practically feasible. This remedy best accords with the principle of industrial justice and the restorative purpose of the Industrial Relations Act.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: It is trite and well-established that reinstatement is the primary and preferred remedy in cases brought pursuant to Section 20 of the Industrial Relations Act 1967(“IRA 1967”). The Federal Court in Wong Chee Hong V. Cathay Organization (M) Sdn Bhd [1988] 1 CLJ (Rep) 298 affirmed that reinstatement is the normal consequence where a dismissal is found to be without just cause or excuse, unless the employer proves compelling reasons why reinstatement should not be ordered.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Section 20 of the IRA 1967 is remedial in nature and seeks to restore the workman to the employment from which he was unjustly removed. The Industrial Court has repeatedly held that reinstatement aims to “place the workman in the position he would have been but for the dismissal”, consonant with the principles of equity, good conscience, and the substantial merits of the case mandated by Section 30(5) IRA.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Court is guided also by the Federal Court in Norizan Bakar V. Panzana Enterprise [2013] 6 MLJ 605, where His Lordship Raus Sharif PCA reiterated that reinstatement must be considered first, and compensation in lieu only where reinstatement is proven impracticable. In Wong Yuen Hock V. Hong Leong Assurance [1995] 3 CLJ 344, the Federal Court further emphasized that reinstatement is the “main and only’ proper remedy unless circumstance show that the employment relationship has irretrievably broken down.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Company did not adduce any evidence demonstrating that reinstatement is impossible, unworkable, undesirable or counterproductive. Neither was it argued that the Claimants’ reinstatement would cause operational disruption, financial hardship, or a breakdown in trust that would make future cooperation untenable.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The evidence before this Court shows no element of dishonesty, fraud or personal gain on the part of the Claimant. The findings above show that the so-called “misconduct” relied upon by the Company was either not proven, partially proven or established to be procedural lapses committed during a period of organizational vacuum, with no improper motive. The Claimant acted at all material times to safeguard the functioning of the Company in the absence of effective governance and absent action by the Board.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant had served the Company for approximately six (6) years and three (3) months with an unblemished record, had shouldered senior responsibilities including Acting Director General and had been entrusted with critical functions without issue until the events culminating in his dismissal. The Company produced no evidence that the Claimant demonstrated any behavior that would preclude a viable employment relationship.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Industrial Court is guided by numbers authorities that reinstatement remains appropriate where the alleged misconduct does not to go the root of trust and confidence. In Ricwil (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd V. Tham Chai Wan [2004] 3 ILR 293 and Abu Samah Othman V. Oriental Assemblers [2007] 3 ILR 1, the High Court intervened where dismissal was disproportionate and held that the workman should be restored unless trust is clearly broken. No such evidence exists here.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Reinstatement as the Most Just Remedy
content: The evidence overall supports the conclusion that the Claimant’s dismissal was substantively unjust, and procedurally tainted by the Company’s failure to undertake a fair and reasonable assessment of the circumstances leading to the alleged wrongdoing.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Reinstatement as the Most Just Remedy
content: Having considered the entire factual matrix, this Court finds no basis to conclude that reinstatement would be oppressive to the Company, unworkable, or detrimental to industry harmony. On the contrary, reinstatement ensure that the workmen receives the full measure of justice contemplated by the IRA 1967.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Reinstatement as the Most Just Remedy
content: As such, reinstatement, without loss of wages, seniority, benefits, and continuity of service, is the most appropriate, equitable and legally correct remedy in this case. Compensation in lieu of reinstatement is inappropriate, as the Company has failed to discharge the burden of proving that reinstament is not feasible.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Reinstatement as the Most Just Remedy
content: In respect of the quantum the Court is mindful of the view taken by Tun Salleh Abas FJ in the case of Hotel Jaya Puri Bhd. V. National Company of Hotel, Bar & Restaurant Workers & Anor [1990] 1 MLJ 109: “..if there is a legal basis for paying the compensation, the amount of course is very much a matter of the discretion which the Industrial Court is fully empowered under s.30 of the IRA 1967 to fix.”

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Back wages are calculated based on the Claimant’s last drawn salary but limited to 24 months. From the back wages, the court is required to make a deduction for any contributory conduct; post dismissal earnings and delay in the hearing of the case but such a deduction need not involve a mathematical calculation.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In determining the appropriate quantum of back wages, this Court is duty-bound to consider whether the Claimant contributed to the circumstances leading to his dismissal. While this Court has found that the dismissal was without just cause or excuse, the Claimant cannot be fully absolved of responsibility regarding the procedural irregularities identified in Second (failure to strictly verify Encik Azman’s bankruptcy status) and Third (the utilization of personal accounts for Company payments). As the Acting Director General, the Claimant was expected to exercise a high degree of administrative diligence.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: However, the evidence establishes that these actions were not driven by malice, dishonesty, or personal gain, but were executed in good faith to ensure the Company's continued operations during a critical shortage of signatories. Therefore, applying the principles of equity and proportionality, this Court finds that a deduction of 20% from the back wages is just and appropriate. This percentage serves to acknowledge the Claimant’s contributory fault in failing to adhere to strict procedural protocols, while reflecting that these errors were minor and technical in nature compared to the severity of the dismissal.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Court is bound by the principle laid down in the case of Dr. James Alfred (Sabah) V. Koperasi Serbaguna Sanya Bhd (Sabah) & Anor [2001] 3 CLJ 541. His Lordship Justice Tan Sri Steve Shim CJ (Sabah & Sarawak) in delivering the judgement of the Federal Court held that: ‘’In our view, it is in line with equity and good conscience that the Industrial Court, in assessing quantum of back wages, should take into account the fact, if established by evidence or admitted, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. Failure to do so constitutes a jurisdictional error of law. Certiorari will therefore lie to rectify it. Of course, taking into account such employment after dismissal does not necessarily mean that the Industrial Court has to conduct a mathematical exercise in deduction. What is important is that the Industrial Court, in the exercise of its discretion in assessing the quantum of back wages, should take into account all relevant matters including the fact, where it exists, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. This discretion is in the nature of a decision-making process.’’

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
This Court have carefully examined the facts and evidence in this case and of the view that there was contributory factor on the part of the Claimant. Hence, under this item, there is deduction shall be made to this contributory factor.
DELAY

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: From an examination of the notes of proceedings, this Court is satisfied that the Claimant did not occasion any delay in connection with the hearing of this ministerial reference. Hence, there is no deduction under this head.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: At the time of dismissal, the Claimant last drawn basic salary with fixed allowance was RM 19,300.00 [as at CLB-3 page 15]. On the facts of this case, there is no evidence of any post- dismissal income after the Claimant was dismissed by the Company. Hence, there shall be no deduction under this item. The Claimant has served the Company for over six (6) years three (3) months and one (1) day, which was from 01.01.2015 until 02.04.2021.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Regarding the issue of gainful employment, the Court is guided by the principle that back wages are compensatory in nature. However, in this present case, the Claimant has adduced evidence that he has remained unemployed and has not secured any alternative employment from the date of his termination on 02.05.2021 until the conclusion of the hearing of this case. Furthermore, there is no evidence before this Court to show that the Claimant had obtained any post-dismissal earnings during the interim period. As the Claimant has generated no income since his dismissal, this Court holds that no deduction shall be made from the back wages under this head.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
After having considered the evidence adduced before this Court as well as the submission by both parties, the remedies are as follows:
i. Back wages for twenty (24) months based on the Claimant’s last drawn salary: RM 19,300.00 X 24 months = RM 463,200.00 Less 20% (Proportionality of Punishment 20 %:)
= (RM 92,640.00)
________________
TOTAL = RM 370,560.00
________________

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In this case, the Claimant also involve in the proportionality of Punishment the facts of the case and the back wages here to be deducted on 20% basis.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The monetary award in a total sum of RM 370,560.00 less statutory deductions, if any, shall be paid by the Company to the Claimant via his representative Messrs. Ganpartnership within 30 days of the award with interest of 8% per annum to be calculated from 30 days of the award until full and final settlement.

case_name: Rizal bin Abdul Kadir v Maritime Institute of Malaysia
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Court verily believe that this Award is just and appropriate in the light of the particular facts of the present case and guided by the principles of equity, good conscience and substantial merits of this case without regard to technicalities and legal forms.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content:
The role of the Industrial Court was lucidly explained by His Lordship Raja Azlan Shah CJ (Malaya) (as His Royal Highness then was) in Goon Kwee Phoy v. J & P Coats (M) Bhd. [1981] CLJU 30; [1981] 1 LNS 30; [1981] 1 MLJ 129, at p. 136 as follows:
“Where representations are made and are referred to the Industrial Court for enquiry, it is the duty of the court to determine whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse. If the employer chooses to give a reason or excuse for the action taken by him, the duty of the Industrial Court will be to enquire whether that reason or excuse has or has not been made out. If it finds as a fact that it has not been proven, then the inevitable conclusion must be that the termination or dismissal was without just cause or excuse. The proper enquiry of the court is the reason advanced by the employer, and that court or the High Court cannot go into another reason not relied on by the employer, or find one for him.”

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content:
The Federal Court in Wong Yuen Hock v. Syarikat Hong Leong Assurance Sdn. Bhd. & Another Appeal [1995] 3 CLJ 344 at p. 352 succinctly stated the function of the Industrial Court in dealing with dismissal cases as follows:
“On the authorities, we were of the view that the main and only function of the Industrial Court in dealing with a reference under s. 20 of the Act (unless otherwise lawfully provided by the terms of the reference) is to determine whether the misconduct or irregularities complained of by the management as the grounds of dismissal were in fact committed by the workman, and if so, whether such grounds constitute just cause or excuse for the dismissal.”

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content:
The said principle was reiterated in Milan Auto Sdn. Bhd. v. Wong Seh Yen [1995] 4 CLJ 449 at pp. 454 and 455 by the Federal Court, where His Lordship Mohamed Azmi FCJ said:
“As pointed out by this court recently in Hong Leong Assurance Sdn. Bhd. v. Wong Yuen Hock [1995] 3 CLJ 344; [1995] 2 MLJ 753, the function in the Industrial Court in dismissal cases on a reference under s.20 is two-fold: first to determine whether the misconduct complained of by the employer has been established and secondly to determine whether the proven misconduct constitutes just cause or excuse for the dismissal of the employee.”

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: The standard of proof applicable to dismissal cases is the civil standard of proof on a balance of probabilities as decided by the Court of Appeal in Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara v. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor [2002] 3 CLJ 314. It was held that: “Thus, we can see that the preponderant view is that the Industrial Court, when hearing a claim of unjust dismissal, even where the ground is one of dishonest act, including "theft", is not required to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the employee has "committed the offence", as in a criminal prosecution... In our view the passage quoted from Administrative Law by HWR Wade & C.F. Forsyth offers the clearest statement on the standard of proof required, that is the civil standard based on balance of probabilities, which is flexible, so that the degree of probability required is proportionate to the nature and gravity of the issue.”

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content:
In Ireka Construction Berhad v. Chantiravathan Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 11 , the Industrial Court had this to say with regards to the burden of proof placed on the company:
“It is basic principle of industrial jurisprudence that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed that offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer to prove that he has just cause and excuse for taking the decision to impose the disciplinary measure of dismissal upon the employee. The just cause must be, either a misconduct, negligence or poor performance based on the facts of the case...”

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: The standard of proof applicable to dismissal cases is the civil standard of proof on a balance of probabilities as decided by the Court of Appeal in Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara v. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor [2002] 3 CLJ 314 as follows: “Thus, we can see that the preponderant view is that the Industrial Court, when hearing a claim of unjust dismissal, even where the ground is one of dishonest act, including "theft", is not required to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the employee has "committed the offence", as in a criminal prosecution... In our view the passage quoted from Administrative Law by H.W.R. Wade & C.F. Forsyth offers the clearest statement on the standard of proof required, that is the civil standard based on balance of probabilities, which is flexible, so that the degree of probability required is proportionate to the nature and gravity of the issue.”

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content:
In Lee Mei Wan v. Ultimate Media Group Pty Ltd. [2017] ILRU 1668; [2017] 2 LNS 1668, it was observed by the learned Chairman that:
“Ex Parte Hearing
[4] Sub-section 29(d) of Act 177 provides for an ex parte hearing without the presence of one of the parties to the dispute as follows:
The court may, in any proceedings before it:
(a) ... (d) hear and determine the matter before it notwithstanding the failure of any party to submit any written statement whether of case or reply to the court within such time as maybe prescribed by the President or in the absence of any party to the proceedings who has been served with a notice or summons to appear.”

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content:
OP Malhotra, "The Law of Industrial Disputes" Volume 1: 6th. Edition, at p. 1062 states:
“If, however, a party wilfully absents himself in such a way that the adjudication is likely to be impede, or wilfully tries to delay or avoid the proceedings, the tribunal may fix a pre-emptory hearing on a particular day. After reasonable notice of hearing has been given to the defaulting party, if he still neglects or refuses to attend, the tribunal may and ought to hear in his absence. Prompt discharge of business is of particular importance before a tribunal adjudicating an industrial dispute....”

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: Therefore, the Court was of the view that in the circumstances of this case, an ex parte hearing was warranted due to the Company's failure to attend Court although the Notice of Hearing and the earlier Notice of Mention had been served on it as stated above. Also see the case of: Zahari Ruslan v. Wajib Cemerlang Sdn. Bhd. [2011] 2 LNS 0450.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content:
On the other hand, this Court is also mindful of its duty to adjudicate the matter on merit, albeit the case proceeded ex parte. The Claimant must be subject to the burden to prove his/her case on the balance of probabilities. This is succinctly set out in the case of Wong Brothers' Building Construction v. Choo Chee Siam [2005] 2 ILR 356 in which the Company was absent during the date of the hearing. The Court continued to hear the case on an ex parte basis, wherein the Court held, inter alia, as follows:
“The Court is mindful of the role in ex parte hearing by referring to the case of Ike Video Distributors Sdn. Bhd. v. Chan Chee Bin [2004] 2 ILR 687 where the Learned Chairman quoted from the book "The Law of Industrial Disputes" by OP Malhotra Vol. 3rd. edition. At p. 716:
“A rule empowering the tribunal to proceed ex parte if a party is absent and sufficient cause is not shown for his absence, would not enable it either to do away with the inquiry or straight away pass on an Award without giving finding on the merits of the disputes. In other words, the absence of a party does not entail the consequence that an Award will straightaway be made against him.”

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content:
In the case of Manimaran Karuvanan v. Tav Facility Solution (M) Sdn. Bhd. [2020] MELRU 1374 the Company failed to turn up when the case was called for a hearing. The Industrial Court had proceeded with an ex-parte hearing on the merit of the case pursuant to s. 29(d) of the IRA 1967. It was held inter alia as follows:
"As such, both parties had been sufficiently informed of the hearing dates fixed for this case. However, the Company failed to turn up in Court on the Hearing date. Hence, the hearing was ordered to proceed Ex-Parte pursuant to s. 29(d) of the IRA 1967".

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: ii) Whether the dismissal was with just cause and excuse Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content:
The dispute before this Court relates to the claim by the Claimant that she was dismissed from her employment without just cause or excuse by the Company. Due to the absence of the Company and its representative, the case proceeded by an ex-parte hearing. Section 29(d) of Act 177 provides for an ex-parte hearing without the presence of one of the parties to the dispute as follows:
“The Court may, in any proceedings before it: (a)...(d) hear and determine the matter before it notwithstanding the failure of any party to submit any written statement whether of case or reply to the Court within such time as maybe prescribed by the President or in the absence of any party to the proceedings who has been served with a notice or summons to appear".

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: ii) Whether the dismissal was with just cause and excuse Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: An ex-parte hearing was necessary in light of the circumstances of the case, given the Claimant's readiness to proceed and the Company's absence from Court, despite having been duly served with the Notice of Hearing and the prior Notice of Mention, as previously indicated.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: ii) Whether the dismissal was with just cause and excuse Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: In the present case, the sole witness is the Claimant herself. The only issue to be decided by this Court is the claim by the Claimant that she had been terminated from her employment without just cause or excuse by the Company on 08/11/2024 vide Dismissal Letter dated 28/10/2024. It is undisputed and unchallenged evidence that throughout the Claimant's employment in the Company, as she had carried out her functions and responsibilities to the best of her ability and capability for the Company, however, she was not treated as a permanent employee but her employment status was changed to "contract staff" without any consultation to obtain her consent and agreement and without taking into account her length of service which clearly violated the fundamental terms and conditions in the employment contract between the parties. This matter and evidence were never answered and challenged by the Company in this claim.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: ii) Whether the dismissal was with just cause and excuse Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: The Claimant asserts that the termination of her service was a termination simpliciter as no reasons was advanced by the Company and no notice of termination was issued to her. The decision of the Company vide letter dated 16/09/2024 by converting the Claimant’s status of employment from permanent staff to contract staff in the Company was a clear breach of fundamental terms and conditions of the Claimant’s employment with the Company at the material time. In addition, it was carried out without obtaining prior consent from the Claimant culminating a clear violation and breach of the Claimant's terms and conditions of service, whereby the Company's unilateral action against the Claimant has never been challenged neither explained by the Company in the proceedings. Nonetheless, the Company did not proffer any reason for the termination of her employment.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: ii) Whether the dismissal was with just cause and excuse Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: It must be said that by being absent from attending the hearing and producing witnesses to contradict the Claimant's evidence during trial, the Company must be taken to agreeing to the Claimant's contentions or that the Company had no interest to challenge the Claimant's testimony. It must be noted that above all, the Company did not file its Statement in Reply to answer the Claimant's Statement of Case.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: ii) Whether the dismissal was with just cause and excuse Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: It is profound finding and abundantly clear that the Company has failed to produce witnesses to adduce evidence to contradict the only evidence available before this Court testified by the Claimant. As such, this Court is of the views that the Claimant has prescribed admissible evidence on the balance of probabilities in support of her case of unfair termination.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: ii) Whether the dismissal was with just cause and excuse Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: This Court is of the considered views that the Claimant had sufficiently proved on the balance of the probabilities that her termination was without just cause or excuse. The Company has failed to comply with due process in taking the action of terminating the Claimant. In the absence of evidence that justify to the contrary, the Company had failed to produce evidence in rebuttal to the evidence led by the Claimant before this Court. Failure to be present in Court by Company's witness thereby enabling cross examination of the Claimant's evidence certainly of no assistance whatsoever to this Court. Given the circumstances, in the course of dispensing justice, this Court is compelled to accept the ex-parte evidence adduced by the Claimant. In the absence of any evidence to the contrary to rebut the submissions presented to this Court by the Claimant, this Court is compelled to accept the truth in the Claimant's complaints in the aforesaid that goes to the fundamental breaches in the Claimant's employment contract.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: ii) Whether the dismissal was with just cause and excuse Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: Notwithstanding that, this Court is of the views that the Claimant had sufficiently proved on the balance of the probabilities that she had been summarily dismissed by the breaches of fundamental terms of the employment contract by the Company. The Company had clearly failed to remedy the said breaches. In any event, the Company had failed to produce any evidence in rebuttal to the evidence led by the Claimant before this Court. The absence of the Company for the hearing merely to confirm that there was no question to be put to the Claimant for cross examination was devoid of any assistance to this Court whatsoever.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: ii) Whether the dismissal was with just cause and excuse Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: In the foregoing, this Court finds that the Claimant in fact was dismissed by the Company on 08/11/2024. Be that as it may, the Company had failed to discharge the burden of proof that the Claimant was terminated with just cause or excuse with the issuance of the Dismissal Letter dated 28/10/2024 against the Claimant. The Company had failed to show that it had acted bona fide in terminating the Claimant's services.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: ii) Whether the dismissal was with just cause and excuse Evaluation of Evidence & Findings
content: Based on totality of the evidence, the Court found that the dismissal of the Claimant was tainted with unfair labour practice and was not carried out with bona fide. Hence, the dismissal was made without just cause and excuse. It is therefore this Court's conclusion based on equity and good conscience that the Claimant had successfully made out her case of termination without just cause or excuse. The Company had failed to prove its case of a valid dismissal of the Claimant by failing to attend and adduce evidence on the hearing date. It must necessarily follow that the Claimant's case be hereby allowed.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
content: As such, in the circumstances, this Court found that the Claimant's dismissal without just cause or excuse. On another note, this Court is mindful of its duty to adjudicate the matter on merit notwithstanding the case proceeded ex-parte. The Claimant must be subject to the burden to prove her case on the balance of probabilities as it was held in Wong Brothers' Building Construction v. Choo Chee Siam (supra). In this case, the burden to prove her case on the balance of probability has been discharged by the Claimant. The Claimant's claim is hereby allowed.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Remedies a) Compensation In Lieu of Reinstatement
content: The Court shall now consider whether the Claimant is entitled for an order of reinstatement to her former position without any loss of seniority, wages or benefits. Based on the Court's assessment of the industrial climate between the parties, it is certainly not conducive to reinstating the Claimant as the relationship between the Company and the Claimant has been badly strained. Considering the factual matrix of this case where the relationship between the Claimant and the Company can only be seen as having deteriorated after the Claimant's dismissal from employment, it is this Court's view that reinstatement of the Claimant to former position in the Company is not a suitable remedy in the circumstances of this case. This Court views that it would be inappropriate in the aforesaid circumstances to so order as the relationship between the parties no longer harmony.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Remedies a) Compensation In Lieu of Reinstatement
content:
In the circumstances, it is inappropriate to order the remedy of reinstatement. Instead, the Claimant will be awarded an appropriate remedy accordingly. This Court referred to the principle discussed by the Federal Court in the case of Dr. A Dutt v. Assunta Hospital [1981] 1 MLRA 472; [1981] 1 MLJ 304 where the Court held that:
"The Industrial Court is authorized to award monetary compensation if it is of the view that reinstatement is not appropriate. We are of the opinion that upon a true interpretation, the Industrial Court may properly award compensation where the dismissal is without just cause or excuse, if, in its considered view, it does not think reinstatement should be ordered".

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Remedies a) Compensation In Lieu of Reinstatement
content: In such a case, monetary compensation in lieu of reinstatement would be appropriate and is hereby granted. Following Practice Note No: 3 of 2019, compensation in lieu of reinstatement must be computed based on one month's salary for each year of completed service.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Remedies a) Compensation In Lieu of Reinstatement
content:
Based on the evidence, this Court finds that the Claimant was employed with the Company since 18/05/2015 until date of her dismissal on 08/11/2024 with her last drawn basic salary of RM5,000.00 based on her last payslip dated 07/08/2024. She had served with the Company approximately for 9 years and 5 months. This would make her years of completed service is for nine (9) years.: RM5,000.00 x 9 years of completed service = RM45,000.00
b) Backwages

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Remedies a) Compensation In Lieu of Reinstatement
content:
In respect of the quantum the Court is mindful of the view taken by Tun Salleh Abas FJ in the case of Hotel Jaya Puri Bhd. v. National Company of Hotel, Bar & Restaurant Workers & Anor [1990] 1 MLJ 109:
".. if there is a legal basis for paying the compensation, the amount of course is very much a matter of the discretion which the Industrial Court is fully empowered under s. 30 of the IRA 1967 to fix."

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Remedies a) Compensation In Lieu of Reinstatement
content:
In determining the quantum for backwages that is discretionary in nature, the Court may award not exceeding the maximum of 24 months based on the last drawn salary; regards shall have to the provision under Section 30(6A) of the IRA 1967 and Clause 1 of the Second Schedule in [Factors For Consideration In Making An Award in Relation To A Reference Under Sub Section 20(3)] which provides:
"1. In the event backwages are to be given, such backwages shall not exceed twenty four months backwages from the date of dismissal based on the latest drawn salary of the person who has been dismissed without just cause or excuse"

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Remedies a) Compensation In Lieu of Reinstatement
content: From the date of her dismissal on 18/11/2024 until the end of hearing date on 23/10/2025, it was 11 months eligible period for backwages: - RM5,000.00 x 11 months = RM55,000.00

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Remedies a) Compensation In Lieu of Reinstatement
content:
There shall be no deduction if the workman has not been able to secure any employment since the date of her dismissal. No evidence has been submitted to show that the Claimant was gainfully employed after her dismissal. As there was no evidence of post dismissal earnings, it would improper to deduct the awarded backwages pursuant to Clause 3 of the Second Schedule of Section 30(6A) Industrial Relation Act 1967.
Total Relief : RM45,000.00 + RM55,000.00 = RM100,000.00

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Remedies a) Compensation In Lieu of Reinstatement
content: As the Court’s final order, the amount totalling RM100,000.00 (Ringgit Malaysia: One Hundred Thousand Only) as awarded above less statutory deduction (if any), shall be paid by the Company to the Claimant within thirty (30) days from the date of service of this Award to parties.

case_name: Khoo Li Li v Alpha Ascent Development Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Zulhelmy bin Hasan
section_title: Remedies a) Compensation In Lieu of Reinstatement
content: At the risk of repetition, this Court had taken into account the evidence adduced ex-parte in its entirety, having borne in mind Section 30(5) of the IRA 1967 by which virtue this Court shall act according to equity, good conscience and the substantial merit of the case without regard to technicalities and legal form.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
The issues to be determined in this case are:-
(i) whether the allegations of misconduct levelled against the Claimant are proven on a balance of probabilities; (ii) whether the allegations of misconduct, if proven, justified the Company in not confirming the Claimant (who was under probation) in her position in the Company.
V. The Court’s Findings And Reasons (i) Whether the charges of misconduct levelled against the Claimant are proven on a balance of probabilities

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant, at the material when the alleged incidents occurred, was still under a probationary period with the Company.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: It is trite law that a probationer cannot be dismissed from his employment whilst being under probation unless he/she has been found guilty of an act of misconduct. In all other instances, the Claimant will have to be assessed on his work performance before the decision to confirm him/her in his/her position is made. In the case of Sulnayah Mohd Isa v. Sekolah Kanak-Kanak Pekak Selangor & Anor [1999] 6 CLJ 34 it was held by Azmel Maamor J:- “The main issue that arose from this application concerned with the right of an employer to dismiss its employee during the period of probation. It was not disputed that the applicant was dismissed by respondent No. 1 during the currency of her probationary period. At p. 3 of the award the Industrial Court had quite rightly stated the legal principle concerning this issue i.e.: In other words the employer has no right to terminate the service of an employee before the period of probation has expired, except on the ground of misconduct or other sufficient reasons in which case even the service of a permanent employee could be terminated. This principle means that an employee cannot be terminated by the employer during the currency of his probationary period. However there is an exception to the rule, i.e. the employee can be terminated if he commits an act of misconduct for which reason even the services of a confirmed employee can be terminated. In the light of the above principle what this court need to examine is whether the dismissal of the applicant who was still on probation was on the ground of misconduct”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: It is clear from the evidence before this Court that the Claimant had been dismissed from his employment due to her acts of misconduct, i.e. conflict of interest, habitual tardiness, absenteeism and insubordination.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
Learned Counsel for the Claimant submits that the only issues before this Court pertain to the 4 allegations contained in the Show Cause letter dated 20 December 2022 (at pp. 7-10 of COB-1), despite the Claimant’s pleadings being peppered with several other side issues related to, amongst others, the whistleblowing and town hall meeting. As such, the Court will only analyse the 4 allegations contained in the said Show Cause letter to determine whether the Company was justified in cutting short the Claimant’s probationary period and not confirming her in her position in the Company.
 Allegation No. 1 : Abuse of Power

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: Allegation No. 1 contained in the Show Cause letter dated 20 December 2022 (at pp. 7-8 of COB-1) reads as follows:- “1. ALLEGATION 1: Abuse of Power – as to the appointment of Encik Azizul Rahman Bin Kamarudin as Senior Executive, Business Development of the Company Based in our finding, Encik Azizul Rahman bin Kamarudin is your brother and you have directly involved in the hiring process of Encik Azizul from the early stage of the said post is advertised which clearly an act of such conflict of interest. However you have failed to disclose your relationship with Encik Azizul at any earliest opportunity, i.e. as soon as you become aware of the conflict to the Company. By the above said act and your conduct in the entire process of hiring Encik Azizul Rahman bin Kamarudin, you have therefore breached your express and/or implied duties as an employee of UMPH Group, with reference to the Conflict of Interest Policy UMPH Group, Topic 8.0 Breach of Policy and Employee Handbook, “Bahagian 7: Prosedur dan Tindakan Disiplin; Topic 7.1 Kesalahan-kesalahan Tatatertib. 7.1.1 Sengaja mengingkari atau enggan mematuhi sama ada secara perseorangan atau kumpulan kepada sebarang perintah yang sah di sisi undang-undang atau yang munasabah dari pihak Pengurusan”. You have further acted beyond your power as the Vice President, Group Human Capital of UMPH Group by amending the position and salary package offered to Encik Azizul Rahman bin Kamarudin as can be seen in the Interview Summary for the interview date of 24.06.2022 despite the fact that the vacancy advertised for the position and salary and agreed proposed salary were different. This is seen as an act of misconduct of gaining benefit for your family member through manipulation of the original advertised vacancy. By the above said act and your conduct of amending the position and salary package offered to Encik Azizul Rahman bin Kamarudin, you have therefore caused the company to incur unnecessary expenditure on recruitment. By the above said act, you have therefore breached your expressed and/or implied duties as an employee of UMPH Group, with reference to the Employee Handbook, “Bahagian 7: Prosedur dan Tindakan Disiplin; Topic 7.1 Kesalahan-kesalahan Tatatertib. 7 7.1.29 Penyalahgunaan kuasa yang diberi bagi tujuan menjatuhkan syarikat atau untuk kepentingan sendiri””.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: Allegation No. 1 pertains to the Claimant’s alleged misconduct wherein she had acted in conflict of interest in the appointment process of one En. Azizul Rahman bin Kamarudin (“En. Azizul”) (who is the Claimant’s brother) to the role of Senior Executive, Business Development in the Company.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
Learned Counsel for the Company had pointed out the Conflict of Interest Policy of the Company which stipulates that an employee should not directly or indirectly be in a position to influence the hiring or assessments of a family member. The relevant provision in the said Conflict of Interest Policy reads as follows (at pp. 79-80 of COB-1):-
“4.0 IDENTIFYING CONFLICTS OF INTEREST 4.1 In general, a conflict of interest would arise where a person’s ability to perform his/her duties effectively and impartially are potentially impaired by personal interests, considerations or relationships. Generally, conflicts of interest may be described under the following broad categories:
“… iv. Personal Relationships A conflict of interest would exist if a family member of an employee has a reporting relationship with the employee. An employee should not be in the same department/division as a family member, and should not directly or indirectly supervise, or be in a position to influence the hiring, work assignments or assessments of the family member…”

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: It is not disputed that the said En. Azizul is the Claimant’s brother and that the shortlisting and interview process of En. Azizul for the position of Senior Executive, Business Development in the Company was done by the Claimant’s subordinates in Group Human Capital, i.e. En. Ahmad Solehin (“En. Solehin”) and En. Ali Saifullah. This was admitted to by the Claimant in her Reply to the Show Cause letter dated 30 December 2022 (at p. 15 of COB-1).

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant states in her Reply to the Show Cause letter dated 30 December 2022 (at p. 15 of COB-1) that in June 2022 the then Senior Vice President, Business Division, i.e. En. Azman bin Ridwan (CLW-2), “was looking high and low for an experienced Business Development personnel” and thus had requested to hire an Executive at senior level and that a Manpower Requisition Form (MRF) was issued by CLW-2 and the Claimant’s Group Human Capital division had proceeded with the recruitment. The Claimant thereafter admits having submitted her brother’s (En. Azizul) CV to CLW-2 and declared to CLW-2 that En. Azizul is her brother and left it to CLW-2 to select his preferred candidates.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: En. Azizul was thereafter interviewed, amongst others, by the Claimant’s subordinate, i.e. En. Solehin. The said En. Solehin had also prepared En. Azizul’s Interview Summary. The said Interview Summary was then not only checked, but also recommended by the Claimant as the Vice President, Group Human Capital. The Interview Summary was thereafter approved by the Interim Chief Executive Officer, i.e. Professor Madya Dr. Ahmad Tarmizi bin Haron.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The matter however did not end there. Subsequent to the approval of the Interview Summary, the Claimant then forwarded a photo of her handwritten notes pertaining to the proposed salary package to another of her subordinate, i.e. Pn. Noor Aidayuwati Binti Zakaria (COW-2) via WhatsApp messages (at pp. 39 - 41 of COB-2).

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: It is evident from the Claimant’s said WhatsApp messages (at pp. 40 – 41 of COB-2) that she had clearly instructed COW-2 to forward the said notes to En. Solehin for him to add to the Interview Summary, which COW-2 duly complied with. En. Solehin had then incorporated the Claimant’s handwritten notes onto the Interview Summary (at p. 32 of COB-2). Thus, upon the Claimant’s instructions, En. Solehin had amended the Interview Summary to now reflect a much higher salary package for her brother, En. Azizul, then what was originally indicated in the said Interview Summary.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The said En. Azizul was then appointed as a Senior Executive, Business Development, Business Division (Grade: E5) effective 14 July 2022 (at pp. 30 – 31 of COB-2) and, more glaringly, his employment contract was signed by the Claimant on behalf of the Company.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: Throughout the proceedings before this Court, the Claimant’s stand had been that she had declared to CLW-2 and Professor Madya Dr. Ahmad Tarmizi bin Haron that En. Azizul is her brother. However, when pressed upon with regard to any documentary evidence of such a declaration, the Claimant was unable to produce any.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant admitted that she did not complete the Conflict of Interest Declaration Form as required under the Conflict of Interest Policy, wherein Clause 6.1 (at p. 82 of COB-1) provides:- “Any conflict of interest must be declared by filling up the Conflict of Interest Declaration Form. The conflict of interest must be escalated to the HOD for further action. In the case of directors, the conflict must be disclosed to the Board of Directors and recorded by the Company’s Secretary. The declaration shall be made as and when the conflict arises, and shall be made at the earliest opportunity, i.e., as soon as the director or employee becomes aware of the conflict”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: It is pertinent to note that Clause 6.1 of the Conflict of Interest Policy makes it mandatory for any conflict of interest to be declared by filling up the Conflict of Interest Declaration Form. Thus, it is insufficient for the Claimant to plead that she had informed her superiors, i.e. CLW-2 and Professor Madya Dr. Ahmad Tarmizi bin Haron. There is no discretion given to the employee to declare in any other form or manner other than completing and submitting the Conflict of Interest Declaration Form to the HOD, wherein the Legal and Governance Department of the Company will then review the conflict and decide on the steps to resolve the conflict. In bypassing the requirement of the submission of the Conflict of Interest Declaration Form and merely verbally informing CLW-2 and Professor Madya Dr. Ahmad Tarmizi bin Haron, the Claimant had wilfully and/or blatantly disregarded the mandatory requirement contained in Clause 6.1 of the Conflict of Interest Policy.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant during examination-in chief testified that she did not submit the Conflict of Interest Declaration Form as Clause 4.1 (iv) of the Conflict of Interest Policy merely provides that a conflict of interest would only exist if a family member of an employee has a reporting relationship with the employee. Since her brother, En. Azizul, was being recruited to the Business Division, and the Claimant being in a different department, i.e. Group Human Capital, thus there was no requirement for the Claimant to submit the Conflict of Interest Declaration of Form.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Court however finds this explanation of the Claimant as being totally misconceived. Even though they were in different departments, nevertheless the nature of the Claimant’s job functions as the Vice President in the Group Human Capital which involves, amongst other things, the recruitment of new staff placed her in a precarious situation when the Claimant herself forwarded En. Azizul’s CV to CLW-2 with a view of having her brother appointed to the role of Senior Executive, Business Development in the Business Division. At the very least, the Claimant, being a senior human resources officer, ought to have realised that she was under an obligation to declare the potential conflict of interest via the Conflict of Interest Declaration Form when she was instructing her subordinates pertaining to the interview of her brother and also the proposed salary package, which the Claimant herself had actively revised via her handwritten notes and forwarded to COW-2 via WhatsApp. In short, the Claimant had actively involved herself in the recruitment process of her brother and thus influenced the Company’s decision in hiring him as the Senior Executive, Business Development in the Business Division.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant held a senior position in the Group Human Capital division, i.e. the human resource department in the Company. Her job functions, amongst other things, would involve recruitment of new staff for the Company. By getting herself involved in the recruitment of her brother, i.e. En. Azizul, she had clearly breached the Company’s Conflict of Interest Policy, whereby she had allowed her personal interests to seep into the recruitment process of her brother, thereby directly or indirectly clouding her judgment in the appointment of En. Azizul.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: In Saifuddin Shah Sowkkatali v. Petroliam Nasional Berhad Petronas [2022] ILRU 0467 it was held by the learned Industrial Court Chairman, Reihana Abd Razak:- “All the undisputed and unchallenged evidence adduced by the Company only goes to show the active role of the Claimant in the recruitment of Amir Alif, his nephew with CEFS PIC. Based on the evidence adduced, the Court is satisfied that the Claimant was in a conflict of interest situation when he was involved in the hiring, supervision, management or career planning at PETRONAS in respect of all those individuals in Charges 1 to 5 and who were all related to him. The Court finds that the Claimant reviewed the Intent to Hire and the Intent to Renew documents of all the individuals who are related to him, took an active role to recommend those related to him in their recruitment, influenced the decision of the interviewers to change their initial decision from "Reject" to "Recommend", asked for the questions and answers before the interviews session for his nephew from the interviewer and even instructed the interviewer to reschedule the interview for his nephew (Amir Alif) who had missed the interview. As the Claimant had not denied his personal relationship with the persons named in Charges 1 to 5, and also no denial by the Claimant that he had not declared to the Company of his relationship with any of these persons prior or at the time they had been interviewed or post their interviews as required of him under Clause 1.3 of the Company's Code of Conduct and Business Ethic (CoBE) Part II: Duties of Good Faith, Fidelity, Diligence and Integrity under Part II A: Conflict of Interest, the Court is satisfied the Company had proven Charges 1 to 5 against the Claimant”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
The Court finds that the Company had succeeded in proving, on a balance of probabilities, Allegation No. 1 against the Claimant.
 Allegation No. 2 – Repeatedly coming late to work

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
Allegation No. 2 contained in the Show Cause letter dated 20 December 2022 (at pp. 8 – 9 of COB-1) reads as follows:- “2. ALLEGATION 2: Repeatedly coming late to the office We refer to the Clause 10 of your Letter of Employment which stated that:-
10.0 HOURS OF WORK Employees are required to work such hours and days as the company from time to time directs.
Without prejudice to the foregoing: The standard working hours per week is 39 hours (Monday to Friday: 8.00 am to 5.00 pm) However, review on the Company’s Log Record of Staff Attendance for the month of November indicated that you have repeatedly reported late to office without prior permission and/or approval from your superior, on the following dates:
No. Date Clock-in Time Lateness of 1 4-11-2022 9.33 AM 1 hour 33 minutes 2 16-11-2022 8.33 AM 33 minutes 3 17-11-2022 8.32 AM 32 minutes 4 21-11-2022 8.45 AM 45 minutes 5 23-11-2022 9.39 AM 1 hour 39 minutes By the above said act, you have therefore breached your expressed and/or implied duties as an employee of UMPH Group as stated in your Letter of Employment and also the Employee Handbook, “Bahagian 7: Prosedur dan Tindakan Disiplin; Topic 7.1 Kesalahan-kesalahan Tatatertib. 7.1.10 Kerap datang lewat ke pejabat tanpa alasan munasabah”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: Allegation No. 2 against the Claimant pertains to the Claimant’s habitual tardiness, in particular during the month of November 2022, i.e. on 4 November 2022, 16 November 2022, 17 November 2022 and 27 November 2022.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
