content: The Claimant in her Reply to the Show Cause letter (at p. 17 of COB-1) had provided an explanation for turning up late for work on 4 November 2022, i.e. a delay of 1 hour 33 minutes, in that she was taken ill on that day. The Claimant states that she had informed the Interim GCEO and Group Human Capital team, but however failed to produce any documentary evidence to support her contention.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: As for turning up late to work on 16 November 2022 (delay 33 minutes), 17 November 2022 (delay of 32 minutes) and 21 November 2022 (delay of 45 minutes), the Claimant failed to given any explanation for her lateness. For the delay on 23 November 2022, the Claimant explained that she had to go to the clinic and that she had already informed the GCEO at 8.28am via WhatsApp (at p. 22 of COB-1) and the Group Human Capital team.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
Under Clause 7 of the UMP Holdings & Subsidiary Staff Policy (“the Employee Handbook”) (at pp. 25-64 of COB-1) it is expressly stated that habitual tardiness without reasonable excuse is an act of misconduct to which disciplinary could be taken against the employee concerned (at p. 53 of COB-1):-
“BAHAGIAN 7: PROSEDUR DAN TINDAKAN DISIPLIN
7.1 KESALAHAN-KESALAHAN TATATERTIB Perkara-perkara berikut merupakan kesalahan-kesalahan yang mana boleh mengakibatkan tindakan disiplin diambil ke atas anggota pekerja:-
… 7.1.10 Kerap datang lewat ke pejabat tanpa alasan munasabah…”

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant was not any ordinary employee in the Company. She held the senior position of Vice President in the Group Human Capital department, overseeing the affairs and welfare of all employees in the Company. Thus, she held a bigger responsibility in ensuring the Company’s Employee Handbook is adhered to. By turning up late to work herself, the Claimant had sent all the wrong signals to the other employees of the Company that any non-compliance of the Employee Handbook and/or Staff Policy will be tolerated by the Company. The Claimant’s explanation in her Reply to the Show Cause letter (at p. 17 of COB-1) that her job responsibilities as a Vice President, Group Human Capital required her to work around the clock and that she did not have time to sleep is certainly no excuse and does not give her carte blanche to turn up for work at whatever time that she deems fit. Rules are there to be obeyed, and the Claimant as the Vice President of Group Human Capital had the responsibility to ensure such compliance of the Employee Handbook and/or Staff Policy, including herself.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant in fact admitted during cross-examination that her late attendance on the stated dates without any reasonable explanation was indeed an act of misconduct.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: In Aezrine Shah Abdullah v. Fat Boys Records Sdn Bhd [2017] 2 ILR 409 it was held by the Industrial Court:- “Coming to work late or lateness is a form of absence without leave for the period between the time the employee is required to arrive and the time he actually does arrive and as a species of unauthorized absence, it too, is misconduct. Cases have held that even lateness for only a few minutes may be misconduct especially when the employee has been warned to be punctual. An employer has every right to demand punctuality up to the very minutes if he chooses. The misconduct is aggravated when the lateness is persistent. In the case of Crystal Products (Eire) v. Irish Transport & Gen Workers' U.Recommendation No.1394, 18 February 1961 (mimeo) the Irish Labour Court held as follow: The Court feels that it must be accepted that, in order to obtain smooth and efficient working, Management is entitled to regular and punctual attendance on the part of the employees, and that is has the right to take disciplinary action amounting, if necessary, to dismissal in order to ensure that these requirements are fulfilled The dismissal of the worker concerned in this dispute must therefore be accepted as a normal measure adopted by an employer to ensure adherence to the regulations governing the question of time keeping. In the case of Hong Voon Holdings Sdn Bhd, Kuantan v. Puan Rosnani Bte Sidin, Jerantut [1986] 2 ILR 1643 (Award No. 378 of 1986), the learned Industrial Court Chairman held as follow: The Company contended that coming to work late habitually was a good ground for dismissal and cited The Chartered Bank and Kuching Bank Employees Union (Award 10 of 1966) to support the contention. I agree with the contention, and dismiss the Claimant's claim. On the facts, the claimant has admitted to his late attendance to work, as frequent as 3 times in a week and the duration varies from ½ hour to 3 ½ hours. The claimant had serious issue of late attendance to work. His tardiness, in duration and frequency were simply excessive and unacceptable”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
The Court finds that the Company had succeeded in proving, on a balance of probabilities, Allegation No. 2 against the Claimant.
 Allegation No. 3 : Absenteeism

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
Allegation No. 3 contained in the Show Cause letter dated 20 December 2022 (at p. 9 of COB-1) reads as follows:-
“3. ALLEGATION 3: Absenteeism You are alleged to be absent from work without leave, prior approval by your immediate superior or medical leave during the working hours on the following dates:- No. Date Day 1 3/10/2022 Monday 2 4/10/2022 Tuesday 3 5/10/2022 Wednesday 4 6/10/2022 Thursday 5 7/10/2022 Friday 6 10/10/2022 Monday 7 11/10/2022 Tuesday 8 12/10/2022 Wednesday 9 13/10/2022 Thursday 10 14/10/2022 Friday 11 17/10/2022 Monday 12 18/10/2022 Tuesday 13 19/10/2022 Wednesday 14 20/10/2022 Thursday 15 21/10/2022 Friday 16 24/10/2022 Monday 17 25/10/2022 Tuesday 18 26/10/2022 Wednesday
As to date, you have failed to produce medical certificates (MC) or any other supporting documents to justify on your continuous absence on the above particular dates. By the above said act, you have therefore breached your expressed and/or implied duties as an employee of UMPH Group, with reference to the Employee Handbook, “Bahagian 7: Prosedur dan Tindakan Disiplin; Topic 7.1 Kesalahan-kesalahan Tatatertib. 7.1.8 Pekerja tidak hadir bertugas tanpa memohon cuti atau kebenaran terlebih dahulu melebihi dua (2) hari berturut-turut”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: As stated earlier, the Claimant’s work days are from Mondays to Fridays between 8.00am to 5.00pm.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
The Employee Handbook provides as follows on the working hours of the employees (at p. 34 of COB-1):-
“BAHAGIAN 2: WAKTU KERJA DAN KERJA LEBIH MASA
2.1 WAKTU KERJA HARIAN 2.1.1 Waktu bekerja yang telah ditetapkan oleh Syarikat adalah selama lapan (8) jam sehari seperti mana berikut:-

Waktu

Hari Waktu
Isnin hingga Khamis 01:00 petang hingga 02:00 petang (1 jam)
Jumaat 12:30 petang hingga 02:30 petang (2 jam) 2.1.3 Semua kakitangan dikehendaki merekodkan kedatangan harian bertugas menggunakan sistem pada masa-masa berikut:
2.1.3.1 Pada masa datang ke pejabat pada waktu pagi. 2.1.3.2 Pada masa meninggalkan pejabat untuk urusan di luar pejabat. 2.1.3.3 Pada masa balik semula ke pejabat selepas selesai urusan di luar pejabat. 2.1.3.4 Pada masa meninggalkan pejabat selepas waktu bekerja. 2.1.4 Pekerja yang tidak dapat merekodkan waktu pergi dan balik atas alasan tugas seperti kerja luar, menghadiri mesyuarat, temu janji dan sebagainya dikehendaki mengisi permohonan Kelulusan Kerja Luar Pejabat melalui sistem dan disahkan oleh Pegawai Atasan/Ketua Unit. 2.1.5 Pekerja yang gagal merekodkan waktu pergi dan balik tanpa alasan yang kukuh dikehendaki menulis memo kepada pihak Sumber Manusia dan disahkan oleh Pegawai Atasan/Ketua Unit”.

chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
Under Clause 7 of the Employee Handbook (at pp. 25-64 of COB-1) it is expressly stated that being absent from work without leave, prior approval by your immediate superior or medical leave during the working hours is an act of misconduct to which disciplinary could be taken against the employee concerned (at p. 53 of COB-1):-
“BAHAGIAN 7: PROSEDUR DAN TINDAKAN DISIPLIN
7.1 KESALAHAN-KESALAHAN TATATERTIB Perkara-perkara berikut merupakan kesalahan-kesalahan yang mana boleh mengakibatkan tindakan disiplin diambil ke atas anggota pekerja:-
… 7.1.8 Pekerja tidak hadir bertugas tanpa memohon cuti atau kebenaran terlebih dahulu melebihi dua (2) hari berturut-turut…”

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: And as stated earlier also, the Claimant as the Vice President in the Group Human Capital department in the Company had the responsibility of ensuring that all staff of the Company, more so herself, adheres to the Employee Handbook and/or staff policy.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant however was absent on various dates in October 2022. The Claimant in her Reply to the Show Cause letter (at pp. 18-19 of COB-1) had stated that out of the 18 dates mentioned under Allegation No. 3:- i. 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 October 2022 - Claimant was on medical leave/working from home ii. 10 October 2022 was a public holiday (Prophet Muhammad’s Birthday); iii. 11 October 2022 – Claimant attended Zumba class at UMPH Hall together with other UMPH & Group employees; iv. 12 October 2022 – Claimant attended discussion with Interim GCEO, Prof. Madya Dr. Ahmad Tarmizi at BIM Office on preparation for the UMPH Board Townhall; v. 13 October 2022 – Claimant attended Budget Meeting 2023 – BOD Meeting Room; vi. 17 October 2022 – Claimant attended UMPH Board Townhall; vii. 18 October 2022 – Claimant attended Zumba class at UMPH Hall together with other UMPH & Group employees; viii. 19 October 2022 – Claimant attended meeting with IGU on Whistle Blowe allegations at Board Meeting Room; ix. 21 October 2022 – Claimant attended UMPH HOD Mesyuarat Khas Lembaga Pengarah Bil 05/2022 (26) at Double Tree By Hilton, Putrajaya; x. 24 October 2022 – Public holiday (Deepavali); xi. 26 October 2022 – Claimant coordinated the Executive and Assistant Level staff sessions with Tn. Haji Basharuddin at Training Room UCTS.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: After the explanation given by the Claimant in her Reply to the Show Cause letter, the Company narrowed down on the following dates where she was alleged to have been absent from work without prior approval:- i. 11 October 2022 – the Claimant contends she was in a Zumba class at UMPH Hall; ii. 12 October 2022 – the Claimant attended discussion with Interim GCEO at BIM Office on preparation for the UMPH Board Townhall; iii. 14 October 2022 – the Claimant did not give any explanation on her absence from work; iv. 18 October 2022 – the Claimant attended Zumba Class at UMPH Hall; v. 19 October 2022 – the Claimant attended meeting IGU on Whistle Blower allegations at Board Meeting Room; vi. 25 October 2022 – the Claimant did not give any explanation on her absence from work.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: With regard to the Claimant’s absence from work on 11 October 2022 and 18 October 2022, despite the Claimant contending that she had attended the Zumba Class at the UMPH Hall, the evidence produced by the Company, in particular the “Zumba Fitness” poster at p. 48 of COB-2, shows that the Zumba classes were only carried out between 4.30pm to 5.30pm, which was after work hours, and certainly does not justify her absence from work the entire day. The Claimant during cross-examination testified that she had no evidence of what she was doing before the Zumba classes on both the dates of 11 and 18 October 2022.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: With regard to the Claimant’s absence from work on 12 October 2022 and 19 October 2022, the Claimant had explained that she had to attend to some discussions with the Interim GCEO on preparation for the UMPH Board Townhall and also the meeting with IGU on the whistleblower allegations at the Board Meeting Room respectively. However the Claimant did not produce any evidence to prove her contention that she was in discussion with the Interim GCEO on 12 October 2022 and how long that discussion had lasted. As for her purported meeting on 19 October 2022 with IGU on the whistleblower allegations, the meeting only took place at 2.00pm and certainly does not justify her absence from work for the whole day.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: As for her absence from work on 14 October 2022 and 25 October 2022, the Claimant failed to give any explanation whatsoever.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: From the evidence produced before the Court, it is evident that the Claimant had been absent from work without any justification on 11 October 2022, 12 October 2022, 14 October 2022, 18 October 2022, 19 October 2022 and 25 October 2022. There was no evidence produced by the Claimant to prove that she had reported for work on the said dates. In fact, the Claimant tried to suggest that she must have been at work on 11 and 18 October 2022 as she had attended the Zumba class at the UMPH Townhall and that it would be illogical for her to travel all the way from her home in Kuantan to the UMPH Hall in Gambang just for Zumba classes. The Claimant may contend that it is illogical, but what is even more shocking is that the Claimant being the Vice President in the Group Human Capital and having control of the employees’ attendance record, could not even find any evidence whatsoever that she had reported for work in accordance with the Company’s work hours as stated in her Employment Contract and the Employee Handbook. This clearly shows the ineptitude of the Claimant in managing her own department, which is the human resource department.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant in fact answered in the affirmative when questioned during cross examination that being the Vice President, Group Human Capital, she must lead by example and be a role model in ensuring compliance with the working hours in the Company. Further, she also admitted that the system that manages the employees’ attendance, “the clock-in, clock-out systems”, fell under her purview as the Vice President, Group Human Capital.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: In Syahrizal Salam @ Mansor v. Desaru Damai Beach Resort Sdn Bhd [2018] 1 ILR 381 it was held by the learned Industrial Court Chairman, Sumathi Murugiah (as Her Ladyship then was):- “This court is of the opinion that being a probationer, the claimant's actions in this case is very unbecoming, as the number of leave days required by the claimant had not been one (1) or two (2) days but much more than that. Especially so, considering the fact that his position in the company was the Human Resource Manager and the responsibilities that come with that position is of great importance, the claimant should have taken the trouble to contact his superior and or the Resort Manager to explain the situation and request for the approval of his leave in order to settle his personal matter and return to work as soon as possible. This situation is made worse by the fact that the claimant was a probationer. As such, this court is reminded by the statement made by the court in the case of Fakir Abdul Jalii Pakir Mohamed v. Shell Refinery Co Bhd (Award No. 20 of 1974), where the following was said: The dictionary meaning of "probation" is given as the "testing of conduct or character of a person" and a "probationer" is one who "is on trial or in a state to give proof of certain qualifications for a place or state". The idea of probation in all cases of services contracts is, therefore, a testing of the character and capabilities of the servant on the employer's side, and also a testing of the conditions of service on the employee's part. The period of probation in a service contract can, therefore, be taken as a communication by the employer that in case the employee proves himself, within the period of probation, to the satisfaction of the employer, that he (the probationer) is a fit and proper person to perform the duties for which he has offered his services, the probationer would be entitled to be confirmed or taken in on a permanent basis. The appointment of a person on probation is, therefore, tentative and dependent on the employer's satisfaction as to his suitability. In echoing the Chairman in the Fakir Abdul Jalil Pakir Mohamed's case, this court finds that based on the evidence and findings produced before this court, the company would be in a better position to judge the performance of the claimant under the circumstances. This court also opines that the claimant's nonchalant attitude in handling this matter left it open to the company to exercise its managerial prerogative of dismissal against him. The number of days where the claimant had been absent from work without prior approval and without informing the company had made the company lose all trust and confidence in the claimant, not only as an employee but more so an employee holding such big responsibility who is incidentally still on probation”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Court finds that the Company had succeeded in proving, on a balance of probabilities, Allegation No. 3 against the Claimant.  Allegation No. 4: Incitement towards creating hatred and insubordination

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: Allegation No. 4 contained in the Show Cause letter dated 20 December 2022 (at p. 10 of COB-1) reads as follows:- “4. ALLEGATION 4: Incitement towards creating hatred and insubordination You are alleged to have used words which are inappropriate, vulgar and uncouth targeted at the GCEO through WhatsApp with your staff members which is deemed to be an act of incitement towards creating hatred and insubordination which is an offence, with reference to the Employee Handbook, “Bahagian 7: Prosedur dan Tindakan Disiplin; Topic 7.1 Kesalahan-kesalahan Tatatertib. 7.1.28 Melakukan perbuatan melawan penyelia secara lisan atau menghasut anggota pekerja lain melakukannya””.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: Allegation No. 4 pertains to the incident where the Claimant had used inappropriate language or word in reference to COW-1, who was the Group Chief Executive Officer at the material point in time, and the said impugned words were stated by the Claimant in the Company’s MyExec WhatsApp group, which consisted of human resource executive employees.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
The impugned words in the WhatsApp group uttered by the Claimant are as follows (at p. 52 of COB-2):-
“Ni dia si laknat syed. Jgn ingat dia baik”

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The term “laknat” is a curse word in the Malay language. The Dewan Bahasa & Pustaka dictionary defines the word “laknat” as “kemurkaan Allah dan jauh drpd petunjuk dan Rahmat-Nya” and “terkutuk, keji, hina, celaka, teruk diseksa” (at p. 173 of COB-2). Whereas the Oxford Fajar dictionary (Kamus Dwibahasa Oxford Fajar, 6th Edn.; Joyce M. Hawkins) defines the word “laknat” as “adj. damned; condemned to hell; condemned as failure, -k.n. & sr. damn; uttered curse”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant, on her part, did not deny uttering the said word in the WhatsApp group but that she had said it out in frustration as she was hospitalised and under medication at that moment in time and COW-1 had allegedly not shown any empathy towards her condition wherein he had purportedly harassed her on how long she would be hospitalised.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: Whether or not COW-1 had shown any empathy towards her condition, it is wholly inappropriate to utter such inappropriate language in reference to her superior at a platform where other employees were also present and participating, i.e. the Company’s MyExec WhatsApp group. Learned Counsel for the Claimant submits that this was a one-off situation and that an employee should be judged by the standards of man and not that of angels. However, that saying is certainly misplaced in the current situation. Usage of curse words and inappropriate language towards a superior or colleague cannot be tolerated, be it by standards of men or even angels. The Claimant typed the inappropriate words against COW-1 in the WhatsApp group for the other employees to look at. A person in a fit of anger may regrettably utter inappropriate language, but when such inappropriate words are instead written or typed out, it shows more often than not, that it was pre-meditated where the person would have had a tiny window of time to think it over and calm down before deciding to write or type such words. As the other famous saying goes, “a pen is mightier than the sword”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant’s conduct in uttering inappropriate language towards her superior and undermining him in front of the other employees certainly speaks volume of her character and personality, and the Company was justified in coming to a decision that she was not suited to the Company’s working culture and environment, and thus not confirming her in her position in the Company.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The usage of inappropriate language towards one’s superior is a serious misconduct, irrespective of the circumstances in which it was uttered. In Acidchem (M) Bhd v. Goh Hock Teong [2003] 1 ILR 904 it was held by the learned Industrial Court Chairman, K. Ramakrishnan:- “The counsel also submitted that the utterance of "India Pariah" from a smoking room of a factory canteen could not positively establish that the remarks were specially directed at the personnel officer and furthermore the personnel officer did not even hear or was aware of such utterance coming from the smoking room. The evidence of the personnel and administrative officer would show that he heard what the claimant had uttered. This evidence is further corroborated by the evidence of Azahar (COW4) who was with the claimant in the room at the material time. COW4 specifically told the claimant not to say such words to COW2. COW2 clearly heard what the claimant uttered. Furthermore COW4 was in the room when the claimant uttered such word to COW2. The claimant also admitted using the word to COW2. There was no denial by the claimant. The use of abusive language towards the superiors is a serious misconduct because it creates such a situation in which it becomes impossible to maintain proper discipline in an establishment. The use of abusive language generally arises when a worker is dissatisfied with some order or action of the superior officer. Such abusive language is also resorted to by workmen when they use the expressions indiscriminately showing laxity in the use of language. This arises out of lack of sense of discipline coupled with the impact of the circumstances existing at a particular time. Whatever may be the reason for use of abusive words, it is a recognised misconduct and unlike use of defamatory words it has no exceptions. It means that use of abusive language will be misconduct irrespective of the circumstances in which it has been uttered. The use of insulting and abusive language towards superiors is an indication of physical and mental resistance to authority and, therefore, misconduct. If rude behaviour towards superiors is allowed then it will not be possible to maintain discipline in the factory which is of utmost importance to the smooth running of all operations. See Misconduct In Employment by BR Ghaiye. On the issue of quantum of punishment, the learned author states that: When an employee uses vulgar and indecent language towards the officers then he is liable to be dismissed and the dismissal cannot be objected to on the ground that the punishment is excessive. The industrial peace will be at stake if the servant is given the immunity of maliciously scandalising the master and other workmen who work under him. The same principle will apply to the allegations of unrestrained and abusive attacks launched upon the proprietors and officers of the Company and cannot be said to be a legitimate trade union activity. If the abuses are made in the presence of others then it is held to be an aggravating factor. When the evidence given by the witnesses in the enquiry clearly shows that the opponent was not only impertinent and insolent towards the foreman but the language used by him was abusive and indecent and the opponent used such language in the presence of his co-workers then his dismissal is justified”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: In M Anathan Muniandy v. HS Optimus Wood Products Sdn Bhd (Formerly Known As KLW Wood Products (M) Sdn Bhd) [2024] ILRU 1841 it was held by the learned Industrial Court Chairman, Mohd Taufik Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff:- “By uttering vulgar words and abusive language in a group which has other members, such an action will surely lower the dignity or the position of Mr. Albert, as a director, in the judgment of the other employees. The claimant should have abstained from doing so. The claimant misconduct will create such a situation where it becomes impossible to maintain proper discipline in an establishment (see B.R Ghaiye in his book "Misconduct of Employment" (2nd Edn), referred to in the case of Barney Production BC Sdn Bhd (supra))”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content:
The Court finds that the Company had succeeded in proving, on a balance of probabilities, Allegation No. 4 against the Claimant.
(ii) Whether the allegations of misconduct justified the Company in not confirming the Claimant (who was under probation) in her position in the Company.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: As can be seen from the findings above, the Company has succeeded in proving, on a balance of probabilities, that the Claimant is guilty of all the allegations levelled against her in the Show Cause letter dated 20 December 2022.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The misconduct complained of by the Company in the said Letter of Termination constitute serious misconduct. Being an officer holding a senior and important position, i.e. the Vice President in the Group Human Capital division, it cannot be gainsaid that the Claimant had added responsibilities and a fiduciary duty to always act in the best interests of the Company. Under the circumstances, the non-confirmation of the Claimant in her position whilst she was under the probationary period is proportionate to the act of misconduct complained of. The Claimant, being a senior human resources personnel, ought to have known that being a probationer, she was an employee on trial at the material point in time. By behaving in the manner in which she did, the Claimant had displayed characteristics and mannerisms which are wholly unsuitable for employment in the Company, let alone the position of a Vice President, Group Human Capital.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant’s conduct was against the Company’s best interest and faithful discharge of her duty to the Company. In the oft-quoted case of Pearce v. Foster [1886] QBD 536 it was held by Lord Esher MR:- “The rule of law is, that where a person has entered into the position of servant, if he does anything incompatible with the due or faithful discharge of his duty to his master, the latter has a right to dismiss him. The relation of master and servant implies necessarily that the servant shall be in a position to perform his duty duly and faithfully, and if by his own act he prevents himself from doing so, the master may dismiss him. It is not that the servant warrants that he will duly and faithfully perform his duty; because, if that were so, upon breach of his duty his master might bring an action against him on the warranty. But the question is, whether the breach of duty is a good ground of dismissal”.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: Upon analysing the evidence and facts of the case in its entirety, the Court is satisfied and do hereby find that the Company was justified in not confirming the Claimant in her position whilst she was still under the probationary period, due to serious acts of misconduct.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Company’s action in not confirming the Claimant in her position was wholly justified in the circumstances.

case_name: Salina binti Kamarudin v UMPSA Holdings Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Paramalingam a/l J. Doraisamy
content: The Claimant’s case is hereby dismissed.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content:
The role of the Industrial Court was succinctly described by Raja Azlan Shah CJ (Malaya) (as His Royal Highness then was) in the celebrated case of Goon Kwee Phoy v J&P Coats (M) Bhd [1981] 1 LNS 30; [1981] 1 MLJ 129 at p.136 (FC) where His Lordship had this to say:
“Where representations are made and are referred to the Industrial Court for enquiry, it is the duty of the Court to determine whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse. If the employer chooses to give a reason or excuse for the action taken by him, the duty of the Industrial Court will be to enquire whether that reason or excuse has or has not been made out. If it finds that it has not been proven, then the inevitable conclusion must be that the termination or dismissal was without just cause and excuse. The proper enquiry of the Court is the reason advanced by the employer, and that court or the High Court cannot go into another reason not relied on by the employer or find one for him.” (emphasis is mine)

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: The Law on Fixed Term Contracts
content: In perusing the Claimant’s Statement of Case, he had contended that his fixed term contract was not a genuine fixed term contract and that it was a permanent one (CLWS-1 paragraph 15). It is established law that the non-renewal of a fixed term contract is considered as a dismissal as envisaged under s.20 of the Act along with constructive dismissals, forced resignation and retrenchments etc. (See the decision of this Court in Colgate Palmolive Sdn. Bhd. v Yap Kok Fong [1998] 3 ILR 843).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: The Law on Fixed Term Contracts
content:
The approach that is to be applied by this Court in determining the issues in regard to a fixed term contract was succinctly stated by Faiza Tamby Chik J in the case of M. Vasagam Muthusamy v Kesatuan Pekerja-Pekerja Resorts World Pahang & Anor [2003] 5 MLJ 262 where His Lordship had this to say:
“I am of the opinion that the Industrial Court had correctly addressed the issue in this case by determining first whether or not the contract in question was a genuine fixed term contract…….If the Industrial Court made a finding that it was not a genuine fixed term contract but was really a contract of employment, then only would the Industrial Court be required to ask whether there was a dismissal or not and that if so whether it was with just cause or excuse. In the instant case, since a finding was reached that the contract concerned was indeed a genuine fixed term contract, the question of there being a dismissal or not does not arise.” “Once it is established that there is a genuine fixed term contract, the dissolution of the contract upon reaching the expiry date of the fixed term would clearly spell the end of the worker’s tenure with the relevant company.” (emphasis is mine)

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: The Law on Fixed Term Contracts
content:
Hence this Court is duty bound to consider the following issues:
a. Whether the contract between the Claimant and the Company is a genuine fixed term contract; b. Should the Court find that the said contract is a genuine fixed term contract, then at the conclusion of the said contract upon reaching the expiry date would mean that claimant’s tenure with the company will come to an end. c. If for any reason the Court finds that the said contract is not a genuine fixed term contract, then the issue of whether or not there was a dismissal and if so, whether it was with just cause or excuse will have to be determined.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: The Law on Fixed Term Contracts
content: It can be gathered from the pleadings as outlined above, that the 3rd Contract of Service was offered to the Claimant during the duration of the 2nd Contract of Service and therefore when Foundation terminated the Claimant on 1.3.2024 under 2nd Contract of Service after its expiry, to my mind this amounted to a pre-mature termination of the Claimant’s 3rd Contract of Service as it was due to expire only on 1.2.2026.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: The Law on Fixed Term Contracts
content: However in addition, apart from what was mentioned above on the law on fixed term contracts, it is also trite law that an employer who pre-maturely terminates a fixed term contract as the Foundation did in the case of the Claimant here, would need to show that it was done with just cause or excuse. (See the decision of the Court of Appeal in Omar Othman v Kulim Advanced Technologies Sdn. Bhd. [2019] 7 CLJ 18).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: It’s trite that the Company bears the burden of prove on a balance of probabilities that the contract between the Company and the Claimant was a genuine fixed term contract and that it had come to an end by effluxion of time. However, it is the employee who bears the evidential burden to prove that there exist elements to show that the fixed term contract is not genuine. (See the decision of the High Court in Toko Inomoto & Ors v Mahkamah Perusahaan Malaysia [2017] 1 LNS 201 and the decision of this Court in Mazwan Mohd Ali v Universiti Islam Antrabangsa [2016] 4 ILR 238).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether the Contract was a Genuine Fixed Term Contract?
content: In order to decide on the issues posed by the parties as adverted to earlier, it is necessary for this Court to refer to the decision of the Federal Court in Ahmad Zahri Mirza Abdul Hamid v AIMS Cyberjaya Sdn. Bhd. [2020] 6 CLJ 557 where it was decided that in determining whether a contract is a genuine fixed term contract there are three issues to consider: (i) The intention of the parties. (ii) Employer’s subsequent conduct during the course of employment. (iii) Nature of the employer’s business and the nature of the work which an employee is engaged to perform.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether the Contract was a Genuine Fixed Term Contract?
content: In perusing Ahmad Zahri Mirza’s case it was clear that there were successive renewals of the employment contract over a period of time and over a number of years which was considered by the Federal Court as continuous employment without a break from 2009 to 2013 as opposed to the facts involving the Claimant and the Foundation where there were two renewal of the contract wherein the Claimant’s first contract was from 1.3.2021 until 1.3.2023 ( the 1st Contract of Service) and subsequently there was a renewal of that contract which commenced from 1.3.2023 to 1.3.2024 (the 2nd Contract of Service) and again the said contract was renewed from 1.8.2023 until 1.2.2026 (the 3rd Contract of Service) Hence, in the circumstances, essentially there was only two renewal of the fixed term contract.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether the Contract was a Genuine Fixed Term Contract?
content: Further, in the Court of Appeal case of A. Gilbert D’Cruz v Sapura Acergy Sdn. Bhd. [2022] 1 ILR 259, the Court of Appeal held that since the Claimant’s contract of employment was renewed continuously from 2008 until 2015 and he was not employed for only a specific project but he was involved in all the Company’s project both local and overseas, the Court found that the employment contract was not a genuine fixed term contract.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether the Contract was a Genuine Fixed Term Contract?
content: It was also pointed out by the Federal Court in Ahmad Zahri Mirza that the total duration or the length of service with the employer is also a factor to be considered and also whether there was a requirement under the contract for the employee to apply for its renewal.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether the Contract was a Genuine Fixed Term Contract?
content: The Foundation’s stand on this issue was that the Claimant’s fixed term contract was not a permanent one but was a genuine fixed term contract.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Evaluation of the Evidence and Findings of this Court
content: Sifting through the evidence, it can be found that the 3rd Contract of Service from the period from 1.8.2023 until 1.2.2026 according to the Claimant was granted by the Chairman of the Board during the subsistence of the 2nd Contract of Service which was from 1.3.2023 until 1.3.2024. The 3rd Contract of Service was executed by both the Claimant and Chairman of the Board by placing their respective signatures to the said contract on 1.8.2023 and it was subsequently stamped (refer COB-1 p.100 -106).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Evaluation of the Evidence and Findings of this Court
content: The Chairman of the Board at the material time was not called as a witness in the proceedings before this Court.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Evaluation of the Evidence and Findings of this Court
content: According to the Claimant in his evidence during re-examination, he had approached the Chairman of the Board as there were no Board of Directors meeting at the material time to renew his 2nd Contract of Service as it was a requirement under the said contract that any application for renewal must be made to the Foundation not less than six months before the expiry of the contract and further, he added that he was running out of time. (refer Clause 4 of the 2nd Contract of Service).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Evaluation of the Evidence and Findings of this Court
content: Upon perusing the Claimant’s contracts of employment for the periods from 1.3.2021 to 1.3.2023 (the 1st Contract of Service) and from 1.3.2023 to 1.3.2024 (the 2nd Contract of Service), it is clearly provided that for the purpose of renewal of the said contracts, the Claimant is required to provide at least 6 months’ notice of renewal to the Foundation.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Evaluation of the Evidence and Findings of this Court
content:
In order to decide on the issues posed by the parties as outlined above, it is necessary for this Court to refer to the decision of the Federal Court in Ahmad Zahri Mirza Abdul Hamid v AIMS Cyberjaya Sdn. Bhd. [2020] 6 CLJ 557 (which was cited by the learned counsel for the Foundation) where it was decided that in determining whether a contract is a genuine fixed term contract there are three issues to consider:
(i) The intention of the parties. (ii) Employer’s subsequent conduct during the course of employment. (iii) Nature of the employer’s business and the nature of the work which an employee is engaged to perform.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Evaluation of the Evidence and Findings of this Court
content: In Ahmad Zahri’s case it was held that since the claimant who was first employed under a one-year fixed term contract as a Consultant in AIMS Data Centre Sdn. Bhd. which was later merged with the respondent’s company and during this material time his contract was renewed annually over three consecutive years, the Federal Court was of the view that it’s only proper to lift the corporate veil and treat both these companies as one single unit/entity and hence, since the renewal of the contract by the respondent was uninterrupted without the claimant having to apply for its renewal, the Court held that it was indeed a permanent contract.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Evaluation of the Evidence and Findings of this Court
content:
The trite principle of law laid down by the Federal Court in Ahmad Zahri Mirza (supra) spells out that the ingredients to prove that a fixed term contract is actually a permanent contract disguised as fixed term contract among others is the fact, that there must not be a requirement where the employee is required to apply for a renewal of the fixed term contract. In stating so, the Federal Court in Ahamd Zahri Mirza had this to say:
[64] The next case is Holiday Villages (supra). In this case, a resort employed both seasonal and permanent employees. Seasonal employees had a fixed term in their contracts which would range from three to six months or for a season. The resort was not open for the whole year and would be closed during the monsoon season which falls between November and January of each year. The employee had begun employment on a fixed term contract for one season. He was subsequently employed for six consecutive seasons. The Industrial Court acknowledged that the resort was only open for nine to ten months in a year and that there was a genuine need for fixed term contracts as it was inconceivable to expect the resort to pay salaries when it was closed. [65] Notwithstanding the genuine need for fixed term contracts, the Industrial Court found that the employee was, by the last fixed term contract in the series of fixed term contracts, a permanent employee of the resort as: (i) he was employed even during the off-season as a laundry supervisor; (ii) he was given a new contract without the need to reapply; and (iii) he was able to continue in employment even after the alleged expiry of his penultimate fixed term contract without an extension. [88] For all the foregoing reasons, the questions posed for our determination are answered as follows: (i) Whether a need for work permit is a material consideration in determining whether an employment contract is a genuine fixed term contract; and In the negative. (ii) Does a contract of employment which is renewed successively without application by the employee and without any intermittent breaks in between, is in reality permanent employment? In the affirmative.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Evaluation of the Evidence and Findings of this Court
content: Hence, based on the evidence of the Claimant himself that he is required to provide at least 6 months’ notice of renewal to the Foundation under the contract, I am of the view that this would mean that the Claimant has to reapply for an extension of the contract by giving at least six months’ notice to the Foundation of his intention to continue serving with the Foundation by seeking an extension of the said contract.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Evaluation of the Evidence and Findings of this Court
content: Hence, following the decision of the Federal Court in Ahmad Zahri Mirza case, it’s my finding that although there were two successive renewals of the contracts namely the 1st and 2nd Contracts of Service without a break in the Claimant’s case, however with the requirement that the Claimant has to reapply for an extension of the said contracts by giving at least six months’ notice to the Foundation, it cannot be said that the 1st and 2nd Contracts of Service are permanent in nature. Hence, I am on all fours with submission of the learned counsel for the Foundation on this pertinent issue and is satisfied that the Foundation has discharged its burden in proving that the said contracts are a genuine fixed terms contract. (Toko Inomoto & Ors v Mahkamah Perusahaan Malaysia (supra))

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Evaluation of the Evidence and Findings of this Court
content: As such, after having considered the totality of the evidence presented and based on the above grounds, I find that there is insufficient evidence to show on record that the Claimant’s 1st and 2nd Contracts of Service with the Foundation was actually a permanent contract of employment disguised or dressed up as a genuine fixed term contract.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Evaluation of the Evidence and Findings of this Court
content: Hence, from the facts and evidence presented to this Court, it is clear that the Claimant was engaged under a genuine fixed term employment contract in regard to the 2nd Contract of Service which was terminated on 1.3.2024 due to effluxion of time. Hence, this Court is not required to ascertain whether the Claimant’s 2nd Contract of Service was terminated with or without just cause and excuse. (M. Vasagam Muthusamy v Kesatuan Pekerja-Pekerja Resorts World Pahang & Anor (supra)). Hence, this to my mind is clearly not an issue for the Courts consideration and determination.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: This brings us to the 3rd Contract of Service. Since, I have decided that the Claimant’s 2nd Contract of Service is a genuine fixed term contract, I am therefore of the view that the Claimant’s 3rd Contract of Service can also be said to be genuine fixed term contract by reason of the fact that the Claimant has to reapply for an extension of the contract by giving at least six months’ notice to the Foundation.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: However, notwithstanding the above finding, since it was the pleaded case that the 3rd Contract of Service was offered to the Claimant during the duration of the 2nd Contract of Service, and since I have already found that when the Foundation terminated the Claimant on 1.3.2024 under the 2nd Contract of Service after its expiry, this amounted to a pre-mature termination of the Claimant’s 3rd Contract of Service as it was due to expire only on 1.2.2026 as adverted to earlier.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: Hence, what is now left to be decided by this Court is whether the Claimant’s pre-mature dismissal under the 3rd Contract of Service of the Claimant from 1.8.2023 up and until 1.2.2026 which was running simultaneously or in tandem with the 2nd Contract of Service was done with or without just cause or excuse. (Omar Othman v Kulim Advanced Technologies Sdn. Bhd. (supra)).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: It must be noted that the 3rd Contract of Service was actually in effect and running during the subsistence of the 2nd Contract of Service, as such, for the purposes of this case, I am of the view that the 3rd Contract of Service should be looked at separately from the 2nd Contract of Service as the 3rd Contract of Service was slated to expire only on 1.2.2026. In fact, under cross-examination COW-1 agreed that the 3rd Contract of Service was offered to the Claimant during the duration of the 2nd Contract of Service.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: Moreover, it is the contention of the Foundation that the 3rd Contract of Service for the period of 1.8.2023 until 1.2.2026 is invalid and void (refer paragraph 60.1 of the Foundations Written Submissions) which was vigorously disputed by Claimant. Hence, it’s now duty of this Court to ascertain whether the 3rd Contract of Service was indeed null and void on the grounds that it was concluded without the approval of the Foundation’s Board of Directors.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: The gravamen of the Foundation’s case against the Claimant was that his appointment as Chief Executive Officer under the 3rd Contract of Service is null and void as it was obtained and concluded without the approval of the Foundation’s Board of Directors.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: It was the contention of the Claimant in his evidence that he applied for a renewal of the 2nd Contract of Service (which had brought about the 3rd Contract of Service) by giving the requisite six months’ notice as he was running out of time. In his evidence (CLWS-1) the Claimant testified that he had applied to the Chairman of the Board to extend his contract during the tenure of his 2nd Contract of Service in or around the month of July 2023.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: He added in his testimony that after his application, he was appointed as the Chief Executive Officer of the Foundation for a tenure of thirty (30) months from 1.8.2023 to 1.2.2026 which was the 3rd Contract of Service.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: The Charter of the Board of Directors
content: I have perused the Foundation’s Charter of the Board of Directors (COB-3 p.26-36) (hereinafter referred to as the ‘Charter’) which was raised by the Claimant at the trial and found that there are four (4) clauses which are pertinent to the case before me. These are Clauses 1.3, 2.2.2, 2.2.3 and 5.0.2. Clause 1.3 simply states that in the event of any uncertainty or inconsistency, the Constitution of the Foundation, laws and regulations would prevail over the terms of the Charter. Clause 2.2 describes the duties of the Chairman of the Board of Directors and Clause 5.0 list down the role and responsibilities of Board of Directors.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: The Charter of the Board of Directors
content:
Clause 1.3 of the Charter provides as follows:
Piagam ini berfungsi sebagai rujukan kepada Ahli Lembaga Pengarah dalam melaksanakan tanggungjawab mereka. Peruntukan yang terkandung dalam Piagam ini tidak mengambil tempat atau menggantikan undang-undang Malaysia atau rangka kerja pengawalseliaan yang terpakai. Sekiranya berlaku ketidakpastian dan / atau timbul percanggahan, Perlembagaan YIPP, undang-undang dan peraturan-peraturan hendaklah mengatasi kandungan Piagam Lembaga Pengarah ini.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: The Charter of the Board of Directors
content:
Clause 2.2.2 of the Charter provides as follows:
Pengerusi Lembaga Pengarah adalah saluran utama antara Lembaga Pengarah dengan Kumpulan Pengurusan.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: The Charter of the Board of Directors
content:
Clause 2.2.3 of the Charter states the following:
Pengerusi memastikan bahawa Lembaga Pengarah dimaklumkan dengan perkara yang berkaitan dan kelulusan Lembaga Pengarah diminta apabila diperlukan.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: The Charter of the Board of Directors
content:
Clause 5.0.2 of the Charter states the following:
Lembaga Pengarah mengagihkan kelulusan kepda Jawatankuasa Lembaga Pengarah, Pengerusi, Pengurus Besar dan mana-mana badan lain yang dianggap patut bagi pengurusan YIPP. Sebarang kuasa yang diagihkan adalah daripada Lembaga Pengarah dan tidak bertujuan untuk menggantikan kuasa Lembaga Pengarah.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: The Charter of the Board of Directors
content:
Having perused the evidence of COW-1, during cross-examination by the learned counsel for the Claimant, I find that COW-1 was well aware of Clauses 1.3, 2.2.3 and 5.0.2 of the Charter. Her evidence in this respect is as follows:
Q. Rujuk COB-3 m/s 28 perenggan 1.3, setuju, apa yang dinyatakan dekat sini, “Piagam ini berfungsi sebagai rujukan kepada Ahli Lembaga Pengarah dalam melaksanakan tanggungjawab mereka.” Dan, “Peruntukan yang terkandung tidak mengambil tempat atau menggantikan undang-undang Malaysia.” Setuju? A. Setuju. Q. Rujuk COB-3 m/s 29. 2.2.3 (Counsel reads 2.2.3) – “Pengerusi memastikan bahawa Lembaga Pengarah dimaklumkan dengan perkara yang berkaitan dan kelulusan Lembaga Pengarah diminta apabila diperlukan” Setuju dengan saya? A. Setuju. Q. Saya rujuk COB-3 Klausa 5 m/s 31 under paragraph 2 – “Lembaga Pengarah mengagihkan kelulusan kepada Jawatankuasa Lembaga Pengarah, Pengerusi, Pengurus Besar, dan mana-mana badan lain yang dianggap patut bagi pengurusan YIPP. Sebarang kuasa yang diagihkan adalah daripada Lembaga Pengarah dan tidak bertujuan untuk mengantikan kuasa Lembaga Pengarah.” A. Setuju.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: COW-1 agreed that the Claimant’s 3rd Contract of Service was signed by the Claimant and the Chairman of the Board at the material time and was subsequently stamped. However, she disagreed that the contract was valid although it was signed and stamped.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: Learned counsel for the Claimant submitted that there was indeed a concluded contract between the Claimant and the Foundation based on the decisions of the Court of Appeal in Cipta Cermat Sdn. Bhd. v Perbadanan Kemajuan Negeri Kedah [2007] 1 CLJ 498 and a decision of the High Court in Melaka Farms Resort (M) Sdn. Bhd. v Hong Wei Seng [2004] CLJU 476.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: Conversely, the Foundation had disputed that there was a concluded contract which was the 3rd Contract of Service that was signed on 1.8.2023 between the parties, premised on the fact that the Chairman of the Board at the material time had no capacity to enter into the 3rd Contract of Service as he was only acting as Chairman of the Foundation in a caretaker role since the Penang State Assembly was dissolved on 28.6.2023 and the Penang State Election was held on 12.8.2023. (Referring to COW-1’s evidence in COWS-1 Q&A no.18(v)).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: In explaining this position, COW-1 testified as follows during re-examination: Q. Rujuk COB-1 m/s 107- pada masa mesyuarat lembaga pengarah pada 13.12.2023 tak ada Pengerusi YIPP yang dilantik? Jelaskan mengenai kehadiran pegawai dalam Lembaga Pengarah pada 13.12.2023? A. Masa itu masa peralihan dimana DUN telah dibubarkan maka Kerajaan yang ada masa itu adalah “caretaker government” jadi walaupun lantikan Pengerusi as TKM (1) its still there, he can’t function as the Pengerusi because it’s a caretaker government.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content:
When a question was put to COW-1 that by reason of Clause 5.0.2 of the Charter, the Chairman of the Board at the material time had the power to appoint the Claimant under 3rd Contract of Service, COW-1 flatly denied the said suggestion. Her answer in this regard was as follows:
Q. Berdasarkan Piagam ini, Dato, Pengerusi mempunyai, that means, Pengerusi yang dinyatakan pada kontrak yang ketiga ini, mempunyai kuasa untuk melantik En. Fitri untuk kali ketiga dan tidak wujud sebarang ketidakpatuhan dalam proses perlantikan En. Fitri untuk kontrak ketiga? A. Tidak setuju.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: The Court observes that the Foundation did not dispute the powers of the Chairman although he was in a caretaker role at the material time on the ground that he had acted ultra vires his powers under the Charter when he entered into the 3rd Contract of Service during the subsistence of the 2nd Contract of Service or that the 3rd Contract of Service is null void on the grounds of duplicity as the Claimant was serving the Foundation under two contracts of service running in tandem with each other.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: Having said that, after having examined Clause 2.2.2 and 5.0.2 of the Charter, and the submissions of the learned counsels, I am of the considered view that the Chairman of the Board had the requisite approval under Clause 5.0.2 of the Charter to enter into the 3rd Contract of Service with the Claimant since the said clause clearly grants the power of approval to the Chairman of the Board solely for the purpose of the management of the Foundation.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: At this juncture I am of the view that even if the Chairman of the Board was acting in caretaker role as contended by the Foundation, the Foundation nevertheless, would still need to function as usual and all its needs, be it from the perspective of human resources, finance and operations etc would still have to be looked into to ensure that the workings of the Foundation is not disrupted in any way. Hence, the Chairman of the Board was for all intents and purpose acting in a caretaker role was under a duty to ensure that the Foundation operates as usual without any disruptions.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: Moreover, by convention, a key public officer in caretaker role under a caretaker government typically avoids making major policy decisions or entering into large scale contracts with huge financial implications to the government, however from the facts and evidence before me, I find that the execution of the 3rd Contract of Service was nothing out of the ordinary as it was a routine employment contract in which its terms and conditions are reasonable and is very much similar with the previous contracts namely the 2nd Contract of Service. In particular, the Claimant’s salary was the same as the 2nd Contract of Service.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: Further, I am of the view that essentials decisions like the renewal of contracts of persons in key position within the organisation, like the Claimant here, can be undertaken by the Chairman of the Board in a caretaker role, more so when the Charter itself under Clause 5.5 provides that the Foundation shall at all times have a General Manger which was later known as Chief Executive Officer of the Foundation.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: I take cognisance that COW-1 had disputed that the Chaiman of the Board had such powers to approve, since according to her in her evidence during re-examination, there was nothing in a documentary form which was presumably a letter from the Foundation’s Board of Directors that gives the Chairman of the Board or any individual such powers of approval.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: Having examined the testimony of COW-1 on this issue, I am unable to accede to her contention and explanation as there is no requirement under the Charter that the Board of Directors have to provide a written approval or a formal authorization of power (a fiat for e.g.) for the Chairman of the Board to act for the proper management of the Foundation.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: Hence, based on the grounds as aforesaid, I find that the Chairman of the Board at the material time had not exceeded his powers that was granted to him under Clause 5.0.2 and/or acted ultra vires the said clause and therefore I am satisfied that he had the capacity to execute the 3rd Contract of Service with the Claimant.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Whether a Contract Has Been Concluded?
content: Thus, after having considered the facts and evidence in totality and in relying on s.10(1) of the Contracts Act 1950 and applying the fundamental elements of contract law on the balance of probabilities, I find that there was indeed a concluded contract in respect of the 3rd Contract of Service as contended by learned the counsel for the Claimant since the said contract was entered into freely by the parties, with parties competent to contract and there was lawful consideration since the Claimant had commenced serving the Foundation as its CEO under the 3rd Contract of Service. (Melaka Farms Resort (M) Sdn. Bhd. v Hong Wei Seng [2004] CLJU 476).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Issue of the Approval of the Board of Directors
content: The minutes of the meeting on 13.12.2023 had mentioned that there was an “irregularity” in the appointment of the Claimant which was in relation to his 3rd Contract of Service (refer COB-1 p.109 item 2.0). From the meeting minutes it can be gathered that the ‘irregularity’ was in respect of the 3rd Contract of Service not being brought for approval to the Foundation’s Board of Directors. Consequently, the Board of Directors which sat on 13.12.2023 decided to annul the appointment of the Claimant under the 3rd Contract of Service (COB-1 p.109 item 2.0 (i)).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Issue of the Approval of the Board of Directors
content: Having considered the Charter and the evidence as a whole, I am of the considered view that the Board of Directors of the Foundation should have approved the 3rd Contract of Service instead of annulling it as it was a concluded contract between the Foundation and the Claimant and was legally enforceable. The irregularity in the Claimant’s appointment that it was not brought to the Foundation’s Board of Directors for approval as required under Clause 2.2.3 of the Charter flies in the face of Foundation’s contention since COW-1 herself had confirmed in cross-examination that the Charter is subjected to existing laws pertaining to the formation of contracts which are offer and acceptance etc and as such the 3rd Contract of Service was in essence a valid contract. In this regard, COW-1 testified as follows: CL-C1: So, Puan. Puan sebelum ini menyatakan Piagam ini merujuk kepada, tertakluk kepada undang-undang sedia ada. Undang-undang kontrak sedia ada menyatakan offer, acceptance, tandatangan. Dia merupakan satu kontrak yang sah. Puan Penasihat Undang-undang. So, Puan sepatutnya tahu benda ini. So, ini merupakan satu kontrak yang sah. Perkara lain. Proses lain itu, kita akan. Kita akan tanya soalan dalam masa akan datang. Rujuk kepada basics. CO-W1: Basics of what? CL-C1: Offer, acceptance. CO-W1: And acceptance. CL-C1: And the signature makes this a valid contract. Would you agree with me? CO-W1: Yes. In the (inaudible) of law.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Issue of the Approval of the Board of Directors
content: Thus, I am of the considered view that the Foundation’s contention that the Claimant’s 3rd Service Contract is invalid based on an irregularity on the ground that it was not brought to the Board of Directors for approval is untenable in the circumstances of this case. To my mind based on the evidence of COW-1 as stated above, COW-1 having known that the 3rd Service Contract had already been concluded legally, should have apprised the Board of Directors about the legality and validity of the said contract at the meeting on 13.12.2023 in order for it to be approved.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Issue of the Approval of the Board of Directors
content: Furthermore, the subsequent approval of the 3rd Contract of Service would not have prejudiced the Foundation in any way in light of the stellar performance of the Claimant during his stint at the Foundation before he was terminated. This was evident in the Claimant’s achievements that was highlighted by the Foundation for the purposes of renewing his contract for the second time (the 2nd Contract of Service) (refer Meeting Minutes dated 15.9.2022 at COB-1 p.91). The Claimant’s achievements were acknowledged COW-1 in her evidence during cross-examination. There were also no issues raised about the Claimant's record of service with the Foundation which may have justified the decision to pre-maturely end the Claimant’s contract.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Issue of the Approval of the Board of Directors
content: Hence, based on the evidence before me, I am of the view that the decision to annul the appointment of the Claimant under Claimant’s 3rd Contract of Service was done mechanically by the Board of Directors of the Foundation without regard to the laws of Malaysia as to the formation of a contract in particular s.10(1) of the Contracts Act 1950 as adverted to earlier and therefore amounted to a unilateral termination of the said contract. Hence, this Court being a Court of equity and good conscience is duty bound strike down any decision to terminate the services of a workmen which was arrived at mechanically.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Issue of the Approval of the Board of Directors
content: It’s the opinion of this Court therefore, that the termination of the Claimant by the Foundation as of 1.3.2024 under the 2nd Contract of Service, in total disregard to the Claimant’s 3rd Contract of Service which was running in tandem during the subsistence of the Claimant’s 2nd Contract of Service was harsh and unjust. The termination of the Claimant from his services on 1.3.2024 under 2nd Contract of Service meant that his services under 3rd Contract of Service was pre-maturely terminated on 1.3.2024 since it was only due to expire on 1.2.2026.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Security of Tenure and the Right to Livelihood
content: Looking at the factual matrix of this case from the point of view of the Federal Constitution which to my mind is the holy book of the nation and a sacrosanct document, it cannot be gainsaid that that a workman like the Claimant who was lawfully appointed by the Foundation via a contract of employment, undoubtedly has security of tenure of employment which has been recognized as a proprietary right to livelihood under Article 5 of the Federal Constitution, meaning, the right to be engaged in lawful and gainful employment until and unless he is dismissed from gainful employment with just cause or excuse (Tan Teck Seng v Suruhanjaya Perkhidmatan Pendidikan & Anor [1996] 2 CLJ 771 and Subramaniam Letchimanan v The United States of America & Another Appeal [2021] 7 CLJ 371).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Security of Tenure and the Right to Livelihood
content: In Hong Leong Equipment Sdn Bhd v Liew Fook Chuan & Other Appeals [1997] 1 CLJ 665, in speaking for the Court of Appeal, Gopal Sri Ram JCA had this to say: “The legislature has willed that the relationship of employer and workman as resting on a mere consensual basis that is capable of termination by the employer at will with the meagre consequence of paying the hapless workman a paltry sum as damages should be altered in favour of the workman. It has accordingly provided for security of tenure and equated the right to be engaged in gainful employment to a proprietary right which may not be forfeited save, and except, for just cause or excuse.” (emphasis is mine)

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Security of Tenure and the Right to Livelihood
content:
The importance of security of tenure in employment was also underscored in Nova Charm Sdn. Bhd. v Ooi Hock Huat 2002 2 ILR 706 where this Court stated:
“The IRA protects the security of tenure of a workman engaged under a contract of service. The principle of security of tenure guarantees an employee’s legitimate expectation to continue in his employment and to earn his livelihood unless his employer has just cause or excuse or excuse to terminate his services….” (emphasis is mine)

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Security of Tenure and the Right to Livelihood
content: Hence, based on the authorities cited above, I am of the view that the right to livelihood cannot be trampled upon merely because of technicalities and irregularities like board of director’s approvals etc. This is not to say that approvals from the board of directors of a company or an organisation are not important or unnecessary, but such a requirement must always be weighed in with reasonableness and objectivity. Like in the instant case, the 3rd Contract of Service could have been approved at the Board of Directors meeting on 13.12.2023 based on existing laws pertaining to contracts and the Claimant could have continued his employment with the Foundation up and until 1.2.2026. Surely a mere irregularity cannot be the basis for dismissing an employee, depriving him/her of their constitutional to right to livelihood.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Security of Tenure and the Right to Livelihood
content: Hence, this Court being a Court of equity and good conscience is emboldened to act based on the substantial merits of a case without regard to technicalities and legal form, and hence, the Court cannot and must not pay mere lip service to this phrase. This phrase to my mind is the very foundation of the Industrial Court and breaths life to it and extends beyond a cosmetic existence, carrying with it the notion of justice and fair play. It is specifically provided under s.30(5) of the Act so as to ensure that the decisions of the Industrial Court are nuanced, tempered with objectivity and reasonableness and not tied to any technicality or irregularities as exposed in the Claimant’s case before this Court.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Security of Tenure and the Right to Livelihood
content: To my mind it is this phrase which has empowered the Industrial Court to assess the proportionality of punishments in relation to acts of misconduct and to strike down any decision to terminate the services of a workmen which was arrived at mechanically without thought and with absolute disregard to concept of fairness and logic.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Security of Tenure and the Right to Livelihood
content: Hence in the upshot, this Court after having considered all the evidence led before it, the pleadings filed, written submissions of the parties and keeping in mind Section 30(5) of Act 177 which behoves upon this Court to act according to equity, good conscience and the substantial merits of the case without regard to technicality and legal form, finds that the Foundation has failed to prove on a balance of probability that the pre-mature termination of the Claimant under the 3rd Contract of Service was done with just cause and excuse. (Omar Othman v Kulim Advanced Technologies Sdn.Bhd. (supra)).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
section_title: Security of Tenure and the Right to Livelihood
content: This Court therefore finds that the termination of the Claimant to be without just cause and excuse.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: This Court finds that the Claimant was employed on a genuine fixed term contract for the period of two years and six months from 1.8.2023 to 1.2.2026 which is yet to expire as of the date of handing down this award. The learned counsel for the Claimant had pleaded for the Claimant’s reinstatement to his former position.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: However, in considering the facts and circumstances of this case, I am of the view that no order of reinstatement should be made as the Claimant had testified that he had found alternative employment since 3.3.2025 and moreover, I am of the opinion that reinstatement is not appropriate as it is apparent from the facts of this case that this may put both parties in a difficult and an intolerable situation which may in turn disrupt peace and harmony in the establishment and therefore it will not be beneficial for both parties.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: The practice in cases of termination of a fixed term contract is to limit backwages to the remainder of the unexpired portion of the fixed term contract of employment. (See Thangasamy Brown v. Pelabuhan Tanjung Pelepas Sdn. Bhd. [2009] 6 CLJ 144 and Kolej Tafe & Anor v. Kalimuthu Arumugam [1999] 1 ILR 171).

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: The Court takes note that since the Claimant was employed on a fixed term contract from 1.8.2023 to 1.2.2026 under the 3rd Contract of Service and he was pre-maturely dismissed effective from 1.3.2024, this means that the Claimant had twenty two (22) months remaining in the said contract before it was pre-maturely terminated by the Foundation.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content:
The Court is aware that any form of compensation awarded to the Claimant must be subjected to a deduction for post-dismissal earnings as required in the case of Dr. James Alfred (Sabah) v. Koperasi Serbaguna Sanya Bhd (Sabah) & Anor [2001] 3 CLJ 541, where the Federal Court held:
"In our view, it is in line with equity and good conscience that the Industrial Court, in assessing quantum of backwages, should take into account the fact, if established by evidence or admitted, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. Failure to do so constitutes a jurisdictional error of law. Certiorari will therefore lie to rectify it." (emphasis is mine)

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: The Claimant in cross-examination informed the Court that after he was dismissed from employment with the Company on 1.3.2024, he tried looking for a job and only managed to secure employment as a Manager in March 2025 with a salary of RM 6,500.00 per month.
