Meaning, the Claimant was unemployed for nearly a year. Hence, I am of the view that a deduction of five (5) percent is reasonable in the circumstances on account of post dismissal earnings for the remaining period of his fixed term contract.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content:
Hence, back-wages for the balance of the unexpired fixed term contract is calculated as follows:
RM 15,121.25 x 22 months = 332,667.50 less 5% on account of post dismissal earnings is equivalent to RM 316,034.13.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: Hence the total sum of compensation payable to the Claimant is RM 316,034.13 only.

case_name: Mohd Fitri bin Ibrahim v Yayasan Islam Pulau Pinang
chairman: Jeyaseelen a/l T. Anthony
content: This Court hereby orders that the total sum of RM 316,034.13 less any statutory deductions is to be paid to the Claimant by the Foundation through his solicitors, the Messrs. Jessy & Associates within 30 days from the date of this award.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Roles and functions of the court
content: It is a trite law that the role of the court is two-fold. Firstly, to determine whether the misconduct complained of by the employer has been established, and secondly whether the proven misconduct constitutes just cause or excuse for the dismissal: see Wong Chee Hong v. Cathay Organisation Malaysia Sdn Bhd [1988] 1 CLJ Rep 298; Milan Auto Sdn Bhd v. Wong Seh Yen [1995] 4 CLJ 449; K A Sanduran Nehru Ratnam v. I-Berhad [2007] 1 CLJ 347.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Roles and functions of the court
content: The burden of proof lies with the employer in proving that he has just cause or excuse for making the decision and not for the employee to prove otherwise: see Ireka Construction Berhad v Chantiravathan Subramaniam James [1995] 2 lLR 11 (Award No. 245 of 1995). The employer must prove the employee guilty, by producing convincing evidence that the employee committed the offence or offences the employee is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed, and it is not the employee who must prove himself not guilty (see Stamford Executive Centre v. Dharsini Ganesan [1986] 1 lLR 101 (Award No. 263 of 1985).

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Roles and functions of the court
content: As regards the standard of proof to prove the case is on a balance of probabilities that is the civil standard, as decided by the Court of Appeal in the case of Menara Panglobal Sdn Bhd v Arokianathan Sivapiragasan [2006] 2 CLJ 501 and Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara v. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor [2002] 3 CLJ 314.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Roles and functions of the court
content:
The test that is applied to a direct dismissal like this case is a “reasonable test”. Reasonable test has been expounded by Salleh Abas FCJ (as His Lordship then was) in the case of Preston Corp Sdn Bhd v. Edward Leong Nim Fay & Ors [1982] CLJ 302; [1982] CLJ (Rep) 272; [1982] 2 MLJ 22 as below:
“The test of reasonableness is what a reasonable, honest and right-minded person considers the usage concerned to be fair and proper. A usage which outrages the sense of justice and commonsense is not reasonable: Produce Broker Co. Ltd v. Olympia Oil and Cake Co. Ltd. The test therefore is one which refers to the normal and ordinary value judgment of a reasonable man.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Roles and functions of the court
content: In the recent Federal Court’s decision, in the case of Tan Lay Peng v. RHB Bank Bhd & Anor [2024] 2 ILR 535, Nordin Hasan FCJ in delivering the judgment of the Court, held: “On the issue of reasonableness, generally, what is reasonable is what a reasonable man considers fair and proper based on the particular facts and circumstances of the case.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Roles and functions of the court
content:
The court must also satisfy that the company has come up with good and convincing proof as required by law pronounced in Federal Aluminium Sdn Bhd, Prai v. Kochunni A/L Kuttan Nair, Penang [1986] 1 ILR 656, to prove misconduct, where the court held:
“It must be realised that in dismissal cases this Court must insist on good and convincing proof of the charge against the workman. This is an absolute prerequisite for the Court to uphold a dismissal if the protection given to workmen by S. 20 of the Industrial Relations Act, 1967 of security of tenure in their jobs against unjustified dismissals is not to be negated. This principle is so basic that ignorance of it can be excuse at all.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: It is a trite law that the relationship between the employer and the employee is fiduciary in nature. Any breach of fiduciary duty will be an act of mala fide. The court wishes to refer to the case of Azahari Shahrom & Anor v. Associated Pan Malaysia Cement Sdn Bhd [2010] 1 ILR 423, where it was held, as follows: "It is trite that the association between employer and employee out of necessity is fiduciary in nature. There has to be mutual trust and confidence that one would deal with the other in all fairness and rectitude over the rights and obligations flowing between the parties under the employment agreement. If one does an act or commits an omission which is inconsistent with that fiduciary relationship then that act or omission will be mala fides. This principle has equal application as against the employer and the employee in their respective positions viz the employment relationship between them." (emphasis added)

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: It must be remembered that the established principle in industrial jurisprudence is that in every employment contract there is an implied term that a party thereto will not without reasonable cause conduct himself in a manner likely to damage or destroy the relationship of trust and confidence between the parties, as employer and employee: see Tian San Sdn Bhd v. Lin Kim Ping [1997] 3 ILR 483 (Award No. 483 of 1997).

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The claimant is also required, as an employee, to act faithfully and in accordance with the interest of his employer, as held in the case of Cellular Communications Network (M) Sdn Bhd v. Ilhami Mohamad [2001] 1 ILR 233 (Award No. 29 of 2001).

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The question to be answered by the court is whether the company was with just cause or excuse while dismissing the claimant.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Learned counsel for the claimant, at the very commencement of the trial, prior to the marking of the bundle of documents, raised objection to the company’s documents at pages 13 and 14, 15 to 25, 26 to 33 and 125 to 192 of COB3 since the maker of the documents were not called and the admissibility of those documents are being directly challenged. The court upon hearing the parties ruled that the documents were to be marked and admitted, whereby, the weight to be decided later.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Generally, failure to call the maker of the document would render documentary evidence to be hearsay.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Learned counsel for the claimant has also cited a recent decision by the Industrial Court in Sabah in the case of Kendy Lim Fang Vui v Sazarice Sdn Bhd [2024] 3 lLR 121, where the Learned Chairman held that the evidence produced by COW2 was hearsay in respect to the second charge since the person who allegedly told COW2 that the claimant had never visited the Speed Mart was not called as a witness.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Learned counsel for the claimant has also distinguished the decision of Mohd Azreen Bin Abd Manap v Petroleum Nasional Berhad [2025] lLRU 0872, where the Learned Chairman had allowed the admissibility of the interview transcript since the counsel had failed to object to the document prior to the marking and the document was taken by Alex Tan who was called to testify by the company. The court in Mohd Azreen, supra, emphasised that the court has the obligation to act in equity and good conscience without strict compliances to legalities and technical form pursuant to s. 30(5) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 (“IRA”).

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content: The question that the court is facing now is a crucial issue as to the admissibility of evidence where the maker or the creator of the document was not called to testify to the accuracy of the document.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content: Under the IRA, the parties will usually quote s. 30(5) in attempting to relax the strict application as stated in the Evidence Act 1950, and, in our case, on the issue of hearsay evidence.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content:
Before we proceed further, it is imperative for the court to highlight what the position of law is on how to tender a document properly during the trial. To answer this, the court wishes to refer to the latest Federal Court’s decision in Live Capital Sdn Bhd v. Pioneer Conglomerate Sdn Bhd [2025] 6 CLJ 855, where Abdul Rahman Sebli CJSS held:
[31] What the Court of Appeal set as precedent, a dangerous one we would say, is that the authenticity and contents of disputed documents, ie, Part C documents need not be verified by the maker of the documents before they can be admitted in evidence and that all that is required of the party seeking to rely on such documents is to have them marked as exhibits, and once that is done, the contents of the documents are deemed to be the truth. [32] With due respect to the learned judges of the Court of Appeal, the procedure they adopted is unknown to law. Unless the authenticity of the two vouchers had been verified by calling the maker or makers of the documents, the contents of the documents remained hearsay as the purpose of producing them was to prove the truth of the contents and not merely to prove that the notation and alterations were made (Subramaniam v. PP [1956] CLJU 115; [1956] 1 LNS 115; [1956] 1 MLJ 220). Clearly, the respondent had no other purpose in producing P1 and P2 as exhibits other than to prove that the RM7 million was an advance and not a commission. They were therefore caught by the rule against hearsay.” (emphasis added)

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content:
What if the document has been tendered and marked like in our case? The answer can also be found in Live Capital Sdn Bhd, supra, where it was held:
“[33] A document cannot be admitted in evidence and marked as such until it has been properly proved: See the judgment of Shankar J (as he then was) in Chong Khee Sang v. Phang Ah Chee [1983] CLJU 57; [1983] 1 LNS 57; [1984] 1 MLJ 377. Such a document has no evidential value, is irrelevant and should not be admitted in evidence and if admitted must be disregarded.” (emphasis added)
Effect of s. 30(5) of IRA

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content:
Now, what is the effect of s. 30 (5) on the decision of the court? S. 30 (5) provides:
(5) The Court shall act according to equity, good conscience and the substantial merits of the case without regard to technicalities and legal form.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content: Before we proceed further, it cannot escape the court’s attention to state in this Award that IRA is a social legislation enacted by the Parliament to ensure that a workman’s right to earn a livelihood is not truncated arbitrarily at the will of the employer (see Maritime Intelligence Sdn Bhd v Tan Ah Gek, [2021] 10 CLJ 663) and the duty of the court is to protect the weaker party in social legislation (see PJD Regency Sdn Bhd v Tribunal Tuntutan Pembeli Rumah & Anor and Other Appeals [2021] 2 CLJ 441).

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content:
In discussing the issue, it is worthwhile referring to the case of Plastic Centre Sdn. Bhd. v. Kesatuan Pekerja-Pekerja Kimia Malaya, [1990] 1 ILR 9A, where the court held:
“While provocation is a factor available as a defence within well defined limits in law, the Industrial Relations Act 1967, s.30(5) of the Act emboldens this Court to act according to equity and good conscience and without regard to legal form. It means that in considering whether the employer acted reasonably or unreasonably, the tribunal should adopt a broad approach of common sense and common fairness, eschewing all legal or other technicality. (Sir John Donaldson in Carl v. Slater & Wheeler (Airlyne) Ltd. ICB, 508 [1973] 1 AER 145.)” (emphasis added)

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content: It must be remembered that Industrial Court is acting and deciding its case based on social justice. In the IRA, s. 30(5) is a concept of social justice. In Jurutera Konsultant (SEA) Sdn. Bhd. v. Yeo Soon Chuan, [1991] 2 ILR 825, the court described social justice as “something more than legal justice in the country. It seeks to unshackle the technicalities of the common law in dealing with industrial disputes. Social justice and legal justice are two different concepts though their common object is to do justice. Nevertheless the methods adopted by social justice are unorthodox. It metes out justice according to the conscience of society according to what is fair and equitable.” (emphasis added)

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content:
In the case of Amran Mahmud v. Syarikat Sesco Berhad, [2025] 4 ILR 17, this court held:
“[81] The court in hearing this case “should not be burdened with the technicalities regarding the standard of proof, the rules of evidence and procedure that are applied in a court of law. The Industrial Court should be allowed to conduct its proceedings as a “court of arbitration”, and be more flexible in arriving at its decision, so long as it gives special regard to substantial merits and decide a case in accordance with equity and good conscience.” – see Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara v. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor [2002] 3 CLJ 314.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content: Social justice is a "Justice that conforms to a moral principle…” (see Kesatuan Pekerja-pekerja Bank Pertanian Malaysia Berhad Sarawak v. Bank Pertanian Malaysia Berhad [2025] 3 ILR 523.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content: Hence, it is the considered view of the court, upon reading the above authorities, that the bounden duty of the court is to balance the duty to call the maker to tender the document according to the requirement in the case of Live Capital Sdn Bhd, supra, and the duty assigned to it under s. 30(5) to ensure social justice be properly observed without binding itself to technicalities and legal form, not only to ensure justice to the claimant but also to the company.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: General rule to call the maker of document
content: Therefore, it is the considered view of the court, to act as realistic as possible and in adopting a broad approach of common sense and common fairness and moral principle, the sacred duty of the court is to make sure that element of technicalities or legal form (“the element”) must be avoided, as far as possible, and, the element, if observed is really necessary due to the substantial prejudice or substantial miscarriage of justice that befell the claimant before the decision was made to dismiss him.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: In our case, the documents on pages 13-14, 15-25 and 26-33 of COB3 are statements by Srithar Sriramulu, Alex Tan and Travis Wong respectively who were the witnesses giving evidence in the DI. Whereas the document on pages 125-192 of COB3 is an interview transcript based on audio recording of a person named Mazrin Ramli (“Mazrin”), the CEO of Deleum Primera .

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: During the trial before this court, COW2 testified that she was the chairperson of the DI held against the claimant. The members of the DI, including COW2, were three (3) people.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
COW2 in her evidence highlighted the court that the documents on pages 13-14, 15-25 and 26-33 of COB3 were tendered as part of the exhibit during the DI. This is her evidence during the examination in chief: Q: Please refer to pages 1 to 390 of the Company’s Bundle of Documents (Volume 3) and pages 1 to 266 of the Company’s Bundle of Documents (Volume 4). What are these documents?
A: These are the exhibits produced by the Company’s presenting officer during the course of the Domestic Inquiry. The exhibits are marked as “Exhibit CE-A” to “Exhibit CE-G” and “Exhibit CE-1” to “Exhibit CE-26”.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Whereby, the document on pages 125 – 192 was also made part of the evidence during the hearing in the DI. It was tendered through Alex Tan during the DI.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
These documents were tendered and marked during the DI, as follows:
a. The document on pages 13-14 of COB3 marked as CE-D. b. The document on pages 15-25 of COB3 marked as CE-E. c. The document on pages 26-33 of COB3 marked as CE-F. d. The document on pages 125-192 of COB3 marked as CE-12.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: It is the considered view of the court, since these documents were tendered during the DI and became part of the evidence in the DI, therefore, they are relevant documents which formed part of the proceeding in the Dl.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
Regarding the procedure to be adopted during a domestic inquiry to show that the rule of natural justice has been properly observed, it is worthwhile for the court to refer to a decision by Mohd Eusoff b Chin J (as he then was) in the case of Nadarajah & Anor. v. Golf Resort (M) Sdn. Bhd. [1991] 1 ILR, where His Lordship held:
“What is required of the Industrial Court to do is that it must observe the rules of natural justice in the conduct of inquiries before it, some of which are.
(a) that a party should have due notice of the
proceeding:
(b) that he should have the opportunity of adducing all relevant evidence on which he relies;
(c) that the evidence of the opposite side should be taken in his presence;
(d) that he should be given the opportunity of cross-examining the witnesses examined by the opposite party, and
(e) that no material should be relied on against him without his having been given an opportunity of explaining the same.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The court was also referred to the case of Sony Electronics (M) Sdn Bhd v. Philip Vincent Rodrigues [2007] ILRU 2058, where the court held: “It is well settled that in a domestic enquiry the strict and sophisticated rules of evidence under the Evidence Act 1950 may not apply. All materials which are logically probative for a prudent mind are permissible. There is no allergy to hearsay evidence provided it has reasonable nexus and credibility.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: It is the considered view of the court that the documents that were challenged and objected to by the claimant are relevant to the issue at hand, as proceeding in the DI together with the exhibits tendered therein became the consideration that led to the forming of reason for the dismissal. This has complied with the principle of law described by the Federal Court in Maritime Intelligence Sdn Bhd, supra, which held that the reason to dismiss must resonate in the employer's mind, prior to, or preceding the decision to dismiss. And based on the cases of Nadarajah, supra and Sony Electronics (M) Sdn Bhd, supra, the court finds that the rules of natural justice were not faulted in the proceeding.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
To show that natural justice had been accorded to the claimant during the DI, the claimant was also not stopped from calling his own witness and in fact he decided not to call any witness, and this can be seen on page 166 of COB2:
Chairman :
Okay, alright. Johnny you have one witness like you mentioned earlier? Accused Employee:
Has my wife lah.
Chairman :
Okay, alright
Accused Employee:
I think, I think we already explained this lah.
Chairman :
Ya
Accused Employee:
I don’t think needed lah.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: There was also no evidence to suggest during the DI that the claimant was stopped or halted by the DI from referring to the documentary evidence for the purpose of cross-examination to any of the company’s witnesses or to ask more time from the DI to peruse the documentary evidence relied on by the company against him.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
Having found that the rules of natural justice have not been faulted during the DI – as the claimant was present and was given opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses – the next duty of the court is to consider the evidence or statements adduced at the Dl. This duty has been stated by the High Court in the case of Metroplex Administration Sdn Bhd v. Mohamed Elias [1998] 5 CLJ 467, a case helpfully cited by the learned counsel for the company. This is what the High Court held:
“…, I am of the view that the learned chairman has failed to consider or failed to consider adequately the evidence or statements adduced at the board of domestic inquiry and the finding of the board of domestic inquiry.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
The court at the same time while preparing this Award is duty bound to examine the notes of proceeding prepared during the Dl, as the document was tendered through the chairperson of the DI, COW2, is relevant and will be accepted as evidence. As the notes of proceeding in the DI were tendered through one of its members, the court will accept them as evidence in this court. In the case of Alam Arena Management Sdn. Bhd. v. Alex Veeramuthu [2006] 1 ILR 485, the court held:
"If the notes had been properly produced by any of the Panel Members, the court would have accepted them as evidence."

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The court is also bound to consider the evidence of the witnesses during the Dl. To this, the court wishes to refer to the judgment of Raus Sharif J (as His Lordship then was) in the case of Bumiputra Commerce Bank Bhd v. Mahkamah Perusahaan Malaysia & Anor [2004] 7 CLJ 77 where His Lordship held: I am of the view in coming to the said conclusion, the Industrial Court had failed to take into consideration the evidence of the second respondent himself at the domestic inquiry, bearing in mind the notes of inquiry had been accepted by court as an exhibit.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
Be that as it may, the court is mindful the duty of the court is to investigate the whole of the evidence presented before the court. The court is not bound to merely rely on the notes of proceeding before the DI, before coming to its decision. The court finds guidance from the Court of Appeal’s decision in the case of Multimedia Development Corporation Sdn Bhd v. Clarence Augustine Tee Teck Huo, [2018] 2 ILR 401 where Hasnah Mohammed Hashim JCA (as Her Ladyship then was) held:
“[31] The factual matrix in Plaintree Wood Products Sdn Bhd v. Mahkamah Perusahaan Malaysia is different from Bumiputra Commerce. His Lordship, Raus J (as he then was) explained in his written judgment that the issues decided in Plaintree Wood Product 's case can be distinguished from that of Bumiputra Commerce 's:
Dengan hormatnya saya berpendapat perkara yang diputuskan di dalam kes tersebut adalah berbeza dengan kes pemohon ini. Di dalam kes Bumiputra Commerce Sdn. Bhd., apa yang saya putuskan adalah mengenai kegagalan Mahkamah Perusahaan untuk mengambilkira nota keterangan domestic inquiry yang telah dikemukakan sebagai keterangan. Mahkamah Perusahaan di dalam kes itu tidak langsung merujuk kepada nota keterangan domestic inquiry dalam membuat penilaian fakta dan kegagalan itu telah saya putuskan sebagai suatu kesilapan undang-undang. Di dalam kes pemohon ini, keadaan adalah berbeza. Kes pemohon di Mahkamah Perusahaan adalah masih diperingkat pembicaraan. Pada saya, responden kedua adalah bebas untuk membentangkan kesnya ini dan untuk menyokong dakwaan bahawa beliau telah dibuang kerja tanpa alasan yang munasabah. Di pihak pemohon pula, jika terdapat keterangan mengenai domestic inquiry, terpulanglah kepada pemohon untuk mengemukakannya. Tugas Mahkamah Perusahaan ialah untuk membuat keputusan berpandukan keseluruhan keterangan yang dikemukakan melalui keterangan-keterangan saksi yang dikemukakan oleh kedua-dua pihak. Sudah tentu Mahkamah Perusahaan tidak semata-mata terikat kepada nota prosiding di dalam domestic inquiry. Jadi Mahkamah Perusahaan adalah tidak silap untuk mengarahkan pembicaraan penuh dijalankan di dalam kes ini. (emphasis added)

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Therefore, based on the spirit of the IRA, the court finds that the challenged and objected documents are relevant, admissible and should be considered by the court to arrive at its fair and right decision. The question of weight to be attached to these documents is different, which the court is readily undertaking in preparing this Award.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: The established evidence in the court
content:
The company has established the evidence as follows:
a. The claimant confirmed during his employment with the company, he was based in Miri.
b. From 1.10.2017 until the dismissal, the claimant held a position as Manager, under Construction, Sarawak – Oil with Petronas Carigali Sdn Bhd.
c. Based on COB3, page 153, lines 8 to 19, the claimant agreed when Mazrin mentioned ‘Johnny’ and the position as the head of construction the statements are consistent with his position in Petronas.
d. The claimant admitted that working with the company he is bound to follow the CoBE and ABC Manual. e. The claimant knows Mazrin as a registered contractor of Petronas, who won the award for the Sponge Jet Contract of which the claimant was the end user.
f. The claimant knows Mazrin through one of his colleagues, Mohd Azreen bin Abd Manap who was also dismissed for similar offences like the claimant.
g. The claimant agreed that the company requires him to make a declaration, if he travels with a contractor, so that the company can assess whether there is a conflict of interest and whether to clear it or to prohibit it.
h. During the DI, the claimant agreed that Mazrin had paid for the flight tickets and the claimant had handed the passport to him to arrange for the flight tickets and physically passed the tickets to him.
i. The claimant also stated in the DI that the trip to Santorini was called a family trip and he went there with his wife, Mohd Azreen and his wife.
j. The claimant agreed that the trip began on 07.03.2018 as per the flight from Miri and ended on 18.03.2018 as per the flight back to Miri. The flight tickets can be seen on pages 3-11of COB4.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Breach of the company’s COBE and ABC Manual
content: It is submitted by the learned counsel for the company that the claimant had breached clauses 1.1. and 1.3 of CoBE and clause 10 of CoBE and section 2B(ii) of the ABC Manual.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Breach of the company’s COBE and ABC Manual
content:
The claimant agreed that the company has stated four (4) corporate core values, and two (2) of them relate to avoiding conflict of interest and refraining from taking advantage of his position for his own personal interest. Clause 2.2 provides:
“CORPORATE VALUES AND CULTURE
2.2. As an employee in the PETRONAS group, you have a duty to serve PETRONAS with good faith, fidelity, diligence and integrity. You are required to act in the best interests of PETRONAS and to refrain from engaging in conduct or activities which may adversely affect the best interests of PETRONAS. You are at all times required to:
• conscientiously maintain the highest degree of integrity, • always exercise proper care and judgment, • avoid conflicts of interest, and •refrain from taking advantage of your position or exercising your authority to further your own personal interest at the expense of PETRONAS. You may not conduct yourself in a manner that might undermine or that is likely to destroy or seriously damage PETRONAS’ confidence and trust in you. These duties are without limitation on duties imposed on you by law.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Breach of the company’s COBE and ABC Manual
content:
Whereas clause 1.1 of CoBE regarding avoidance of conflict of interest provides:
“1. DUTY REGARDING AVOIDANCE OF CONFLICT OF INTEREST
1.1. A conflict of interest arises in any situation in which an individual is in a position to take advantage of his or her role in PETRONAS for his or her personal benefit, including the benefit of his or her family and friends. A conflict of interest can make it difficult for an individual to fulfil his or her duties impartially and correctly. A conflict of interest can exist even if it results in no unethical or improper acts. Even the appearance of improper influence in your decision-making may be an issue. A conflict of interest will undermine the values of good faith, fidelity, diligence and integrity in the performance of your duties and obligations as expected by PETRONAS. You must therefore avoid conflicts of interest between your personal dealings and your duties and responsibilities in the conduct of PETRONAS' business. In particular, the use of PETRONAS office position, confidential information, assets and other PETRONAS resources for personal gain, or for the advantage of others with whom you are associated, is prohibited.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Breach of the company’s COBE and ABC Manual
content:
The duty of the claimant to inform the company of any conflict of interest that may arise is provided by clause 1.3 of CoBE as follows:
“1. DUTY REGARDING AVOIDANCE OF CONFLICT OF INTEREST
1.3 In certain instances, a conflict of interest that has been fully disclosed to PETRONAS may be tolerated by PETRONAS (for example, because measures are taken to ensure that it poses no risk to PETRONAS). Any conflict situations should be cleared by your Human Resource Department (or, in case of directors, with the relevant company secretary). A failure to disclose fully the nature and scope of the conflict of interest may result in disciplinary action against you.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Breach of the company’s COBE and ABC Manual
content:
Regarding receiving entertainment, it is stated in CoBE as follows:
“6. SOLICITATION, BRIBERY AND CORRUPTION 6.5 Even the appearance of conduct prohibited by this Section 6, or any other measure that is unethical or that will tarnish PETRONAS’ reputation for honesty and integrity, must be avoided. If you are unsure whether an action is permitted, seek guidance before acting.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Breach of the company’s COBE and ABC Manual
content:
Clause 10 of CoBE provides:
“10. Receiving Gifts and Entertainment
10.1 You are required to comply with the policies and procedures of your Human Resource Department relating to the receipt of gifts and entertainment.
10.2 In no event, however, may you or any of your family/household members accept gifts or entertainment in exchange for an exercise or non-exercise of your PETRONAS authority or otherwise to the detriment of PETRONAS.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
section_title: Breach of the company’s COBE and ABC Manual
content:
Meanwhile, section 2B(ii) of ABC Manual provides:
“2B(ii): Receiving Entertainment
PETRONAS recognises that occasional acceptance of a reasonable and modest level of entertainment provided by third parties in the normal course of business is a legitimate way to network and build good business relationships.
However, it is important for employees and directors to exercise proper care and judgment before accepting entertainment offered or provided by a third party. This is not only to safeguard the Company’s reputation, but also to protect employees and directors from allegations of impropriety or undue influence.
You are required to comply with the policies and procedures of your Human Resources Department in relation to receiving entertainment from third parties.
As set forth in Part IIB paragraph 10.2 of CoBE, in no event, however, may you or any of your family/household members accept entertainment in exchange for an exercise of non-exercise of your PETRONAS authority or otherwise to the detriment of PETRONAS.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: For this charge, the allegation of misconduct is that the claimant had received the total amount of RM260,000.00 from Deleum Primera Sdn Bhd (DPSB), a Petronas’s registered contractor. DPSB as Petronas’ registered contractor can also be seen at pages 37-185 of COB4.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: To establish this charge, the company relied on the evidence which is in the possession of DPSB’s staff’s laptop.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The investigation that led to this charge showed that the sum of RM260,000.00 is recorded in spreadsheets belonging to DPSB. This evidence can be seen on page 66 of COB3 stated as “Johny-trip to KL family 12-16Jan:RM10K”, on page 71 of COB3 as “Jony Baram G 50,000” and on page 80 of COB3 as “Johny-Temana: RM200K”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: According to the evidence from COW1, who was at that material time holding the position of Manager (Special Review), whose duty was to manage investigations and carry out special review work as instructed by the company.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: COW1 narrated to the court, in September 2020, during a meeting with the President, Group CEO and company’s Chief Integrity Officer, where in that meeting it was highlighted that PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) found a tender plan belonging to PETRONAS Carigali Sdn Bhd (PCSB) and several spreadsheets containing records of payout to PETRONAS staff. The discovery was made by PwC during their forensic investigation work at DPSB.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Due to seriousness of the issue, an investigation taskforce was formed to establish facts relating to the documents retrieved through PwC’s forensic investigation work. The company also according to COW1 had engaged PwC to assist on investigation work as part of ensuring information pertaining to DPSB could be verified. In order to verify the veracity of the documents and information by PwC, the company looked through the documents received and validated the information and documentation against its internal data.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The duty of COW1 in the taskforce was predominantly validating documents and information found by PwC in the possession of DPSB.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Based on the evidence, PCSB and DPSB entered two contracts, collectively referred to by COW1 as “the Sponge Jet Contract”.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The validation was done by looking through the spreadsheets and other documents surrendered by PwC and extracting all the names given by PwC alleged to be the PETRONAS personnel. The taskforce also requested documentation for the Sponge Jet Contract to validate the alleged contract as per PwC’s finding. Upon checking with the PETRONAS internal data, it was confirmed that the claimant was one of the PETRONAS’s employees stated in the spreadsheets.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
COW2 in her evidence told the court that to determine the accuracy of the spreadsheets, the DI referred to:
a. spreadsheet line item i.e. PO to SS (with 8%) at RM409, 415.04 as can seen on page 39 of COB3.
b. DPSB purchase order No. 6002707 to Synergy Spectacular Sdn. Bhd. on page 267 of COB3 showing the amount shown in the spreadsheet at RM409, 415. 04. c. spreadsheets containing names of PETRONAS acronyms such as KAKG, TEPB etc, for example at pages 39 to 42 and 71 of COB3.
d. confirmation by the company’s witness during the Dl by the name of Jason that the spreadsheet line item i.e. Work Order No. 32 for work on KAKGA HP and LP Flare Tim Maintenance and Repair at Main Deck at pages 39 to 42 of COB3 was the same Work Order No. 32 raised and paid by PCSB as can be seen at pages 80 to 81 of COB3
Allegations of receiving RM50,000.00 and RM200,000.00

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Regarding the allegation of receiving RM50,000.00, the court finds that the company has successfully proved the charge. There is sufficient evidence to link the claimant with receiving the amounts of RM50,000.00 and RM200,000.00. From the evidence, there is no other employee by the named Johnny working in Miri with the company. Further, the document also showed the spouse of the claimant as Kong Siew Ling, who forms part of charges 2, 3 and 4. This can be seen on pages 242-242 of COB4 i.e. the Staff & Family Details.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Furthermore, as admitted by the claimant during the cross examination, he agreed when Mazrin referred to ‘Johnny’, based in Miri and is the head of construction – as shown on page 153 of COB4 – he was referring to him.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
The court would like to refer to the evidence of COW2 to show that reference to Johnny in the spreadsheets referred to the claimant:
(b) To ensure that the name “Johnny” stated in the spreadsheet referred to the Claimant, the domestic inquiry panel referred to:
(i) Mazrin’s interview transcript at page 153, Lines 8 &10 of Company’s Bundle of Document (Volume 3), which he confirmed that that “Johny” in the spreadsheet was based in Miri, which indicated this referred to the Claimant. Mazrin Bin Ramli was the Chief Executive Officer of DPSB (“Mazrin”)
(ii) Confirmation by the Company’s witness during domestic inquiry (Jason) that that the name “Johny” found in the spreadsheet referred to the Claimant after internal verification [page 80, line 20 of Company’s Bundle of Document (Volume 2)].
(iii) Emails at pages 23 to 25, 28 & 29 of Company’s Bundle of Document (Volume 4)] showing the names of the Claimant. These are emails found by PwC from DPSB’s laptop. (iv) Confirmation by the Claimant himself that he was involved in the Sponge Jet Contract as end user [page 113 of Company’s Bundle of Document (Volume 2)].

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Further, the claimant during the DI never challenged Alex Tan that ‘Johny’ referred to by Mazrin in his interview transcript tendered during the DI is not him. It is the considered view of the court that the conduct of the claimant bearing something towards the case during the DI, which does not require the DI to investigate further who is the actual person ‘Johny’.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Based on the evidence, the DI has taken into consideration the claimant received the payments through Mazrin or through Azreen who will then be paid through Synergy Spectacular Sdn. Bhd. This finding can be seen in the evidence of COW2 when she found such evidence from Mazrin’s interview transcript.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Based on the available evidence, there was sufficient evidence for the company to reasonably imply that “Johny” as stated in the spreadsheets referred to the claimant.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Learned counsel for the claimant submitted that the company should have produced the employment and placement record to show he was posted to Baram-G and Temana site.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
However, the court finds sufficient evidence has been produced to show that the name in the spreadsheet referred to the that without employment and placement record as allegedly required by the counsel is not going to affect the quality of evidence produced to link the claimant to the spreadsheets.
Allegation of receiving RM10,000.00

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The court also finds that the allegation of accepting RM10,000.00 as stated “Johny trip to KL family 12-16 Jan: RM10K” in the spreadsheet has been successfully proved by the company.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
In our case, the claimant during the DI has clearly admitted that he was in KL from 12.01.2016 to 16.01.2016. This was taken into consideration by the DI when they arrived at their decision. COW2 in her evidence told the court that there was high probability that the claimant received the amount of RM10,000.00 when she said:
“(ii) Confirmation by the Claimant that he was in KL between 12 January 2017 until 16 January 2017 [page 140, lines 35 to 45 of Company’s Bundle of Document (Volume 2] which matched with the spreadsheet item related to “Johny Trip to KL family 12 – 16 Jan: RM10K” at page 58, item 6 of Company’s Bundle of Document (Volume 3])

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
During the trial in court, the claimant when he was under cross-examination agreed that there was a trip to KL from 12.01.2016 to 16.01.2016. Q. Refer to the Domestic Inquiry Minutes as COB-2, page 140, lines 35 to 40. Please read out what you stated here during the DI.
So you confirm you were at KL on a family trip between 12 – 16 January 2017 as per what’s stated in the spreadsheet and in Charge 1, agree?
A. Yes, that is my own trip.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Furthermore, there is other evidence to link the claimant with the receiving of RM10,000.00 when there is an email dated 19.11.2016, adduced by the claimant, which contains a confirmation receipt for booking at Cititel, Mid Valley in Kuala Lumpur for the period between 12.01.2016 to 16.01.2016. These dates matched with the dates stated in the spreadsheet to link the offence for receiving such amount.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
The court finds that the dates from 12.01.2016 to 16.01.2016 corresponds with “Johny trip to KL family 12-16 Jan: RM10K”, as stated in the spreadsheet. Hence, based on the available evidence, it is reasonably or highly probable that the claimant has received the amount of RM10,000.00
Charge 2

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: For this charge, the court finds that the company has also successfully proved the misconduct.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
There was admission by the claimant regarding the trip to Santorini, Greece. The evidence by the claimant is as follows:
Q: Refer to Domestic Inquiry Minutes at COB-2, page 149, lines 25 to 40.
This is regarding your Santorini trip.
You called it a family trip and you went with your wife, Mohd Azreen and his wife, correct?
A: Yes
Q: You also stated here that Mazrin, his wife and his kids went on the Santorini trip too, agree?
A: Yes

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The claimant also agreed in his evidence when he was cross examined that the trip began on 07.03.2018 from Miri, as shown on page 3 of COB4, and ended on 18.03.2018, as shown on page 7 of COB4.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The claimant was also asked during the cross-examination when he was shown the flight tickets on pages 3 to 11 of COB4, which contained his name and his wife’s name, Kong Siew Ling.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
The claimant also admitted during the cross-examination that Mazrin paid for his flight tickets. This is his evidence: Q: Refer to Domestic Inquiry Minutes at COB-2, page 139, lines 25-60 [read out for emphasis]
You stated during the DI that Mazrin paid for your flight tickets and that you gave him your passport details for him to arrange for your flight tickets, agree?
A: Yes. I fully refunded him later.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
During the DI the claimant clearly admitted that Mazrin paid for the tickets when he was asked at page 139 of COB2:
Assistant Presenting Officer 1:
Question to you, who did who paid for your flight tickets for this trip?
Accused Employee:
What I know is from Mazrin. Because he said he help me to he help to arrange. So from him lah I didn’t know him.
Assistant Presenting Officer 1:
So he paid so he paid your flight ticket?
Accused Employee:
It should be lah if if he didn’t pay then, how am I going to fly?

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: From the above evidence and the claimant’s own admission, it is the considered view of the court that the company has sufficiently proved that Mazrin paid for the flight tickets to Santorini for the claimant and his wife. The documentary evidence from the company, which is the Staff & Family Details on page 242 of COB4, shows that the wife of claimant is Kong Siew Ling.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Regarding this charge, the company has produced a tax invoice dated 22.03.2018 issued by Mitra Tours & Travel to Mazrin for coverage of insurance for international travel in the name of the claimant and his wife.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
Apart from that there is evidence from the claimant to show that travel insurance was paid by Mazrin as can be seen during the cross-examination of the claimant:
Q: Refer to COB-4, page 12
This is a tax invoice issued by Mitra Tours & Travel to Mazrin Ramli of DPSB on 22 March 2018. The travel insurance here bears your name, your wife’s name and your colleague Mohd Azreen’s name, agree?
A: Yes Q: Agree that the coverage period of the insurance for yourself and your wife is 7 March 2018 to 18 March 2018 which coincides with your travel dates for the Santorini trip?
A: Yes
Q: Agree that based on page 12, COB-4, you had allowed Mazrin Ramli of DPSB, a registered Petronas contractor to arrange or pay for the travel insurance of yourself and your wife?
A: Yes. I refunded him after the trip.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Upon considering the available evidence, the court satisfies that the company has produced good and convincing proof to show the commission of misconduct, as per the charge.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
Regarding this charge, the court finds that there was admission by the claimant during the DI that Mazrin also went to Santorini. He told the court when learned counsel for the company referred him to the notes of proceeding in the DI, page 149 of COB2, that he went to Santorini with his wife, Mohd Azreen and his wife. He was also asked regarding page 149, and he answered: Q : You also stated here that Mazrin, his wife and his kids went on the Santorini trip too, agree?
A : Yes

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: During the examination in chief the claimant admitted that he crossed path with Mazrin but he did not stay with Mazrin or share any room with him. The claimant said that he stayed at a location called Porto Fira Suites (Porto Fira) which is in the centre of Santorini and to his knowledge Mazrin also stayed at the same hotel.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The claimant also during the DI admitted that he and Mazrin stayed at Porto Fira and they stayed not in the same apartment but separated (see page 136 of COB2, paras 5-6).

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The abovementioned evidence showed that the claimant did meet Mazrin and stayed together at the same hotel. This can reasonably be indicated or implied that they went to Santorini together.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The claimant later attempted by denying they stayed together at the same hotel during the cross-examination when he was referred to lines 5-55, on page 136-137 of COB2.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: It is trite law that if a person demonstrably tells lies on one or two points then he is not a reliable witness, and the rest of his evidence must be scrutinised with great care and suspicion (see Selva Rani a/p Sinnathamby v Concorde Hotel Kuala Lumpur [2015] 2 ILJ 491). The High Court in the case of Mohamed Bin Kasdi [1968] CLJU 78; [1969] 1 MLJ 135 referred to by Selva Rani, supra, laid down a principle of law that when a witness gives or makes two statements which differ in material particulars there must necessarily be ground for believing that he is not a truthful witness.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: In our case, the claimant has narrated two material particulars which differ to each other with respect to his trip with Mazrin to Santorini. It is the considered view of the court that such a difference goes to the root of the claimant’s case, and which affected his credibility. By shifting to another narrative, the claimant obviously tried to tell lies in court.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The claimant has lied to this material issue. Therefore, his evidence that he did not stay at Porto Fira should be discarded and must not be believed. There was an act of an afterthought on the part of the claimant to deny what he already says during the DI.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The fact that the claimant and Mazrin met and stayed at the same hotel raised reasonable probability that they were travelling together. Upon taking into consideration that all the expenses were paid by Mazrin, there cannot be any coincidence that they merely bumped into each at the same hotel in Santorini, let alone at the same destination i.e. Santorini.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
Therefore, the court finds that the company has proved that the dismissal was made with just cause or excuse. Based on the evidence, it is the considered view of the court that any reasonable employer would have found that the claimant has committed the acts of misconduct levelled against him.
Defence

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The claimant in his defence told the court that upon coming back to Malaysia, he had paid the expenses occurred for the trip to Santorini including hotel, flite tickets and travel insurance around RM34, 604.00 and he paid Mazrin RM35,000.00.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Be that as it may, even if the claimant was true that he paid all the expenses when he came home, that would not be a good defence. In this case, he was not supposed to ask Mazrin to make any payment for the trip, knowing very well that DPSB was the registered contractor of the company.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
In fact, the claimant was aware that when he travels with the company’s contractor, he must make a declaration to the company. This is his evidence during the cross-examination:
Q: When you travel with the Company’s contractor, you must make a declaration so that the Company can assess whether there is a conflict of interest and whether to clear it or prohibit it.
A: If I travel with contractor, yes.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: As a senior managerial employee, the claimant knew that he had to comply with CoBE and ABC Manual and report to the company anything that will compromise his duty, which is not to cause conflict of interest between him and the company.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The claimant’s admission that he knows his duty to report any conflict of interest that may arise from his conduct by allowing Mazrin to pay for his expenses before going for Santorini’s trip showed his blatant refusal to follow the rules and regulations formulated by the company to discipline its employees.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: In this case, regardless of whether DPSB will receive any benefit from the claimant’s position is irrelevant. What is important is the duty of the claimant is not to act or conduct in a manner that will create conflict of interest and not to accept any gratification which clearly the serious misconduct under the CoBE and ABC Manual. It bears considerable question in mind of the court, why DBSB should give the claimant RM260,000.00 and pay the trip to Santorini, if not because of his position in the company.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Therefore, it is the considered view of the court that the defence mounted by the claimant cannot stand.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
Learned counsel for the claimant attempted to impress the court by submitting that the charge filed during the DI should also be subjected to the principle of “one transaction rule” as per the criminal trial. This is what the submission by the counsel:
“The Company’s charges 2 to 4 falls directly under the “one transaction rule” and should be treated as one single on-going charge. Instead, the Company was found guilty of and punished for the same offence 3 times. This is tantamount to unnatural punishment which is manifestly unjust and not in line with proper operating system or management system.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
With due respect, the court finds that submission by the learned counsel is without merit. It must be remembered that drafting or preparing a charge under industrial jurisprudence is different from any charge under criminal law. The court wishes to refer to the case of Amran Mahmud, supra, where the court held:
“[77] The position of law with respect to the filing of charge for misconduct is as decided by the case of Shahrin Abdul Mutalib v. Worldwide Fund For Nature Malaysia [2019] ILRU 2233; [2019] 2 LNS 2233 (Award No. 2233 of 2019), whereby, the court held that in the context of employee misconduct, the framing of charge is not like in criminal matters or quasi criminal. The court further held what matters is that the accusation made against the employee must be unambiguous and comprehensible and which will not cause material prejudice to the employee for being unable to put forward his defence.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: It is the opinion of the court that the charges against the claimant were clear and unambiguous. There is no issue of material prejudice against the claimant which has inhibited him from adducing his defence.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
In the context of employee misconduct, the drafting of the charge should be left with the employer, and the court should not disturb how the charges were drafted, let alone apply criminal application in drafting a charge. In industrial jurisprudence, the law only recognises the charge is bad or defective only if the charge was unclear, ambiguous and has caused material prejudice to the claimant which deprived him of the right to properly put forward his defence. And, in our case, none of this has happened to the claimant.
Punishment

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The correct test to be applied in deciding this issue is “whether any reasonable employer, based on the established facts, in that line of business, would have dismissed the Claimant, even though some other employers may not have dismissed him?”. This test has been enunciated by NH Chan JCA in the case of Tan Tek Seng @ Tan Chee Meng v Suruhanjaya Perkhidmatan Pendidikan & Anor [1996] 2 CLJ 771; [1996] 2 AMR 1617, where His Lordship has referred to the English cases of NC Watling & Co Ltd v Richardson [1978] ICR 1049 and British Leyland UK Ltd. v. Swift [1981] IRLR 91.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content:
The test was adopted by another Court of Appeal’s case in Subramanyah AJ Karuppiah v. Bank Negara Malaysia, [2011] 2 CLJ 178, which held:
“[46] The court is satisfied that the BNM's decision to dismiss the appellant on all the five charges of misconducts against him was a reasonable decision in view of the circumstances of the case. His misconducts are serious in nature. Being the employer, BNM is in the best position to determine the seriousness of the appellant's misconducts. In this respect the court is in full agreement with NH Chan JCA (dissenting) in the case of Tan Teck Seng v. Suruhanjaya Perkhidmatan Pendidikan & Anor [1996] 2 CLJ 771, when he said:
... The correct test is: Was it reasonable for the employers to dismiss him? If no reasonable employer would have dismissed him, then the dismissal was unfair. But if a reasonable employer might reasonably have dismissed him, then the dismissal was fair. It must be remembered that in all these cases there is a band of reasonableness, within which one employer might reasonably take one view; another quite reasonably take a different view. One would quite reasonably dismiss the man. The other would quite reasonably keep him on. Both views may be quite reasonable. If it was quite reasonable to dismiss him, then the dismissal must be upheld as fair: even though some other employers may not have dismissed him.
[47] In the present case, the court is satisfied that it was reasonable for BNM to have taken the view that dismissal was the appropriate punishment. The 'offences' or misconducts for which the appellant had committed were serious and grave in any establishment and that it was quite reasonable for BNM as the employer, to dismiss him.”

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: In allowing the finding of the company to dismiss the claimant, the court finds that the claimant has committed serious misconduct with all the charges. It is important to observe the company through the evidence of COW3 adopts a zero-tolerance policy against all forms of bribery and corruption. Further, the company also adopts core values of Loyalty, Integrity, Professionalism and Cohesiveness and hence has zero tolerance on any breaches committed by the claimant which cannot be tolerated.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Serious misconduct is where an employee’s act or behaviour is so severe that it fundamentally breaches the employment agreement and the trust and confidence required to continue the employment relationship. It is without doubt that the act of receiving gratification and gifts or entertainment is serious misconduct and not trifling in nature. COW3 in his evidence told the court that the serious acts of misconduct committed by the claimant involving integrity and breach of fiduciary duty that would tantamount to dismissal as the claimant who was holding a senior position was expected to maintain a higher standard of care and professionalism in ensuring that his conduct was consistent with the requirement of CoBE and ABC Manual.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Regarding the relationship between employer and employee, honesty and integrity are virtues that cannot be compromised in an employee no matter what position he holds in an organisation (see Zulkifli Abdul Latif v. Sistem Penerbangan Malaysia Berhad [2006] 3 ILR 1923).

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: The court finds that the position held by the claimant and the length of his employment demanded him to uphold the values and cores held by the company to ensure the company’s reputation and character as a renowned national oil company in Malaysia be highly preserved, not only internally but also internationally.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Hence, it is the considered view of the court that any reasonable employer in the position of the company would have been taken the same position by the company in dismissing the claimant.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: In conclusion, the court, having taken into account the totality of the evidence adduced by both parties as well as their submissions and bearing in mind s. 30(5) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967, to act according to equity and good conscience and the substantial merits of the case without regard to technicalities and legal form, finds that the company has discharged its legal and evidential burden of proving on a balance of probabilities to dismiss the claimant with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Johnny Lau Kah Beng v Petroliam Nasional Berhad (PETRONAS)
chairman: Mohd Taufik bin Mohd @ Mohd Yusoff
content: Therefore, the claimant’s claim is dismissed.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: C. DUTY OF THE INDUSTRIAL COURT
content: The Federal Court in Milan Auto Sdn. Bhd. v. Wong Seh Yen [1995] 4 CLJ, 449 at 455 held that the function of the Industrial Court in dismissal cases on a reference under section 20 is two-fold. Firstly, to determine whether the misconduct complained of by the employer has been established, and secondly whether the proven misconduct constitutes just cause or excuse for the dismissal.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: C. DUTY OF THE INDUSTRIAL COURT
content:
In K A Sanduran Nehru Ratnam v I-Berhad [2007] 1 CLJ 347, the Federal Court outlined the function of the Industrial Court :
“the main and only function of the Industrial Court is dealing with reference under s20 of the IRA 1967 is to determine whether the misconduct or irregularities complained of by the management as to the grounds of dismissal were in fact committed by the workmen. If so, whether such grounds constitute just cause or excuse for the dismissal”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: C. DUTY OF THE INDUSTRIAL COURT
content:
First and foremost, it is the duty of the Industrial Court to determine whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse. The Federal Court in the case of Goon Kwee Phoy v. J&P Coats (M) Bhd [1981] 1 MLRA 415, where His Lordship Raja Azlan Shah, CJM (as he then was) stated at p 430:
“Where representations are made and are referred to the Industrial Court for enquiry, it is the duty of that court to determine whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse. If the employer chooses to give a reason for the action taken by him the duty of the Industrial Court will be to enquire whether that excuse or reason has or has not been made out. If it finds as a fact that it has not been proved, then the inevitable conclusion must be that the termination or dismissal was without just cause or excuse.”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: C. DUTY OF THE INDUSTRIAL COURT
content:
It is also the role of the Industrial Court that it must act according to equity, good conscience and substantial merits of the case without regard to technicalities and legal forms. In Nadarajah v Golf Resort (M) Bhd [1992] 1 MLJ 506, Eusoff Chin J (as he than was) says :
“ It is therefore to be observed that in view of the provision of s. 30(5) of the Act , the Industrial Court must act according to equity, good conscience and substantial merits of the case without regard to technicalities and legal forms. Technical rules such as estoppel, limitation, laches, acquiescence, etc … have no place in industrial adjudication and they should not be allowed to be invoked for defeating claims which are just and proper ”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: D. THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: Whenever a company had caused the dismissal of the workman, it is incumbent on the part of the company to discharge the burden of proof that the dismissal was with just cause or excuse .

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: D. THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: It is trite law that the Company bears the burden to prove that the Claimant had committed the alleged misconduct and the conduct warrants the Claimant’s dismissal. The Company must prove the Claimant guilty and it is not the Claimant who must prove himself not guilty.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: D. THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content: The burden of proof in an unfair dismissal claim lies on the employer to prove on a balance of probabilities that the employee is guilty of the allegation or the reason for the dismissal. This principle was expounded in Stamford Executive Centre v Dharsini Ganeson [1986] ILR 101 : “In a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer. The employer must prove the workman guilty and it is not the workman who must prove himself not guilty. This is so basic a principle of industrial jurisprudence that no employer is expected to come to this Court in ignorance of it.”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: D. THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content:
In Ireka Construction Bhd. v. Chantiravathan Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 11 it was held that :
“It is a basic principle of industrial jurisprudence that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer to prove that he has just cause and excuse for taking the decision to impose the disciplinary measure of dismissal upon the employee. The just cause must be, either a misconduct, negligence or poor performance based on the facts of case.”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: D. THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content:
In Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara v. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor [2002] 3 CLJ 314 at the Court Appeal held that the standard of proof for cases heard before the Industrial Court is “on the balance of probabilities” :
In our view the passage quoted from Administrative Law by H.W.R. Wade & C.F. Forsyth offers the clearest statement on the standard of proof required, that is the civil standard based on the balance of probabilities, which is flexible so that the degree of probability required is proportionate to the nature of gravity of the issue.”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: D. THE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF
content:
In Tyco Engineering And Construction (M) Sdn Bhd v James Francis Trimble [2000] 2 MELR 678, the Industrial Court outlined the law on the burden of proof as follows:
“The burden of proof that the dismissal was with just cause or excuse is on the employer which is on the balance of probabilities to adduce cogent and convincing evidence being the real reason by dismissing the employee. This is the principle of industrial jurisprudence”.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: In this case, it is an undisputed fact from the evidence that the Claimant was a workman within the meaning of the IRA 1967 and her employment with the Company was terminated on 24.02.2022.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: Based on the case of Colgate Palmolive (M) Sdn Bhd v. Yap Kok Foong & Another Appeal [2001] 3 CLJ 9, it now remains to be considered whether the termination was with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: H. THE COURT’S FINDINGS DOMESTIC INQUIRY AND SHOW CAUSE LETTER
content: In relation to Domestic Inquiry , the general principle of good industrial practice and natural justice require that the employer ought to hold a domestic inquiry prior to dismissing a workman for misconduct. In the present case, a Domestic Inquiry was never conducted prior to the dismissal of the Claimant by the Company.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: H. THE COURT’S FINDINGS DOMESTIC INQUIRY AND SHOW CAUSE LETTER
content: The Claimant contends that she was not accorded with proper inquiry for her to state her defence as the Company did not issue show cause letter and hold a domestic inquiry in the instant case. The Claimant further states that the Company failed to observe procedural fairness and that failure on the part of the Company to issue show cause letter and to conduct a Domestic Inquiry is a clear violation of an express contractual term and a denial of natural justice.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: H. THE COURT’S FINDINGS DOMESTIC INQUIRY AND SHOW CAUSE LETTER
content: The Claimant further states that her Letter of Appointment (Clause 23.1) makes a domestic inquiry a contractual precondition to disciplinary action. The Company’s failure to issue a show cause letter and conduct a domestic inquiry prior to the Claimant’s termination deprived the Claimant of a meaningful opportunity to be heard.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: H. THE COURT’S FINDINGS DOMESTIC INQUIRY AND SHOW CAUSE LETTER
content: The Company avers that the absence of Show Cause letter and Domestic Inquiry is not fatal and is curable as the Industrial Court has the jurisdiction to hear the matters de novo through a complete hearing of the evidence given by witnesses in the full trial before this Court.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: H. THE COURT’S FINDINGS DOMESTIC INQUIRY AND SHOW CAUSE LETTER
content:
This Court is guided by the principle enunciated in the case of Hong Leong Equipment Sdn. Bhd. v. Liew Fook Chuan & Other Appeals [1997] 1 CLJ 665; Gopal Sri Ram JCA as he then was said :
