“The fact that an employer has conducted a domestic inquiry against his workman is, in my judgment, an entirely irrelevant consideration to the issue whether the latter had been dismissed without just cause or excuse. The findings of a domestic inquiry are not binding upon the Industrial Court which rehears the matter afresh. ”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: H. THE COURT’S FINDINGS DOMESTIC INQUIRY AND SHOW CAUSE LETTER
content:
In the case of Ang Bee Hoon v. Be-P Pharmacy Sdn Bhd [202314 ILR 204, there was no show cause letter nor domestic inquiry held against the claimant. In dismissing the claimant's claim, the Industrial Court held that : "The claimant pleaded that there was no show cause letter and no DI held by the company. It is undisputed that there was no show cause letter issued to the claimant and there was no DI held against the claimant with regard to the allegations preferred against her which brought about her dismissal. On the authority of Wong Yuen Hock v. Syarikat Hong Leong Assurance Sdn Bhd & Another Appeal [199513 CLJ 344 which followed the decision of the Supreme Court in Dreamland Corporation (M) Sdn Bhd v. Choong Chin Sooi & Anor [198811 CLJ 1, a defective inquiry or failure to hold a DI is not a fatality but only an irregularity' curable by de novo proceedings before this court….
….. The hearing before this court itself which indeed provides a better and impartial forum for the claimant should be taken as a sufficient opportunity for the claimant to be heard to satisfy natural justice. Indeed, the Minister's reference is a de novo hearing by this court and it therefore rehear the matter afresh.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: H. THE COURT’S FINDINGS DOMESTIC INQUIRY AND SHOW CAUSE LETTER
content: It is trite law that the hearing before the Industrial Court is a de novo hearing and the Industrial Court should proceed to determine on the merits of the case, and the validity or failure to hold a Domestic Inquiry is not fatal as any procedural breach of natural justice could be cured at the hearing before the Industrial Court. This principle was laid down by the Federal Court in Wong Yuen Hock v Syarikat Hong Leong Assurance Sdn Bhd & Anor [1995] 2 MLJ 753 : “.. It was not within the ambit of the reference for the Industrial Court to determine whether Hong Leong ought to be punished for failing to hold a domestic inquiry. The Industrial Court was not competent to declare the dismissal void for failure to comply with the rule of natural justice. …. The very purpose of the inquiry before the Industrial Court was to give both parties to the dispute an opportunity to be heard irrespective of whether there was a need for the employer to hold a contractual or statutory inquiry. We were confident that the Industrial Court as constituted at present was capable of arriving at a fair result by fair means on all matters referred to it. If therefore there had been a procedural breach of natural justice committed by the employer at the initial stage, there was no reason why it could not be cured at the rehearing by the Industrial Court”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: H. THE COURT’S FINDINGS DOMESTIC INQUIRY AND SHOW CAUSE LETTER
content: Applying the above principles into the present case, this Court is of the view that the Claimant had all the opportunity to present her case afresh by having the entire matter referred and heard before this Court.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: H. THE COURT’S FINDINGS DOMESTIC INQUIRY AND SHOW CAUSE LETTER
content:
As mentioned earlier, a failure to hold a Domestic Inquiry or the presence of a defective and/or biased inquiry is not a fatality but only an irregularity curable by de novo proceedings before the Industrial Court. It was held in Dreamland (M) Corp Sdn Bhd v Choong Chin Sooi & Industrial Court of Malaysia [1987] 1 MLRA 357 that :
“…The absence of DI or the presence of a defective inquiry is not fatality but merely an irregularity, it is open to the employer to justify his action before the Industrial Court by leading all relevant evidence before it and by having the entire matter referred before the Court..”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: H. THE COURT’S FINDINGS DOMESTIC INQUIRY AND SHOW CAUSE LETTER
content: In the circumstances, if therefore there had been a procedural breach of natural justice committed by the Company at the initial stage, including during and after the Domestic Inquiry, there was no reason why it could not be cured at the rehearing by this Court.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content:
In cases where an employee is dismissed on the grounds of misconduct, it is trite in Malaysian industrial jurisprudence that the two-fold test is to be adopted by the Court, as follows:
i. Whether the Claimant had committed the misconduct complained of by the Company; and
ii. If the misconduct is proven, whether the Company had just cause and excuse for the dismissal.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content:
In Ong Ho Hoo v Sunway Resort Hotel Sdn Bhd & Anor [2020] 4 ILR 493 , the Industrial Court stated that :
“OP Malhotra in his book “The Law of Industrial Disputes”, 6th Edn at p. 1116 defined “misconduct” as follows:
Any conduct on the part of an employee inconsistent with the faithful discharge of his duties towards his employer would be a misconduct. Any breach of the express or implied duties of an employee towards his employer, therefore, ..would constitute an act of misconduct....(emphasis added)

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content:
Based on the evidence adduced before this Court and after having perused and duly considered the relevant documents , the relevant decided cases as well as the submissions by both parties , the conclusion are as follows:
1 In the present case, whether the Claimant had committed the alleged misconducts, this Court will take into consideration the grounds of dismissal of the Claimants as stated in the Letter of Termination.
The Claimant was handed with a Termination Letter dated 24.02.2022, terminating her employment with immediate effect for alleged “serious misconduct and negligence” and directing her to vacate her post as General Manager and leave the office immediately. The contents of the Termination Letter dated 24.02.2022 are inter alia as follows :
…TERMINATION OF WONG CHIEW LEE JULIE, GENERAL MANAGER OF WAKIKI MANAGEMENT CORPORATION
We regret to inform you that by a Resolution dated 7th February 2022, the Wakiki Management Corporation (WMC) has decided to terminate your services as the General Manager of the WMC with immediate effect, i.e. as of the date of service of this letter on you, on grounds of serious misconduct and negligence in the execution of your duties…..
2 Based on the Termination Letter dated 24.02.2022 signed by CoW1, the Company decided to terminate the Claimants’ employment with immediate effect “on grounds of serious misconduct and negligence in the execution of your duties”.
It is obvious that the Termination Letter did not provide details of the alleged misconduct and negligence. The Termination Letter merely stated “serious misconduct and negligence” as the grounds for dismissal. It contained no particulars or examples of the alleged misconduct, nor did it refer to any specific incidents.
3 In the present case, this Court is of the opinion that the Termination Letter lack in clarity. The Company was merely alleged “serious misconduct and negligence” as the grounds for dismissal against the Claimant without even specifying which Code of Conduct was breached by the Claimant, what regulation or rules were allegedly violated or not complied with, what duty was owed and allegedly breached by the Claimant, and what expressed or implied term was breached by the Claimant.
4 This Court is of the opinion that the Claimant is prejudiced because the Claimant would not know which rule or regulations that were purportedly violated or not complied with as per the Company's allegation in the Letter of Termination.
In line with the rule of natural justice, the material particulars of the “serious misconduct and negligence” as the grounds for dismissal must be disclosed to the Claimant. Hence, this Court is convinced that the dismissal was therefore procedurally unfair for lack in clarity and particulars of the alleged misconduct and negligence.
5 This Court is also of the view that it is insufficient for the Company to merely allege, “serious misconduct and negligence” against the Claimant without even specifying in the Termination Letter of what duties or expressed or implied terms were breached by the Claimant and without stating what section of the policy or regulations was involved and allegedly breached by the Claimant. This Court is convinced that the Termination Letter with the allegation of “serious misconduct and negligence” leveled against the Claimant is unfair and unreasonable.
6 In addition, this Court is of the view that the Company could not go into other reasons not relied on by the Company in terminating the Claimants. In the present case, the allegations of misconduct against the Claimant as per Paragraph 25 of this instant Award were never mentioned and/or included in the Termination Letter dated 24.02.2022.
In the case of Mohd Azizi Sohan V. Asian Kitchen (M) Sdn Bhd [2017] 3 MELR 601 it was held that:
“(1) On the present facts, the reason given by the company in terminating the claimant’s services was posting of the Facebook Comments. The court could not go into other reasons not relied on by the company in terminating the claimant.” In Maritime Intelligence Sdn Bhd v Tan Ah Gek [2021] MLJU 2189, the Federal Court made it clear that in proceedings under section 20(3) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967, the Industrial Court is confined to considering only those reasons which operated in the employer’s mind at the time of dismissal. Allegations raised only post-dismissal, whether in pleadings or in submissions, amount to impermissible ex post facto justifications and cannot be considered.
In BSC Manufacturing (M) Sdn Bhd v Value Plus Industries Sdn Bhd [2022] MLJU 2825, it was held inter alia that allegations raised belatedly or only after pleadings have closed amount to mere afterthoughts and cannot constitute a genuine defence.
Applying the above principles into the present case , this Court could not go into other reasons not relied on by the Company in terminating the Claimant.
7 On top of that it is trite law that parties are strictly bound by their pleadings. This principle was applied in the case of Tyco Engineering & Construction Sdn Bhd v Jescon Sdn Bhd [2006] 3 CLJ 1 :
“It deserves mention here that the Company in its submission, at length suggested retrenchment as a reason for the termination of the Claimant. This Court observes that there was no such plea in the Statement of Reply of the Company. Parties are bound by their pleadings. … Not only is the Company in this case bound to prove the facts of a fair dismissal of an employee but it must also not find or give reasons that are not pleaded or made out in the pleadings.
In R. Rama Chandran v. The Industrial Court of Malaysia & Anor. (1997) 1 CLJ 147 at page 162 His Lordship Eusoff Chin CJ said :
“It is trite law that a party is bound by its pleadings. The Industrial Court must scrutinise the pleadings and identify the issues, take evidence, hear the parties’ arguments and finally pronounce its judgements having strict regard to the issues. It is true that the Industrial Court is not bound by all the technicalities of a civil court (s. 30 of the Industrial Relations Act 1967) but it must follow the same general pattern. The object of pleadings is to determine what are the issues and to narrow the area of conflict. The Industrial Court cannot ignore the pleadings and treat them as mere pedantry or formalism, because if it does so, it may lose sight of the issues, admit evidence irrelevant to the issues and come to the wrong conclusions. The Industrial Court must at all times keep itself alert to the issues and attend to matters it is bound to consider”. (Underlining is mine).” [Emphasis added]
Applying the above principles in Tyco Engineering [supra] and R. Rama Chandran [supra] into the present case , this Court concurs with the Claimant on the issues raised at Paragraph 30 (14 to 19) of this instant Award that parties are bound by their pleadings . This Court is confined to the issues pleaded and to the reasons that were actually operating in the employer’s mind at the material time of dismissal. Fresh grounds raised only in submissions are amount to ex post facto justifications, afterthought and must be disregarded
8 On matters stated at Paragraph 30 (12) of this instant Award , this Court has no hesitation to agree that none of those allegations were pursued in the Company’s Submissions. They must therefore be treated as abandoned, being mere afterthoughts, either bare assertions devoid of evidential support or allegations raised belatedly in an attempt to justify the dismissal of the Claimant .
9 With respect to Paragraph 30 (20) of this instant Award, applying the principles in Mohd Azizi Sohan [supra], Maritime Intelligence Sdn Bhd [supra] and BSC Manufacturing (M) Sdn Bhd [supra] , this Court could not deal into other reasons not relied on by the Company in terminating the Claimant.
10 In conclusion, scrutinizing the evidence and the testimonies of CLW1 and CLW2 as well as the testimonies of CoW1, CoW2 and CoW3, this Court is of the view that the Claimant’s version are inherently probable than the Company’s version .

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: In the circumstances , this Court is satisfied that the Company had failed to established on a balance of probabilities its case of misconducts levelled against the Claimant.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: The Claimant submits that the dismissal was disproportionate to the seriousness of the allegation of misconducts. The Company , on the other hand states that the dismissal of the Claimant was appropriate with just cause and excuse.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: The Federal Court in Norizan bin Bakar v Panzana Enterprise Sdn Bhd [2013] 6 MLJ 605 held that the Industrial Court is duty bound to consider proportionality of punishment when exercising its powers under section 30(5) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 to act according to equity, good conscience and substantial merits of the case.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: The proportionality principle requires the Court to strike a balance between the severity of an employee’s conduct and the sanction imposed.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content:
In passing a just and appropriate order, the Industrial Court is obliged to do a balancing exercise. It was held by the Court of Appeal in Tan Poh Thiam v Industrial Court of Malaysia and Daily Fresh Foods Sdn Bhd ( Civil Appeal J-01-414-12/2013) that :
“[4] Industrial law jurisprudence does not permit any form of oppressive conduct on the part of an employer having the objective of dismissing the employee on “just cause or excuse” based on trivial allegations; based on matters that could have been dealt with appropriately with proper operating system or management system instead of taking drastic steps to dismiss the employee.
The Industrial Court in the Malaysian context is obliged to do a balancing exercise taking into account such factors as the nature of complaint the conduct of the employer, the operating and management system that is in place, the reason advanced by the employee as well as his conduct, and the gravity of the allegation; in order to ascertain whether the employee’s act or omission qualifies as a misconduct to attract section 20 on Industrial Relations Act 1967 (IRA 1967). The proposition is fortified by section 30 of IRA 1967.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: This Court agrees that the decision to terminate the Claimant with immediate effect vide a letter dated 24.02.2022 was executed not in accordance with Clause 12 of the Letter of Appointment, which stipulates that, after confirmation of employment, either party may only terminate the contract with three (3) months’ written notice or payment of three (3) months’ salary in lieu. The Claimant was summarily dismissed without notice, salary in lieu, or payment of her contractual or statutory dues for February 2022.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: In the instant case , this Court is of the view that the punishment of dismissal was too harsh for the Claimant. The Company could have opted for other lesser forms of disciplinary action inter alia suspension without pay or demotion which would have been more appropriate.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: It is the opinion of this Court that even if the Claimant had committed the alleged misconducts, it does not warrants immediate dismissal. Instead, the Company was obliged to impose a punishment in order of its magnitude starting from the less punitive , inter alia : stern warning, suspension without pay, a demotion, and finally a dismissal.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content:
In passing a just and appropriate order, the Industrial Court is obliged to do a balancing exercise. It was held by the Court of Appeal in Tan Poh Thiam v Industrial Court of Malaysia and Daily Fresh Foods Sdn Bhd ( Civil Appeal J-01-414-12/2013) that :
“[4] Industrial law jurisprudence does not permit any form of oppressive conduct on the part of an employer having the objective of dismissing the employee on “just cause or excuse” based on trivial allegations; based on matters that could have been dealt with appropriately with proper operating system or management system instead of taking drastic steps to dismiss the employee.
The Industrial Court in the Malaysian context is obliged to do a balancing exercise taking into account such factors as the nature of complaint the conduct of the employer, the operating and management system that is in place, the reason advanced by the employee as well as his conduct, and the gravity of the allegation; in order to ascertain whether the employee’s act or omission qualifies as a misconduct to attract section 20 on Industrial Relations Act 1967 (IRA 1967). The proposition is fortified by section 30 of IRA 1967.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: In the present case, as mentioned earlier , this Court is satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Company had failed to made out the case of misconduct against the Claimant . As such the termination of the Claimant is now rendered as null and void.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: In any event, this Court is convinced that the Claimant who served the Company for almost 2 years with clean disciplinary record could have been dealt with appropriately with proper management system. The Company could have opted for other lesser forms of punishment instead of taking drastic steps by terminating her service.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content:
In Goodyear Malaysia Bhd and National Union of Employees in Companies Manufacturing Rubber Products ( Award 88 of 1986) it was held that ;
“It must be noted that not all misconduct deserves dismissal, which has been described as the capital punishment in industrial relations. Important circumstances, which mitigate the offence of the workman, should be taken into account by the employer before he can be said to have made a fair and reasonable decision to dismiss. For example, a workman's past record of good service, or the management's own actions or omission which contributed to the misconduct, are mitigating factors which any reasonable employer would take into account before dismissing Length and quality of service, good untainted record, and past service awards and recognition must also be taken as extenuating circumstances when an employer decides the appropriate punishment for the misconduct.”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: In addition, when carrying out the termination , the employer must ensure that the existing law, rules and procedures are adhered to. In this regard, it has been the practice of the Industrial Court to look at the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony 1975 (“the Code”) in determining the issue of fairness.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: Though the Code has no legal force and its acceptance is voluntary, it is still relevant for the purpose of considering the overall reasonableness of the employer’s action.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: The Code is an agreement made and signed in Kuala Lumpur on 9 February 1975 between the Human Resources Ministry and the Malaysian Council of Employers’ Organizations.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: The Code is aim to lay down principles and guidelines to employers and employees on the practice of industrial relations for achieving greater industrial harmony. Though the Code has no legal force and its acceptance is voluntary, it is still relevant for the purpose of considering the overall reasonableness of the employer’s action.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: The High Court in Credit Corporation (M) Bhd v Choo Kam Sing & Anor [1998] 2 MELR 256 noted that although the Code has no legal force, it is nevertheless relevant factor to be looked at for the purpose of considering the overall reasonableness of the employer’s action in dismissal cases.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content:
This means the court can take into account established guidelines and practices within industries, particularly in dismissal cases, when determining whether an employer's actions were fair. In fact, section 30(5A) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 empowers the Industrial Court in making an award to take into consideration the requirements of the Code.
section 30(5A) : “In making its award, the Court may take into consideration any agreement or code relating to employment practices between organisations representative of employers and workmen respectively where such agreement or code has been approved by the Minister.”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: Essentially, section 30(5A) provides a mechanism for the Industrial Court to incorporate industry-specific best practices and standards into its decision-making process, promoting fairness and consistency in industrial relations.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: In the instant case , the decision to terminate the Claimant with immediate effect was indeed, a hasty decision by the Company. This Court is of the view that the alleged misconduct does not warrants immediate dismissal. The Company could have opted for other lesser forms of disciplinary action which would have been more appropriate instead of taking drastic steps by terminating her services.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: WHETHER THE DISMISSAL IS PROPORTIONATE TO THE ALLEGED MISCONDUCT
content: In view of all the above and after taking into consideration the evidence adduced during the Trial, this Court is satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the termination of the Claimant was without just cause or excuse .

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: SALARY FOR FEBRUARY 2022 AND PAYMENT OF 10 DAYS ANNUAL LEAVE
content: The Claimants prays that she be paid her salary for February 2022 and payment of 10 days unused annual leave .

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: SALARY FOR FEBRUARY 2022 AND PAYMENT OF 10 DAYS ANNUAL LEAVE
content: It was never disputed by the Company that the Claimant was never paid of her salary for February 2022 and payment of 10 days unused annual leave.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: SALARY FOR FEBRUARY 2022 AND PAYMENT OF 10 DAYS ANNUAL LEAVE
content:
In Nadarajah v Golf Resort (M) Bhd [1992] 1 MLJ 506, Eusoff Chin J (as he than was) says :
“ It is therefore to be observed that in view of the provision of s. 30(5) of the Act , the Industrial Court must act according to equity, good conscience and substantial merits of the case without regard to technicalities and legal forms. Technical rules such as estoppel, limitation, laches, acquiescence, etc … have no place in industrial adjudication and they should not be allowed to be invoked for defeating claims which are just and proper ”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: SALARY FOR FEBRUARY 2022 AND PAYMENT OF 10 DAYS ANNUAL LEAVE
content: In Tamil Nesan (M) Sdn. Bhd. V K. Ganesan 1 MELR 493; [1987] 2 ILR 147 [unreported], Mohd. Yusof J ( as he then was ) applied with approval the following passage appearing at page 1591 in the second volume of the Law of Industrial Disputes by Malhorta , 4th edition, a leading treatise on the subject : Estoppel and waiver The technicalities of the procedural law i.e Code of Civil Procedure or the Evidence Act do not apply to industrial adjudication. But fundamental principles of procedural law, cannot be given go-by whether called the rules of natural justice or by any other name. For instance, even if some workmen accept certain amount ‘in full and final settlement of their account’, they cannot be estopped from further claiming their legitimate dues nor can there be waiver in this respect of the rights accruing to them under the industrial law. The principle of estoppel or waiver cannot be rigorously applied against the workmen especially when it is not clear that they accept compensation given by the management in full satisfaction of their claim after having been made aware that they were entitled to higher compensation.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: SALARY FOR FEBRUARY 2022 AND PAYMENT OF 10 DAYS ANNUAL LEAVE
content: The propositions established in Nadarajah (supra) and Tamil Nesan (supra) was quoted with approval by the Supreme Court in Kumpulan Perangsang Selangor Bhd v Zaid Hj. Mohd Noh [1997] 2 CLJ 11 .

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
section_title: SALARY FOR FEBRUARY 2022 AND PAYMENT OF 10 DAYS ANNUAL LEAVE
content: Applying the abovementioned principles in Nadarajah (supra) and Tamil Nesan (supra), this Court is satisfied that it is just and appropriate that the Claimant be paid of the salary for February 2022 as well as for the 10 days unused annual leave. It caused no prejudiced to the Company as it is in line with the terms of the Claimant’s employment.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: Pursuant to section 30(5) of the IRA1967 and after having considered the totality of the evidence adduced, this Court is satisfied that the Company had failed on a balance of probabilities to prove its case of misconduct against the Claimant . Hence, this Court finds that the Company had failed to prove on the balance of probabilities that the dismissal of the Claimant from her employment with the Company was with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: As mentioned earlier, the Claimant was terminated as General Manager with immediate effect for alleged “serious misconduct and negligence”. However the Termination Letter dated 24.02.2025 did not particularise or provide details of the alleged misconduct or negligence.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: The Claimant was also not given sufficient opportunity to explain and to defend herself. The Claimant was also not given the right to mitigate as well as right to appeal against the decision of the Company. Hence, this Court is satisfied that there was an issue of lack of procedural fairness as the Company had failed to adopt a reasonable procedure in dismissing the Claimant.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: This Court is convinced that this is a case of unlawful dismissal against the Claimant and that the termination of the Claimant was carried out not in accordance with fair labour practice and without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: Based on the Court’s assessment of the industrial climate between the parties, it is certainly not conducive to reinstate the Claimant as the relationship between the Company and the Claimant has been badly strained. In the circumstances, it is inappropriate to order for reinstatement.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: Instead, this Court having ruled that the Claimant was dismissed without just cause or excuse, will now consider the appropriate remedy for the Claimant.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content:
In respect of the quantum the Court is mindful of the view taken by Tun Salleh Abas FJ in the case of Hotel Jaya Puri Bhd. V National Union of Hotel, Bar & Restaurant Workers & Anor [1990] 1 MLJ 109 :
“.. if there is a legal basis for paying the compensation, the amount of course is very much a matter of the discretion which the Industrial Court is fully empowered under s.30 of the IRA 1967 to fix.”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: Back wages is calculated based on the Claimant’s last drawn salary but limited to 24 months. From the back wages, the court is required to make a deduction for any contributory conduct, post dismissal earnings and delay in the hearing of the case but such a deduction need not involve a mathematical calculation.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content:
This Court is bound by the principle laid down in the case of Dr. James Alfred (Sabah) v. Koperasi Serbaguna Sanya Bhd (Sabah) & Anor [2001] 3 CLJ 541.His Lordship Justice Tan Sri Steve Shim CJ (Sabah & Sarawak) in delivering the judgement of the Federal Court held that:
In our view, it is in line with equity and good conscience that the Industrial Court, in assessing quantum of back wages, should take into account the fact, if established by evidence or admitted, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. Failure to do so constitutes a jurisdictional error of law. Certiorari will therefore lie to rectify it. Of course, taking into account such employment after dismissal does not necessarily mean that the Industrial Court has to conduct a mathematical exercise in deduction. What is important is that the Industrial Court, in the exercise of its discretion in assessing the quantum of back wages, should take into account all relevant matters including the fact, where it exists, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. This discretion is in the nature of a decision-making process.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content:
This Court have carefully examined the facts and evidence in this case and of the view that there was no contributory factor on the part of the Claimant. As such, there is no deduction under this item.
Delay

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: From an examination of the notes of proceedings, this Court is satisfied that the Claimant did not occasion any delay in connection with the hearing of this ministerial reference. Therefore, there is no deduction under this head.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: At the time of dismissal, the Claimant last drawn salary was RM 5,500.00 inclusive of monthly fixed allowances. On the facts of this case, there is evidence of a post-dismissal income of RM2,500.00 per month from December 2022 to May 2023 after the Claimant was dismissed by the Company on 24.02.2022. Hence, a deduction of 10% under this item is just and reasonable.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content:
After having considered the evidence adduced before this Court as well as the submission by both parties, the remedies are as follows:
i. Compensation in lieu of reinstatement , based on the formula of one month salary for every completed year of service . There is no dispute on the fact that the Claimant has completed 1 full year of service calculated from 19.09.2020 until the date of dismissal on 24.02.2022:
RM 5,500.00 x 1
= RM 5,500.00
ii. Back wages for 24 months based on the Claimant’s last drawn salary with deduction of 10% for post-dismissal income:
RM 5,500.00 x 24 ( RM 132,000.00 – 10% ) = RM 118,800.00
iii. Salary for February 2022
= RM 5,500.00
iv. Payment of 10 days unused annual leave = RM 1,833.30

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: The monetary award in a total sum of RM 131,633,30, less statutory deductions, if any, shall be paid by the Company to the Claimant through Messrs. Chung & Lee Advocates on or before 16.01.2026 with interest of 8% per annum to be calculated from 17.01.2026 until full and final settlement.

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: Last but not least , it is pertinent to note the following passage taken from Kuching Plywood Bhd v Ngu Tiong Hie @ Ngu Tiong Hea (Award No 172 / 1994) which make reference to the Supreme Court of India judgment in the case of Delhi Transport Corporation. v D.T.C. Mazdoor Congress & Ors (1991)AIR 101 : “The right to life includes a right to livelihood. The right to livelihood therefore cannot hang on to the fancies of individuals in authority. The employment is not a bounty from them nor can its survival be at their mercy. Income is the foundation of many fundamental rights and when work is the sole source of income, the right to work becomes as much fundamental. Fundamental rights can ill afford to be consigned to the limbo of undefined premises and uncertain applications. That will be a mockery of them.”

case_name: Wong Chiew Lee v Waikiki Management Corporation
chairman: Datuk Indra bin Haji Ayub
content: This Court verily believe that this Award is just and appropriate in the light of the particular facts of the present case and guided by the principles of equity, good conscience and substantial merits of this case without regard to technicalities and legal forms.

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The sole issue is whether the termination of the Claimant was with just cause or excuse. In an unfair dismissal reference under s.20 (3) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967, the Court’s duty is to determine “whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse”. If the employer gives a reason for dismissal, the Court must inquire whether that reason has been made out in evidence. Retrenchment is a dismissal in operational redundancy, so s.30 of the Act applies, the Company must show a genuine redundancy situation and that the dismissal was made in good faith (s.30 (5) IRA).
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Normally retrenchment selections follow the industry-recognised “last-in-first-out” rule; deviations are allowed only for valid and bona fide reasons. The Company must prove on balance that the Claimant’s post had indeed become redundant and that his retrenchment was not a sham (Goon Kwee Phoy V. J&P Coats [1981] 2 MLJ 127; Ng Chang Seng V. Technip Geoproduction [2021] 1 MLJ 447). The Court apply these principles to the evidence.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: It is imperative to consider the law on redundancy prior to considering the conduct of the Company, as it will show that the Company at all times acted in a bona fide manner and the redundancy was bona fide. Therefore, it will be evident that the Company complied with the principles of law.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The adjudication of retrenchment disputes in Malaysia is governed by a well-established framework of legal principles derived from the Industrial Relations Act 1967 and judicial precedent
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In the Court of Appeal case of William Jacks & Co (M) Sdn Bhd V. S Balasingam [1999] 3 CLJ235,3 MLJ 411, redundancy was defined as follows: "Retrenchment" has been defined as the discharge of surplus labour or staff by an employer for any reason whatsoever. Whether the retrenchment exercise in a particular case is bona fide or otherwise is a question of fact and of degree depending in the peculiar circumstances of the case. It is well settled that the employer is entitled to organize his business in the manner he considers best. So long as the managerial power is exercised bone fide, the decision is immune from examination even by the Industrial Court. However, the Industrial Court is empowered and indeed duty bound to investigate the facts and circumstances of the case to determine whether the exercise of power is in fact bone fide".
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: The term "retrenchment" was authoritatively defined by the Court of Appeal in William Jacks & Co (M) Sdn Bhd V. S. Balasingam 3 CLJ 235 [supra] as: "The discharge of surplus labour or staff by an employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action.”
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: The Court further held that the right to reorganize business is a managerial prerogative. Provided the decision is made bona fide (in good faith), it is immune from interference. However, the Industrial Court is "duty-bound to investigate the facts and circumstances of a particular case to determine whether that exercise of power was in fact bona fide."
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: In the case of Stephen Bong V. Fcb (M) Sdn Bhd [1999] 3 MLJ 411 redundancy has been stated as follows:- ‘’that it is not that the law that redundancy means the Job or work no longer exist. Redundancy situations arise where the business requires fewer employees of whatever kind".
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: Redundancy has also been considered, where the Company has to close down or downsize the business, as stated in the case of Yusoff Othman V. Felda Engineering Services Sdn Bhd [Award No 778 OF 2022], where it was stated that:- "It is well established in industrial jurisprudence that an employer is entitled to close down the whole of part of his business as long as he acts bona fide. The right to reorganize a business and/or a company's restructuring is a managerial prerogative. " In the said case, the Court further stated that: - “lt Is well established that it is for the management to decide the strength of its staff which it considers necessary for efficiency in its undertaking. The Court will not intervene unless it is shown that the decision was capricious or without reason or was made mala fide or was actuated by victimization or unfair labour practice... the employer has a right to determine the volume of his labour force consistent with his business and organization and if the implementation of a reorganization scheme adopted for reasons of economy and better management of the business, the services of some of the employees become excess of the requirement of the business, the employer is entitled to discharge such excess".
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: The right of a Company to reorganize is evident from the case of Thomas Hans Raab V. Nokia Services And Networks Malaysia Sdn Bhd [2022] 3 ILR 371 and George Kent (M) Sdn Bhd V. Tan Tai Wai, Mak Kin Kung & Wong Khoon Sand [1988] 1 ILR 342 where it is stated that: - "Redundancy connotes that the functions of the Claimant became excess. lt is settled law that it is up to the Company to decide the strength of its staff which it considers necessary for efficiency its undertaking... ".
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: In view of the above, it is indisputable and accepted industrial jurisprudence, that a company has every right to reorganize or to restructure the Company, so as to maintain operational and financial sustainability so as to avoid any complete shutdown of the winding up of a Company.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: A case similar to the situation as in the matter before this Honourable Court, Mohd Nor Hassan & Ors V. Continental Sime Tyre PJ Sdn Bhd [2014] 3 ILR 144 where the expenses were reduced and thereafter the redundant staff were terminated, where the Court found that retrenchment was bona fide. The Court stated that:- "..the measures taken by the company were insufficient and the company was compelled to undertake a retrenchment exercise. The company carried out a reorganisation exercise if the manufacturing department of the company in Petaling Jaya which resulted in a total of 70 employees including the claimant who were found to be redundant and were accordingly retrenched.. ".
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: Further, in the case of Vithylingam Letchumanan V. Ice Room Food & Beverage Management Sdn Bhd [2015] 4 ILR 655, the Court on the issue of rights of a company stated that:- "It is the right of every employer to reorganize his business in any manner for the purpose of economy or convenience. The law recognises that a company has the right to organize its business in the manner it considers best".
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE TERMINATION OF THE CLAIMANT BY REASON OF REDUNDANCY
content: In the case of How Zheng Hong V. Air Asia Berhad [2023] 3 ILR 113, the Court considered the Aviation Industry and stated that:- "It is common knowledge that the aviation industry was among the worst affected industries by the COV/D-19 pandemic. The pandemic wrecked financial devastation across the aviation value chain, most notably for airlines save and except for freight forwards and cargo airlines. The grounding of aircrafts by the company is genuine"
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE TERMINATION OF THE CLAIMANT BY REASON OF REDUNDANCY
content: In the case of George Kent (M) Sdn Bhd V. Tan Tai Wai, Mak Kin Kung & Wong Khoon Sang [1992] 2 ILR 400, redundancy and the situation that prevails has been stated as follows:- "We are in full agreement with the learned author C.P, Mills on Industrial Disputes Law in Malaysia, that it is settled law that it is up the Company to decide the strength of its staff which it considers necessary for the efficiency in its undertaking and the Court will not interfere unless it is shown that the decision was capricious or without reason or was mala fide or was actuated by victimisation or unfair labour practice."
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE TERMINATION OF THE CLAIMANT BY REASON OF REDUNDANCY
content: In the case of Premalata Vincent Ramesh V. Nestle Products Sdn Bhd [1992] 3 ILR 277, the Court stated that in determining that the dismissal was done with just cause or excuse by the retrenchment exercise undertaken by the company, this Court will ask these pertinent questions:- (i) Whether there was a genuine need for reorganization exercise by the company; (ii) Whether a genuine redundancy situation had a rise and which led to the retrenchment of the claimant; and (iii) Whether the company had complied with the accepted standards and procedure when selecting and retrenching the claimant.’
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Principles from Ng Chang Seng
content:
The recent landmark decision of the Court of Appeal in Ng Chang Seng V. Technip Geoproduction (M) Sdn Bhd & Anor 1 MLJ 447 has significantly raised the bar for employers. The key principles established are:
a) Selection Criteria: The employer must provide clear evidence explaining why a specific employee was selected over others.
b) Comparative Evidence: To prove redundancy and fair selection, the court must look at the employees who were retained as well as those retrenched. A failure to produce comparative data is fatal.
c) LIFO: To justify a departure from LIFO, clear evidence of special skills possessed by retained juniors must be shown. d) Foreign Labour: Employers should retrench foreign workers before locals unless there are overriding reasons (though less relevant to the facts here, the principle of rigorous selection scrutiny applies).
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony
content: While the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony is not a statute, judicial decisions such as Equant Integration Services and Ng Chang Seng have elevated its status to the "gold standard" of industrial practice. Failure to comply with the Code, particularly regarding consultation and early warning, can be evidence of mala fides.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE FUNCTION OF THE INDUSTRIAL COURT
content: The role of the Industrial Court pertaining to a reference under section 20 (3) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 is to ask itself a question whether there was a dismissal; and, if so, whether it was with or without just cause or excuse Wong Chee Hong V. Cathay Organisation (M) Sdn Bhd [1988] 1 MLJ 92; [1987] 1 MLRA 346.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Burden Of Proof on Employer to Prove Genuine Redundancy
content: The primary responsibility lies with the employer to establish that the redundancy is genuine. It is insufficient to merely assert financial constraints or lack of work. The Industrial Court, in William Jacks & Co. (M) Sdn Bhd V. S. Balasingham [1997] 3 CLJ 235, affirmed that the employer must provide credible evidence to justify retrenchment. Employers must not use redundancy as a convenient excuse to terminate employees for other reasons, such as poor performance or personal bias.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Burden Of Proof on Employer to Prove Genuine Redundancy
content: As a result of the financial difficulties, the Company had embarked on a cost-cutting and reorganization exercise, where it ultimately led to some of its employees being unfortunately retrenched from the employment. The Claimant was one of those selected for retrenchment.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Burden Of Proof on Employer to Prove Genuine Redundancy
content: In order for an employee to be retrenched from his employment, the burden is on the employer to prove that there was a redundancy in the first place. The term redundancy is defined by Dunston Ayadurai in his book Industrial Relations in Malaysia (2ndEd.) at p. 159:- “Redundancy refers to a surplus of labour and is normally the result of a reorganisation of the business of the employer; and its usual consequence is retrenchment, i.e. the termination by the employer of those employees found to be surplus to his requirements after the organisation. Thus, there must first be redundancy or surplus of labour before there can be retrenchment or termination of the surplus”.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Once redundancy had occurred in any particular position, a retrenchment exercise may then be carried out by the employer to discharge the surplus labour. This was explained in the case of William Jacks & Co (M) Sdn Bhd V. S Balasingam [1997] 3 CLJ 235 [supra] where the Court of Appeal defined the term “retrenchment” as follows:- “Retrenchment had been defined as the discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action (per SK Das in Hariprasad V. Divelkar AIR [1957] SC 121 at p 132). Whether the retrenchment exercise in a particular case is bona fide or otherwise is a question of fact and of degree depending on the peculiar circumstances of the case”.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
Thus, a situation of redundancy in a job position must occur in the first place before the subsequent exercise of retrenchment is carried out whereby the employer will then set out to discharge those employees whose position had already been identified as redundant. This was succinctly explained in the book Retrenchment Law and Procedure in Malaysia by Thavalingam Thavarajah & Raymond TC Low (at pp. 4 – 5):- “An employee is said to be ‘redundant’ when their job is no longer available and the employer either cannot offer the employee any alternative position or, any alternative position offered by the employer cannot be accepted by the employee concerned. Redundancy occurs where the employer’s requirements for employees to carry out work of a particular kind has ceased or diminished. Where the same number of employees is no longer required by the employer’s business, then that will result in a redundancy. There is redundancy where:
(i) The number of employees required to carry out work of a particular nature is reduced, or is expected to be reduced and this results in dismissals; or
(ii) The work itself ceases or diminishes permanently or temporarily, or is expected to do so, so that fewer employees are needed and this results in dismissals.
In summary, ‘retrenchment’ is the expression used to describe what occurs to an employee whose employment is terminated by reason of their job becoming redundant. ‘Redundancy’ is the process of identifying employees who are surplus to the organisation’s requirements and the end result is the retrenchment of such employees”.

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
In Sistem Televisyen Malaysia Bhd & Anor V. Suzana Zakaria [2005] 1 ILR 853 it was held:- “The learned author, Dunstan Ayadurai, in his book 'Industrial Relations in Malaysia' at p. 121 defined redundancy as follows: Redundancy refers to a surplus of labour and is normally the result of reorganization of the business of an employer; and its consequence is retrenchment, i.e. the termination by the employer of those employees found to be surplus to his requirements after the reorganization. Thus, there must first be redundancy or surplus of labour before there can be retrenchment or termination of the surplus. “In Soonavala's 'The Supreme Court on Industrial Law’ Vol. 11, 2nd Edition at p. 424, the learned author stated: “Retrenchment is a necessary incidence of running an industry, but retrenchment is justified only when due to shrinkage of work, whether permanently or for an indefinite or indeterminate period, there has arisen a surplus in the number of workmen in the employment of a Company. Therefore, when a Company gives notice of retrenchment to its workmen and the dispute arising therefrom is referred to a tribunal, the only question for its decision are (a) whether the retrenchment was justified by the circumstances of the case (b) whether the grounds for the retrenchment given by the Company are true, that is, whether there had in fact occurred a reduction in the business of the Company due to circumstances such as scarcity of raw materials on the availability of which the running of the factory depends, or stoppage of work under the orders of government or changes in the economy which made it impossible to continue the business except at a loss or on meagre profits, and (c) whether the order of retrenchment was motivated by bad faith and a desire to victimize or harass the workmen whom for some ulterior reasons the employer wanted to discharge or dismiss. Additionally the High Court in Stephen Bong V. Fcb (M) Sdn Bhd [1999] CLJ 131; [1999] 1 LNS 131; [1999] 3 MLJ 411 held that: It is settled law now that redundancy does not mean the job or work no longer exist. Redundancy situation may arise where the business requires fewer employees of whatever kind.
Hence to justify the retrenchment, there must first be redundancy. To prove redundancy, the company must prove that there is surplus of labour or that the requirement of the job functions of the employee has ceased or has greatly diminished to the extent that the job no longer exists or that the business requires fewer employees of whatever kind resulting from a reorganisation exercise or due to whatever other legitimate reasons”.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
In Woo Chee Khoon V. Citibank Berhad [2011] 2 LNS 495 it was held:-
“Before there can be retrenchment or termination of the surplus, there must be redundancy or surplus of labour. It is for the management to decide on the strength of the staff, which it considers necessary for efficiency in its undertaking. When the management decides that workmen are surplus and that there is therefore a need for retrenchment, an arbitration tribunal will not intervene unless it is shown that the decision was capricious or without reason, or was mala fide, or was actuated by victimization or unfair labour practice. It is the right of every employer to reorganize its business in any manner for the purposes of economy or convenience, provided it acts bona fide”.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In the case of Yusoff Othman V. Felda Engineering Services Sdn Bhd, Award No, 778 Of 2022 it states that the term "redundancy" has been defined as:- "Redundancy refers to a surplus of labour and is normally the result of a reorganization of the business of an employer; and its usual consequence is retrenchment, i.e. termination by the employer of those employees found to be surplus to the requirement after the reorganization. Thus, there must be first be redundancy or surplus labour before there can be retrenchment of termination of the surplus"
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
A critical factor in determining the fairness of a retrenchment exercise is the application of the LIFO principle, where the employer must prioritize the retention of longer -serving employees over newer ones. In Dynacraft Industries Sdn Bhd V. Kamaruddin bin Kana Mohd Sharif & Ors [2012] 6 MLJ 453, the Federal Court held as follows:
“[13] We will deal with the first question posed in this appeal. It concerns the correctness of the application of the LIFO principle by the Industrial Court. The LIFO (last in first out) or ‘last come first go’ principle requires the most junior employee to be retrenched before the more senior ones in the same category. The principle is intended to afford a healthy safeguard against discrimination of workmen in the matter of retrenchment (as at Swadesamitran Ltd V. Their Workmen, 1960 (SC) 762). Explaining this principle, in Workmen of Sudder Workshop of Jorehaut Tea Co Ltd The Management of Jorehaut Tea Co Ltd AIR 1980 SC 1454, the Supreme Court said: The rule is that the employer shall retrench the workman who came last, first, popularly known as ‘last come first go’.”
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
For the reasons stated above, it is evident that the Claimant’s termination on the grounds of redundancy was not conducted in good faith. The Company has failed to adhere to the principles of fairness, including the burden of proof, application of LIFO, exploration of alternatives, and transparency in its decision-making process.
ISSUES FOR DETERMINATION
(a) Was the Claimant’s dismissal with just cause or excuse under Section 20(1) Industrial Relation Act 1967 [ACT 177]. (b) Was there a genuine redundancy and bona fide closure and termination of the Claimant. (c) Did the Company comply with the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony 1975, including the principles of consultation, LIFO, and transparency. (d) Was the Claimant’s dismissal procedurally fair and in accordance with the principles of industrial justice and natural justice. (e) What is the appropriate remedy if the dismissal was without just cause or excuse.
THIS HONOURABLE COURT’S EVALUATION
a)
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Whether There Was Just Cause or Excuse
content: The burden of proof lies on the employer to affirmatively justify that the dismissal was with just cause or excuse as per Goon Kwee Phoy V. J & P Coats (M) Sdn Bhd [1] 2 MLJ 129 (Federal Court).
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: b) Whether There Was Bona Fide Redundancy and Closure
content: While retrenchment may be justified if a business faces genuine closure, this must be supported by clear evidence and must be bona fide, not a mask for selective unfair removal as at Ireka Construction Berhad V. Chantiravathan Subramaniam James 2 ILR 11 (Federal Court).
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: b) Whether There Was Bona Fide Redundancy and Closure
content: This factual matrix closely mirrors principles established by the Federal Court in Holiday Inn, Penang V. National Union Of Hotel, Bar & Restaurant Workers 1 MLJ 130, where contradictions in the defines and continuing business activity nullify the genuineness of alleged redundancy. The Court is not satisfied that the Company proved an irreversible and total cessation as asserted. The documentary record exposes substantial contradictions and an absence of transparency and can be dour in the Company’s position.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: c) Procedural Fairness & Adherence to Code of Conduct
content:
Employer obligations prior to retrenchment are prescribed by the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony 1975: consultation, consideration of alternatives to retrenchment, application of the LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) principle (unless objectively justified departure is proven) and adequate notice. Here, overwhelming evidence including unchallenged testimony from the Claimant shows that:
(i) No meaningful consultation occurred. (ii) No objective matrix for selection was disclosed; persons less senior than the Claimant remained in employment for a period after her termination. (iii) The Company deviated from the LIFO principle without adducing special circumstances, violating the expectation in Colgate Palmolive (M) Sdn Bhd V. Yap Kok Foong 3 ILR 313 (Court of Appeal), and guided by the Court of Appeal's reasoning in Ng Chang Seng V. Technip geoproduction (M) Sdn Bhd & Anor [2021] 1 MLRA 261 (iv) No evidence of alternative roles, redeployment options or voluntary separation schemes was offered to the Claimant.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: c) Procedural Fairness & Adherence to Code of Conduct
content: Industrial court findings in Malaysia underscore that retrenchment and especially redundancy for the Airline cannot be sustained where business or its core functions are demonstrably ongoing, and the selection process is not transparent or uniformly applied. While operational loss may in justified cases allow rationalization of the workforce, the particular facts here point to inconsistency, poor disclosure, and poor industrial practice.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: d) Natural Justice and Industrial Harmony
content: This Honourable Court notes as persuasive the ongoing scholarly and comparative literature emphasizing natural justice as a foundational element in labour dispute resolution, even where formal legal duties are balanced against other practicalities. Both judicial practice and industrial relations literature highlight the centrality of the right to be heard, procedural consistency, and an equitable (not arbitrary) selection for retrenchment in fostering workplace stability and legitimacy. This is especially so in the Malaysian industrial context with its hybrid model of industrial pluralism and evolving workforce flexibility.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: It is undisputed that the Company faced severe financial distress due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Its witnesses (Head of Finance) testified to massive losses and debt. For example, the Company projected that without urgent cost cuts it would incur an additional RM644 million loss in 2021. The audited accounts show Malindo revenue plunged from RM2.52 billion in 2019 to only RM650.5 million in 2020. The Company introduced multiple memoranda (unpaid leave, salary cuts, VSS) from February through October 2020 and did not immediately retrench pilots after the first lockdowns.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In these respects, the Company’s case is supported; it clearly needed to reduce costs to survive. Indeed, the Industrial Court in Luqman Bin Mikail Lim V. Air Asia X (Award NO. 270 OF 2023) and Mohamad Zahid V. Air Asia Sdn Bhd (Award NO. 631 OF 2025) Recognised that during the pandemic employers could depart from traditional selection processes because of the “unprecedented” crisis.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: However, “good faith” under s.30 IRA also requires fair treatment of employees. Here the Company admitted it did not pay the Claimant his contractual salary for March to Oct 2020. In cross-examination, the Claimant denied ever applying for any unpaid leave or separation plan. The Company never produced any signed application from him. Simply withholding wages (while invoking “voluntary” schemes that the Claimant did not join) suggests coercive treatment. By common law, an employer cannot contract out of paying agreed wages during employment. The withholding of pay for 8 months, when the Claimant continued to fly on request, undermines the Company’s plea of bona fide.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

Kamaruddin bin Kana Mohd Sharif & Ors [2012] 9 CLJ 21; [2012] 6 MLJ 453, the Federal Court held as follows: "[13] We will deal with the first question posed in this appeal. It concerns the correctness of the application of the LIFO principle by the Industrial Court. Explaining this principle, in Workmen of Sudder Workshop of Jorehaut Tea Co Ltd V. The Management of Jorehaut Tea Co Ltd AIR 1980 SC 1454, the Supreme Court said: "The rule is that the employer shall retrench the workman who came last, first, popularly known as ' last come first go'."
