case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In Dynacraft ‘s case [supra] decision makes clear that prima facie the LIFO rule applies, an employer should retrench the latest recruits first, “where other things are equal”.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: A lawful deviation requires objective justification. The Company argues it departed from LIFO for “performance, safety and disciplinary” reasons. Even if merit-based selection is permitted in principle (as Wong Zi Chuang V. Air Asia X [2025] 1 ILJ 1 held, provided it is done bona fide and not arbitrarily), those reasons must be substantiated.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The adjudication of retrenchment disputes in Malaysia is governed by a well-established framework of legal principles derived from the Industrial Relations Act 1967 and judicial precedent.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: A. The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: The term "retrenchment" was authoritatively defined by the Court of Appeal in William Jacks & Co (M) Sdn Bhd V. S. Balasingam 3 CLJ 235 as: "The discharge of surplus labour or staff by an employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action.”
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: A. The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: The Court further held that the right to reorganize business is a managerial prerogative. Provided the decision is made bona fide (in good faith), it is immune from interference. However, the Industrial Court is "duty-bound to investigate the facts and circumstances of a particular case to determine whether that exercise of power was in fact bona fide."
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The burden of proof lies squarely on the employer to justify the retrenchment. As held in Bayer (M) Sdn Bhd V. Ng Hong Pau 4 CLJ 155; 3 MELR 484: "On redundancy it cannot be gainsaid that the appellant must come to the Court with concrete proof. The burden is on the appellant to prove actual redundancy on which the dismissal was grounded."
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Mere assertions of financial difficulty or reorganization are insufficient; the employer must adduce "concrete proof" of the redundancy and the fairness of the selection.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: C. The Principles from Ng Chang Seng’ Case
content:
The recent landmark decision of the Court of Appeal in Ng Chang
Seng V. Technip Geoproduction (M) Sdn Bhd & Anor 1 MLJ 447 has significantly raised the bar for employers. The key principles established are:
a) Selection Criteria: The employer must provide clear evidence explaining why a specific employee was selected over others.
b) Comparative Evidence: To prove redundancy and fair selection, the court must look at the employees who were retained as well as those retrenched. A failure to produce comparative data is fatal.
c) LIFO: To justify a departure from LIFO, clear evidence of special skills possessed by retained juniors must be shown.
d) Foreign Labour: Employers should retrench foreign workers before locals unless there are overriding reasons (though less relevant to the facts here, the principle of rigorous selection scrutiny applies).
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: D. The Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony
content: While the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony is not a statute, judicial decisions such as Equant Integration Services and Ng Chang Seng have elevated its status to the "gold standard" of industrial practice. Failure to comply with the Code, particularly regarding consultation and early warning, can be evidence of mala fides.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Evidence and Proof on Company’s Burden
content: Having chosen to retrench the Claimant, the Company bore the onus of proof that its stated reasons were genuine. Moreover, by common practice, the Company should have produced documentary justification for its choices.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The evidence here suffers from notable gaps
content: As the authorities point out, the very person who decides on dismissals should testify. In CJ Polymers Sdn Bhd V. Sim Chin Hu & Ors & Other Appeals [2025] 5 MLRA 473 (CA), the Court stressed that failing to call the dismissing authority warrants an adverse inference. By analogy, we find it significant that the people “behind the scenes” were not examined.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
The Court has scrutinized the extensive evidence and submissions. The evaluation is structured into four distinct areas:
A. Financial Necessity B. Selection Criteria and LIFO C. Adverse Inference and Witnesses D. Procedural Fairness.
A. Financial Necessity and Bona Fides
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The threshold question is whether the Company was in a genuine redundancy situation. The Company paints a picture of apocalyptic financial collapse; the Claimant argues the Company was in "recovery" and acted opportunistically.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Court has examined the audited accounts (COBD-1) and the testimony of COW-1. The sheer scale of the revenue collapse from RM2.5 billion to RM650 million cannot be overstated. The aviation industry was grounded. The reduction of the fleet from 47 to 15 aircraft creates a prima facie case of redundancy. Logic dictates that a 68% reduction in aircraft requires a commensurate reduction in pilots.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: ii. The "Recovery Mode" Argument in (Osram Opto’case)
content: The Claimant relies on Osram Opto Semiconductors (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd V. Ooi Mei Chien [2024] 6 CLJ 716 to argue that the retrenchment was unlawful because the Company’s loss margin improved from -153% (Sept 2020) to -110% (Oct 2020). In Osram’s [supra] case the Court of Appeal (and recently affirmed by the Federal Court regarding reinstatement remedies) held that retrenchment is not bona fide if the business is on an "expansion mode" with positive growth.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: ii. The "Recovery Mode" Argument in (Osram Opto’case)
content:
However, this Court finds a material distinction. In Osram, [supra] the company was expanding and hiring. In the present case, Malindo Airways was not "expanding." An improvement in loss margin from -153% to -110% does not constitute "profitability" or "growth." It indicates that the Company was losing money at a slightly reduced rate but was still technically insolvent.
i. Fact: The Claimant’s own data shows that in November 2020 (post-retrenchment), the loss worsened to -157%. ii. Inference: This suggests the "recovery" in October was a statistical fluctuation, not a stabilized trend.
Finding: The Court finds that the Company has successfully established a genuine redundancy situation. The financial distress was real, severe, and external. The Osram [supra] principle does not apply because the Company was in survival mode, not expansion mode.
B. Selection Criteria and the LIFO Principle
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: ii. The "Recovery Mode" Argument in (Osram Opto’case)
content:
Establishment of redundancy is only the first hurdle. The second, and often more difficult hurdle, is Selection. Why was the Claimant selected? The Company claims it strictly followed LIFO.
C. The Evidence of Selection (COB-2,(2) page 62-65)
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: ii. The "Recovery Mode" Argument in (Osram Opto’case)
content:
The Company relied on Exhibit COB-2 (2) page 62-65 as the definitive "Retrenchment List." However, under cross-examination, COW-2 made startling admissions regarding this document:
i. It contained only names, positions, and hire dates of the retrenched staff.
ii. It did not contain a comparative list of the retained staff. iii. It lacked any details on skills, disciplinary records, or qualifications.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: ii. The "Recovery Mode" Argument in (Osram Opto’case)
content:
When pressed by Claimant’s counsel on whether he had proof that the Claimant was junior to those retained, COW-2 replied: "It’s impossible to bring them to the Court because there are tonnes and tonnes of paper."
D. The "Tonnes of Paper" Defence
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: ii. The "Recovery Mode" Argument in (Osram Opto’case)
content:
This Court rejects the "tonnes of paper" defence. In a court of law, the burden of proof is static. If an employer asserts LIFO, it must demonstrate LIFO. This requires a Master List showing:
i. All employees in the category (Co-Pilots). ii. Their dates of joining. iii. The specific "cut-off" line. iv. Verification that every person below the line was retrenched and every person above was retained.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: ii. The "Recovery Mode" Argument in (Osram Opto’case)
content:
The Company failed to produce this Master List. Without it, the Court cannot verify the Company’s assertion that the Claimant (Rank 71 on the retrenchment list) was junior to the last retained pilot. The Court is asked to accept the Company’s word without the supporting data.
E. Application of Ng Chang Seng’ Case
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: ii. The "Recovery Mode" Argument in (Osram Opto’case)
content: This evidentiary gap is precisely what the Court of Appeal condemned in Ng Chang Seng [supra]. In that case, the failure to produce evidence comparing the claimant to retained staff was fatal to the company's defence. The Court held: "The company deftly deflected the issue by not producing any evidence as to the number of years of employment of the staff that still enjoyed employment... mere ‘say so’ fell short of discharging the burden of proof."
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: ii. The "Recovery Mode" Argument in (Osram Opto’case)
content: Here, the Company has offered "mere say-so" regarding the seniority of the retained pilots.

section_title: Failure to Call Material Witnesses and Adverse Inference
content: Procedural History and Non-Compliance. It is a matter of record that this Court had, on three separate occasions, directed the Company’s Counsel to file the Witness Statements of its intended witnesses, specifically the decision-makers responsible for the Claimant's dismissal (identified as Mr. Muzaffar and Captain Syafiq). Despite these repeated opportunities and the Court’s clear indulgence, the Company failed to file said statements or produce these witnesses.

section_title: Failure to Call Material Witnesses and Adverse Inference
content: The Court’s Order Consequently, due to the Company’s blatant non-compliance with the Court’s directions, this Court was compelled to issue an order prohibiting the Company from calling these witnesses and directed the proceedings to continue with the Claimant’s evidence alone. The Company, therefore, stands before this Court without having adduced oral testimony from the primary actors who made the decision to dismiss the Claimant.

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Failure to Call Material Witnesses and Adverse Inference
content: Burden of Proof and Adverse Inference In a claim for unfair dismissal under Section 20 of the Act, the burden of proof lies squarely on the employer to prove the misconduct and the justification for dismissal. The Company cannot discharge this burden by merely relying on pleadings or documentary bundles without the oral testimony of the makers to speak to the truth of their contents.

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Failure to Call Material Witnesses and Adverse Inference
content: The failure to call Mr. Muzaffar and Captain Syafiq, who were arguably the material witnesses to the decision-making process, is fatal to the Company’s case. This Court is therefore entitled to and indeed does invoke Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act 1950, which provides that: "The Court may presume that evidence which could be and is not produced would, if produced, be unfavorable to the person who withholds it."

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Failure to Call Material Witnesses and Adverse Inference
content: Distinguishing the Decision in Syafiq Hamdi Case. The Company attempted to rely on the decision Syafiq Hamdi Case to bolster its defense. This Court firmly rejects this reliance. The doctrine of stare decisis or the reliance on precedent requires similar facts and, crucially, similar evidentiary weight.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Failure to Call Material Witnesses and Adverse Inference
content: A party cannot rely on a victory in a previous case to cure a lack of evidence in the present trial. In Syafiq Hamdi, it appears the issue of missing material witnesses was not litigated with the same ferocity, or perhaps the necessary proofs were successfully adduced in that specific instance. However, litigation is case-specific. The Company’s failure to bring the necessary proof, specifically the testimony of the decision-makers, to this specific trial cannot be remedied by pointing to one success in another.
source_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Failure to Call Material Witnesses and Adverse Inference
content: Conclusion on this Issue. Without the testimony of the decision-makers to explain the reason for the termination, to refute the Claimant's evidence of approved leave, or to justify the lack of due inquiry, the Company’s defense collapses. The "mind" of the Company was not present in Court to answer the Claimant’s case. Accordingly, the Court holds that the Company has failed to prove the grounds for dismissal.

content: The legal principle regarding the withholding of evidence is codified in Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act 1950. The Federal Court in Takako Sakao V. Ng Pek Yuen & Anor 6 MLJ 751 held that if a party fails to call a material witness who could elucidate the facts, the Court is entitled to presume the evidence would be unfavourable.

content:
This is an importance case for adverse inference. The Company relied on a witness (COW-2) who lacked personal knowledge ("hearsay evidence") while withholding the witnesses who had personal knowledge.
i. Inference Drawn: The Court infers that had Captain Syafiq and Mr. Muzaffar testified, their evidence would have revealed irregularities in the selection process. It is probable that the selection was not based strictly on LIFO but was influenced by other factors specifically, the Claimant’s refusal to sign the LTU or VSS.

content: The Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony (Clause 22(a)) mandates "early warning" and consultation. COW-2 admitted under cross-examination that there were "no avenues or channels for employees to discuss with the Company for not being retrenched".

chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Company argues that "Town Hall" meetings constituted consultation. This Court disagrees. A Town Hall is a briefing; it is a one-way transmission of information. Consultation implies a dialogue where the employee can propose alternatives (for example, opting for a lower rank, part-time work or extended unpaid leave). The 48-hour notice precluded any such dialogue.

content: The Claimant raised a significant issue regarding the Training Bond Waiver. COW-2 admitted that employees who accepted the VSS/LTU had their training bonds waived, while those retrenched (who refused LTU) were potentially still liable or treated differently.

content: This creates a perception of victimization. It suggests that the "Selection Criteria" was not just LIFO, but also "Compliance." Those who complied with the LTU were safe (and got bond waivers); those who refused were retrenched. This conflation of a temporary measure (LTU) with a permanent selection criterion indicates mala fides (bad faith).

section_title: Distinguishing This Present Case with Syafiq Hamdi’s Case
content: The doctrine of stare decisis does not strictly apply to the Industrial Court, though consistency is desirable. However, this Court finds a critical factual distinction between Syafiq Hamdi and the present case. In Syafiq Hamdi’s case, the learned Chairman found: "No evidence was adduced to suggest that the principle was applied selectively or arbitrarily."

chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Distinguishing This Present Case with Syafiq Hamdi’s Case
content: In the present case, the Claimant has adduced such evidence or rather, has successfully exposed the absence of Company evidence. The successful invocation of the adverse inference regarding the missing witnesses (Mr.Muzaffar and Captain Syafiq) is the turning point. In Syafiq Hamdi, it appears the issue of the missing witnesses or the incomplete LIFO list was not litigated with the same ferocity or result. A party cannot rely on a previous victory if they fail to bring the necessary proofs to this specific trial. The failure to call the decision-makers in this proceeding is fatal, regardless of the outcome in Syafiq Hamdi.

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
The Court synthesizes its findings as follows:
a) Genuine Redundancy: The Company successfully proved that the pandemic and fleet reduction created a genuine surplus of labour. The Claimant’s "financial recovery" argument is rejected. b) Failed Selection: The Company failed to prove that the Claimant was selected based on LIFO. The failure to produce a Master List of all pilots and the reliance on hearsay evidence (COW-2 (p.62-65) means the Company failed to discharge its burden of proof under Ng Chang Seng [supra].
c) Adverse Inference: The wilful withholding of material witnesses (Mr.Muzaffar and Captain Syafiq) warrants an adverse inference under Section 114(g) Evidence Act 1950, leading the Court to conclude the selection process was flawed or arbitrary.
d) Procedural Breach: The 48-hour notice and lack of individual consultation constituted a breach of the Code of Conduct and principles of natural justice.

content: This Court is bound by the principle laid down in the case of Dr. James Alfred (Sabah) V. Koperasi Serbaguna Sanya Bhd (Sabah) & Anor [2001] 3 Clj 541.His Lordship Justice Tan Sri Steve Shim CJ (Sabah & Sarawak) in delivering the judgement of the Federal Court held that: ‘’In our view, it is in line with equity and good conscience that the Industrial Court, in assessing quantum of back wages, should take into account the fact, if established by evidence or admitted, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. Failure to do so constitutes a jurisdictional error of law. Certiorari will therefore lie to rectify it. Of course, taking into account such employment after dismissal does not necessarily mean that the Industrial Court has to conduct a mathematical exercise in deduction. What is important is that the Industrial Court, in the exercise of its discretion in assessing the quantum of back wages, should take into account all relevant matters including the fact, where it exists, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. This discretion is in the nature of a decision-making process.’’

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The sole issue is whether the termination of the Claimant was with just cause or excuse. In an unfair dismissal reference under s.20 (3) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967, the Court’s duty is to determine “whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse”. If the employer gives a reason for dismissal, the Court must inquire whether that reason has been made out in evidence. Retrenchment is a dismissal in operational redundancy, so s.30 of the Act applies, the Company must show a genuine redundancy situation and that the dismissal was made in good faith (s.30 (5) IRA).

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Normally retrenchment selections follow the industry-recognised “last-in-first-out” rule, deviations are allowed only for valid and bona fide reasons. The Company must prove on balance that the Claimant’s post had indeed become redundant and that his retrenchment was not a sham (Goon Kwee Phoy V. J&P Coats [1981] 2 MLJ 127; Ng Chang Seng Technip Reproduction [2021] 1 MLJ 447). The Court apply these principles to the evidence.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: It is imperative to consider the law on redundancy prior to considering the conduct of the Company, as it will show that the Company at all times acted in a bona fide manner and the redundancy was bona fide. Therefore, it will be evident that the Company complied with the principles of law.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In the Court of Appeal case of William Jacks & Co (M) Sdn Bhd V. S Balasingam [19991 3 MLJ 411, redundancy was defined as follows: "Retrenchment" has been defined as the discharge of surplus labour or staff by an employer for any reason whatsoever. Whether the retrenchment exercise in a particular case is bona fide or otherwise is a question of fact and of degree depending in the peculiar circumstances of the case. It is well settled that the employer is entitled to organize his business in the manner he considers best. So long as the managerial power is exercised bone fide, the decision is immune from examination even by the Industrial Court. However, the Industrial Court is empowered and indeed duty bound to investigate the facts and circumstances of the case to determine whether the exercise of power is in fact bone fide".

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In the case of Stephen Bong V. FCB (M) Sdn Bhd [1999] 3 MLJ 411 redundancy has been stated as follows: - ‘’that it is not that the law that redundancy means the Job or work no longer exist. Redundancy situations arise where the business requires fewer employees of whatever kind".

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Redundancy has also been considered, where the Company has to close down or downsize the business, as stated in the case of Yusoff Othman V. Felda Engineering Services Sdn Bhd [Award No. 778 of 2022], where it was stated that: - "It is well established in industrial jurisprudence that an employer is entitled to close down the whole of part of his business as long as he acts bona fide. The right to reorganize a business and/or a company's restructuring is a managerial prerogative. " In the said case, the Court further stated that: - " lt Is well established that it is for the management to decide the strength of its staff which it considers necessary for efficiency in its undertaking. The Court will not intervene unless it is shown that the decision was capricious or without reason or was made mala fide or was actuated by victimization or unfair labour practice... the employer has a right to determine the volume of his labour force consistent with his business and organization and if the implementation of a reorganization scheme adopted for reasons of economy and better management of the business, the services of some of the employees become excess of the requirement of the business, the employer is entitled to discharge such excess".

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The right of a Company to reorganize is evident from the case of Thomas Hans Raab V. Nokia Services and Networks Malaysia Sdn Bhd [2022] 3 ILR 371 and George Kent (M) Sdn Bhd V. Tan Tai Wai, Mak Kin Kung & Wong Khoon Sand [1988] 1 ILR 342 where it is stated that: - "Redundancy connotes that the functions of the Claimant became excess. lt is settled law that it is up to the Company to decide the strength of its staff which it considers necessary for efficiency its undertaking... ".

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In view of the above, it is indisputable and accepted industrial jurisprudence, that a company has every right to reorganize or to restructure the Company, so as to maintain operational and financial sustainability so as to avoid any complete shutdown of the winding up of a Company.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: A case similar to the situation as in the matter before this Honorable Court, Mohd Nor Hassan & Ors V. Continental Sime Tyre PJ Sdn Bhd [2014] 3 ILR144 where the expenses were reduced and thereafter the redundant staff were terminated, where the Court found that retrenchment was bona fide. The Court stated that: - “...the measures taken by the company were insufficient and the company was compelled to undertake a retrenchment exercise. The company carried out a reorganisation exercise if the manufacturing department of the company in Petaling Jaya which resulted in a total of 70 employees including the claimant who were found to be redundant and were accordingly retrenched. ".

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Further, in the case of Vithylingam Letchumanan V. Ice Room Food & Beverage Management Sdn Bhd [2015] 4 ILR 655, the Court on the issue of rights of a company stated that: - "It is the right of every employer to reorganize his business in any manner for the purpose of economy or convenience. The law recognises that a company has the right to organize its business in the manner it considers best".

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE TERMINATION OF THE CLAIMANT BY REASON OF REDUNDANCY
content: In the case of How Zheng Hong V. Air Asia Berhad [2023] 3 ILR 113, the Court considered the Aviation Industry and stated that: - "It is common knowledge that the aviation industry was among the worst affected industries by the COV/D-19 pandemic. The pandemic wrecked financial devastation across the aviation value chain, most notably for airlines save and except for freight forwards and cargo airlines. The grounding of aircrafts by the company is genuine"

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE TERMINATION OF THE CLAIMANT BY REASON OF REDUNDANCY
content: In the case of George Kent (M) Sdn Bhd V. Tan Tai Wai, Mak Kin Kung & Wong Khoon Sang [1992] 2 ILR 400, redundancy and the situation that prevails has been stated as follows: - "We are in full agreement with the learned author C.P, Mills on Industrial Disputes Law in Malaysia, that it is settled law that it is up the Company to decide the strength of its staff which it considers necessary for the efficiency in its undertaking and the Court will not interfere unless it is shown that the decision was capricious or without reason or was mala fide or was actuated by victimisation or unfair labour practice."

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE TERMINATION OF THE CLAIMANT BY REASON OF REDUNDANCY
content:
In the case of Premalata Vincent Ramesh V. Nestle Products Sdn Bhd [1992] 3 ILR 277, the Court stated that in determining that the dismissal was done with just cause or excuse by the retrenchment exercise undertaken by the company, this Court will ask these pertinent questions: -
(i) ‘’Whether there was a genuine need for reorganization exercise by the company;
(ii) Whether a genuine redundancy situation had a rise and which led to the retrenchment of the claimant; and
(iii) Whether the company had complied with the accepted standards and procedure when selecting and retrenching the claimant.’’

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE FUNCTION OF THE INDUSTRIAL COURT
content: The role of the Industrial Court pertaining to a reference under section 20 (3) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 is to ask itself a question whether there was a dismissal; and, if so, whether it was with or without just cause or excuse Wong Chee Hong V. Cathay Organisation (M) Sdn. Bhd. [1988] 1 MLJ 92; [1987] 1 MLRA 346).

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: BURDEN OF PROOF ON EMPLOYER TO PROVE GENUINE REDUNDANCY
content: The primary responsibility lies with the employer to establish that the redundancy is genuine. It is insufficient to merely assert financial constraints or lack of work. The Industrial Court, in William Jacks & Co. (M) Sdn Bhd V. S. Balasingham [1997] 3CLJ 235, affirmed that the employer must provide credible evidence to justify retrenchment. Employers must not use redundancy as a convenient excuse to terminate employees for other reasons, such as poor performance or personal bias.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: BURDEN OF PROOF ON EMPLOYER TO PROVE GENUINE REDUNDANCY
content: As a result of the financial difficulties, the Company had embarked on a cost cutting and reorganization exercise, where it ultimately led to some of its employees being unfortunately retrenched from the employment. The Claimant was one of those selected for retrenchment.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: BURDEN OF PROOF ON EMPLOYER TO PROVE GENUINE REDUNDANCY
content: In order for an employee to be retrenched from his employment, the burden is on the employer to prove that there was a redundancy in the first place. The term redundancy is defined by Dunston Ayyadurai in his book Industrial Relations in Malaysia (2ndEd.) at p. 159: - “Redundancy refers to a surplus of labour and is normally the result of a reorganisation of the business of the employer; and its usual consequence is retrenchment, i.e., the termination by the employer of those employees found to be surplus to his requirements after the organisation. Thus, there must first be redundancy or surplus of labour before there can be retrenchment or termination of the surplus”.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Once redundancy had occurred in any particular position, a retrenchment exercise may then be carried out by the employer to discharge the surplus labour. This was explained in the case of William Jacks & Co (M) Sdn Bhd V. S Balasingam [1997] 3 CLJ 235 [supra] where the Court of Appeal defined the term “retrenchment” as follows: - “Retrenchment had been defined as the discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action (per SK Das in Hariprasad v. Divelkar AIR [1957] SC 121 at p 132). Whether the retrenchment exercise in a particular case is bona fide or otherwise is a question of fact and of degree depending on the peculiar circumstances of the case”.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
Thus, a situation of redundancy in a job position must occur in the first place before the subsequent exercise of retrenchment is carried out whereby the employer will then set out to discharge those employees whose position had already been identified as redundant. This was succinctly explained in the book Retrenchment Law and Procedure in Malaysia by Thavalingam Thavarajah & Raymond TC Low (at pp. 4 – 5): - “An employee is said to be ‘redundant’ when their job is no longer available and the employer either cannot offer the employee any alternative position or, any alternative position offered by the employer cannot be accepted by the employee concerned. Redundancy occurs where the employer’s requirements for employees to carry out work of a particular kind has ceased or diminished. Where the same number of employees is no longer required by the employer’s business, then that will result in a redundancy. There is redundancy where:
(i) The number of employees required to carry out work of a particular nature is reduced, or is expected to be reduced and this results in dismissals
(ii) The work itself ceases or diminishes permanently or temporarily, or is expected to do so, so that fewer employees are needed and this results in dismissals. In summary, ‘retrenchment’ is the expression used to describe what occurs to an employee whose employment is terminated by reason of their job becoming redundant. ‘Redundancy’ is the process of identifying employees who are surplus to the organisation’s requirements and the end result is the retrenchment of such employees”.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In Sistem Televisyen Malaysia Bhd & Anor V. Suzana Zakaria [2005] 1 ILR 853 it was held: - “The learned author, Dunstan Ayadurai, in his book 'Industrial Relations in Malaysia' at p. 121 defined redundancy as follows: Redundancy refers to a surplus of labour and is normally the result of reorganization of the business of an employer; and its consequence is retrenchment, i.e., the termination by the employer of those employees found to be surplus to his requirements after the reorganization. Thus, there must first be redundancy or surplus of labour before there can be retrenchment or termination of the surplus. “In Soonavala's 'The Supreme Court on Industrial Law’ Vol. 11, 2nd Edition at p. 424, the learned author stated: “Retrenchment is a necessary incidence of running an industry, but retrenchment is justified only when due to shrinkage of work, whether permanently or for an indefinite or indeterminate period, there has arisen a surplus in the number of workmen in the employment of a Company. Therefore, when a Company gives notice of retrenchment to its workmen and the dispute arising therefrom is referred to a tribunal, the only question for its decision are (a) whether the retrenchment was justified by the circumstances of the case (b) whether the grounds for the retrenchment given by the Company are true, that is, whether there had in fact occurred a reduction in the business of the Company due to circumstances such as scarcity of raw materials on the availability of which the running of the factory depends, or stoppage of work under the orders of government or changes in the economy which made it impossible to continue the business except at a loss or on meagre profits, and (c) whether the order of retrenchment was motivated by bad faith and a desire to victimize or harass the workmen whom for some ulterior reasons the employer wanted to discharge or dismiss. Additionally, the High Court in Stephen Bong V. FCB (M) Sdn Bhd [1999] CLJ 131; [1999] 1 LNS 131; [1999] 3 MLJ 411 held that: It is settled law now that redundancy does not mean the job or work no longer exist. Redundancy situation may arise where the business requires fewer employees of whatever kind. Hence to justify the retrenchment, there must first be redundancy. To prove redundancy, the company must prove that there is surplus of labour or that the requirement of the job functions of the employee has ceased or has greatly diminished to the extent that the job no longer exists or that the business requires fewer employees of whatever kind resulting from a reorganisation exercise or due to whatever other legitimate reasons”.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In Woo Chee Khoon V. Citibank Berhad [2011] 2 LNS 495 it was held: - “Before there can be retrenchment or termination of the surplus, there must be redundancy or surplus of labour. It is for the management to decide on the strength of the staff, which it considers necessary for efficiency in its undertaking. When the management decides that workmen are surplus and that there is therefore a need for retrenchment, an arbitration tribunal will not intervene unless it is shown that the decision was capricious or without reason, or was mala fide, or was actuated by victimization or unfair labour practice. It is the right of every employer to reorganize its business in any manner for the purposes of economy or convenience, provided it acts bona fide”.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
In the case of Yusoff Othman V. Felda Engineering Services Sdn Bhd, (Award No. 778 of 2022 ) it states that the term "redundancy" has been defined as: - "Redundancy refers to a surplus of labour and is normally the result of a reorganization of the business of an employer; and its usual consequence is retrenchment, i.e., termination by the employer of those employees found to be surplus to the requirement after the reorganization. Thus, there must be first be redundancy or surplus labour before there can be retrenchment of termination of the surplus"
ISSUES FOR DETERMINATION
(a) Was the Claimant’s dismissal with just cause or excuse under Section 20(1) Industrial Relation Act 1967 [ACT 177].
(b) Was there a genuine redundancy and bona fide closure and termination of the Claimant. (c) Did the Company comply with the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony 1975, including the principles of consultation, LIFO, and transparency.
(d) Was the Claimant’s dismissal procedurally fair and in accordance with the principles of industrial justice and natural justice.
(e) What is the appropriate remedy if the dismissal was without just cause or excuse.
THIS HONOURABLE COURT’S EVALUATION
a)

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Whether There Was Just Cause or Excuse
content: The burden of proof lies on the employer to affirmatively justify that the dismissal was with just cause or excuse, per Goon Kwee Phoy V. J & P Coats (M) Sdn Bhd [1] 2 MLJ 129 (Federal Court) and reaffirmed in Statement in Reply and both parties’ written submissions.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: b) Whether There Was Bona Fide Redundancy and Closure
content: While retrenchment may be justified if a business faces genuine closure, this must be supported by clear evidence and must be bona fide, not a mask for selective unfair removal as at Ireka Construction Berhad V. Chantiravathan Subramaniam James 2 ILR 11 (Federal Court).

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: b) Whether There Was Bona Fide Redundancy and Closure
content: This factual matrix closely mirrors principles established by the Federal Court in Holiday Inn, Penang V. National Union of Hotel, Bar & Restaurant Workers [3] 1 MLJ 130, where contradictions in the defines and continuing business activity nullify the genuineness of alleged redundancy. The Court is not satisfied that the Company proved an irreversible and total cessation as asserted. The documentary record exposes substantial contradictions and an absence of transparency and can be dour in the Company’s position.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: c) Procedural Fairness & Adherence to Code of Conduct
content:
Employer obligations prior to retrenchment are prescribed by the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony 1975: consultation, consideration of alternatives to retrenchment, application of the LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) principle (unless objectively justified departure is proven), and adequate notice. Here, overwhelming evidence including unchallenged testimony from the Claimant shows that:
(i) No meaningful consultation occurred. (ii) No objective matrix for selection was disclosed; persons less senior than the Claimant remained in employment for a period after her termination.
(iii) The Company deviated from the LIFO principle without adducing special circumstances, violating the expectation in Colgate Palmolive (M) Sdn Bhd V. Yap Kok Foong 3 ILR 313 (Court of Appeal), and guided by the Court of Appeal's reasoning in Ng Chang Seng V. Technipgeo production (M) Sdn Bhd & Anor [2021] 1 MLRA 261.
(iv) No evidence of alternative roles, redeployment options or voluntary separation schemes was offered to the Claimant.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: c) Procedural Fairness & Adherence to Code of Conduct
content: Industrial court findings in Malaysia underscore that retrenchment and especially redundancy for the Airline cannot be sustained where business or its core functions are demonstrably ongoing and the selection process is not transparent or uniformly applied. While operational loss may in justified cases allow rationalization of the workforce, the particular facts here point to inconsistency, poor disclosure, and poor industrial practice.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: d) Natural Justice and Industrial Harmony
content: This Honourable Court notes as persuasive the ongoing scholarly and comparative literature emphasizing natural justice as a foundational element in labour dispute resolution, even where formal legal duties are balanced against other practicalities. Both judicial practice and industrial relations literature highlight the centrality of the right to be heard, procedural consistency, and an equitable (not arbitrary) selection for retrenchment in fostering workplace stability and legitimacy. This is especially so in the Malaysian industrial context with its hybrid model of industrial pluralism and evolving workforce flexibility.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: It is undisputed that the Company faced severe financial distress due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Its witnesses COW-1 (Head of Finance) testified to massive losses and debt. For example, the Company projected that without urgent cost cuts it would incur an additional RM644 million losses in 2021. The audited accounts show Malindo’s revenue plunged from RM2.52 billion in 2019 to only RM650.5 million in 2020. The Company introduced multiple memoranda (unpaid leave, salary cuts, VSS) from February through October 2020 and did not immediately retrench pilots after the first lockdowns.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In these respects, the Company’s case is supported, it clearly needed to reduce costs to survive. Indeed, the Industrial Court in Luqman Bin Mikail Lim V. Air Asia X (Award No. 270 of 2023) And Mohamad Zahid V. Air Asia Sdn Bhd (Award No. 631 of 2025) Recognised that during the pandemic employers could depart from traditional selection processes because of the “unprecedented” crisis.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: However, “good faith” under s.30 IRA also requires fair treatment of employees. Here the Company admitted it did not pay the Claimant his contractual salary for March to Oct 2020. In cross-examination, the Claimant denied ever applying for any unpaid leave or separation plan. The Company never produced any signed application from him. Simply withholding wages (while invoking “voluntary” schemes that the Claimant did not join) suggests coercive treatment. By common law, an employer cannot contract out of paying agreed wages during employment. The withholding of pay for 8 months, when the Claimant continued to fly on request, undermines the Company’s plea of bona fide.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: A retrenchment is lawful only if the position is truly surplus. No evidence was tendered to show that the Claimant’s specific duties would permanently cease. In fact, the Company continued limited flights even in late 2020 and no evidence shows the Claimant’s route or unit was closed for good. The Company did not explain how the Claimant (a senior B737 captain) became redundant in preference to those it retained. By the Company’s own testimony, 25 of B737 captains were retained.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant, also a B737 captain, was placed in the retrenchment list. As the Claimant’s counsel pointed out, this effectively created two classes: a “retained” group of 25 captains and a “retrenchment” group of the rest. Yet the Company did not produce the list of retained pilots or explain why each was kept or cut. Without such documentation, the only indication of selection criteria was the oral evidence of one HR witness.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: A critical factor in determining the fairness of a retrenchment exercise is the application of the LIFO principle, where the employer must prioritize the retention of longer -serving employees over newer ones.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Federal Court’s Dynacraft Industries Sdn Bhd V. Kamaruddin bin Kana Mohd Sharif & Ors [2012] 9 CLJ 21; [2012] 6 MLJ 453, the Federal Court held as follows: "[13] We will deal with the first question posed in this appeal. It concerns the correctness of the application of the LIFO principle by the Industrial Court. The LIFO (last in first out) or 'last come first go' principle requires the most junior employee to be retrenched before the more senior ones in the same category. The principle is intended to afford a healthy safeguard against discrimination of workmen in the matter of retrenchment (see Swadesamitran Ltd v. Their Workmen, 1960 (SC) 762). Explaining this principle, in Workmen of Sudder Workshop of Jorehaut Tea Co Ltd V. The Management of Jorehaut Tea Co Ltd AIR 1980 SC 1454, the Supreme Court said: "The rule is that the employer shall retrench the workman who came last, first, popularly known as ' last come first go'."

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In Dynacraft ‘s case [supra] decision makes clear that prima facie the LIFO rule applies, an employer should retrench the latest recruits first, “where other things are equal”.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: A lawful deviation requires objective justification. The Company argues it departed from LIFO for “performance, safety and disciplinary” reasons. Even if merit-based selection is permitted in principle (as Wong Zi Chuang V. AirAsia X [2025] 2 MELR 43 held, provided it is done bona fide and not arbitrarily), those reasons must be substantiated.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
The core “reasons” offered by the Company for retrenching the Claimant were:
(a) a purportedly “high rate” of medical leaves (MCs), and (b) certain Safety Hazard Occurrence Reports (CO3, CO4, CO5) involving the Claimant. We find none of this constitutes proven misconduct.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: “High rate of MCs”: The only evidence was a terse remark in Company records listing the Claimant for retrenchment due to “high rate of MCs.” However, no medical certificate logs or statistics were produced. No witness (for example the pilot’s direct supervisor or the leave approver) was called to explain what “high” meant. It was not shown how many sick days he took, whether it exceeded his contract’s entitlement of 18 days/year, or whether any gap in performance resulted. The Claimant denied any unusual absence record. On this point, the burden lay on the Company. Its failure to supply the records or call relevant personnel is telling: under the Evidence Act, failure to produce a document in its control may justify an adverse inference. We accept the Claimant’s submission that if this mattered the Company “could produce the Claimant’s MC records” but did not. Thus, “high MCs” remains an unsubstantiated allegation and cannot justify preferring other pilots over him.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Safety Reports (CO3–CO5): These documents were also tendered by the Company as evidence against the Claimant, but they tell a different story. CO3 and CO4 were reports filed by the Claimant himself on 21 Feb 2019, complaining of last-minute roster changes (multiple trips to difficult Bandung Airport and too many night flights).

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Company’s management responded by investigating and recommending corrective measures (adjusting crew rotations), even praising the Claimant’s concern as beneficial to safety. Far from showing wrongdoing, the reports show a conscientious pilot raising safety issues. CO5 was a complaint by another about the Claimant allegedly refusing night stops (due to his wife’s pregnancy); this too was closed without investigation (marked “No” under investigation).

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The short of it is that none of CO-3–CO-5 constitutes any proven infraction. The Company sought to “denigrate” the Claimant with them, but the documents themselves undermine that effort. In sum, nothing in the evidence shows the Claimant had disciplinary or performance deficiencies; on the contrary, he had a clean record (no warnings, no hearings ever).

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Importantly, even if such issues had existed, case law forbids using prior discipline to mask a sham retrenchment. The Court of Appeal in Ng Chang Seng V. Technip Geoproduction (M) Sdn Bhd & Anor [2021]1MLJ, 447, [2021]1MLRA 261 held that “a Company may not use disciplinary issues as justification for retrenchment”. In that case, the employee had been terminated ostensibly for poor performance, but in reality, because he complained to a subordinate.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Court found the retrenchment “colourable and for a collateral purpose”. Similarly, the Company’s own admission, through its witness, is that it “departed from LIFO” and treated the Claimant differently on the basis of unidentified “disciplinary matters”. The Claimant’s submissions (which we accept) demonstrate that these matters were at best trivial or mischaracterised.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: As the Claimant notes, penalising a loyal employee twice for the same old incident for example, citing case Wong Zi Chuang V. Air Asia Berhad [2025] 2 MELR 143 is arbitrary. Another recent Industrial Court award similarly criticized use of past disciplinary records to effect retrenchment as not bona fide.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Given all this, we conclude the Company has failed to justify any departure from LIFO. Without doubt the Claimant was more senior than all those placed in the retained list (twelve (12) years in the industry, seven (7) years and six (6) months with Malindo, and originally among the first batch of pilots). He had a clean service history and never faced any performance review issues. The admitted selection criteria (“performance and safety issues”) were not substantiated. On these facts, the Company has not shown the Claimant’s post was truly redundant in any legitimate sense.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Having chosen to retrench the Claimant, the Company bore the onus of proof that its stated reasons were genuine. Moreover, by common practice, the Company should have produced documentary justification for its choices. The evidence here suffers from notable gaps:

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The evidence at trial was given only by one Company witness (the present Head of HR, Mr. Visvaratnam) and the finance head. Neither the HR General Manager (Mr. Muzaffar, who was involved in planning retrenchments) although this Honourable Court already gave the instruction to the Company’s Counsel to file the Witness Statements of Mr. Muzaffar and the other witness but the Counsel did not file the Witness Statement nor anyone from flight operations testified, even though counsel conceded they “would be the best” to explain the criteria.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: As the authorities point out, the very person who decides on dismissals should testify. In CJ Polymers Sdn Bhd V. Sim Chin Hu & Ors & Other Appeals [2025] 5 MLRA 473 (CA), the Court stressed that failing to call the dismissing authority warrants an adverse inference. By analogy, we find it significant that the people “behind the scenes” were not examined.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Company did not tender its internal lists or minutes. It did not show the approved roster of the 25 retained captains with seniority rankings. Nor did it exhibit any written records of the “performance” comparisons (apart from the vague Exhibit COB-2(1) as tendered at the Court and mentioned in submissions.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant pointed out that had such documents existed, MC logs, VSS/LTU application records, selection matrices, they were in the Company’s custody and should have been produced. Their absence leads this Court to invoke Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act: we can presume they would have been unfavourable to the Company.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Weighing all evidence and gaps, the Company has not discharged its burden that the retrenchment was bona fide. The witness testimony was uncorroborated and self-serving, and many material issues were left unexplained.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: On the balance of probabilities, the Claimant’s termination was not for a valid redundancy with just cause. In circumstances of a generalized downturn, the Company was entitled to retrench, but it must do so fairly. Here, it failed to follow the usual seniority rule and gave no credible reason for treating the Claimant as surplus.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The only “reasons” offered was, high MCs and safety reports, do not withstand scrutiny and viewed objectively, appear perpetual.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant’s long service, clean record and refusal to waive pay cuts all point to mala fides in selecting him over more junior colleagues. Accordingly, the dismissal was made without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This conclusion is compelled by Ng Chang Seng V. Technip Geoproduction (M) Sdn Bhd & Anor [2021] 1MLJ477; [2021] 1MLRA 261 and related authorities, which condemn retrenchments that are in truth punitive exercises in disguise.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Honourable Court give the order that therefore award relief under Section 20 IRA. Reinstatement is impracticable after many years’ separation (and indeed the Claimant did not seek reinstatement). The appropriate remedy is compensation and back wages. In addition, the Claimant is entitled to the salary arrears owed for the eight months pre-termination during which he remained on the payroll.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Court finds the Company has failed to discharge its onus of proof that the Claimant’s dismissal was with just cause or excuse under Section 20(1) Industrial Relation Act 1967 [ACT 177].

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The plea of closure is unconvincing in light of continued operations, dividends paid, and survival of business infrastructure post-termination date.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: There was non-compliance with the Code of Conduct on consultation, retrenchment alternatives, LIFO principle and objective selection.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The lack of consultation itself constitutes a fundamental breach of natural justice and the duty of industrial fair dealing, as reinforced by authorities.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: No evidence was provided concerning the Claimant’s performance, conduct, or any reason unrelated to alleged redundancy.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant, with seven (7) years and (seven) 7 months of service, was denied his basic industrial rights at the point of becoming most vulnerable. For the reasons stated above, it is evident that the Claimant’s termination on the grounds of redundancy was not conducted in good faith. The Company has failed to adhere to the principles of fairness, including the burden of proof, application of LIFO, exploration of alternatives, and transparency in its decision-making process.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The dismissal of the Claimant, by the Company, MALINDO SDN BHD on is declared without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Pursuant to section 30(5) of the IRA1967 and after having considered the totality of the evidence adduced, this Court is of the view that the Company had failed to establish on the balance of probabilities that the dismissal of the Claimant from his employment with the company was with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Court having ruled that the Claimant was dismissed without just cause or excuse, will now consider the appropriate remedy for the Claimant.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Based on the Court’s assessment of the industrial climate between the parties, it is certainly not conducive to reinstate the Claimant as the relationship between the Company and the Claimant has been badly strained. In the circumstances, it is inappropriate to order for reinstatement. Instead, the Claimant will be awarded with an appropriate remedy accordingly.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In respect of the quantum the Court is mindful of the view taken by Tun Salleh Abas FJ in the case of Hotel Jaya Puri Bhd. V. National Company of Hotel, Bar & Restaurant Workers & Anor [1990] 1 MLJ 109: “.. if there is a legal basis for paying the compensation, the amount of course is very much a matter of the discretion which the Industrial Court is fully empowered under s.30 of the IRA 1967 to fix.”

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Back wages are calculated based on the Claimant’s last drawn salary but limited to 24 months. From the back wages, the court is required to make a deduction for any contributory conduct; post dismissal earnings and delay in the hearing of the case but such a deduction need not involve a mathematical calculation.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Court is bound by the principle laid down in the case of Dr. James Alfred (SABAH) V. Koperasi Serbaguna Sanya Bhd (SABAH) & Anor [2001] 3 CLJ 541. His Lordship Justice Tan Sri Steve Shim CJ (Sabah & Sarawak) in delivering the judgement of the Federal Court held that: ‘’In our view, it is in line with equity and good conscience that the Industrial Court, in assessing quantum of back wages, should take into account the fact, if established by evidence or admitted, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. Failure to do so constitutes a jurisdictional error of law. Certiorari will therefore lie to rectify it. Of course, taking into account such employment after dismissal does not necessarily mean that the Industrial Court has to conduct a mathematical exercise in deduction. What is important is that the Industrial Court, in the exercise of its discretion in assessing the quantum of back wages, should take into account all relevant matters including the fact, where it exists, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. This discretion is in the nature of a decision-making process.’’

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
This Court have carefully examined the facts and evidence in this case and of the view that there was no contributory factor on the part of the Claimant. Hence, under this item, there is no deduction shall be made to this contributory factor.
DELAY

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: From an examination of the notes of proceedings, this Court is satisfied that the Claimant did not occasion any delay in connection with the hearing of this Director General of Industrial Relation of Malaysia reference. Hence, there is no deduction under this head.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: At the time of dismissal, the Claimant last drawn basic salary was RM 20,000.00. On the facts of this case, there is evidence of post-dismissal income after the Claimant was dismissed by the Company. Hence, there shall be deduction under this item. The Claimant has served the Company for seven (7) years and seven (7) months, which was from 01.04.2013 until 01.11.2020.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
After having considered the evidence adduced before this Court as well as the submission by both parties, the remedies are as follows:
(i) Back wages for twenty-four (24) months based on the Claimant’s last drawn salary: RM20, 000.00 X 24 months = RM 480,000.00
Less 5% (Post Dismissal of = RM 24,000.00 the Claimant)
Total = RM 456,000.00
Add (ii) Compensation in lieu of reinstatement, based on the formula of one month’s salary for every completed year of service. The Claimant has completed seven (7) full years of service calculated from until the date of employment, which was on 01.04.2013 until the date of dismissal on 01.11.2020.
RM 20,000.00 X 7 months = RM 140,000.00
Total = RM 596,000.00

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The monetary award in a total sum of RM 596,000.00 less statutory deductions, if any, shall be paid by the Company to the Claimant via his Counsel Messrs. Thevan Maniam within 30 days of the award with interest of 8% per annum to be calculated from 30 days of the award until full and final settlement.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Court verily believe that this Award is just and appropriate in the light of the particular facts of the present case and guided by the principles of equity, good conscience and substantial merits of this case without regard to technicalities and legal forms.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: THE APPLICABLE LAW, BURDEN AND STANDARD OF PROOF
content: The role of the Industrial Court was lucidly explained by His Lordship Raja Azlan Shah CJ (Malaya) (as His Royal Highness then was) in Goon Kwee Phoy v. J & P Coats (M) Bhd [1981] 1 LNS 30; [1981] 1 MLJ 129 (Federal Court) as follows: “Where representations are made and are referred to the Industrial Court for enquiry, it is the duty of the Court to determine whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse. If the employer chooses to give a reason or excuse for the action taken by him, the duty of the Industrial Court will be to enquire whether that reason or excuse has or has not been made out. If it finds as a fact that it has not been proven, then the inevitable conclusion must be that the termination or dismissal was without just cause or excuse. The proper enquiry of the Court is the reason advanced by the employer, and that Court or the High Court cannot go into another reason not relied on by the employer, or find one for him".

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: THE APPLICABLE LAW, BURDEN AND STANDARD OF PROOF
content: The burden of proving that the employee is guilty of the allegation of misconduct or negligence as the case may be and establishing the reasons for dismissal rests squarely upon the employer. This was aptly stated by the Learned Industrial Court Chairman in Stamford Executive Centre v. Puan Dharsini Ganesan [1986] 1 ILR 101 as follows: “16. It may further be emphasised here that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer. He must prove the workman guilty, and it is not the workman who must prove himself not guilty. This is so basic a principle of industrial jurisprudence that no employer is expected to come to this Court in ignorance of it.”

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The standard of proof applicable to dismissal cases is the civil standard of proof on a balance of probabilities as decided by the Court of Appeal in Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara v. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor. [2002] 3 CLJ 314 as follows: “Thus, we can see that the preponderant view is that the Industrial Court, when hearing a claim of unjust dismissal, even where the ground is one of dishonest act, including “theft”, is not required to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the employee has “committed the offence”, as in a criminal prosecution… In our view the passage quoted from Administrative Law by H. W. R. Wade & C.F. Forsyth offers the clearest statement on the standard of proof required, that is the civil standard based on balance of probabilities, which is flexible, so that the degree of probability required is proportionate to the nature and gravity of the issue.”

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: Hence, the onus is on the Company to prove that it had dismissed the Claimant with just cause and excuse on the basis of the Claimant's poor performance whilst in employment with the Company. It ought to be made out that the Claimant's poor performance relates to the deficiencies in his work or standard of work, and involves inefficiency, incompetence or plain inaptitude.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: "Inefficiency”, “incompetency”, or “incapability" means the workman is found to be incapable of performing the work which he was employed to do, or incapable of performing the basic work functions as required by the employer. Poor performance may possibly bring about another aspect of ground for dismissal. Although not misconduct per se, it had been held that poor performance is an acceptable basis for an employer to dismiss an employee with just cause and excuse. In this regard, it was held in Khor Eng Khye V. Guiness Anchor Marketing Sdn Bhd [2006] 2 LNS 178442 (supra) that: “Although the Industrial Court has held that poor performance is not misconduct per se, it is trite law that poor performance affords an acceptable basis for an employer to establish that the dismissal is with just cause or excuse under section 20 of Industrial Relations Act 1967. The reason for this is that inefficiency or in competence resulting in failure to perform the duties of the service destroys the whole reality of the contract from the point of view of the employer. The vast majority of the employees make their employers the judges of their competence. Hence, so long as the employer acts bona fide ie if he is genuinely discontented with an employee, he is quite entitled to dismiss the employee. (see Samsudin Amin v. Austral Enterprises Bhd Award 47 of 1974).”

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: This court is well minded of the principle that the Company need not prove that the Claimant was in fact incapable or incompetent but is sufficient enough if the Company honestly believes on reasonable grounds that the Claimant is incapable or incompetent. This was held by the Industrial Court in the case of Choong Poh Ling v CIMB Aviva Assurance Berhad [2016] 2 LNS 1032 quoting Lord Denning MR in the case of Alidair LTD v Taylor [1978] LCR 445 which was cited in Saw David Thien v BASF (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd [2020] 2 LNS 07174 (David Thien (supra) and Khor Eng (supra), respectively, as follows: “whenever a man is dismissed for incapacity or incompetence it is sufficient that the employer honestly believes on reasonable grounds that the man is incapable or incompetent. It is not necessary for the employer to prove that he is in fact incapable or incompetent.”

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: Reasonable grounds can be surmised from the following extract from lan Smith and Aaron Baker, Smith and Woods Employment Law, 10th edn (2010, Oxford University Press), p 461 referred to in the case of Azman Zanoo v Firefly Sdn. Bhd. (Award No. 956 of 2015), which sums up the position in this regard: "...The question for the tribunal is whether the employer has satisfied them that he genuinely believed on reasonable grounds that the employee was incapable. The requirement of reasonable grounds means that the employer should make a proper and full investigation into the facts of the case and give careful consideration to the decision to dismiss; amongst other things, this consideration may include as a factor whether the employee was given proper training for the job, adequate supervision, and where appropriate proper support from the employer. Also, it is well established that this area is amenable to the application of a warning procedure, although the emphasis may be different from that in misconduct cases, for here the constructive side of a warning may be more important, not only pointing out the employer's ground of complaint, but also instructing the employee how to improve and giving her reasonable time in which to do so. Of course, warnings are not essential in every case, and may perhaps be irrelevant where it is clear that the employee is completely incapable of improvement or where she already clearly knows what is expected of her. That apart, however, the importance of a fair procedure in this area should not be understated, and the lack of it [particularly if it leads to inadequate investigation by the employer] may make the dismissal of an incompetent employee unfair...".

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
The test to be applied in assessing if the Company has dismissed the Claimant with just cause and excuse on the basis that the Claimant was a poor performer is succinctly laid out in the case of Ireka Construction Berhad v Chantiravathan all Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 1146 (Ireka (supra) which held as follows:
“The only issue for this Court to determine now is whether the Company, on a balance of probabilities has established the poor performance of the Claimant. As far as unsatisfactory performance is concerned the Industrial Court has laid down that in order to justify the dismissal of the Claimant on this ground, the Company has to establish: i) that the Claimant was warned about his poor performance; ii) that the Claimant was accorded sufficient opportunity to improve; and iii) that notwithstanding the above, the Claimant failed to sufficiently improve his performance. In the case of Rooftech Sdn. Bhd. v. Holiday Inn, Penang, Award No. 166/86, the Court stated: “Inefficiency which discloses a course of negative conduct, no doubt is a sufficient ground for termination but there must necessarily be sufficient proof that a procedure has been followed. Ordinarily there must be sufficient written communications to the Claimant in order to establish inefficiency or poor performance before the Company can rely on it to justify dismissal. The Company has failed to do so.”
