case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: Nevertheless it must also be reminded that targets set for the employee who is performing poorly cannot be unrealistic or grossly harsh and must be in line with documentary proof [See Cisco (M) Sdn Bhd v Raja Mohan PV Nathan [2003] 3 ILR 40 (supra)], affirmed by the High Court and Court of Appeal.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: Bearing in mind the principles laid down in the above authorities, in particular the 3 tests enunciated in Ireka Construction Berhad v Chantiravathan a/l Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 1146 (supra), this court however is of the considered views that in order to arrive at an equitable and conscienable decision as required of by Section 30(5) of the Act, the fundamental issues to be determined by this Court in this case are as follows: i. whether the company had successfully proved the Claimant's poor performance; ii. whether the Company had oppressed and victimised the Claimant; iii. whether the PIP was designed to fail the Claimant. EVALUATION OF EVIDENCE AND FINDINGS CHARGES AGAINST THE CLAIMANT 1st CHARGE Habitual Not Being Punctual In Submitting Report As Per Instructed

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The first charge against the Claimant was in respect of submitting the 2 reports namely: (a) Drawings of the 26 tools; and (b) Molding jig #37082 for part number 446135 buy off report.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: Failure to complete the Drawings of 26 tools In his evidence, the Claimant explained as follows: (a) That the number of drawings that he need to draw was 130 drawings. (b) He needed to refer to the old drawings and re-draw the drawings into the Auto-Cad System. He had completed the drawings in the Auto-Cad system. (c) He was unable print the drawings for approval by the Head of Department as he was ordered to stop printing and not to touch his computer when he wanted to print the drawings.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: On the issue of nozzle, the Claimant explained as follows: a. Based on the previous method, the nozzle was drawn separately. b. When he had completed drawing the tools, he was then informed by Mr. Hoa that his drawings were incomplete as some of the drawings where the tools have nozzle but the nozzle was not drawn. c. He started to redo the drawings and had drawn the nozzle.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
On the allegation that the Claimant was unable to complete the drawings within time stipulated, the Claimant had explained that whilst working on the drawings, he also had to attend to his current work and due to the workload, he was not able to complete the drawings within time. The claimant went on to submit that based on the evidence presented before the Court, he had commenced drawing the 26 tools as ordered by his superior and has completed the drawings in the Auto Cad System.
Moulding Jig #87082 for Part No. 446135 Buy Off Report

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: With regard to the issue of buy off report, the buy off report was submitted by the Claimant on the 25.5.2022 (page 3 of COB3). The Claimant in his evidence explained that the reason for delay was because the supplier from Hong Kong took time in sending the molding jig which resulted in the delay in preparing the buy off report. The Claimant had explained that the jig was only received from the Hong Kong Supplier on the 20.5.2025. Upon receiving the molding jig from the supplier, the jig needs to be run first then the molding report could be prepared. The Claimant in his evidence had denied Mr. Hoa Kim Huat’s contention that the molding jig buy off report could be done within one day. It was further explained that the 4 rounds of extensions as alleged by the Company in respect to the delay in submitting the buy off report was not due to the Claimant but due to external factors i.e. as stated above, the delay from receiving the molding jig from the supplier.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Issue of Report submitted using the recycled paper
content:
Another issue in respect of the Buy Off report was the issue of using recycled paper which was forbidden by the IATF Requirements. The evidence before the Court disclosed that upon being notified by Mr. Hoa that the Claimant had inadvertently print the report using recycled paper, the Claimant had then reprinted and resubmit the report to Mr. Hoa. Mr. Hoa (COW2) in his evidence confirmed that the mistake of using the recycled paper had been rectified by the Claimant.
2ND. CHARGE Wilful Disobedience To Any Lawful And Order Of The Superior

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Issue of Report submitted using the recycled paper
content: The second charge against the Claimant was that the Claimant had wilfully disobeyed the lawful and reasonable order of his superior in the following instances: a. No improvement on commitments in PIP in spite of many extensions given by the Head of Department and the Operation Director; and b. No initiative or commitment to learn Meco Plating Line as agreed in PIP Item 5.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Whether the Claimant has improved on Commitment in Performance Improvement Plan (PIP)
content: The Claimant in his evidence stated that: a. He had submitted daily reports on the PIP to show the progress b. There is improvement in the items committed in the PIP.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Whether the Claimant has improved on Commitment in Performance Improvement Plan (PIP)
content: The Claimant's evidence was supported by COW1 (TAY LEE FONG) when she agreed that the Claimant had made improvement although the improvement was not enough. During the Domestic Inquiry, the Claimant had given his explanation as per pages 230 — 275 of the COB1. His explanation on the issue of improvement on commitment in PIP among others are: a. Claimant denied the allegation of wilful disobedient as he followed all instructions from his Superior b. At page 265 of the CLB1 — Claimant had explained that he had made improvement on the commitment in PIP. He had submitted daily reports to show the progress of work.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Whether the Claimant has improved on Commitment in Performance Improvement Plan (PIP)
content: Documents at pages 54 — 178 of the COB1 i.e. the emails from the Claimant to his Superior, Mr, Hoa Kim Huat - clearly support the Claimant’s explanation that he had made improvement on the task assigned to him and on the commitment in the PIP.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Whether the Claimant has improved on Commitment in Performance Improvement Plan (PIP)
content: This is supported by COW1 (TAY LEE FONG) in her evidence during cross examination which confirmed that the Claimant had made improvement. As such, this court found that the impugned allegation that the Claimant had made no improvement on the commitment in the PIP is unfounded, unsubstantiated and not supported by evidence. It is also unsupported in evidence that the Claimant had wilfully disobeyed to follow lawful and reasonable orders of his superior.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The Claimant had been charged for wilful disobedience when he failed to show initiative or commitment to learn Meco Plating Line as stated in Item 5 of the PIP. This allegation was challenged by the Claimant; in that in his evidence he explained that: a. The process of learning of Meco Plating Line was in progress. b. All In along he was assigned to and used to Mitomo Plating Line. c. In 2020, the Claimant was instructed by his Superior Mr. Hoa Kim Huat to learn Meco Plating Line. d. He had no experience in operating the Meco Plating Line. He had been Plating Line. e. He had been learning on his own on the operation of the Meco Plating Line. f. The Company had not provided official training for him to learn Meco Plating Line. g. The Claimant had informed Mr. Hoa Kim Huat that the learning of Meco Plating Line was in progress. h. The Claimant had taken initiative to learn Meco Plating Line.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: COW2 (Hoa Kim Huat) in his evidence has confirmed that the Claimant had informed him that the Claimant had taken initiative to learn Meco Plating Line and that the learning was in progress. COW2 (Hoa Kim Huat) also confirmed in his evidence that the Claimant did not refuse to learn Meco Plating Line when the Claimant was instructed to learn Meco Plating Line.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The evidence before the Court disclosed: a. That the Claimant had taken the initiative to learn Meco Plating Line; b. That the learning of Meco Plating Line was in progress. That the Claimant had taken time to learn the Meco Plating Line due to the fact that he was inexperienced in operating Meco Plating Line and the fact that the Company did not provide official training for him. c. That the Claimant did not disobey his superior’s order in learning the Meco Plating Line.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: In the above evidence, this court found that the Company’s allegation that the Claimant had wilfully disobeyed the legal and reasonable order of his superior is an exaggeration. This court further found that the allegation that the Claimant did not take any initiative or commitment to learn Meco Plating Line is not well supported.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Whether Misconduct by The Claimant Proven
content: It has not been proved by the company to this court’s satisfaction that the Claimant’s dismissal was with just cause or excuse. There was no convincing evidence tendered by the Company to prove the charges of misconduct against the Claimant. In Ahmad Fadzrul Misrah v Brahim’s Sats Food Services Sdn Bhd [2024] ILRU 1708, the Court held that: “Burden Of Proof [20] Whenever a Company has caused the dismissal of the workman, it is then incumbent on part of the Company to discharge the burden of proof that the dismissal was with just cause or excuse. This Court will now refer to the case of Ireka Construction Berhad v. Chantiravathan a/l Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 11 in which case it was stated that: "It is a basic principle of industrial jurisprudence that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer to prove that he has just cause and excuse for taking the decision to impose the disciplinary measure of dismissal upon the employee. The just cause must be, either a misconduct, negligence or poor performance based on the facts of the case.”

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The Claimant submits that the Domestic Inquiry conducted by the Company was flawed and that the findings of the Domestic Inquiry were erroneous based on the following grounds: a. The issues deliberated during the domestic inquiry were not part of the Show Cause Notice dated 10.6.2022; The b. The findings of the Inquiry Panel were made based on the fact that Claimant had accepted the contents of the allegation in the Warning Letters dated 24.12.2021 and 19.5.2021; by virtue of signing the Acceptance of the said letters. c. No evidence of wilful disobedience or insubordination and non- performance of duty was tendered by the Company during the Domestic Inquiry. Matters not part of the Show Cause Notice dated 10.6.2022

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: This can be seen at page 224 of the COB1 where the Prosecuting Officer (COW1) had referred to incidents that occurred on the 12.04.2021 and 14.12.2021 as stated as follows: (PO handed over the invitation print out for Action Plan Report 2nd. Review) Prior to the 12 April 2022 Action Plan and 2nd. Warning Letter dated 19 May 2022, the accused was issued Action Plan dated 19 May 2021. Due to 60% work force restriction during the pandemic last year, review was not able to be followed through and this actually indirectly given the Accused more time to focus in his area for improvement. When the government lifted the 60% work force restriction in September 2021, Mr Hoa continue to monitor the progress of the Accused. However, the Accused still unable to show significant improvement and counselling sessions conducted with Warning Letter was issued on 24.12.2021 for the same misconduct; habitual non- performance of duty.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: COW1 in her evidence also confirmed that the matters stated at page 224 of the COB1 were not part of the Show Cause Notice dated 10.06.2022. During the hearing before this court, the Company had also made reference to the issue of the Claimant’s failure to revert on the Temporary Document Change Notice (TDCN) and it took him numerous reminders to give his response on the TDCN issue.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: However, it is pertinent to note that the issue pertaining to the failure to response to the TDCN issue was not part of the Show Cause Notice and as such irrelevant to the charge. COW2 in his evidence confirmed that the issue pertaining to TDCN was not part of the Show Cause Letter and the Domestic Inquiry. In this respect, this court follows Aziz Yaakob v. Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd [2005] 3 ILR 502 wherein the Industrial Court held that the matters and/or issues which are not part of the charge should not be considered by the Court.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Whether there is Evidence of Wilful Disobedience or Insubordination
content: In the instant case; the Claimant’s employment with the Company was terminated due to non-performance of duty and disobedience [please refer to the Decision of the Panel of Inquiry at page 278 of the COB1]

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Whether there is Evidence of Wilful Disobedience or Insubordination
content: On issue of disobedience; COW1 in her evidence during the Cross Examination had confirmed as follows: a. That the Claimant had given his explanation on each and every charge made against him; b. That the Claimant’s explanation can be seen in his evidence during Domestic Inquiry at pages 230 — 275 of the COB1. c. The Claimant did not on purpose refuse to carry out the orders of Superiors.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Whether there is Evidence of Wilful Disobedience or Insubordination
content: On the issue of non-performance of duty; the evidence before the court are as follows: a. The Claimant had drawn the tools in the Autocad; however he was not able to print the drawings. b. Some of the tools had no nozzle and some had nozzles. Initially the nozzles were drawn separately from the tools. Therefore, initially he did not draw the nozzles. However upon being informed that he needed to draw as per the physical tools, he had redone the drawings and drawn the nozzles as well. c. He had submitted daily reports to his Superior Mr. Hoa Kim Huat. However there were delays in submitting the daily reports. This was confirmed by COW2 in his evidence during Cross Examination. d. On the issue that the Claimant printed a report on the recycled paper; the issue had been rectified immediately by the Claimant upon being informed by his Superior.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Whether there is Evidence of Wilful Disobedience or Insubordination
content:
Hence, this court is of the opinion that the findings of the Inquiry Panel that the Claimant was guilty of non-performance of duty and disobedience was unfounded and unjustified.
Whether the basis of the Panel’s Findings was tainted with irrelevant factor

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Whether there is Evidence of Wilful Disobedience or Insubordination
content: At page 278 of the COB1; the Panel findings are as follow: "Based on 1st. Warning Letter dated 24.12.2021 and the 2nd. Warning Letter dated 19.5.2022, it stated clearly of “Habitual — Non-performance of duty” which the accused fully understood and accepted the content of allegation with his signature”

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Whether there is Evidence of Wilful Disobedience or Insubordination
content: The claimant submitted that the Inquiry Panel’s findings of guilt was made based on that since the Claimant had merely signed the 1st. Warning Letter and the 2nd. Warning Letter, the claimant was taken to having admitted to the charges. Without further elaboration on how the finding was arriving at, this finding does not hold water, clearly without merit and contrary to the principle of natural justice.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: PRESSURE FROM THE SUPERIOR TO RESIGN
content: It is the claimant’s pleading in his Statement of Case and evidence was adduced to support his assertion that he was pressured by his Superior Mr. Hoa Kim Huat to resign from the Company. At page 201 of the COB1; the Company had vide letter dated 06.07.2022 admitted that Mr. Hoa Kim Huat had discussed with the Claimant and requested the Claimant to resign from the Company. The letter stated inter - alia as follow: “Further, seeing that you have committed major misconduct and in order to avoid disciplinary action being taken against you, he had discussed with you, on a friendly basis, other ways to resolve the matter including the possibility of you resigning from the company. However, as you are not agreeable, he left the matter as it is.”

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: PRESSURE FROM THE SUPERIOR TO RESIGN
content:
COW1 when asked about the issue of pressuring the Claimant’s to resign stated as follow: Q: Tab J CLB1. This is the 2nd. explanation letter dated 16.6.2024. At paragraph 4 of the letter the Claimant stated that "Mr. Hoa recently pressuring me to resign. This is what he said. A: Yes Q: The Company actually admitted that Mr. Hoa did ask him to resign. Agree? A: No.
Q: Look at COB1 page 210. This is a letter from your Company dated 6.7.2022 at paragraph 3. Your Company agrees that Mr. Hoa had requested him to resign. A: From here I understand that he discussed with him to resign. But I don’t know if he pressured him.
Q: Do you agree that before the Notice to Show Cause was issued, Mr. Hoa had discussed with the Claimant on resigning? A: Yes.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: PRESSURE FROM THE SUPERIOR TO RESIGN
content: When COW2 was asked during cross-examination about the issue of him pressuring the Claimant to resign, COW2 conceded as follows: Q: You discussed with him and you told him to resign. A: What this mean is if he resigned the problem is solved ...

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: PRESSURE FROM THE SUPERIOR TO RESIGN
content:
Clearly, there was no denial by COW2 in his evidence that he had told the claimant to resign, and this may reasonably be understood as a subordinate being pressured by his superior to resign. As such, there is reason to believe that the Company had already decided to terminate the Claimant’s employment prior to the Domestic Inquiry being conducted.
SUMMARY AND CONCLUSION Whether Drawings of Mitomo Plating Tools not completed

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: PRESSURE FROM THE SUPERIOR TO RESIGN
content: In conclusion, this court emphasized that on the impugned issues of the Claimant has failed to complete the drawings of Mitomo Plating tools within the timeframe; it was never satisfactorily challenged that the delay was due to that whilst working on the drawings, the claimant also had to attend to his current work and due to the workload, he was not able to complete the drawings within time. It was also unrefuted that the claimant had commenced drawing the 26 tools as ordered by his superior and had eventually completed the drawings in the Auto Cad System.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: PRESSURE FROM THE SUPERIOR TO RESIGN
content: With regards to the issue of the nozzle drawings, the Claimant’s evidence must not be entirely dismissed; that it was an issue of misunderstanding of the instruction given to him. The miscommunication and Claimant in his evidence had explained that all along; it was the practice that the nozzle was drawn in a separate drawing as the nozzle was made separately and the nozzle will be assembled together with the tools upon fabrication. As such, this court agrees that the claimant has sufficiently explained the reason why he did not draw the nozzle in the first draft.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: PRESSURE FROM THE SUPERIOR TO RESIGN
content: Upon being highlighted on the issue of nozzle drawings by COW2; the claimant had made the necessary amendments to the drawings and had incorporated the nozzle drawings. This court agrees that such errors should not warrant any dismissal. The dismissal of the Claimant’s employment merely on the issue of incomplete drawings was disproportionate to the “alleged misconduct” and it reflects the Company’s bad faith conduct in terminating the Claimant.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: PRESSURE FROM THE SUPERIOR TO RESIGN
content: In the considered views of this court, the company disproportionately equates poor performance - the issue of incomplete drawings with misconduct that are distinctively dissimilar. Such equation is unwarranted and unbecoming to occur on a senior employee; and prejudicial against the claimant. Issue of 2nd. Misconduct: Buy Off Report using Recycled Paper

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: PRESSURE FROM THE SUPERIOR TO RESIGN
content: The Company has relied on a hypothetical situation that if the mistake was not detected and was found during audit; it would lead to serious repercussion to the Company and that the Company could have suffered financial loss. However, such a hypothetical situation did not occur and hence financial loss was never proven. No explanation was given by any of the company’s witnesses as to how financial losses would have been suffered if the mistake was only detected.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: PRESSURE FROM THE SUPERIOR TO RESIGN
content: What transpired was that the mistake was brought to the Claimant’s attention by COW2 and the mistake was corrected immediately by the Claimant. To dismiss the Claimant’s employment based on a hypothetical situation is clearly unjustified and plainly wrong.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: Improvement on commitment in the PIP
content: The issues raised in the PIP and the Counselling were that the Claimant had made no improvement on commitment in the PIP despite numerous Counselling conducted. The following issues were raised: a. Drawings of the Mitomo plating tools; b. Punctuality in the daily report; c. Completion of tasks within the given timeline;

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: d. Email to external parties must be reviewed; and e. Learning MITOMO and MECO
content: For the above incompetency, the charge levelled against the Claimant in this respect was that the Claimant had wilfully disobeyed the lawful and reasonable order of his superior. The company concluded that the claimant has wilfully disobeyed the lawful and reasonable order of his superior.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: d. Email to external parties must be reviewed; and e. Learning MITOMO and MECO
content: However, this court is not satisfied that ample evidence has been tendered by the company in support of its contention that the claimant had wilfully disobeyed his superior and committed insubordination. The mere fact that the Claimant had signed the comment made by his superior COW2 during the counselling and/or review only meant that the Claimant had acknowledged that there was room for improvement on the matters enumerated in the PIP.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: d. Email to external parties must be reviewed; and e. Learning MITOMO and MECO
content:
It is clear to this court that the PIP process initiated by the company supposedly in order for the claimant to improve, had merely served as an instrument to drive the claimant out of the company, reflective of mala fide, oppression and ulterior motive. This court relies on the case of Azman Zanoo V_Firefly Sdn Bhd [2015] ILRU 0956 where Smith and Woods Employment Law 10th. Edition was referred and adopted inter alia as follows: "The question for the tribunal is whether the employer has satisfied them that she genuinely believed on reasonable grounds that the employee was incapable. The requirement of reasonable grounds means that investigation the into employer should make a proper and full the facts of the case, and give careful consideration to the decision to dismiss; (See Cook v. Thomas Linnell & Sons Ltd. [1977] ICR 770, [1977] IRLR 132) amongst other things, this consideration may include as a factor whether the employee was given proper training for the job, adequate supervision and, where appropriate, proper support from the employer. Also, it is well established that this area is amenable to the application of a warnings procedure, though the emphasis may be different from that in misconduct cases, for here the constructive side of a warning may be more important, not only pointing out instructing the employer's ground for complaint but also employee how to improve and giving her reasonable time in which to do so. Of course, warnings are not essential in every case, and may perhaps be irrelevant where it is clear that the employee is completely incapable of improvement or where she clearly knows what is expected of her. That apart, however, the importance of a fair procedure in this area should not be underestimated, and lack of it (particularly if it leads to inadequate investigation by the employer) may make dismissal of an incompetent employee unfair (though it may still be open to the employer to argue that there should be little or no compensation where there was wilful default on the part of the employee, such as failure or refusal to improve).”
[emphasis added]

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: d. Email to external parties must be reviewed; and e. Learning MITOMO and MECO
content: It is on evidence during cross-examination on 07.04.2025 of COW-2 when it was put to the witness that MECO was new to the claimant and despite that, no training was provided.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: d. Email to external parties must be reviewed; and e. Learning MITOMO and MECO
content: Moreover, it is much left to be seen why the claimant who was regarded as High Potential & Essential Employment for the year 2017/18 had been unable to sustain his good performance allegedly since 2020.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: d. Email to external parties must be reviewed; and e. Learning MITOMO and MECO
content: This court is also of the views that the claimant was denied of the opportunity to improve. This is evident when COW-2 confirmed during cross-examination that the performance review was conducted on the claimant on 09.06.2022 and on the next day itself i.e. 10.06.2022 the claimant was issued a Show Cause Letter.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
section_title: d. Email to external parties must be reviewed; and e. Learning MITOMO and MECO
content: There were unresolved issues in particular the claimant was pressured to resign and when he refused to do so, the PIP was set in by the company. These irregularities invariably point to the conclusion, that the dismissal was without just cause or excuse and inequitable that warrants intervention of this court.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: In the upshot, upon scrutinizing the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence adduced in its entirety and having considered the Written Submissions filed by both parties, it is this Court’s findings that the Company had failed to prove dismissal with just cause or excuse on the ground of poor performance, misconduct and insubordination on the balance of probabilities. In arriving at the above decision, the Court had taken into account the totality of evidence, bearing in mind Section 30(5) of the IRA 1967 by which virtue this Court shall act according to equity, good conscience and the substantial merit of the case without regard to technicalities and legal form.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: Having ruled against the Claimant’s dismissal the Court shall now consider whether the Claimant is entitled for a reinstatement to his former position without any loss of seniority, wages or benefits, from the date of dismissal to the date of reinstatement. This Court agrees that it would be inappropriate in the circumstances to order a reinstatement, given the Claimant’s position that he has been pressured by his superior to resign. In such a case, monetary compensation in lieu of reinstatement would be more appropriate.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: In Dr James Alfred (Sabah) v Koperasi Serbaguna Sanya Bhd (Sabah) & Anor [2001] 3 CLJ 541, the Federal Court held that: "In our view, it is in line with equity and good conscience that the Industrial Court, in assessing quantum of backwages, should take into account the fact, if established by evidence or admitted, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. Failure to do so constitutes a jurisdictional error of law. Certiorari will therefore lie to rectify it. Of course, taking into account of such employment after dismissal does not necessarily mean that the Industrial Court has to conduct a mathematical exercise in deduction. What is important is that the Industrial Court, in the exercise of its discretion in assessing the quantum of backwages, should take into account all relevant matters including the fact, where it exists, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. This discretion is in the nature of a decision- making process".

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
It must be emphasized that the quantum of Compensation to be awarded is one of discretionary as enunciated in Hotel Jayapuri Bhd V National Union of Hotel, Bar & Restaurant Workers & Anor [1979] 1 LNS 32. In assessing the amount to be awarded as compensation in lieu of reinstatement, the completed years of service shall be taken into consideration.
b) Backwages

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: In determining the quantum for backwages that is discretionary in nature, this Court may award not exceeding the maximum of 24 months last drawn salary; regards shall have to the provision of Clause 1 of the Second Schedule in [Factors For Consideration In Making An Award in Relation To A Reference Under Sub Section 20(3)] of Section 30(6A) of the IRA 1967 which provides: “1. In the event backwages are to be given, such backwages shall not exceed twentyfour months backwages from the date of dismissal based on the latest drawn salary of the person who has been dismissed without just cause or excuse”

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case, this Court awards backwages for fifteen (15) months to multiply with the Claimant’s last drawn salary of RM6,836.00 considering the length of service that the claimant had with the Company since 16.03.2010 until being terminated on 29.07.2022. As there was evidence of post dismissal earnings, it would be proper to deduct a percentage of the earnings against the awarded backwages pursuant to Clause 3 of the Second Schedule of Section 30(6A) of the Industrial Relation Act 1967.
DEDUCTIONS AGAINST BACKWAGES a.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The Claimant in his evidence stated that he managed to secure new employment in Singapore in May 2024 with salary of SD2230. Prior to May 2024; he made his earning by working part time by drawing the tool parts on a commission basis. Claimant in his evidence stated that the commission he received doing part times are not fixed, around RM70.00 to RM80.00 per job.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: On average; the claimant earned around RM2,000.00 per month; which means that he would have earned at least RM30,000.00 for a period of 15 months post dismissal. This court is of the views that a deduction of 10% equivalent to RM3,000.00 would be just and proper in the circumstances. This court makes no deduction for the claimant’s earnings that he earns in Singapore.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: In addition, this court is of the considered views that it is equitable to order a deduction for contributory misconduct pursuant to clause 5 of the Second Schedule of section 30 (6A) of the Industrial Relations Act 1957; and for the purpose of which, a deduction of 30% from the awarded backwages would be just and proper in the circumstances.

case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
The role of the Industrial Court was lucidly explained by His Lordship Raja Azlan Shah CJ (Malaya) (as His Royal Highness then was) in Goon Kwee Phoy v. J & P Coats (M) Bhd. [1981] 1 LNS 30; [1981] 1 MLJ 129 (Federal Court) at page 136 as follows:
“Where representations are made and are referred to the Industrial Court for enquiry, it is the duty of the Court to determine whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse. If the employer chooses to give a reason or excuse for the action taken by him, the duty of the Industrial Court will be to enquire whether that reason or excuse has or has not been made out. If it finds as a fact that it has not been proven, then the inevitable conclusion must be that the termination or dismissal was without just cause or excuse. The proper enquiry of the Court is the reason advanced by the employer, and that court or the High Court cannot go into another reason not relied on by the employer, or find one for him.”

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
The Federal Court in Wong Yuen Hock v. Syarikat Hong Leong Assurance Sdn. Bhd. & Another Appeal [1995] 3 CLJ 344 at page 352 succinctly stated the function of the Industrial Court in dealing with dismissal cases as follows:
“On the authorities, we were of the view that the main and only function of the Industrial Court in dealing with a reference under s. 20 of the Act (unless otherwise lawfully provided by the terms of the reference) is to determine whether the misconduct or irregularities complained of by the management as the grounds of dismissal were in fact committed by the workman, and if so, whether such grounds constitute just cause or excuse for the dismissal.”

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
The said principle was reiterated in Milan Auto Sdn. Bhd. v. Wong Seh Yen [1995] 4 CLJ 449 at page 454 and 455 by the Federal Court, where His Lordship Mohamed Azmi FCJ said:
“As pointed out by this Court recently in Hong Leong Assurance Sdn. Bhd. v. Wong Yuen Hock [1995] 3 CLJ 344; [1995] 2 MLJ 753, the function in the Industrial Court in dismissal cases on a reference under section 20 is two-fold: first to determine whether the misconduct complained of by the employer has been established and secondly to determine whether the proven misconduct constitutes just cause or excuse for the dismissal of the employee.”

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
The standard of proof applicable to dismissal cases is the civil standard of proof on a balance of probabilities as decided by the Court of Appeal in Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara v. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor [2002] 3 CLJ 314. It was held that:
“Thus, we can see that the preponderant view is that the Industrial Court, when hearing a claim of unjust dismissal, even where the ground is one of dishonest act, including “theft”, is not required to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the employee has “committed the offence”, as in a criminal prosecution… In our view the passage quoted from Administrative Law by H. W. R. Wade & C.F. Forsyth offers the clearest statement on the standard of proof required, that is the civil standard based on balance of probabilities, which is flexible, so that the degree of probability required is proportionate to the nature and gravity of the issue.”

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
In Ireka Construction Berhad v Chanthiravathan a/l Subramaniam James [1995] 2 ILR 11 - (Award No. 245/1995), the Industrial Court had this to say with regards to the burden of proof placed on the Company:
“It is basic principle of industrial jurisprudence that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed that offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer to prove that he has just cause and excuse for taking the decision to impose the disciplinary measure of dismissal upon the employee. The just cause must be, either a misconduct, negligence or poor performance based on the facts of the case…”

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The standard of proof applicable to dismissal cases is the civil standard of proof on a balance of probabilities as decided by the Court of Appeal in Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara v. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor. [2002] 3 CLJ 314 as follows: “Thus, we can see that the preponderant view is that the Industrial Court, when hearing a claim of unjust dismissal, even where the ground is one of dishonest act, including “theft”, is not required to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the employee has “committed the offence”, as in a criminal prosecution… In our view the passage quoted from Administrative Law by H. W. R. Wade & C.F. Forsyth offers the clearest statement on the standard of proof required, that is the civil standard based on balance of probabilities, which is flexible, so that the degree of probability required is proportionate to the nature and gravity of the issue.”

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
In Lee Mei Wan v. Ultimate Media Group Pte Ltd [2017] 2 LNS 1668, it was observed by the learned chairman that:
Ex-parte Hearing [4] Subsection 29(d) of Act 177 provides for an ex-parte hearing without the presence of one of the parties to the dispute as follows:
"The Court may, in any proceedings before it:
(a)
... (d) hear and determine the matter before it notwithstanding the failure of any party to submit any written statement whether of case or reply to the Court within such time as maybe prescribed by the President or in the absence of any party to the proceedings who has been served with a notice or summons to appear”.
[5] OP Malhotra, The Law of Industrial Disputes Volume 1: 6th Edition, at page 1062 states:
“If, however, a party wilfully absents himself in such a way that the adjudication is likely to be impede, or wilfully tries to delay or avoid the proceedings, the tribunal may fix a pre-emptory hearing on a particular day. After reasonable notice of hearing has been given to the defaulting party, if he still neglects or refuses to attend, the tribunal may and ought to hear in his absence. Prompt discharge of business is of particular importance before a tribunal adjudicating an industrial dispute….”
[6] Therefore, the Court was of the view that in the circumstances of this case, an ex-parte hearing was warranted due to the Company’s failure to attend Court although the Notice of Hearing and the earlier Notice of Mention had been served on it as stated above. Also see the case of: Zahari Ruslan v Wajib Cemerlang Sdn Bhd [2011] 2 LNS 0450

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
On the other hand, this Court is also mindful of its duty to adjudicate the matter on merit albeit the case proceeded ex-parte. The Claimant must be subject to the burden to prove his/her case on the balance of probabilities. This is succinctly set out in the case of Wong Brothers' Building Construction V. Choo Chee Siam [2005] 2 ILR 356 in which the Company was absent during the date of the hearing. The Court continued to hear the case on an ex-parte basis, wherein the Court held inter alia, as follows:
“The Court is mindful of the role in ex parte hearing by referring to the case of Ike Video Distributors Sdn. Bhd. v. Chan Chee Bin [2004] 2 ILR 687 where the Learned Chairman quoted from the book “The Law of Industrial Disputes” by O.P. Malhotra Vol. 3rd Edition. At p 716: “A rule empowering the tribunal to proceed EX-PARTE if a party is absent and sufficient cause is not shown for his absence, would not enable it either to do away with the inquiry or straight away pass on an Award without giving finding on the merits of the disputes. In other words, the absence of a party does not entail the consequence that an Award will straightaway be made against him”

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
The issues before this court are:
i. whether there is termination, ii. if the answer is yes, whether the termination is with just cause or excuse; and iii. Whether the purported offer of reinstatement genuine.
COURT’S EVALUATION AND FINDINGS Issues on Delay in Payment of Salary AUGUST 2023 SALARY PAID IN APRIL 2024

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: On 9th April 2024, the Company credited August 2023 salary to the Claimant’s bank account with an amount of RM7,833.65 despite the Company claimed that the Claimant was absent for 9 days in August as per alleged in the Letter of Termination dated 16th April 2024. The sum of RM7,833.65 represents the amount without any deductions for the 9 days in August 2023, during which the Company alleged that the Claimant was absent. The company must be construed to having waived its allegation of absenteeism for 9 days in August 2023 against the claimant.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: It is pertinent to note that the company has failed to reply the claimant’s appeal letter dated 2nd May 2024 titled “Surat Rayuan: Permohonan dan Pembatalan Surat Pemecatan Kerja (“Letter of Termination”) Bertarikh 16.04.2024” (“the appeal letter”) wherein the issue of inconsistencies and/or discrepancies between the allegations set out in the “Show Cause Letter” e-mail, “Show Cause Notice” letter both dated 2nd April 2024, and the reasons to terminate the Claimant’s employment in the “Letter of Termination” dated 16th April 2024 were raised at length (from clause 5.2 until clause 5.8.14) (refer CLB-1, pages 51 to 60). This could only lead to the presumption that the company has no explanation to support the allegation of misconduct levelled against the claimant.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: In a discussion between the Claimant and the Executive Chairman/CEO on 09th May 2024 in response to the Claimant’s appeal letter, the Company (its Executive Chairman/CEO) offered the Claimant a reinstatement via a phone call on 21.05.2024 and instructed the claimant to work as usual commencing on 1st July 2025 and promised that a letter of reinstatement be issued before 01.07.2024 (refer CLB-1, page 76).

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The date to commence employment by way of reinstatement was unilaterally changed to 15th July 2024 via a telephone call made again by the Executive Chairman/CEO to the Claimant on 01.07.2024 at around 10:58 a.m.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The Claimant seemingly prepared to accept the purported reinstatement offer, has on 15th July 2024 arrived at the office premises area to start working. However, she did not enter the company’s premises because the company did not issue any letter on the reinstatement and/or the retraction of termination letter against the claimant despite Hussfazellah (the HR personnel) was ready to hand over the office access card. This court is of the views that the company has failed to give an official authorization to the claimant to enter the company premises and effectuate the claimant’s reinstatement notwithstanding the oral assurance given vide telephone call on 01.07.2024.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: There were 6 follow-ups by the claimant for the reinstatement letter from 30th June 2024 until 16th July 2024; alas, the Executive Chairman/CEO has failed and/or refused to issue a letter and/or a written statement with regards to his verbal reinstatement offer.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: In the aforesaid, the company’s purported offer of reinstatement is nothing more than an illusion to camouflage the company’s fundamental breach to pay salaries due and outstanding to the claimant. The company’s non-committal to the offer to reinstate the claimant was clearly reflected by the reluctance of the company to issue a formal letter of reinstatement, simultaneously revoking the termination. The unchallenged fact remains that the claimant was in fact terminated and the termination was without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The fact that the claimant’s application to work from home was approved by the Executive Chairman/CEO on 30.4.2024 was never challenged. The approval can be seen at page 47 and 48 of Claimant’s Bundle of Documents (CLB1). The claimant was working from home as she had used up her financial resources that she received, denied of further monthly salaries that she deserved to make ends meet despite having shown her loyalty to serve the company without contractual pay, until she was terminated for oppressive reasons seriously tainted by mala fide.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: Screenshot/s of WhatsApp messages to the Executive Chairman/CEO that are before the court had proved prima facie that the Executive Chairman/CEO has ignored and/or failed to answer 64 phone calls in total made by the Claimant, only to request for the Reinstatement Letter and the unpaid salaries which are promised to be paid to the Claimant (refer to the Claimant’s Bundle of Documents (Volume 2) page 36).

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: Notwithstanding that nowhere it was adduced that the claimant was confirmed in her emplyment, nevertheless, it is reasonable to construe otherwise. The claimant had worked for the company for more than a year during which the claimant’s probation was never emphasised. As such it is safe to make a reasonable inference that the claimant was a confirmed employee after the probationary period of 3 months according to the letter of offer.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: In view of the oppression that the claimant had endured in particular having to sustain working without and/or on an excessively prolonged delay of payment of salaries, this court hereby Order punitive compensation of one (1) month salary for the claimant pursuant to section 30(6) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The company was absent during the entire proceedings and has failed to produce witnesses to adduce evidence to contradict the evidence available before this court adduced by the Claimant. As such, this court is of the views that the Claimant has prescribed admissible and credible evidence on the balance of probabilities in support of her case of termination without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: Failure to be present in court in order to cross examine the Claimant’s witnesses and challenge the claimant’s evidence has denied this court to evaluate any evidence to the contrary. Given the circumstances, this court is compelled to accept and there is nothing to dispute the ex-parte evidence adduced by the Claimant.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
As such, this court found that the Claimant’s dismissal without just cause or excuse. On evidence, the offer to reinstate was never meant or intended to be executed and therefor a sham. On another note, this Court is mindful of its duty to adjudicate the matter on merit notwithstanding the case proceeded ex-parte. The Claimant must be subject to the burden to prove her case on the balance of probabilities as it was held in Wong Brothers' Building Construction V. Choo Chee Siam (supra). In this case, the burden to prove her case on the balance of probability has been prima facie discharged by the Claimant. Hence, the Claimant’s claim is hereby allowed.
REMEDIES Reinstatement

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
This court has considered the claimant’s evidence that she has worked for the company until 7.5.2024. This essentially means that the claimant has completed one year of service for the company. This court is of the views that the claimant is not entitled to an Order for Reinstatement since the relations is no longer harmony. In such a case, compensation in lieu of reinstatement would be just and proper.
Backwages

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: In determining the quantum for backwages that is discretionary in nature, the Court may award not exceeding the maximum of 24 months based on the last drawn salary; regards shall have to the provision of Clause 1 of the Second Schedule in [Factors For Consideration In Making An Award in Relation To A Reference Under Sub Section 20(3)] of Section 30(6A) of the IRA 1967.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The claimant’s document “Table of Salary Payments Credited into the Claimant’s Bank Account” has listed payments of salaries she had received that is of assistance to this court, albeit the Bundle Documents (Volume 2) being unmarked as it was filed after the conclusion of the hearing. The company had only paid monthly salaries to the claimant for the months of February, March, April, May, June, July and August 2023 (refer: page 11, Claimant’s Bundle of Documents Volume 2). The claimant’s evidence that she had worked until 7.5.2024 effectively means that the company has failed to pay her approximately 8 months’ salaries from September 2023 until 7 May 2024. The claimant was to have rightfully continued working for the company for 9 more months until the end of her tenure i.e. 15 February 2025 but for the termination.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: Since the claimant’s employment was for a duration of a fixed term of 24 months from 15.02.2023 to 15.02.2025, the claimant was entitled for backwages being the payment of salaries for the months of September 2023 until December 2023, January 2024 until December 2024, and January 2025 until 15 February 2025; accumulatively 17.5 months of her last drawn salary of RM10,000.00. Insofar as the unpaid contributions and deductions to EPF and SOCSO is concerned, the issues had to be escalated to the governing authorities for the purpose of enforcement.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content:
Having considered the fact and circumstances of the case and evidence adduced ex-parte by the claimant, this Court Awards in favour of the Claimant as follows:
a) Compensation in lieu of reinstatement RM10,000.00 b) Backwages: RM10,000.00 x 17 months RM170,000.00 c) Punitive compensation RM10,000.00
TOTAL: RM190,000.00

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: At the risk of repetition, this Court had taken into account the evidence adduced ex-parte in its entirety, having borne in mind Section 30(5) of the IRA 1967 by which virtue this Court shall act according to equity, good conscience and the substantial merit of the case without regard to technicalities and legal form; and Section 30(6) of the same act, in making this award, the court shall not be restricted to the specific relief claimed by the parties.

case_name: Fatin Adilah binti Norhadzlan v Greentech Axis Berhad
chairman: Syed Noh bin Said Nazir @ Syed Nadzir
content: The amount totalling RM190,000.00 awarded above less statutory deduction (if any), together with interest at the rate of 8% per annum, the interest to be calculated commencing on the 31st. day from the date of the making of the award until the day the award was satisfied pursuant to section 30(1A) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 shall be paid by the Company to the Claimant through the claimant’s solicitors. For the avoidance of doubt, the interest shall not be accrued if the award was fully satisfied within thirty (30) days from the date of the making of this award.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
section_title: D. The Role and Function of the Industrial Court
content:
In Milan Auto Sdn Bhd v. Wong She Yen [1995] 4 CLJ 449, His Lordship Mohd Azmi bin Kamaruddin, FCJ explained the role of the Industrial Court under section 20 of the IRA as follows–
As pointed out by this court recently in Wong Yuen Hock v. Syarikat Hong Leong Assurance Sdn Bhd & Another Appeal [1995] 3 CLJ 344; [1995] 2 MLJ 753, the function of the Industrial Court is dismissal cases on a reference under s.20 is two-fold firstly, to determine whether the misconduct complained of by the employer has been established, and secondly whether the proven misconduct constitutes just cause or excuse for the dismissal. Failure to determine these issues on the merits would be a jurisdictional error. (emphasis is added)

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: It has been settled that in cases where the dismissal was caused by the employer, it is the employer that must discharge the burden of proof that the dismissal is with just cause and excuse. This long-settled principle was demonstrated in the case of Ireka Construction Berhad v. Chantiravathan Subramaniam James [1995] 2ILR 11 (Award No. 245 of 1995), wherein the Learned Chairman opined that: “It is a basic principle of industrial jurisprudence that in a dismissal case the employer must produce convincing evidence that the workman committed the offence or offences the workman is alleged to have committed for which he has been dismissed. The burden of proof lies on the employer to prove that he has just cause and excuse for taking the decision to impose the disciplinary measure of dismissal upon the employee. The just cause must be either a misconduct, negligence or poor performance based on the facts of the case”.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The onus or burden of proof is based on a standard of proof on the balance of probabilities as laid down by the Court of Appeal in Telekom Malaysia Kawasan Utara v. Krishnan Kutty Sanguni Nair & Anor [2002] 3 CLJ 314 wherein His Lordship Abdul Hamid Mohamad, JCA opined– Thus, we can see that the preponderant view is that the Industrial Court, when hearing a claim of unjust dismissal, even where the ground is one of a dishonest act, including “theft”, is not required to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the employee has “committed the offence”, as in a criminal prosecution. On the other hand, we see that the courts and learned authors have used such terms as “solid and sensible grounds”, “sufficient to measure up to a preponderance of the evidence”, “whether a case … has been made out”, “on the balance of probabilities” and “evidence of probative value”. In our view the passage quoted from Administrative Law by H.W.R. Wade & C.F. Forsyth offers the clearest statement on the standard of proof required, that is civil standard based on the balance of probabilities, which is flexible, so that the degree of probability required is proportionate to the nature of gravity of the issue. But again, if we may add, these are not “passwords” that the failure to use them or if some other words are used, the decision is automatically rendered bad in law. (emphasis is added)

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content:
The issues before this Court to be determined are as follows: (a) Whether the misconduct complained of by the Company had been established; and (b) Whether the proven misconduct constitutes just cause or excuse for the dismissal.
F. Evaluation of Evidence and Findings of the Court
Whether the misconduct complained of by the Company had been established

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The Claimant joined the Company on 8 December 2003. It is among other terms of the Claimant’s appointment contract that employment shall be governed by the Rules and Regulations as stated in the Company Handbook. A copy of the relevant clause of the Appointment Letter dated 9.03.2003 and 21.07.2016 is reproduced as follows:

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content:
It is clear from the confidentiality clause of the employment contract that there are warnings and prohibitions on employee acts and actions that warrant immediate termination for serious misconduct. For clarification, there were four (4) charges leveled against the Claimant as follows: Charge 1 Pursuant to the Companies Commission Malaysia’s records, it is undeniable that you are and/or held yourself out to be, sole proprietor of Logistic Master Enterprise. During Q & A Session, you had admitted, amongst others that Logistic Master is involved in transportation business, a business which is in direct competition to the services provided by DHL, and further failed to declare the same to the Company. You had also made false declaration in the Declaration of Interest document wherein you failed to declare, as annually required to do so, any potential conflict of interest.
This was while you are employed and paid a salary by DHL, and despite company’s policy requiring your exclusivity and fidelity towards the Company. You received no authorisation from DHL to involved with Logistic Master and/or any other business and/or work outside DHL. Your acts/admissions amount to unauthorised breached of your duties and contractual obligations as to exclusivity and fidelity, gross misconduct and failure to adhere to applicable rules and policies pertaining to discipline and work ethics.
Charge 2
From the Companies Commission Malaysia records, Key Master Enterprise (Reg. No: PG0198599-T), it is undisputed that your wife, Gowri A/P Ramiah, your nephew Sathishvaran A/L Ramasamy and your cousin Nanthakumar A/L Ragvan has been proprietors for various time period at Key Master Enterprise. Not only you had failed to declare and/or bring to the Company’s attention your family’s involvement, you had also made false declaration in Declaration of Interest document, wherein you failed to declare any potential conflict of interest with regards to Key Master Enterprise.
Charge 3
During the Q & A Session, you had admitted that you and your wife own a Honda Jazz and BMW car. Further you and/or your family members own about 32 motorcycles which includes a Harley Davidson. Also, you have been frequently travelling overseas. Given your remuneration scale in the Company and your declaration to the Company, it appears to be you are holding properties disproportionate to the known sources of income.
Charge 4 Further during Q&A Session, it was disclosed by you that you have set up TS Master of Martial Arts an entity which is of an income generating business. Non-Disclosure of the same is in clear conflict of DHL’s code of conduct.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: Following the “Whistleblower” email dated 25 October 2022, which linked the Claimant with allegations of financial impropriety, illegal money, mafia activities. The “Whistleblower” email named the perpetrator as the Claimant who owns the business known as Logistic Master Enterprise, the Claimant was called for a Q&A session on 28 October 2022.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: Considering the registration records issued by SSM confirming that the Claimant owns LME, the Claimant was instructed to submit a bank statement for a period of three years. The Claimant’s Representative submits that during the Q & A session, the Claimant was instructed to sign a “CONSENT” letter, submit bank statements for a period of three (3) years, and hand over his mobile phone for investigation of its contents.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: It was found that upon completion of the Q & A session, he was given a letter of suspension from work for a period of fourteen (14) days with full salary effective 28.10.2022. Upon considering the “whistleblowing” issue, the Company, through a letter dated 1.11.2022, had issued a show cause letter listing all four charges copies of Letter of Suspension dated 28.10.2022 is represented as follows:-

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content:
As regards the four charges levelled against the Claimant, an investigation Question & Answer (Q&A) session was conducted by the HR Team from Kuala Lumpur, whom include COW-2. The session was conducted on two occasions, 28.10.2022 and 09.11.2022. The learned counsel for the Company submits that the panel found that: (i) Logistic Master Enterprise (LME) - The Competing Business: Official SSM searches confirmed the Claimant was the sole proprietor of LME, a transportation business. The Claimant also admitted that LME’s business nature was the same as the Company's and explicitly agreed that this constituted a "clear conflict of interest".
(ii) Key Master Enterprise (KME) - The Undisclosed Vendor: It was discovered that the Claimant's wife, Gowri a/p Ramiah, was a proprietor of KME. It is noted that KME was a registered vendor for the Company for the transportation task between 2012 and 2015. The Claimant also failed to declare this direct familial and commercial conflict to the Company regarding KME.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The obligation of employees to declare their income, assets, and interests in other companies is strictly provided for under the Employment Handbook. Failing to declare the same, it may create a conflict of interest. This mandatory requirement ensures that the Company's interests are protected.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The employees are prohibited from competitive businesses such as transportation and logistics. Upon the completion of the investigation and inquiry session, the Company found that there were several offences alleged to be committed by the Claimant. Having gathered all the evidence, the Company issued a Show Cause Letter on 01.11.2022 to the Claimant, allowing him to formally explain himself in relation to four main allegations of misconduct: A copy of the Show Cause Letter dated 1.11.2022 is reproduced as follows: Operating an undeclared competing business (LME);

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content:
The Company submits that the Claimant operated LME, a transportation business in the same industry, and knowingly failed to declare this direct competition, an act he himself admitted was a "clear conflict of interest. It is a trite fact that every employee in DHL is required to submit an annual Declaration of Interest. The Claimant, during the cross-examination, admitted that he never declared LME since it’s establishment as stated in the first charge as follows: RK Kamu sahkan kamu dinyatakan sebagai pemilik tunggal LME TAMIL Ya RK Sole proprietorship, lepas itu owner dia Tamil Selvam, betul? TAMIL Betul RK LME ini ditubuhkan pada tahun 2013, di mana kamu masih bekerja dengan DHL sehingga kamu ditamatkan pekerjaan dan sehingga ke hari ini.
