TAMIL Ya RK Saya cadang, kamu sebagai pemilik tunggal LME, menjalankan business transportation adalah clear conflict of interest dengan DHL, semasa kamu jadi pekerja DHL. Setuju?
TAMIL Semasa bekerja setuju RK Kamu setuju kamu tidak pernah declare mengenai syarikat LME kepada DHL pada bila-bila masa melalui DOI, setuju? TAMIL Ya RK Setuju, kamu sedia arif bahawa Logistic Master Enterprise... adalah violation to DHL Code of Conduct?
TAMIL Setuju

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: Having perused the evidence adduced, the Court finds that the Claimant had actively engaged in the transportation business, the same nature of business as the Company. It is a trite fact that the Claimant, while still the Company’s employee, had a direct interest that he concealed from his employer.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content:
The Court in the case of Teh Seng Kay v United Coatings Technology Sdn Bhd [2014] MELRU 256 held that : "[17] Under these circumstances it is reasonable for COW-1 to infer that Claimant through Jamax Industries was also doing business in competition with the Company while working for the Company. This fact do give rise to a conflict of interest situation and for COW-1 to have lost his trust and confidence on the Claimant. The Claimant never revealed to the Company his interest in Jamax Industries until COW-1 found out on his own. COW-1 under the circumstances cannot be said that he can trust the Claimant to protect the interest of the Company.
[18] Taking into considerations of all these factors this Court finds that the dismissal of the Claimant was not unfair and Claimant was dismissed with just cause and excuse”.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The Court in that case, which has quite similar facts to our case, concluded that the employer’s loss of trust was a reasonable and inevitable consequence of the employee’s deceptive conduct. Having considered that the Claimant controls the LME operation, which competes directly with DHL's services, his failure to declare his relationships with LME represents a serious breach of trust and transparency. A copy of SSM Search on LME is reproduced as follows:

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The Claimant admitted that LME is involved in the transportation business, a business which is in direct competition with the services provided by the Company. He had made a false declaration in the Declaration of Interest (DOI) document wherein he failed to declare any conflict of interest and/or potential conflict of interest. Therefore, the Claimant had committed serious misconduct that would warrant a dismissal.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content:
It is a settled principle that an employee cannot faithfully serve two masters, especially when their interests are in direct opposition. Having read the submissions of both parties, the Claimant has failed to adhere to the rules and regulations of the Company’s Employment Handbook and Code of Conduct. Therefore, the Claimant has committed serious misconduct as stated in the first charge.
Failing to disclose his family’s interest in a Company vendor (KME);

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The learned counsel for the Company submits that the Claimant committed a serious and calculated breach of his duty of fidelity and the Company’s Code of Conduct by failing to declare that his wife Gowri A/P Ramiah, nephew Sathiswaran A/L Ramasamy and his cousin Nanthakumar A/L Ragvan were proprietors of Key Master Enterprise (KME), an active vendor of the Company between 2012 and 2015. This concealment created a clear conflict of interest, placing his family's financial gains in direct intersection with his duties and responsibilities to the Company.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: In the case of Teh Seng Kay v United Coatings Technology Sdn Bhd (supra), where the Claimant who was a sales manager failed to disclose a competing business registered under his wife’s name. The Claimant also said that it was his wife who registered a company by the name of Jamax Industries Sdn Bhd and it was registered on 7 August 2012, five days before Claimant was compelled to resign. In upholding the dismissal, the Court rejected the notion that the employee was a mere "inactive shareholder”.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content:
The SSM search confirms that the Claimant’s wife, Gowri, was a proprietor of KME during the material time, and Company’s invoices prove that KME was actively engaged as a vendor, billing DHL directly for services from 2012 to 2015. The Claimant, during the evidence in Court, has testified as follows:
CHM Kamu tidak declare kepada DHL, Perniagaan isteri dan Nanda Kumar adik ipar kamu itu kepada DHL, setuju ke tak? TAMIL Setuju

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The Representative for the Claimant's submission that the Claimant was "not aware" of the requirement to declare such a relationship is not only incredible but is an affront to reason. As a Lead of Operations Agent with 19 years of service was required to submit an annual Declaration of Interest forms; his claim of ignorance was untenable. It is transparent self-avoidance to adhere to the stipulated provision in the employment handbook and the Company’s Code of Conduct.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: It is also a basic requirement that if someone wishes to submit a quotation or bid for a service contract, the bidder or price quoter must declare that they have no relations or conflicts of interest with the company. In the case of Azliyah binti Samsi v Petronas Management Training Sdn Bhd [2019] MELRU 1033, the Court held that the dismissal of an employee for failing to disclose family-owned vendors was upheld. It was further held: “In ethics, integrity is the honesty, truthfulness and accuracy of dealings; all unfortunately and conspicuously found wanting in the Claimant's conduct in this case. It was therefore unsafe and indeed unreasonable to expect the Company to continue her employment. [I take comfort in this ruling from the authority of the following cases”.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: It is an established principle that the legal test for such non-disclosure of the interest in the competing companies, the employer’s burden is not to prove the consequences of the concealment, such as financial loss, but simply the concealment itself. On the other hand, the misconduct is not contingent on proving financial loss or malicious intent. The act of non-disclosure itself points directly to a fundamental lack of integrity and is a dismissible offense. Therefore, the Claimant has committed serious misconduct as stated in the second charge. Holding properties disproportionate to his known sources of income, raising concerns about the integrity of his dealings

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: Disproportionate assets owned by the Claimant are not primary evidence to describe a situation where the Claimant’s asset value significantly exceeds the assets he should possess after accounting for the assets that he previously held and all legal sources of income. An undisclosed wealth is an actionable however, it is not deemed a crime until and unless it is proven that the wealth was acquired by illegal means.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The Company’s investigation into the Claimant’s assets was not conclusive evidence that the Claimant was involved in illegal money and mafia activities. Money laundering, if proven, is a serious offense and punishable with imprisonment. Without proving it beyond a reasonable doubt, the allegation via the whistle email is untenable due to insufficient evidence.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content:
Furthermore, the Company also failed to prove that the Claimant’s luxurious life was the proceeds of undisclosed activities and was gained throughout his employment with the Company that would warrant a dismissal.
Operating another undeclared income-generating business (TS Master of Martial Arts).

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The Company’s counsel submits that the Claimant's failure to declare his third business, TS Master of Martial Arts, and the subsequent investigation into his disproportionate assets are not standalone charges. Rather, they are crucial corroborating evidence that demonstrates the concealment of LME and KME were not isolated oversights.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content:
The Company’s counsel further submits that the Claimant admitted that every year, when submitting the annual Declaration of Interest (DOI) form, he was given a clear opportunity to rectify his omissions. Instead, he made a conscious choice to submit a declaration that he knew to be false. During cross-examination, the Claimant agreed that his failure to list LME, KME, and TS Master of Martial Arts rendered his official submissions to the Company "wrong and untrue". The evidence is reproduced as follows:
RK Dengan demikian kamu telah membuat satu declaration yang salah dan tidak benar apabila kamu gagal untuk menyatakan syarikat LME, KME dan TS Master Art dalam declaration kamu kepada syarikat. CHM Setuju ke tak dengan cadangan pihak syarikat? TAMIL Ya. Setuju

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The evidence indicates the Claimant was aware that failing to disclose his interest in the three companies, LME, KME, and TS Master Martial Arts, was dishonest and improper from the beginning. His failure to disclose other business interests, in addition to his employment at DHL, suggests a lack of integrity and a disregard for company policies. Consequently, this Court finds that the intentional concealment of his personal interests in those companies, while employed by the Company, constitutes serious misconduct, justifying termination of his employment.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: This Court refers to the case of Azliyah binti Samsi v Petronas Management Training Sdn Bhd (supra), which provides powerful authority on the nature of misconduct in conflict of interest. The Court decisively held that the core wrongdoing is the failure to disclose, and the employer's burden of proof does not extend to proving the consequences of that failure, such as malicious intent or financial loss. Consequently, the Company terminated the Claimant's employment through a Termination letter dated with immediate effect on 10.11.2022. The decision was made because the Claimant had committed serious misconduct that demonstrated a fundamental lack of integrity and irrevocably destroyed the trust and confidence essential to the employer-employee relationship.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The Claimant owes the Company a fiduciary duty, trust, and confidence. In the case of Sitt Tatt Industrial Gases Sdn Bhd v. Puvananderan Ganasamoorthy [2003] 2 ILR 485 (Award No. 396 of 2003), the Court held that: “Since the employer-employee relationship carries with it the duty of fidelity on the part of the employee and also a relationship of trust and confidence; dishonesty on the part of the employee is an attack upon the trust and confidence of the employer.”

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content:
The Court of Appeal in Zaharen bin Hj Zakaria v Redmax Sdn Bhd & Other Appeals [2016] 7 CLJ 3805 first distinguished the duty of fidelity from the stricter fiduciary duty, making it clear that all employees owe a duty of loyalty:
“[4] Under the law, an employee of a company has a duty of fidelity to be observed at all times during his employment with the company. What is this duty of fidelity? Every employment contract contains an implied term that an employee will serve his employer with good faith and fidelity (the duty of fidelity). The duty of fidelity is owed by all employees and is to be distinguished from a fiduciary duty. A fiduciary duty requires an employee to act in the interests of his employer, whereas the duty of fidelity requires an employee to have regard to his employer's interests. Inherent in that duty to have regard to his employer's interests must be a duty not to act in a manner which would be to disregard his employer's interests. Such acts must include acts that are inherently detrimental to his company's interests.
(emphasis is added)

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: This Court is of the view that, being Lead of Operation Agent with almost 20 years of service, the Claimant owed a duty to the Company to be diligent in discharging his duties to protect its interest provided for in his employment contract. The Court, having carefully considered his reply to the show cause notice through his written reply dated 02.11.2022 and his explanation on disregard of his employer’s interest, found his reply to be unsatisfactory and lacking in credibility, specifically for the first, second and fourth charges.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: Following the Q&A sessions, the Company was satisfied that it had proved the allegations made against the Claimant. The Company found that the Claimant has committed grave misconduct that justified the issuance of the Termination Letter dated 10.11.2022 as follows: Whether the proven misconduct constitutes just cause or excuse for the dismissal.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The Court is satisfied that the Company has been fair in dealing with the issue of the Claimant's misconduct. There was no evidence to suggest that the Claimant was confused or misled when responding to the allegations made against him in the inquiry. The Claimant has been given the space and time to dispute the allegations against him. The Claimant also did not challenge the validity of the evidence tendered in court.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: There is also no evidence to show that from the very beginning of the establishment of the Companies LME, KME and TS Master of Martial Arts, the Claimant was honest and declared his relationship and interest in all three Companies. For several years, the Claimant has received benefits in the form of salary and other fixed remuneration from the Company. Unfortunately, the Company's kindness has been reciprocated by generating personal profits using his position and experience in the Company.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The Claimant's failure to declare his interest and actively participate in LME and KME, whose business type in question is transportation, indicates that the Claimant exploited and misused his role at DHL for personal benefit. Furthermore, the Claimant's position within the Company may also be leveraged by KME, which is owned by the Claimant's spouse and family.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The employees entrusted with responsibilities must act in good faith and shall not abuse the confidence and trust placed in them by the Company. confidence and trust reposed in him by the company. BR Ghaiye in Misconduct in Employment; Chapter XIX at pp 650 and 651 described the fiduciary relationship as follows: “The servant stands in fiduciary relation. The relation between an employer and an employee is of fiduciary character. The word 'fiduciary' means belonging to trust or trusteeship. It means that whenever an employer engages a worker, he puts trust that the worker will faithfully discharge the service and protect the interest of the employer. ….If the employee continues in service, then one of the obvious remedies for breach of faith is to dismiss him”.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: Given the circumstances, an employer is entitled to dismiss an employee who acts in a manner inconsistent with the faithful discharge of his duties toward his employer. In Asahi Industries (M) Sdn Bhd v. Lim Mui Lin [2000] 1 MELR 726; [2000] 2 ILR 29, the Industrial Court held: “In any establishment, be it public or private, trust and confidence are of utmost importance, if any of the two is lacking then it becomes very difficult for the employer to continue keeping the employee in his employment”.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The gravity of the Claimant's misconduct is too serious for the Company to compromise, even though the Claimant has served the Company for 19 years. The trust and confidence placed in the Claimant for years by the Company to safeguard the interests and generate profits for the Company have been violated by the Claimant. If this behavior is not curbed, it will be followed by all employees which will ultimately destroy the Company's long-established organization.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The Claimant's untrustworthiness and dishonesty are the causes of broken relationships between the employee and the employer that justified immediate dismissal. In the case of Mohd Aminuddin Md Zain & Ors v. Perbadanan Usahawan Nasional Berhad [2006] 3 ILR 2172; [2006] 2 MELR 692, wherein the Learned Chairman opined: "The relationship between the employer and employee is fiduciary character. What this means is that whenever an employer engages an employee, he puts trust that the employee will faithfully discharge his service and protect the interests of the employer. Once the trust is breached, it causes the employer to lose trust and confidence in the employee, as in the instant case, to protect his interest and hence justifies an immediate dismissal."

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: Having considered all facts and evidence, the Company cannot reasonably be expected to retain the Claimant's employment due to a deliberate act of dishonesty on his part, which constitutes serious misconduct.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: The proportionality principle requires the court to strike a balance between the severity of the workman's conduct and the punishment imposed. In Norizan Bakar v. Panzana Enterprise Sdn Bhd [2014] 1 MELR 1; [2013] 6 MLRA 613; [2014] 1 ILJ; [2013] 6 MLJ 605; [2013] 4 ILR 477; [2013] 9 CLJ 409; [2013] 6 AMR 338 278, the Federal Court held: “The appellant had knowingly made a false declaration and with respect, which in our view, in the circumstances and facts of this case is not a minor misconduct, given the fact that the appellant had signed and accepted the code of conduct which clearly stipulates that: "an employee shall not be employed, engaged or be concerned in any kind of trade or business nor shall he/she serve on the Board of Directors of any other company, while in the employment within the PANZANA GROUP OF COMPANIES”.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: Having borne in mind s 30(5) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967, acting in equity and good conscience and the substantial merit of the case without regard to technicality and legal form, the Court finds that the Company had proven on the balance of probabilities that the Claimant's dismissal was with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Rusita binti Md Lazim
content: Hence, the Claimant's claim against the Company is hereby dismissed.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: It is imperative to consider the law on redundancy prior to considering the conduct of the Company, as it will show that the Company at all times acted in a bona fide manner and the redundancy was bona fide. Therefore, it will be evident that the Company complied with the principles of law.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The adjudication of retrenchment disputes in Malaysia is governed by a well-established framework of legal principles derived from the Industrial Relations Act 1967 and judicial precedent.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In the Court of Appeal case of William Jacks & Co (M) Sdn Bhd V. S Balasingam [1997] 3 CLJ 235, redundancy was defined as follows: "Retrenchment" has been defined as the discharge of surplus labour or staff by an employer for any reason whatsoever. Whether the retrenchment exercise in a particular case is bona fide or otherwise is a question of fact and of degree depending in the peculiar circumstances of the case. It is well settled that the employer is entitled to organize his business in the manner he considers best. So long as the managerial power is exercised bone fide, the decision is immune from examination even by the Industrial Court. However, the Industrial Court is empowered and indeed duty bound to investigate the facts and circumstances of the case to determine whether the exercise of power is in fact bone fide".

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: The term "retrenchment" was authoritatively defined by the Court of Appeal in William Jacks & Co (M) Sdn Bhd V. S. Balasingam 3 CLJ 235 [supra] as: "The discharge of surplus labour or staff by an employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action.”

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: The Court further held that the right to reorganize business is a managerial prerogative. Provided the decision is made bona fide (in good faith), it is immune from interference. However, the Industrial Court is "duty-bound to investigate the facts and circumstances of a particular case to determine whether that exercise of power was in fact bona fide."

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: In the case of Stephen Bong V. Fcb (M) Sdn Bhd [1999] 3 MLJ 411 redundancy has been stated as follows: - ‘’that it is not that the law that redundancy means the Job or work no longer exist. Redundancy situations arise where the business requires fewer employees of whatever kind".

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content:
Redundancy has also been considered, where the Company has to close down or downsize the business, as stated in the case of Yusoff Othman V. Felda Engineering Services Sdn Bhd [Award No 778 of 2022], where it was stated that: - "It is well established in industrial jurisprudence that an employer is entitled to close down the whole of part of his business as long as he acts bona fide. The right to reorganize a business and/or a company's restructuring is a managerial prerogative. "
In the said case, the Court further stated that: - “lt Is well established that it is for the management to decide the strength of its staff which it considers necessary for efficiency in its undertaking. The Court will not intervene unless it is shown that the decision was capricious or without reason or was made mala fide or was actuated by victimization or unfair labour practice... the employer has a right to determine the volume of his labour force consistent with his business and organization and if the implementation of a reorganization scheme adopted for reasons of economy and better management of the business, the services of some of the employees become excess of the requirement of the business, the employer is entitled to discharge such excess".

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: The right of a Company to reorganize is evident from the case of Thomas Hans Raab V. Nokia Services and Networks Malaysia Sdn Bhd [2022] 3 ILR 371 and George Kent (M) Sdn Bhd V. Tan Tai Wai, Mak Kin Kung & Wong Khoon Sand [1988] 1 ILR 342 where it is stated that: "Redundancy connotes that the functions of the Claimant became excess. lt is settled law that it is up to the Company to decide the strength of its staff which it considers necessary for efficiency its undertaking... ".

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: In view of the above, it is indisputable and accepted industrial jurisprudence, that a company has every right to reorganize or to restructure the Company, so as to maintain operational and financial sustainability so as to avoid any complete shutdown of the winding up of a Company.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: A case similar to the situation as in the matter before this Honourable Court, Mohd Nor Hassan & Ors V. Continental Sime Tyre PJ Sdn Bhd [2014] 3 ILR 144 where the expenses were reduced and thereafter the redundant staff were terminated, where the Court found that retrenchment was bona fide. The Court stated that: - “...the measures taken by the company were insufficient and the company was compelled to undertake a retrenchment exercise. The company carried out a reorganisation exercise if the manufacturing department of the company in Petaling Jaya which resulted in a total of 70 employees including the claimant who were found to be redundant and were accordingly retrenched... ".

Ice Room Food & Beverage Management Sdn Bhd [2015] 4 ILR 655, the Court on the issue of rights of a company stated that: - "It is the right of every employer to reorganize his business in any manner for the purpose of economy or convenience. The law recognises that a company has the right to organize its business in the manner it considers best".

Air Asia Berhad [2023] 3 ILR 113, the Court considered the Aviation Industry and stated that: - "It is common knowledge that the aviation industry was among the worst affected industries by the COVID-19 pandemic. The pandemic wrecked financial devastation across the aviation value chain, most notably for airlines save and except for freight forwards and cargo airlines. The grounding of aircrafts by the company is genuine"

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE TERMINATION OF THE CLAIMANT BY REASON OF REDUNDANCY
content: In the case of George Kent (M) Sdn Bhd V. Tan Tai Wai, Mak Kin Kung & Wong Khoon Sang [1992] 2 ILR 400, redundancy and the situation that prevails has been stated as follows: - "We are in full agreement with the learned author C.P, Mills on Industrial Disputes Law in Malaysia, that it is settled law that it is up the Company to decide the strength of its staff which it considers necessary for the efficiency in its undertaking and the Court will not interfere unless it is shown that the decision was capricious or without reason or was mala fide or was actuated by victimisation or unfair labour practice."

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE TERMINATION OF THE CLAIMANT BY REASON OF REDUNDANCY
content:
In the case of Premalata Vincent Ramesh V. Nestle Products Sdn Bhd [1992] 3 ILR 277, the Court stated that in determining that the dismissal was done with just cause or excuse by the retrenchment exercise undertaken by the company, this Court will ask these pertinent questions:
‘’(i) Whether there was a genuine need for reorganization exercise by the company;
(ii) Whether a genuine redundancy situation had a rise and which led to the retrenchment of the claimant; and
(iii) Whether the company had complied with the accepted standards and procedure when selecting and retrenching the claimant.’

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Principles from Ng Chang Seng’ case
content:
The recent landmark decision of the Court of Appeal in Ng Chang Seng V. Technip Geoproduction (M) Sdn Bhd & Anor 1 MLJ 447 has significantly raised the bar for employers. The key principles established are:
a) Selection Criteria: The employer must provide clear evidence explaining why a specific employee was selected over others.
b) Comparative Evidence: To prove redundancy and fair selection, the court must look at the employees who were retained as well as those retrenched. A failure to produce comparative data is fatal.
c) LIFO: To justify a departure from LIFO, clear evidence of special skills possessed by retained juniors must be shown.
d) Foreign Labour: Employers should retrench foreign workers before locals unless there are overriding reasons (though less relevant to the facts here, the principle of rigorous selection scrutiny applies).

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony
content: While the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony is not a statute, judicial decisions such as Equant Integration Services and Ng Chang Seng have elevated its status to the "gold standard" of industrial practice. Failure to comply with the Code, particularly regarding consultation and early warning, can be evidence of mala fides.

chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE FUNCTION OF THE INDUSTRIAL COURT
content: The role of the Industrial Court pertaining to a reference under section 20 (3) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 is to ask itself a question whether there was a dismissal; and, if so, whether it was with or without just cause or excuse Wong Chee Hong V. Cathay Organisation (M) Sdn Bhd [1988] 1 MLJ 92; [1987] 1 MLRA 346. Burden of Proof on Employer to Prove Genuine Redundancy.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE FUNCTION OF THE INDUSTRIAL COURT
content: The primary responsibility lies with the employer to establish that the redundancy is genuine. It is insufficient to merely assert financial constraints or lack of work. The Industrial Court, in William Jacks & Co. (M) Sdn Bhd V. S. Balasingham [1997] 3 CLJ 235, affirmed that the employer must provide credible evidence to justify retrenchment. Employers must not use redundancy as a convenient excuse to terminate employees for other reasons, such as poor performance or personal bias.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE FUNCTION OF THE INDUSTRIAL COURT
content: As a result of the financial difficulties, the Company had embarked on a cost-cutting and reorganization exercise, where it ultimately led to some of its employees being unfortunately retrenched from the employment. The Claimant was one of those selected for retrenchment.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THE FUNCTION OF THE INDUSTRIAL COURT
content: In order for an employee to be retrenched from his employment, the burden is on the employer to prove that there was a redundancy in the first place. The term redundancy is defined by Dunston Ayadurai in his book Industrial Relations in Malaysia (2ndEd.) at p. 159: - “Redundancy refers to a surplus of labour and is normally the result of a reorganisation of the business of the employer; and its usual consequence is retrenchment, i.e., the termination by the employer of those employees found to be surplus to his requirements after the organisation. Thus, there must first be redundancy or surplus of labour before there can be retrenchment or termination of the surplus”.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Once redundancy had occurred in any particular position, a retrenchment exercise may then be carried out by the employer to discharge the surplus labour. This was explained in the case of William Jacks & Co (M) Sdn Bhd V. S Balasingam [1997] 3 CLJ 235 [supra] where the Court of Appeal defined the term “retrenchment” as follows: - “Retrenchment had been defined as the discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action (per SK Das in Hariprasad v. Divelkar AIR [1957] SC 121 at p 132). Whether the retrenchment exercise in a particular case is bona fide or otherwise is a question of fact and of degree depending on the peculiar circumstances of the case”.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
Thus, a situation of redundancy in a job position must occur in the first place before the subsequent exercise of retrenchment is carried out whereby the employer will then set out to discharge those employees whose position had already been identified as redundant. This was succinctly explained in the book Retrenchment Law and Procedure in Malaysia by Thavalingam Thavarajah & Raymond TC Low (at pp. 4 – 5): “An employee is said to be ‘redundant’ when their job is no longer available and the employer either cannot offer the employee any alternative position or, any alternative position offered by the employer cannot be accepted by the employee concerned. Redundancy occurs where the employer’s requirements for employees to carry out work of a particular kind has ceased or diminished. Where the same number of employees is no longer required by the employer’s business, then that will result in a redundancy. There is redundancy where:
(i) The number of employees required to carry out work of a particular nature is reduced, or is expected to be reduced and this results in dismissals; or
(ii) The work itself ceases or diminishes either permanently or temporarily, or is expected to do so, so that fewer employees are needed and this results in dismissals.
In summary, ‘retrenchment’ is the expression used to describe what occurs to an employee whose employment is terminated by reason of their job becoming redundant. ‘Redundancy’ is the process of identifying employees who are surplus to the organisation’s requirements and the end result is the retrenchment of such employees”.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
In Sistem Televisyen Malaysia Bhd & Anor V. Suzana Zakaria [2005] 1 ILR 853 it was held: - “The learned author, Dunstan Ayadurai, in his book 'Industrial Relations in Malaysia' at p. 121 defined redundancy as follows: Redundancy refers to a surplus of labour and is normally the result of reorganization of the business of an employer; and its consequence is retrenchment, i.e., the termination by the employer of those employees found to be surplus to his requirements after the reorganization. Thus, there must first be redundancy or surplus of labour before there can be retrenchment or termination of the surplus. “In Soonavala's 'The Supreme Court on Industrial Law’ Vol. 11, 2nd Edition at p. 424, the learned author stated: “Retrenchment is a necessary incidence of running an industry, but retrenchment is justified only when due to shrinkage of work, whether permanently or for an indefinite or indeterminate period, there has arisen a surplus in the number of workmen in the employment of a Company. Therefore, when a Company gives notice of retrenchment to its workmen and the dispute arising therefrom is referred to a tribunal, the only question for its decision are (a) whether the retrenchment was justified by the circumstances of the case (b) whether the grounds for the retrenchment given by the Company are true, that is, whether there had in fact occurred a reduction in the business of the Company due to circumstances such as scarcity of raw materials on the availability of which the running of the factory depends, or stoppage of work under the orders of government or changes in the economy which made it impossible to continue the business except at a loss or on meagre profits, and (c) whether the order of retrenchment was motivated by bad faith and a desire to victimize or harass the workmen whom for some ulterior reasons the employer wanted to discharge or dismiss. Additionally, the High Court in Stephen Bong V. Fcb (M) Sdn Bhd [1999] CLJ 131; [1999] 1 LNS 131; [1999] 3 MLJ 411 held that: It is settled law now that redundancy does not mean the job or work no longer exist. Redundancy situation may arise where the business requires fewer employees of whatever kind.
Hence to justify the retrenchment, there must first be redundancy. To prove redundancy, the company must prove that there is surplus of labour or that the requirement of the job functions of the employee has ceased or has greatly diminished to the extent that the job no longer exists or that the business requires fewer employees of whatever kind resulting from a reorganisation exercise or due to whatever other legitimate reasons”.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In Woo Chee Khoon V. Citibank Berhad [2011] 2 LNS 495 it was held: - “Before there can be retrenchment or termination of the surplus, there must be redundancy or surplus of labour. It is for the management to decide on the strength of the staff, which it considers necessary for efficiency in its undertaking. When the management decides that workmen are surplus and that there is therefore a need for retrenchment, an arbitration tribunal will not intervene unless it is shown that the decision was capricious or without reason, or was mala fide, or was actuated by victimization or unfair labour practice. It is the right of every employer to reorganize its business in any manner for the purposes of economy or convenience, provided it acts bona fide”.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In the case of Yusoff Othman V. Felda Engineering Services Sdn Bhd, [Award No.778 of 2022] it states that the term "redundancy" has been defined as: - "Redundancy refers to a surplus of labour and is normally the result of a reorganization of the business of an employer; and its usual consequence is retrenchment, i.e., termination by the employer of those employees found to be surplus to the requirement after the reorganization. Thus, there must be first be redundancy or surplus labour before there can be retrenchment of termination of the surplus"

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: A critical factor in determining the fairness of a retrenchment exercise is the application of the LIFO principle, where the employer must prioritize the retention of longer -serving employees over newer ones. In Dynacraft Industries Sdn Bhd V. Kamaruddin bin Kana Mohd Sharif & Ors [2012] 6 MLJ 453, the Federal Court held as follows: “[13] We will deal with the first question posed in this appeal. It concerns the correctness of the application of the LIFO principle by the Industrial Court. The LIFO (last in first out) or ‘last come first go’ principle requires the most junior employee to be retrenched before the more senior ones in the same category. The principle is intended to afford a healthy safeguard against discrimination of workmen in the matter of retrenchment (as at Swadesamitran Ltd V. Their Workmen, 1960 (SC) 762). Explaining this principle, in Workmen of Sudder Workshop of Jorehaut Tea Co Ltd the Management of Jorehaut Tea Co Ltd AIR 1980 SC 1454, the Supreme Court said: “The rule is that the employer shall retrench the workman who came last, first, popularly known as ‘last come first go’.”

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: For the reasons stated above, it is evident that the Claimant’s termination on the grounds of redundancy was not conducted in good faith. The Company has failed to adhere to the principles of fairness, including the burden of proof, application of LIFO, exploration of alternatives, and transparency in its decision-making process.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The sole issue is whether the termination of the Claimant was with just cause or excuse. In an unfair dismissal reference under s.20 (3) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967, the Court’s duty is to determine “whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse”. If the employer gives a reason for dismissal, the Court must inquire whether that reason has been made out in evidence. Retrenchment is a dismissal in operational redundancy, so s.30 of the Act applies, the Company must show a genuine redundancy situation and that the dismissal was made in good faith (s.30 (5) IRA).

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Normally retrenchment selections follow the industry-recognised “last-in-first-out” rule; deviations are allowed only for valid and bona fide reasons. The Company must prove on balance that the Claimant’s post had indeed become redundant and that his retrenchment was not a sham (Goon Kwee Phoy V. J&P Coats [1981] 2 MLJ 127; Ng Chang Seng V. Technip Geoproduction [2021] 1 MLJ 447). The Court apply these principles to the evidence.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
The Court frames the issues for determination as follows:
a) Did the Company discharge the burden of proving a bona fide necessity for retrenchment due to the genuine and compulsory closure of the C&P Division (Substantive Fairness)
b) Did the Company comply with procedural obligations, specifically the duty to find alternative employment (Redeployment), prior to termination.
c) Did the Company discharge the heightened statutory burden under the Employment Act 1955, as amended, to prove the termination was not linked to the Claimant's pregnancy.
d) Was the Claimant’s dismissal with just cause or excuse under Section 20(1) Industrial Relation Act 1967 [ACT 177].
e) Were there a genuine redundancy and bona fide closure and termination of the Claimant. f) Did the Company comply with the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony 1975, including the principles of consultation, LIFO, and transparency
g) Was the Claimant’s dismissal procedurally fair and in accordance with the principles of industrial justice and natural justice.
h) What is the appropriate remedy if the dismissal was without just cause or excuse.
THIS HONOURABLE COURT’S EVALUATION
a)

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Whether There Was Just Cause or Excuse
content: The burden of proof lies on the employer to affirmatively justify that the dismissal was with just cause or excuse, per Goon Kwee Phoy V. J & P Coats (M) Sdn Bhd [1981] CLJV 30; [1981] 1MLRA 413 (Federal Court) and reaffirmed in Statement in Reply and both parties’ written submissions.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: b) Whether There Was Bona Fide Redundancy and Closure
content: While retrenchment may be justified if a business faces genuine closure, this must be supported by clear evidence and must be bona fide, not a mask for selective unfair removal as at Ireka Construction Berhad V. Chantiravathan Subramaniam James [1995] 2ILR 11(Award No.235 of 1995) (Federal Court).

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: b) Whether There Was Bona Fide Redundancy and Closure
content: This factual matrix closely mirrors principles established by the Federal Court in Holiday Inn, Penang V. National Union of Hotel, Bar & Restaurant Workers [1988] 1 MLJ 130, where contradictions in the defines and continuing business activity nullify the genuineness of alleged redundancy. The Court is not satisfied that the Company proved an irreversible and total cessation as asserted. The documentary record exposes substantial contradictions and an absence of transparency and can be dour in the Company’s position.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: c) Procedural Fairness & Adherence to Code of Conduct
content:
Employer obligations prior to retrenchment are prescribed by the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony 1975: consultation, consideration of alternatives to retrenchment, application of the LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) principle (unless objectively justified departure is proven), and adequate notice. Here, overwhelming evidence including unchallenged testimony from the Claimant shows that: i. No meaningful consultation occurred.
ii. No objective matrix for selection was disclosed; persons less senior than the Claimant remained in employment for a period after her termination.
iii. The Company deviated from the LIFO principle without adducing special circumstances, violating the expectation in Colgate Palmolive (M) Sdn Bhd V. Yap Kok Foong & Another Appeal[2001] 3 CLJ 885; [2001]4 AMR 4539 (Court of Appeal) and guided by the Court of Appeal's reasoning in Ng Chang Seng V. Technip geoproduction (M) Sdn Bhd & Anor [2021] 1 MLRA 261.
iv. No evidence of alternative roles, redeployment options or voluntary separation schemes was offered to the Claimant.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: c) Procedural Fairness & Adherence to Code of Conduct
content: Industrial court findings in Malaysia underscore that retrenchment and especially redundancy for the Airline cannot be sustained where business or its core functions are demonstrably ongoing, and the selection process is not transparent or uniformly applied. While operational loss may in justified cases allow rationalization of the workforce, the particular facts here point to inconsistency, poor disclosure, and poor industrial practice.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: d) Natural Justice and Industrial Harmony
content: This Honourable Court notes as persuasive the ongoing scholarly and comparative literature emphasizing natural justice as a foundational element in labour dispute resolution even where formal legal duties are balanced against other practicalities. Both judicial practice and Industrial Relations literature highlight the centrality of the right to be heard, procedural consistency and an equitable (not arbitrary) selection for retrenchment in fostering workplace stability and legitimacy. This is especially so in the Malaysian industrial context with its hybrid model of industrial pluralism and evolving workforce flexibility.

chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: A critical factor in determining the fairness of a retrenchment exercise is the application of the LIFO principle, where the employer must prioritize the retention of longer -serving employees over newer ones.
