chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Federal Court’s Dynacraft Industries Sdn Bhd V. Kamaruddin bin Kana Mohd Sharif & Ors [2012] 9 CLJ 21; [2012] 6 MLJ 453, the Federal Court held as follows: "[13] We will deal with the first question posed in this appeal. It concerns the correctness of the application of the LIFO principle by the Industrial Court. The LIFO (last in first out) or 'last come first go' principle requires the most junior employee to be retrenched before the more senior ones in the same category. The principle is intended to afford a healthy safeguard against discrimination of workmen in the matter of retrenchment (see Swadesamitran Ltd V. Their Workmen, 1960 (SC) 762). Explaining this principle, in Workmen of Sudder Workshop of Jorehaut Tea Co Ltd V. The Management of Jorehaut Tea Co Ltd AIR 1980 SC 1454, the Supreme Court said: "The rule is that the employer shall retrench the workman who came last, first, popularly known as ' last come first go'."

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In Dynacraft ‘s case [supra] decision makes clear that prima facie the LIFO rule applies, an employer should retrench the latest recruits first, “where other things are equal”.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: A lawful deviation requires objective justification. The Company argues it departed from LIFO for “performance, safety and disciplinary” reasons. Even if merit-based selection is permitted in principle (as Wong Zi Chuang v AirAsia X [2025] 1 ILJ 1 held, provided it is done bona fide and not arbitrarily), those reasons must be substantiated.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The adjudication of retrenchment disputes in Malaysia is governed by a well-established framework of legal principles derived from the Industrial Relations Act 1967 and judicial precedent.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: A. The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: The term "retrenchment" was authoritatively defined by the Court of Appeal in William Jacks & Co (M) Sdn Bhd V. S. Balasingam [1997] 3 CLJ 235 as: "The discharge of surplus labour or staff by an employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action.”

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: A. The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: The Court further held that the right to reorganize business is a managerial prerogative. Provided the decision is made bona fide (in good faith), it is immune from interference. However, the Industrial Court is "duty-bound to investigate the facts and circumstances of a particular case to determine whether that exercise of power was in fact bona fide."

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The burden of proof lies squarely on the employer to justify the retrenchment. As held in Bayer (M) Sdn Bhd V. Ng Hong Pau[1999] 4 CLJ 155; [1999] 4 AMR 3913 (Court of Appeal): "On redundancy it cannot be gainsaid that the appellant must come to the Court with concrete proof. The burden is on the appellant to prove actual redundancy on which the dismissal was grounded."

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Mere assertions of financial difficulty or reorganization are insufficient the employer must adduce "concrete proof" of the redundancy and the fairness of the selection.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: C. The Principles from Ng Chang Seng’ case
content:
The recent landmark decision of the Court of Appeal in Ng Chang Seng V. Technip Geoproduction (M) Sdn Bhd & Anor [2021] 1 MLJ 447 has significantly raised the bar for employers. The key principles established are:
a) Selection Criteria: The employer must provide clear evidence explaining why a specific employee was selected over others. b) Comparative Evidence: To prove redundancy and fair selection, the court must look at the employees who were retained as well as those retrenched. A failure to produce comparative data is fatal.
c) LIFO: To justify a departure from LIFO, clear evidence of special skills possessed by retained juniors must be shown.
d) Foreign Labour: Employers should retrench foreign workers before locals unless there are overriding reasons (though less relevant to the facts here, the principle of rigorous selection scrutiny applies).

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: D. The Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony
content:
While the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony is not a statute, judicial decisions such as Equant Integration Services Sdn Bhd V. Wong Wai Hung [2012] 1LNS 1296; [2013]; 1 MLRA 150 and Ng Chang Seng case [Supra] have elevated its status to the "gold standard" of industrial practice. Failure to comply with the Code, particularly regarding consultation and early warning, can be evidence of mala fides. THE COMPETING SUBMISSIONS
The Court has scrutinized the written submissions filed by both parties and Notes of Evidence in this case. The arguments present a stark conflict between the employer's right to manage its business and the employee's statutory rights, particularly regarding maternity protection.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
The Claimant’s Representative, advances the following core arguments:
A. No Genuine Redundancy of the "Business".

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant argues that RLA Polymers (M) Sdn Bhd, as the employer, is still in operation. COWS-1 admitted during cross-examination that "RLA is still running as a business entity as a whole" and that "Business 1 is running as usual," while "Business 2 have been downsizing". The Claimant submits that the "Closure of the Employer's Business" exception in the Employment Act was not met because the entire business did not close only a division was downsized.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
The Claimant contends she was the only employee forcefully retrenched from the C&P Division at that specific time. The Internal Memo listed roughly ten (10) employees. The Company’s witness admitted that others had either resigned previously or were transferred. The Claimant argues she was targeted because of her pregnancy or that the Company used the "closure" as a convenient excuse to terminate a pregnant employee to avoid maternity liabilities.
C. Failure to Redeploy

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant asserts she possessed transferable skills. Her resume details experience in Quality Assurance, R&D and Technical Support applicable to "liquids, polymers, epoxy," which are products handled in BU1 (the surviving division). She specifically requested a transfer but was refused. She argues this refusal while other staff were retained or transferred, indicates bad faith.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant challenges the Company's allegation of "unbearable losses." She points out that the Company failed to tender any audited financial statements or management accounts specific to the division to prove these losses. In contrast, the Claimant produced SSM Financial Reports showing the Company (RLA Polymers) made a profit in the financial years 2022 and 2023. She argues the Court cannot accept the mere oral testimony of COWS-1 against documentary proof of the Company's overall profitability.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant places heavy reliance on Section 41A, which prohibits the termination of a pregnant employee except for limited grounds. She argues the "closure of business" exception in Section 41A must be interpreted strictly to mean the cessation of the entire trade of the employer, not just a department otherwise, the statutory protection is rendered toothless.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Counsel for the Company, defends the termination on the grounds of managerial prerogative and genuine commercial necessity:

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: A. Bona Fide Closure of Division
content: The Company submits that the closure of the C&P Division was genuine and absolute. COWS-1 testified that no new orders were taken and production ceased on 1 November 2023. The Company relies on William Jacks & Co (M) Bhd V. S. Balasingam [1997] 3 CLJ 235 to argue that an employer has the right to organize its business as it sees fit, including closing unprofitable divisions.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Company argues the Claimant was employed specifically for the C&P Division. Once that division closed, her role as "Technical Services Manager (Cementitious)" ceased to exist. There is no legal obligation to create a post where none exists.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Company contends that "closure of the employer's business" in Section 41A (1) (c) encompasses the closure of a specific business unit or division. They cite cases like Haslinda Idris V. Sky Park Properties [Award No. 1297 of 2025] to argue that redundancy arising from the closure of a department is a valid ground for dismissal, even for protected employees. They argue that preventing a company from retrenching staff in a defunct division simply because of pregnancy would create an absurdity where the company must pay for non-existent work.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Company argues that under Ng Chiaw Loong V. Duta Jasa Sdn Bhd [Award No. 37 of 2022], the production of audited accounts is not mandatory if the witness testimony is credible. They argue confidentiality prevented the disclosure of detailed accounts and COWS-1’s testimony regarding the division’s losses should be accepted as she had direct access to the financial records.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Company asserts there were no suitable vacancies in BU1. The skills for cementitious products (powder/grout) are distinct from Adhesives/Polymers (liquids/glue), and thus the Claimant could not be automatically transferred.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
The sequence of events leading to the termination is as follows:
Date Event Description Early 2023 Cost Cutting Company Closes “Blister Division” in BU2. 23 Aug 2023 Notification of Pregnancy Claimant formally informs Mr. Tan Kay Inn (Technical Director) of her pregnancy 11 Oct 2023 Internal Memo Company issues a memo titled "Closing down of Cementitious & Powder divisions." The memo states the division will be "no longer active" from 1 Nov 2023. 30 Oct 2023 Termination Notice Claimant is issued a letter titled "Termination of Employment Due to Redundancy." 31 Oct 2023 Dismissal Claimant's last day of service.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: It is a crucial evidentiary point that the Internal Memo dated 11 October 2023, while announcing the "closing down" of the division did not explicitly use the words "retrenchment" or "termination" regarding the staff. The Claimant testified that she was only informed of her termination via the specific notice on 30 October 2023, merely 24 hours before her effective dismissal date.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: At the heart of this dispute lies the undisputed fact that the Claimant was pregnant at the time of her dismissal. She was approximately seven months into her pregnancy when her employment was terminated. The Company through COW-1, admitted knowledge of this condition. This fact triggers the application of Section 41A of the Employment Act 1955, a relatively new statutory provision introduced by the Employment (Amendment) Act 2022, which strictly restricts the termination of pregnant employees.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In a reference under Section 20(3) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967, the burden of proof invariably rests upon the employer to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities that the dismissal was with just cause or excuse. This principle was firmly established in the seminal case of Goon Kwee Phoy V. J & P Coats (M) Bhd [1981] 2 MLJ 129, where the Federal Court held that the Industrial Court must determine whether the misconduct (or in this case, redundancy) complained of by the employer was in fact established by the evidence.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
Retrenchment is defined as the discharge of surplus labour. The leading authority on the subject is William Jacks & Co (M) Bhd V. S. Balasingam [1997] 3 CLJ 235 [supra]. The Court of Appeal in William Jacks held that: "It is well-settled that an employer is entitled to organize his business in the manner he considers best. So long as that managerial power is exercised bona fide, the decision is immune from examination even by the Industrial Court. However, the Industrial Court is empowered, and indeed duty-bound, to investigate the facts and circumstances of a particular case to determine whether that exercise of power was in fact bona fide."
Therefore, the Court's inquiry is two-fold:
i. Substantive Fairness: Was there a genuine redundancy? Did the surplus of labour actually exist. ii. Procedural Fairness: Was the selection of the employee for retrenchment fair? Did the Company comply with the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony (CCIH).

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
This case is distinguished from a standard retrenchment dispute by the application of Section 41A of the Employment Act 1955. This section, effective from 1 January 2023, imposes a statutory prohibition on terminating pregnant employees.
Section 41A (1) states:
"Where a female employee is pregnant... it shall be an offence for her employer to terminate her services... except on the grounds of
(a) Wilful breach of a condition of the contract of service...; (b) misconduct...; or (c) closure of the employer’s business.".
Section 41A (2) explicitly shifts the burden of proof: "Where the service of a female employee under subsection (1) is terminated, the burden of proving that such termination is not on the ground of her pregnancy... shall rest on the employer." This creates a "heightened" burden. The Company must not only prove "just cause" under the Industrial Relations Act but also demonstrate that the termination falls strictly within the narrow exceptions of the Employment Act and was not discriminatory.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: FIRST ISSUE: SUBSTANTIVE FAIRNESS, THE QUESTION OF GENUINE REDUNDANCY
content: The first issue for determination is whether the Company has discharged the burden of proving a bona fide necessity for retrenchment. The Company relies on the closure of the C&P Division as the sole ground for redundancy.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The "Losses" Justification and the Evidentiary Gap
content: The Company submits that the closure of the C&P Division was a commercial necessity driven by "unbearable losses." COW-1 testified extensively on the financial struggles of the division, claiming that despite investments in R&D and machinery, the products failed to gain market traction.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The "Losses" Justification and the Evidentiary Gap
content: However, a critical examination of the evidence reveals a significant lacuna in the Company's case. While COW-1 asserted financial losses, the Company failed to tender any audited financial statements or detailed management accounts to substantiate these claims. When cross-examined on this failure, COW-1 stated: "RLA Polymer Malaysia Sdn Bhd is a private limited company and all the informations, detail informations of the company are actually PNC [Private and Confidential] ... we might risk letting off informations to competitors and apart from that, we will need to get approval from our HQ.".

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The "Losses" Justification and the Evidentiary Gap
content: The Claimant aggressively challenged this, arguing that financial statements of a Malaysian Sdn Bhd are public documents available via the Companies Commission of Malaysia (SSM) and cannot be deemed "confidential" in a court of law where the very justification for dismissal is financial loss.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: This Honourable Court's Evaluation of the Financial Evidence
content:
The Court finds the Company's refusal to produce financial document to be fatal to its argument of "unbearable losses."
i. The Best Evidence Rule: In a court of law, he who asserts must prove. If an employer asserts financial incapacity or loss as the reason for destroying an employee's livelihood, it must produce the primary evidence of that loss, namely the accounts. Mere verbal testimony from a manager, unsupported by documentary evidence, carries little weight when challenged.
ii. Adverse Inference: Under Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act 1950, the Court may presume that evidence, which could be and is not produced, would if produced be unfavourable to the person who withholds it. The Company had the accounts. They refused to show them.
iii. The Claimant's Rebuttal: The Claimant took the initiative to obtain the Company's financial data from SSM. These documents indicate that RLA Polymers (M) Sdn Bhd was profitable in the financial years 2022 and 2023.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: This Honourable Court's Evaluation of the Financial Evidence
content: The Company attempts to rely on the case of Muhammad Firdaus Murad V. L&O Collections Sdn Bhd 1LNS 814[2023] CLJU 814 [2023]1LNS 814, where the High Court held that the absence of audited accounts is not automatically fatal if other evidence (like bank statements or credible testimony) exists. However, this Court distinguishes Muhammad Firdaus on the facts. In that case, there was corroborating evidence of the loss of major contracts (Telekom Malaysia projects). Here, the Company relies solely on the internal assertion of "lack of demand" while the external evidence (SSM reports) shows overall profitability. The contradiction between the Company's verbal claim of loss and the documentary proof of profit requires explanation that only the granular accounts could provide. The Company chose not to provide them.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Closure of Division against Closure of Business
content: The Company argues that it is entitled to close a losing division even if the overall company is profitable. They cite Haslinda Idris V. Sky Park Properties Sdn Bhd [Award No. 1297 of 2025] and Florentius Henry Toyad V. Cahya Mata Sarawak Berhad[2015] 4 ILR 662 to support the proposition that the closure of a specific department justifies retrenchment of employees in that department.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Closure of Division against Closure of Business
content: The Court accepts the principle that a company has the right to close a division. The evidence confirms that the production activities of the C&P Division ceased. The Claimant admitted that the manufacturing line was stopped. Therefore, a technical redundancy existed, the specific job of "Technical Manager for Cementitious Production" was no longer required in its original form.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Closure of Division against Closure of Business
content: However, recognizing a technical redundancy does not automatically validate the dismissal. The Court must look beyond the label. If the Company is profitable and continues to trade in similar products (outsourcing or trading finished goods) the core functions of a "Technical Manager", quality control, customer inquiries, product specification, do not necessarily vanish. They may simply shift.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Court finds that whilst there was a reorganization involving the cessation of manufacturing in the C&P Division, the Company has failed to prove the financial necessity of the retrenchment. The suppression of financial evidence, coupled with the overall profitability of the Company, suggests that the "unbearable losses" narrative was exaggerated. While the closure of the division created a surplus of labour, the bona fides of selecting the Claimant for retrenchment, rather than absorption, is questionable. This leads the Court to the critical issue of procedural fairness and redeployment.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: SECOND ISSUE: PROCEDURAL FAIRNESS, THE DUTY TO REDEPLOY
content: Even where redundancy is genuine, Malaysian industrial jurisprudence demands that the retrenchment exercise be carried out fairly. This duty is enshrined in the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony (CCIH).

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Requirements of the Code of Conduct industrial Harmony
content: Clause 20 of the Code of outlines measures to avert retrenchment, explicitly recommending: "Re-training and/or transfer to other department/work.".

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: The Requirements of the Code of Conduct industrial Harmony
content: While the Company correctly submits (citing Equant Integration Services Sdn Bhd V. Wong Wai Hung)[2012] ILNS 1296; [2013] MLRA 150 that the CCIH does not have the force of law, the Industrial Court is mandatorily required under Section 30(5A) of the Industrial Relations Act 1967 to take the Code into consideration. Flagrant non-compliance with the Code without valid reason often points to a lack of bona fides.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The central contention here is whether the Claimant could have been transferred to BU1 (Adhesives/Polymers).

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant argues that she was contractually employed to work on "all the company’s products." She possesses a chemistry background and 5 years of tenure. She specifically requested a transfer to other departments, a request she claims was summarily dismissed. She argues that her skills in quality assurance and technical support are transferable between cementitious products and polymer adhesives.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Company argues that the Claimant was a specialist. COW-1 testified that BU1 deals with different chemical compositions (liquids/epoxies vs. powders) and that the Claimant lacked the specific technical competence for BU-1. The Company relies on Teo Chin Wern V. Vizeum Media Services (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd [2024] ILRU 0520: [2024] 3MERL 402 arguing that an employer is not obliged to create a post where none exists.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
This Honourable Court finds the Company's failure to redeploy the Claimant to be procedurally unfair for several reasons:
i. Contractual Estoppel: The Company cannot argue the Claimant is "too specialized" when they themselves drafted an employment contract stating her duties covered "all the company's products." This clause acts as a contractual acknowledgement of her potential utility across divisions. The Company is estopped from narrowing her scope to justify retrenchment when the contract allows for broader deployment. ii. Lack of Assessment: There is no evidence that the Company conducted any formal skills assessment, interview, or evaluation to determine if the Claimant could handle BU1 duties. COW-1's testimony that "she was not suitable" appears to be a subjective assertion rather than an objective finding.
iii. Failure to Retrain: The CCIH obliges employers to consider "re-training." If the Claimant lacked specific knowledge of epoxies, a profitable company with a 5-year employee should reasonably offer retraining rather than immediate termination. The Company offered no such option.
iv. Disparity of Treatment: The evidence suggests that lower-level employees (operators) were transferred or offered voluntary separation schemes (VSS). The Claimant was the sole employee in the division retrenched without option. While managers and operators have different transferability the complete lack of effort to save the Claimant's employment stands in stark contrast to the treatment of others.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Court distinguishes Teo Chin Wern’s case. In that case, the company was ceasing operations or the specific role was unique. Here RLA Polymers continued to operate BU1 a parallel technical division. The refusal to consider the Claimant for BU1, despite her request and contractual scope indicates a pre-determined decision to exit her.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THIRD ISSUE THE HEIGHTENED STATUTORY BURDEN (PREGNANCY DISCRIMINATION)
content:
This pivotal issue distinguishes this case from standard retrenchment disputes. The Claimant was pregnant. The Employment effective 01 January 2023, introduced Section 41A, of Employment Act 1955 [ACT 265] providing explicit protection against the termination of pregnant employees.
Statutory Interpretation of Section 41A.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THIRD ISSUE THE HEIGHTENED STATUTORY BURDEN (PREGNANCY DISCRIMINATION)
content:
The section prohibits termination of a pregnant employee except on three grounds:
a) Wilful breach of contract. b) Misconduct. c) Closure of the employer’s business.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THIRD ISSUE THE HEIGHTENED STATUTORY BURDEN (PREGNANCY DISCRIMINATION)
content: The Company relies on exception (c): "Closure of the employer’s business."

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: THIRD ISSUE THE HEIGHTENED STATUTORY BURDEN (PREGNANCY DISCRIMINATION)
content:
The Conflict of Interpretation:
i. Company's Interpretation: "Closure of the employer's business" should be read to include the closure of a specific business unit or division. They argue that for the C&P Division employees, the "business" effectively closed.
ii. Claimant is Interpretation: "Employer" refers to the legal entity (the Sdn Bhd). RLA Polymers (M) Sdn Bhd did not close. It is still trading, profitable, and employing staff in BU1. Therefore, the exception does not apply.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
The Court must apply the canons of statutory interpretation. Section 41A of Employment Act 1955 [Act 265] is a piece of social legislation designed to align Malaysia with international labour standards (such as ILO Convention No. 183). Its purpose is to provide security of tenure to women during the vulnerable period of pregnancy.
a) Literal Rule: The statute uses the definitive phrase "closure of the employer's business" (singular). It does not say "closure of a department" "closure of a division" or "redundancy." In other sections of the Employment Act (e.g., relating to retrenchment benefits), the law recognizes redundancy as a broader concept. The limitation in Section 41A to "closure of the employer's business" indicates a legislative intent to set a very high threshold for terminating pregnant women.
b) Purposive Rule: If "closure of the employer's business" were interpreted to mean "closure of any department," the protection would be rendered toothless. An employer could simply "close" a department, retrench the pregnant employee, and then restructure. The intent of Parliament was clearly to prevent retrenchment of pregnant employees unless the employer itself ceases to exist or ceases operations entirely.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Court holds that "closure of the employer's business" in Section 41A (1) (c) refers to the complete cessation of operations of the legal entity or at the very least, a substantial shutdown akin to winding up. It does not cover the strategic closure of a single product line while the Company continues to operate other profitable lines. Since RLA Polymers (M) Sdn Bhd continued to operate BU1 and remained profitable, the "closure of the employer's business" exception was NOT triggered.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Failure to Discharge the Burden of Proof
content: Even if, arguendo, the Court were to accept the Company's broader interpretation, the Company failed to discharge the burden under Section 41A (2) to prove the termination was not due to pregnancy.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Failure to Discharge the Burden of Proof
content:
The circumstances raise a strong presumption of discrimination:
a) Timing: The Claimant informed the Company of her pregnancy in August 2023. The "closure" memo was issued in October 2023.
b) Selection: The Claimant was the only manager retrenched.
c) Financial Motivation: By terminating the Claimant at 7 months pregnant, the Company avoided paying 98 days of Maternity Allowance (approximately (3.2 months’ salary) and the costs of a replacement. d) Refusal to Redeploy: As noted in second Issue, the refusal to transfer her to BU1, despite her contract allowing it, suggests an intent to remove her specifically.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
section_title: Failure to Discharge the Burden of Proof
content: The Company offered no evidence to rebut this presumption other than the "losses" of the division, which (as noted in First Issue) were unproven by documents. The Company relied on Boral Plasterboard (M) Sdn Bhd V. Noor Zalila Talib [2004] 1MELR 877 where the Court upheld the retrenchment of a pregnant employee. However, Boral Plasterboard was decided before the enactment of Section 41A. It applied general principles of "bona fide redundancy." The 2022 Amendment fundamentally changed the landscape, removing "redundancy" as a valid ground for terminating pregnant employees unless it amounts to a full business closure. Boral Plasterboard is therefore no longer good law in the face of the new statutory bar.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The termination of the Claimant was a violation of Section 41A of the Employment Act 1955. It was an offence under the Act and, by extension, a dismissal without just causes or excuse.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
After a thorough evaluation of the evidence and the law, the Court arrives at the following conclusions:
a) On Substantive Fairness: The Company failed to prove the financial necessity of the retrenchment due to the suppression of audited financial statements.
b) On Procedural Fairness: The Company failed to adhere to the Code of Conduct for Industrial Harmony. Specifically, it failed to discharge the duty to redeploy the Claimant to BU1 or other functions, despite her contractual scope covering "all products" and her request for transfer.
c) On Statutory Legality: The termination was in direct contravention of Section 41A of the Employment Act 1955. The partial closure of the C&P Division does not constitute "closure of the employer's business" under the Act. The Company failed to discharge the statutory burden of proving the dismissal was not linked to pregnancy.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Court finds the Company has failed to discharge its onus of proof that the Claimant’s dismissal was with just cause or excuse under Section 20(1) Industrial Relation Act 1967 [ACT 177].

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The plea of closure is unconvincing in light of continued operations, dividends paid, and survival of business infrastructure post-termination date.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: There was non-compliance with the Code of Conduct on consultation, retrenchment alternatives, LIFO principle, and objective selection.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The lack of consultation itself constitutes a fundamental breach of natural justice and the duty of industrial fair dealing, as reinforced by authorities.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: No evidence was provided concerning the Claimant’s performance, conduct, or any reason unrelated to alleged redundancy.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant, with 7(seven) and 7(seven) month of service, which was from 01 April 2013 until 01 November 2021 denied his basic industrial rights at the point of becoming most vulnerable.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Accordingly, the Court finds that the dismissal of the Claimant, Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum, was WITHOUT JUST CAUSE OR EXCUSE.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Pursuant to section 30(5) of the IRA1967 and after having considered the totality of the evidence adduced, this Court is of the view that the Company had failed to establish on the balance of probabilities that the dismissal of the Claimant from his employment with the company was with just cause or excuse.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Court having ruled that the Claimant was dismissed without just cause or excuse, will now consider the appropriate remedy for the Claimant.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: On the balance of probabilities, the Claimant’s termination was not for a valid redundancy with just cause. In circumstances of a generalized downturn, the Company was entitled to retrench, but it must do so fairly. Here, it failed to follow the usual seniority rule and gave no credible reason for treating the Claimant as surplus.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The Claimant’s long service, clean record and refusal to waive pay cuts all point to mala fides in selecting him over more junior colleagues. Accordingly, the dismissal was made without just cause or excuse.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This conclusion is compelled by Ng Chang’ Seng [supra] and related authorities, which condemn retrenchments that are in truth punitive exercises in disguise.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Honourable Court give the order that therefore award relief under Section 20 IRA. Reinstatement is impracticable after many years’ separation (and indeed the Claimant did not seek reinstatement). The appropriate remedy is compensation and back wages.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Based on the Court’s assessment of the industrial climate between the parties, it is certainly not conducive to reinstate the Claimant as the relationship between the Company and the Claimant has been badly strained. In the circumstances, it is inappropriate to order for reinstatement. Instead, the Claimant will be awarded with an appropriate remedy accordingly.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: In respect of the quantum the Court is mindful of the view taken by Tun Salleh Abas FJ in the case of Hotel Jaya Puri Bhd. V. National Company of Hotel, Bar & Restaurant Workers & Anor [1990] 1 MLJ 109: “.. if there is a legal basis for paying the compensation, the amount of course is very much a matter of the discretion which the Industrial Court is fully empowered under s.30 of the IRA 1967 to fix.”

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: Back wages are calculated based on the Claimant’s last drawn salary but limited to 24 months. From the back wages, the court is required to make a deduction for any contributory conduct, post dismissal earnings and delay in the hearing of the case but such a deduction need not involve a mathematical calculation.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Court is bound by the principle laid down in the case of Dr. James Alfred (Sabah) V. Koperasi Serbaguna Sanya Bhd (Sabah) & Anor [2001] 3 CLJ 541. His Lordship Justice Tan Sri Steve Shim CJ (Sabah & Sarawak) in delivering the judgement of the Federal Court held that: ‘’In our view, it is in line with equity and good conscience that the Industrial Court, in assessing quantum of back wages, should take into account the fact, if established by evidence or admitted, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. Failure to do so constitutes a jurisdictional error of law. Certiorari will therefore lie to rectify it. Of course, taking into account such employment after dismissal does not necessarily mean that the Industrial Court has to conduct a mathematical exercise in deduction. What is important is that the Industrial Court, in the exercise of its discretion in assessing the quantum of back wages, should take into account all relevant matters including the fact, where it exists, that the workman has been gainfully employed elsewhere after his dismissal. This discretion is in the nature of a decision-making process.’’

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
This Court have carefully examined the facts and evidence in this case and of the view that there was no contributory factor on the part of the Claimant. Hence, under the item there is no deduction shall be made to this contributory factor.
DELAY

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: From an examination of the notes of proceedings, this Court is satisfied that the Claimant did not occasion any delay in connection with the hearing of this Director General of Industrial Relation of Malaysia reference. Hence, there is no deduction under this head.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: At the time of dismissal, the Claimant last drawn basic salary was RM 9,231.00 [as at p.8-1, CLB-1]. On the facts of this case, there is evidence of post- dismissal income after the Claimant was dismissed by the Company. Hence, there shall be deduction under this item. The Claimant has served the Company for five (5) years two (2) months and twenty-two (22) days which was from 09 August 2018 until 31 October 2023.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content:
After having considered the evidence adduced before this Court as well as the submission by both parties, the remedies are as follows:
i. Back wages for twenty-four (24) months based on the Claimant’s last drawn salary:
RM 9,231.00 X 24 months = RM 221,544.00
Less 5% (Post-Dismissal -The Claimant was employed at another Company) = (RM 11,077.20)
TOTAL = RM 210,466.80
Add
i. Compensation in lieu of reinstatement, based on the formula of one month’s salary for every completed year of service. The Claimant has completed five (5) full years of service calculated from until the date of employment, which was on 09 August 2018 until the date of dismissal on 31 October 2023.
RM 9,231.00 X 5 months = RM 46,155.00
TOTAL = RM 256,621.80

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: The monetary award in a total sum of RM 256,621.80 less statutory deductions, if any shall be paid by the Company to the Claimant via his Representative, Union Network International Malaysia Labour Centre (UNI-MLC) within 30 days of the award with interest of 8% per annum to be calculated from 30 days of the award until full and final settlement.

case_name: Anusiah a/p Ramasindarum v RLA Polymers (M) Sdn. Bhd.
chairman: Hajah Zalina binti Haji Awang @ Mamat
content: This Court verily believe that this Award is just and appropriate in the light of the particular facts of the present case and guided by the principles of equity, good conscience and substantial merits of this case without regard to technicalities and legal forms.
